I may return to this game later, because giving it a negative review feels unjust (I wish I could vote somewhere in the middle). 

On a good note the gameplay is engaging, if somewhat initially unwelcoming in it's difficulty. But one's persistence pays off, and soon you'll be winning those unwinnable battles. Consumables feel a little useless but that may be a build-craft issue on my part. It's a little strange that the game is hard capped at 60fps but honestly you barely notice. Enemies look absolutely great too, especially some of the nighttime-only field bosses.

On a VERY good note mounted combat in this game feels wonderful. I did not expect this and was pleasantly surprised. While it would've been nice to have a little more going on with mount(s) via stats or items, compared to most games this actually feels like you're twice as dangerous from atop a horse rather than just using it to cover ground.

It also must be said that the logistical design of the open world is a feat of great technical and artistic talent. The world blocks and guides you in ways that feel organic and natural. The fact that this is the first time FromSoft has made an open world game almost defies belief. To the world designers at FromSoft: congratulations! A debut of this quality is a generation win.

Sadly Elden Ring's storytelling style does not suit me. I can't connect to any character as they all feel extremely hollow and everything about the world and setting feels empty and boring. This lack of characterization and the absence of meaningful relationships is where the game lost me. 

The player character is kind of just a emotionless murder puppet who says next to nothing and has basically no motivation aside from "You're Tarnished, so go become Elden Lord". I found the open world to be painfully empty of anything to do other than kill kill and kill some more. 

Going out to fight an enemy or explore the open world felt as though I was only doing so to level up my stats and find better items, not because the story has provided me a reason to do so. "I'm just playing a game" versus "I'm doing something this character needs or wants to do."

There are no moments of beauty or peace to offset a persistently depressing tone. Elden Ring is joyless in a way I've seldom encountered. I found it to be overwhelming monotonous and with the story being very obscure I was starving for a relatable goal and yearning for a purpose that felt remotely human.

I feel I gave the game a fair shot with 118 hrs at the time of review. It really pains me to say that whatever everyone sees in this game is lost on me. It's simply a different type I game. Different isn't bad, but can be subjectively bad enough not to carry on. And while I leave a review that I do not recommend Elden Ring at this time, I plan to return someday give it another chance. Perhaps the magic will catch me and I'll join the great and large group of gamers who truly love this game, a group I'm sad to say I cannot yet count myself among.

EDIT: My review was a little too ranty so I'm revising it to be more comprehensive.

Before I get into why I'm leaving this as a thumbs down, the positives:

The Start: The early and mid game is extremely addictive. Deciding on a build, working towards improvements, findings items that make it better, exploring the map, all genuinely top tier. 
Leveling: Leveling stats feels impactful from the very beginning. Your bars get longer, your damage numbers go up, a hit that used to kill you no longer does, a weapon you couldn't efficiently wield is now stronger, etc.
Weapon variety: The amount of variety is so high it's bordering on coming full circle and being too much. Each weapon type has it's own feel, you can mix and match with your off-hand, switch on the fly to holding either one with both hands for certain benefits, the fluidity and sheer number of options available is genuinely impressive and I deeply respect the modelling and animating work that went into all these choices.
The World: Theme, music, sound design in general, armor designs, NPCs, they are all great too. I have gameplay issues with the world and NPCs, but as a theme, they are A+.

Now the bad, starting with:
The World: More does not always equal better, and this open world is a good example. Many times it feels like things are extremely large just to pad out the game. At first, the scale of all the architecture is awe-inspiring and fills you with wonder as to what is out there. As I said, the visual design and the world building is amazing. But, as the newness wears off and you focus more on the gameplay aspect, the obnoxiously long ladders, elevators and sprinting from A to B for literal minutes, gets old. There are fast travel locations, but a lot of areas are perfectly inbetween those spots, especially if you're trying to do NPC quests. More on that after bosses.
The Bosses: This ties into the above about the world feeling padded. Bosses are reused so much it's actually silly. You will fight the same bosses over, and over, and over, and over. The first time you fight them, you may die a lot trying to learn their moveset. Imagine how it feels to finally beat them, just to encounter them again in another part of the map. And again, and again, and again. More does not equal better.
NPCs: While their designs are top tier, the execution of their questlines is genuinely terrible. So much love and care clearly went into their aesthetics and story, only for at least half of them to be hidden behind some of the most obscur pathing I've ever experienced. You will absolutely need to follow a checklist guide to do them, and I think that undermines the fun and the quality of it all. I don't need or expect a quest marker floating in front of my eyes at all times, but having an ingame list with genuine hints on where to head to find an NPC and talk to them more is noticebly missing here. On a lesser note, most of the questlines ending in 'loot xyz from their corpse' is wild. We have become loot goblins for sure.

The combat: While the animations and weapon/skill designs are all genuinely impressive, there is a jank underneath it all that is persistent across FromSoftware games. Attacks are well telegraphed, but sometimes the hitbox just doesn't line up with what you can see. Areas where you fight often have stuff on the ground for you or your attacks to hit/get stuck on. Enemies jump around, going up and down depending on where their body is, or their limbs. It can be quite frustrating to watch and try to interact with in a consistent manner. Ranged is also heavily favored almost all the time, which becomes a problem for enjoying a variety of builds when up-close melee emphasizes the jank.

Lastly, the pricing structure: I'll give just one example to make my point. Sekiro has gone on sale for 50% off, 4 times in the past 12 months alone. Elden Ring on the other hand has been 35% only twice. This doesn't sound that extreme, but add in the fact that the DLC, which costs as much as other soulslikes, has literally never been on sale, and you can see the issue. It is a flawed game, so the price just doesn't make sense after all this time.

In conclusion, it's hard to hate Elden Ring even with all it's issues. But after spending a good amount of time with it, I can't honestly say it's worth full price, as much as there is to like here. There's an equal amount of fun to be had elsewhere these days, for less money. So unless it's on sale, I'd pass.

[h2]To figure out if you will like game or not, here's a simple question.[/h2]
Imagine playing a videogame, and coming across some obstacle. Some friction, some issue. What is your thinking process? Is it "[i]I should try better next time[/i]"? If so, this is game that will bring you some joy, and ALOT of misery and grief. I advice sticking to Dark Souls series in this case.
On the other hand, if at this moment you think "[i]How can I utterly break this game, what option I have to completely invalidate whatever opposition I'm facing?[/i]", then you will have alot of fun, and maybe some dissatisfaction when things fold in front of you a bit [b]too[/b] quickly. Go for it, I suppose.

[h3]If you want my opinion on the game, it can be found below.[/h3]
On one hand, this is a very good game. It's high quality, it's most beautiful open world game out there, and you MAY get hours upon hours of fun out of it (as long as you comply with certain unwritten, unexplained rules that go beyound just clicking buttons at right times). At it's worst ER is still above plenty other games of simillar genre.

On other hand, it's a display of complete lack of control and self-restrain in chase of some nebulous ideas and ideals that end up running contrary to what elevated studio to heights it's enjoying now. It's a game that shows that sometimes "more more more" doesn't equal "better". A silly comparison - think of a person who does so many plastic surgeries that they look nothing like person they used to be, all to end up looking utterly ghastly, even though lots of money, care and skill went into creating the look they now sport. That is Elden Ring and it's DLC "Shadow of the Erdtree".
I'm confident that ER2, or whatever else game will be next in Elden's Soulsborne pseudo-series will shock everyone, and not in positive way, unless From Software finally stops and rethinks their approach.

**Elden Ring – Ein gutes Souls-like, aber kein gutes Open-World-Spiel**

Die Open World von Elden Ring überzeugt mich nicht. Es fehlt ein Questlog, NPCs sind teilweise kaum wiederzufinden, und ihre Dialoge geben oft zu wenig Hinweise darauf, wie ihre Quests weitergehen. Erst im dritten Durchlauf konnte ich Rannis Quest vollständig abschließen. Dass man für solche Quests teilweise externe Guides benötigt, empfinde ich als schlechtes Questdesign.

Abseits der Bosskämpfe gibt es für mich wenig, was die offene Welt wirklich interessant macht. Katakomben und Bergwerke bieten gelegentlich spannende Erkundung, aber vieles andere fühlt sich wie Beschäftigungstherapie an, um den Charakter für die nächsten Bosskämpfe vorzubereiten. Die eigentliche Geschichte bleibt dabei erstaunlich banal: Man besiegt mächtige Gegner, um selbst Eldenfürst zu werden.

Die Bosskämpfe sind dagegen anspruchsvoll, fordernd und teilweise hervorragend gestaltet. Hier liegen die größten Stärken des Spiels. Die Kämpfe verlangen Geduld, Ausdauer und die Bereitschaft, aus Fehlern zu lernen.

**Mein Fazit:** Elden Ring ist für mich ein sehr gutes Souls-like, aber kein überzeugendes Open-World-Spiel. Die offene Welt wirkt eher wie ein Mittel zum Zweck, um die Bosskämpfe miteinander zu verbinden. Wer herausfordernde Bosskämpfe liebt, kommt auf seine Kosten. Wer eine gut erzählte Geschichte, nachvollziehbare Quests und eine lebendige Open World erwartet, wird dagegen enttäuscht.

Don't listen to the gleaming positive reviews of this game: They aren't people who *actually* play soulslike games for fun.

I wouldn't recommend it because:

>It has a major problem with what's known as "twinking" - people abusing the multiplayer mechanics to invade new players. It's not your normal "Oh it's dark souls and I'm getting invaded" - it's legitamately people save-editing in souls or "runes" as ER calls them, dropping high level items for new characters, and so on. This was a problem in Dark souls, yes, but ER it's even worse because they will spawn the invader right next to you - and furthermore, the game isn't as mechanically complex as in Dark souls. So They will just kill you. you can't really fight back unless they're bad. That takes some of the fun out of the concept of "getting invaded".

There are some serious flaws with the game: The exploring to get crafting items feels not very fleshed out and feels like an afterthought to force the player to engage with the open-world aspect, and is more monotonous than adds to the gameplay. None of the crafting items have detailed descriptions so you just have to grab everything not really knowing why. 

The Merchants and so on are generic NPCS - another big gripe with the game, the lack of NPC story characters. And the goods they sell seem completely useless - spells which aren't better than the basic magic bolt yet cost more mana. weapons and armour that are shittier than the starting armor. etc. Only useful shit is the crafting kit and the torch.

Let's talk about the spells and mana: They made the decision to move from spell casts to a mana bar. However, the mana and health system is woeful. Why invest in more mana, more health, when the flasks don't actually replenish it fully? You'll end up finding the next key flaw with the game which revolves around investing in level ups into stat increases.

Essentially: No point in investing in vitality, because don't have enough flasks and not enough flask enhancements. No point in investing in mana for the same reason. 

No point investing in endurance, because you start with SO MUCH STAMINA. Your stamina bar is bigger than both your health and your mana. It comes back so quickly. Investing in endurance does increase equipment load, but you virtually never find any equipment requiring more load so what's the point? 

And so you're just going to be investing in either dex or strength, depending on the scaling of your starter weapon. Another big gripe? Investing in either of those two stats will increase your physical defences across the board in all stats - so what's the point of investing in *both* when I should just invest in whichever one scales the quickest? The outcome: You'll just invest shittons into e.g Dex and basically nothing else.

Next: Let's talk about levelling up, and runes. The enemies in this game drop essentially no runes. The low level enemies are cheap chaff that the game expects you to farm to engage in the open world aspect. The bosses equally drop very little. So why bother? They also don't really drop terrible useful items. You could legitimately just go for the strongest bosses and ignore 80% of the open world - so why on earth would you design an open world with so little depth?

With so few new items, getting new armor or weapons to upgrade seems pointless. It makes you feel unsure about whether or not you're meant to use the smithing stones to upgrade gear. People like choice. And they're more likely to upgrade their gear if they have some idea about whether or not they'll find something better around the corner. You don't have that sort of frame of reference in ER. 

The magic and range in this game sucks for different reasons: As a magic user, or fighting magic users - all of the magic is essentially homing. This is a major deviation form Dark souls games. That makes it infuriating to fight against because you can't just dodge or walk around it - and it takes all the fun out of playing a mage too. There is no point in using a bow because it opens up a clunky ass menu where you have to manually move the crosshair over an enemy - unlike any other game where using a bow is just semi auto-locking but dodgeable ranged attack. 

Let's talk now about the multiplayer co-op: You need to craft these dragon flowers to spend the consumable to do coop and see your friend's summon sign. However this feels really pointless because those flowers are everywhere, and it just means every time you die you've got to use a random consumable that isn't even hard to get. This is clearly *trying* to mimic human effigies in dark souls, but because there's no negative, you don't lose max health when dying or so on, it just feels shallow and monotonous.

Lets talk about the enemies and the bosses: Very few enemies or bosses seem to be unique or have mechanical depth in the combat. So, So many of them are just "I'm a little goblin, I'm small and you can't hit me easily, I'm fast and dart around, I will attack you really fast three times in a row" - and the same sort of goes for the bosses too. you can backstab bosses, which feels sort of neat I guess, but it also makes it less hard and fulfilling. Furthermore, a lot of the bosses you seem to just be able to stun and stop them from attacking you, at least early game. Stunlocking bosses isn't particularly fun. Nor is it fun when *you* get stunlocked by an enemy that attacks quickly and that is *every* enemy. In dark souls, the enemies and bosses had clear movesets, cues to dodge attacks, and combat had mechanical depth. ER doesn't. The biggest exceptions to this seem to be Giants, Kaiden, and the golden sentinel, at least early game. But even then, be prepared for the boss/enemy to spam the same move 17-thousand times.  

The choice between taking health or mana ( flasks are interchangeable) means being a spellcaster is squishy while being a swordsman means you'll never engage with the magic aspect and be a spellsword.

Because all the enemies are so fast, it's deadly to be a greatsword or heavy weapon user - most likely you'll just choose a rogue-like playstyle and stunlock enemies with your quick attacks and your dex build. When there's little choice, the game becomes less fun.

Elden Ring – A master...piece of shit

Elden Ring is a weird game. Beautiful graphics, fantastic combat, incredible world design, yet I spent much of my playthrough wondering whether I was having fun.
The world is full of memorable places, classic FromSoftware gameplay, and some genuinely fun enemies and bosses.
And then there's Torrent. The horse. The legend. The actual secret weapon. Forget legendary swords. Running past 90% of the nonsense is probably the most useful ability in the game.

Elden Ring has two gameplay modes: explore endlessly or git gud.

Exploration becomes exhausting. The world is enormous, yet regular enemies are barely a threat. You spend hours checking every cliff and cave, collecting hundreds of items you'll never use.
Another cookbook? Fantastic. Another crafting material? Just what I needed.
The game makes you explore every edge of the map because maybe something useful is hidden there. Spoiler: usually there isn't. Or it's not what you need.

Then there's the difficulty balance.

Without Mimic Tear, some bosses feel like beating a brick wall with a toothpick. With Mimic Tear, suddenly you're the brick wall. There's little middle ground between getting destroyed and watching your clone do half the work.
I love challenging combat, but I'd rather feel I won than found the unofficial easy-mode switch. 

And finally, the story.

Cryptic lore, depressing characters, dying worlds, NPCs speaking in riddles. Classic FromSoftware. But Elden Ring feels particularly bleak. I never felt like a hero.
The Chosen Undead in DS1 and Ashen One in DS3 weren't traditional heroes either. These games are about struggling through broken worlds. But Elden Ring gave me little reason to care about becoming Elden Lord.

The verdict?

Brilliant ideas, fantastic combat, breathtaking environments, memorable moments.
Also bloated, repetitive, frustrating, and obsessed with rewarding exploration with stuff nobody needs.
When it's good, it's brilliant. When it's bad, you're riding Torrent around another cliff looking for an item you'll never use.

A game I can admire more easily than I can love.

It was a major disappointment for me. While on paper this game has everything that it needs to be crowned as a masterpiece DLC, and while the first impression upon entering into the DLC provides further merit to that sentiment, very quickly does it fall on its face. 

We have seen this before? This is just an extension of the vanilla late game. Sure a ton of weapons, a ton of bosses and enemies, but at this stage of the game its a bit redundant unless you are ready to reset your character. Its fine to do that but ultimately its just a different path up the same trajectory. 

This vast DLC is... largely empty. It feels like a copy-paste of the altus plateau with slightly darker shades. 

The story, same as in the vanilla, seems very irrelevant. And while this is a staple of From Soft Souls game, in ER it is getting a bit too tiring and not cohesive considering the scale of the game. 

The bosses are the worst offenders. While I'll be the first to admit that I am not a speed/challenge runner, I played all the previous games and enjoyed them vastly. Struggled, sure. But still the bosses were enjoyable. In Shadow of the Erdtree, and ER by and large, the bosses seem without vision or balance. From the peaks of Sekiro and DS3, to bosses here that simply spam attacks, are too large to properly track and read, and generally contain levels of unprecedented bull...  

I wanted to like this DLC and the game. I even gave it a long break, upgraded to fully modern hardware, and watched a bunch of videos about how to properly implement jumping, strafing, and unlocking the camera to better move around bosses and enemies. But putting aside the fact that I am not the best player, the game had failed for me at the simplest level. It had failed to be FUN. Trudging through ER late game and the DLC is a slog. And while the vistas are astonishing... the content and the mechanics fall far, far behind.

Is it a recommendation? Sure, on a technical level it is still a masterpiece that needs to be experienced. The scale of it (while also its downside) is alone a cause for celebration. But a more polished experience with better executed ideas lies in DS3 and Sekiro.

Also on a similar note, the game doesn't explain extremely important topics like leveling a weapon is more important than stats.  Or when a weapon scales with some attribute as "B" or "D", what does that even mean?

You find a boss and it barely takes damage.  Is it resistant to your damage type or are you just not high enough level?  Who knows!  Hey let's sink a ton of smithing stones into a blunt weapon just to find out and I sure hope I didn't just waste them.

Poor affordance and esoteric drops basically gating progression gives you two choices in the game: spend 10s of hours banging your head against the game to figure out the special place you need to go, to kill the miniboss, to get a drop you didn't know it had, to then give the drop to another NPC on the other side of the map, which will cause them to then sell you Smithing Stone[2] so you don't have to spend 20 hours farming Limgrave mines with a drop rate so low you aren't even sure it drops there..... OR you go to YouTube, find the cheese/needed steps and you're done in 30 minutes.

It shows you how to run around picking up all the somber smithing stones, open tons of chests and finally cheese a dragon so you have an incredibly powerful character.  All with zero real combat.  But yeah, Elden Ring is "hard" and you need to "git gud" and totally not a poorly crafted unbalanced and clunky mess of a game.

I will probably beat it in anger.  But if you don't own it, don't buy it.

Okay so I'm rewriting this review after having played several more hours, and beaten the first 3 main boss fights. Of course, all opinions are my own, and it's very subjective as to what a "good" playstyle is. 

     My biggest problem with the game is the combat, which obviously significantly hinders my experience with such a combat-focused game/genre. It feels generally "clunky" to me, not smooth and intuitive. Not to say that the motions aren't smooth, they are, it's more so that you can't adapt as frequently as I think you should be able to during a battle. 

     So for example, in the first main boss battle with a guy named Margit, I would like to run in when there's an opening, get a few strikes in, and then dodge out of the way when he's about to strike. However, one thing that this game doesn't do that I think it really should is give command priority. So I might strike 3 times, but right after I try to strike for the 3rd time, I realize Margit is about to strike and my hit won't land, so I need to doge early and cancel my strike. But because you already pressed the attack button, you can't doge until the game finishes that strike. So what happened is I ended up playing very conservatively, only risking a maximum of two hits before running away. Having to play that reserved makes the fight drag on and isn't necessarily overly difficult, it just feels boring to me. 

     Another thing I found very infuriating, especially with Margit, is the insane amount of variability in the time between the start and execution of an attack. Sometimes Margit raises his weapon and strikes immediately, the next try he raises it and strikes 3 seconds after holding in the air doing nothing, the next attempt he does it for 5 seconds. Again this contributes to only getting one or two hits in when sometimes you could get 5 or 6 in, but because you don't know, you have to play conservatively instead. 

     Now the second boss's attack pattern was actually much more intuitive for me. He had the right amount of variability. Not the exact same script, which would be too easy, but not the insane range of variance that Margit had. Sadly, the third boss, felt exactly like Margit all over again. Just a frick ton of attacks, then a short window to get a few hits in, then back to dodge city. 

     Which leads me to my next point: repetitiveness. See, all three of these bosses have felt extremely similar, just each one having subsequently faster attacks. Godrick's (the second boss) pattern differed, for the better, but it still followed the same principal of needed to overuse dodge's a bunch, be very conservative, and keep doing the same thing for 5 minutes. I found it boring. Essentially, up to the third boss anyways, the game's battles felt very "same-y". 

     Now, the last big thing I'll point out is the game's exploration. It doesn't make me want to go explore the world at all, and when I have gone exploring, the world feels very "empty" to me, to say the least. Most of the people you encounter are either enemies (which are trivially easy and repetitive), and the NPCs you encounter, at least by 10 hours into the game still, are few and far between. Plus they're just not very interesting. 

     I also think the entire UI, specifically the Inventory and Equipment menus etc., are overly complicated but that's a nitpick, once you get used to them they aren't that bad. 

     Overall, I just think the game's combat is too repetitive, clunky, and the exploration is very lackluster. Even if the game gets a lot more interesting as it progresses, I still feel confident leaving this review now, as a game shouldn't need more than 10 hours to hook you. Steam's refund policy even suggests that Valve believes hours should be plenty of time to understand if a game is good or not, but at the same time, I do understand the appeal, after all I've played for 10 hours now.

This isn't a good Souls game.

Firstly, let's get this out of the way: Souls fans, this review is not for you. You already bought the game, completed it six times and are busily posting a long rant nobody will read about why whatever weapon is underrated/overpowered. 

For the rest of us, who might dip in and out of Souls games from time to time: this is just a Souls game but worse. The only thing that makes it any different from Dark Souls 1, 2, 3 or any other Fromsoft game is the open world - and the open world makes literally everything worse. 

Don't get me wrong - it was the correct decision to put an open world in. The game isn't for me, it's for the Souls fans who've played every game FromSoft release a dozen times over and just need something new. For those people, the open world is the least harmful breath of fresh air possible. 

If you're not sick of the sight of Souls games, though, the open world is a terrible addition. Pacing is dead and buried, the usually stellar map design is relegated to only existing in dungeons, and you have no idea where you're supposed to go next. If you don't look it up you can guarantee you'll miss a region entirely, then have to choose between never experiencing it or doing it while horribly overlevelled. Speaking of which, if you like to explore and find everything, you'll be overlevelled anyway; I didn't grind once and yet was 30+ levels ahead of where I should be for virtually the entire game simply because I refused to skip content.

The worst thing, though, is the bosses. Bosses are FromSoft's selling point, and they're usually both well-designed encounters and also very visually impressive. In this game, however, thanks to the open world they have to put 300 more of them into the game than there should be - gotta put SOMETHING in the open world after all. They can't design 300+ unique bosses, so that means reprints. A LOT of reprints. By the time I gave up on the game I'd fought an estimated six Crucible Knight versions, dozens of lesser versions thereof, half a dozen gargoyles, seven (I think) Ulcerated Tree Spirits, over a dozen Watchdog Statues... the list goes on. The anticipation and impact Dark Souls usually has with its bosses is entirely eliminated because nine times out of ten you'll see the boss health bar pop up and realise it's the same thing you've already fought before. Repeatedly.

To conclude, if you're NOT someone who plays every Souls game relentlessly, do yourself a favour - buy Dark Souls 3 instead. Hell, buy ANY Dark Souls game. If you already own one, play that instead. They'll have proper gameplay pacing, proper map design, and most of the bosses you fight will be unique and interesting. 

They'll be better than this, in other words. This was legitimately a boring game.

The open world just destroys the flow of the game. It doesn't feel like exploring, but more like working a 9-to-5 just to reach the next legacy dungeon and finally get another taste of actual level design.

More than half of the game is made up of useless horizontal planes with different textures or, when the game feels generous, those same planes decorated with good-looking solid objects planted into the ground.

The game can often be visually impressive, but that alone contributes very little to the actual enjoyment of the exploration itself.

And the legacy dungeons aren't that much better, to be honest. Excluding Farum Azula, I don't feel like any of them really tries to propose a distinctive or interesting way of exploring in the way almost every area of Dark Souls did. Stormveil is basically a castle, Raya Lucaria is a castle with mages, Volcano Manor is a castle with lava, Leyndell spends most of its time feeling like a traditional dungeon crawler, and the Haligtree is okay but ultimately forgettable.

This doesn't mean the game looks bad. Quite the opposite: very often it looks fantastic. But visuals are only part of the job in a medium built around interaction. It's crazy to me that, despite being the first entry with a dedicated jump button, this somehow feels like the Souls game where exploration is least enjoyable.

The reward structure makes things even worse. The game fills the world with useless items in an attempt to create the illusion that wandering around is worthwhile. Half the time you go out of your way to reach some distant corner of the map only to find a crafting material or recipe whose function you'll forget five seconds after picking it up.

And then there are the catacombs and mines.

I hope you really like those assets, because you're going to see them a lot. They feel almost procedurally assembled: repetitive, unimaginative, full of dead space and absurdly unrewarding considering how much of a slog many of them are.

The entire map could have been one quarter of its current size. If that smaller space had been properly filled and given more attention, I'd probably be the happiest Souls player alive.

But thank God there are the incredibly rewarding boss fights.

Yes, I absolutely love being input-read into an AoE, roll-catching, delayed one-shot attack during a seven-hit tracking true combo. At some point you genuinely start wondering whether having somebody punch you while you're playing would improve the experience, if only because the physical pain might distract you from the spiritual hassle of fighting yet another random boss.

And that's assuming the boss isn't recycled. Be prepared to fight the same fucking thing over and over again, or, even better, a normal enemy arbitrarily promoted to boss status for the occasion. It's lazy design taken to an absurd level. There isn't a single boss in the entire game that I genuinely look forward to fighting again. Maybe Malenia and Morgott.

Regular enemies aren't much better, although their biggest problem is less the movesets themselves and more the absurd damage numbers. After a certain point, even with a full tank build, almost everything can practically two-shot you.

That doesn't mean their movesets aren't filled with bullshit, because they absolutely are, but the damage is so aggressively overtuned in an attempt to inflate difficulty that every other problem almost becomes secondary.

That constant feeling of unfairness, combined with some of the least rewarding exploration I've experienced in this kind of game, pushes the frustration to another level.

What keeps Elden Ring afloat is its build diversity and lore. In combat, you can use almost anything and create an enormous variety of viable builds, while the world and its mythology are genuinely compelling. The problem is that the experience surrounding those strengths is often so exhausting that eventually you stop caring about what is in front of you, because everything starts feeling like another chore.

Worst entry in the series, and overall an average to below-average game.

If I also judge it against the minimum level of progress one should reasonably expect from a later installment in an established series, I have to mention how unacceptable the state of the AI is. Enemies are frequently just braindead.

The environmental storytelling has also become strangely self-celebratory. It was one of the defining strengths of the earlier games, but an open world should have been the opportunity to expand that formula and communicate the setting in more organic ways: through cities, settlements, populated spaces, or basically anything that made the world feel more alive.

Instead, despite having exponentially more space to work with, the game often falls back on the exact same formula: empty ruins, cryptic environmental details and item descriptions carrying most of the narrative burden.

At that point it stops feeling elegant and starts feeling lazy.

Before I start, I would like to say that this it not a negative review. I have very complicated feelings towards this game. Feelings that could not be measured by a simple like or dislike. 

Let's start with the positives. I fucking LOVE the art direction of this game. Each region feels distinct and full of detail, conveying a beautifully tragic war-torn world so well, albeit one that feels as though it can be saved and its not all hopeless, and yet despair lurks around every corner.

I loved a lot of the NPCs, they feel considerably more fleshed out than some of the previous Souls games, not to say they didn't have any, but a lot of them made me really question the choices I was making along the way, in particular Varre, who I found intriguingly creepy as hell. It has some of my favorite character designs as well! Blaaid, Alexander, Godrick, Mohg, Malenia, I could go on! The voice acting is top notch as well, some of the best I've heard in a game. 

The music was pretty nice too, unfortunately I'm usually too distracted by my mission or fighting a tough boss to really appreciate it for what it is. 


What made me leave a "negative" review, however, was the difficulty. Not that it was HARD, this genre is known for its relatively high difficulty. It was brutally hard, moreso than every other Souls game I have played, (1 and 3, 3 I have the most experience with) but it's not even that!

The difficulty of this game is....is just....all OVER the fucking place!!!

Like...ok. You start out in Limgrave. You have barely any health to speak of, so you need to start leveling Vigor. My advice to you all, get that shit to 40 IMMEDIATELY. And then towards the mid-late game, get it to 60. I have gripes with this, more on that later. Liurnia, a bit more difficult, but not a huge step up.
Every region after that has a rather large jump in difficulty. ESPECIALLY Caelid. FUCK Caelid! But wait!! It gets even WORSE!!

When you get to the late game areas, (Leyndell, Mountaintops of the Giants, Crumbling Farum Azula) the game just throws as much BULLSHIT at you as it possibly can, and doesn't ever hold back. JESUS. FUCKING. CHRIST. I have NEVER seen such a horrific difficulty spike in any game up until this point! 

The Fire Giant was the first boss to really question my sanity. It is INSANELY tanky, and while largely telegraphable, it will destroy you in 3-4 hits. With 60 VIGOR. 

60 Vigor is practically MANADATORY at this stage of the game. Everyone and everyONE will fuck you up in 3-4 hits. I say 60 because it's the second softcap. After that you get barely anything from Vigor. Which FUCKING SUCKS BECAUSE YOU DON'T EVER GET ENOUGH HP TO WORK WITH!!!

As are summons. The PC version is the definitive version because the online is free. You NEED co-op to beat most of these bosses. Especially towards the end. Spirit Ashes can work too, but here's the thing I fucking hate about this. NOT. EVERY. BOSS. WILL LET YOU. SUMMON. SPIRITS!!!! WHY?!!! This is a HORRIBLE design choice!! They're not even as good as a player can be! Just let me USE them for Christ's sake!!


But THEN....Maliketh.

Maliketh, and the boss you fight at phase 1, the Beast Clergyman, might just be the worst boss I've ever dealt with. And right before, in my mind it was the Fire Giant. 

Imagine a fucker as tanky as the Fire Giant. Now make him INSANELY mobile, have multiple AOE projectiles, and make much of his attacks go through the pillars that LOOK like they're safe, but oftentimes won't protect you from SHIT. I mean this to BOTH bosses by the way.

Maliketh, is even worse. Now give him a sword that can DRAIN YOUR HEALTH OVER TIME, AND! Reduce your Max HP, Make him even MORE mobile, and make him tanky too. 

I am stuck on this boss right now. You need two summons. Not one, TWO. One is not enough. And many times for some godforsaken reason I hardly get anyone online to help! 


There's another aspect of Elden Ring I really don't like, unrelated to difficulty.

It is, by far, the most walkthroughiest game, I have ever played. You NEED a walkthrough for most of this game. After a while I just gave up playing it blind. There's no shame in using one either, especially for games like this. Dark Souls 3 could be like this too, but I used it more for building my character rather than much of the game itself!

NPCs have the most obtuse questlines in the world. They practically DEMAND a guide. How are you supposed to know what to do next, what items to get to progress a questline, without using a guide?! It's ridiculous!!

Pages upon pages, videos upon videos, all just to be able to play this game without losing my mind. And I'm still losing my mind. 


Dark Souls 3 could be like this at times, I remember Irithyll being absolute HELL in regards to difficulty. But in regards to difficulty CURVE, that is the big ass difficulty spike of the game, but a lot of lategame areas tend to generally be more fair relative to the area. The final boss of the game was notably easier than Irithyll's own. And, fuck, Margit the Fell is harder than most Dark Souls 3 bosses, and is the FIRST major story boss! That tells you everything about this game. 

Speaking of which, I have yet to beat the final bosses, (yes there are TWO of them in a row, and if you die at the second one, you have to start from the first one all over again, FUCK THAT.) But I CAN tell you that both of them have twice as much health as the final boss of Dark Souls 3. BOTH. OF. THEM.


It all combines into the most unaccessible, harder than hardcore, not for the faint of heart or the short of temper Souls game, I have ever played. For their first attempt at an open world Souls game, I'd say FromSoft did a pretty good job, but its also meandered with questionable design choices that ultimately lessen what I would've otherwise called the best Souls game! It shows a lot of promise!!....but holy FUCK, are the lows some of the lowest I've seen in a game. 

I wouldn't give it a flat out thumbs down because I DO like a lot of this game. I ultimately did have fun most of the way through, and if a video game is fun, that's great! I would give it a more, thumbs sideways, I guess???

I say "not recommended" not in the sense that the game sucks, it doesn't, I know I sound like I think it sucks, but its moreso certain aspects that really get under my skin, enough to make me not recommend it for most people. I would just start out playing either Dark Souls Remastered, or Dark Souls 3, if you want to get into these games. Elden Ring is for the most hardcore motherfuckers on the planet, clearly. 

And from what I heard the DLC gets even worse due to certain mechanics, and DLC of Souls games generally being even more brutal than the main game, but that is standard at this point. The late game is brutal enough for me, and honestly I'd say it's too much. I'm not ever getting the DLC.

Also also, WHO CHARGES MONEY FOR CHARACTER CLASSES, ARE WE REAL, PEOPLE?!! CHRIIIIIST!!!


If FromSoft makes another open world in this style, I would like to see FromSoft do a much better job with the difficulty curve, making it a lot smoother and fairer in regards to where you are, and make the NPC questlines easier to follow without a guide. Quest design in a 9th gen game this obtuse is beyond stupid. That is not to say show markers pointing every step of the way, just make it so we don't need a guide. There's a lot FromSoft can do in regards to making a game like this so much more accessible without really "dumbing down" the difficulty. 

At the end of the day, I DID like this game. Unfortunately, I wanted to like it even more. But once I realized how massively flawed this game can be, I don't really think I can. It's far from the masterpiece everyone makes it out to be. But it's still a good game! I just feel like it can be so much better than what it actually is.

I spent a few weeks a while back working non-stop, day and night, to prove a massive conspiracy that Elden Ring (and possibly FromSoftware games in general) had synthetic review scores and inflated critic praise. While I don't still think there's a conspiracy, I'll leave some parts of the research that I found interesting below.

1. Elden Ring launched on Steam at about 60% positive from ~19,000 reviews, then rapidly climbed into the 80s and eventually mid-90s, an exceptionally large and fast sentiment reversal.

2. Other major GOTY/blockbuster games I compared—Baldur’s Gate 3, Hogwarts Legacy, Cyberpunk 2077, RDR2, and The Witcher 3—did not show anything close to Elden Ring’s rapid 60%→70s→80s review-score transformation; their launch scores either stayed stable or changed gradually even when receiving comparable or greater review volume.

2.5. Other low-scoring launches like Cyberpunk and RDR2 showed a fairly normal recovery pattern, where later reviewers were somewhat more positive and the score gradually stabilized; Elden Ring instead appeared to shift from roughly 60% → ~78% incoming sentiment → ~95% incoming sentiment, causing its aggregate score to rise unusually fast.

3. Its biggest historical Steam review week contained roughly 210,000 reviews, and that huge volume arrived during the same period the score was rapidly recovering.

4. On February 26, 2022, Steam users explicitly organized a positive counter-review campaign urging fans to review the game to offset negative reviews and push it toward “Overwhelmingly Positive.”

5. By February 27, users were already accusing the positive review wave of containing suspiciously short or low-effort reviews and asking whether bots were involved.

6. Elden Ring had an enormous launch gap between critics, who rated it around 96–98/100, and the first large Steam player population, which rated it around 60% positive.

7. Critics gave Elden Ring almost universally high scores despite well-documented PC problems like stuttering, shader issues, limited graphics options, and a 60 FPS cap.

8. Developers from major studios including Ubisoft and Sony/Nixxes publicly questioned why critics seemed unusually willing to overlook Elden Ring’s technical, UX, and quest-design flaws.

9. Many critics had only about one week with Elden Ring before review embargoes lifted, despite the game often taking 100–150 hours to fully evaluate. A later critic who played roughly 150 hours without guides gave Elden Ring 7/10 and said the final 30–40% became repetitive and dragged, weaknesses early reviewers may not have reached.

10. Roughly 95% of Elden Ring’s critic reviews were published early or around launch, meaning its permanent reputation was largely set inside the prerelease access window.

It seems that Fromsoftware was too afraid to place weapons and armour out in the open world except in a few specific cases, perhaps concerned people wouldn't find it. Overall it's recommended, but it isn't recommended because these developers need to learn a lesson, that they refuse to learn. It truly has the worst camera you can imagine in gaming. Fromsoftware just thinks it's the best thing ever, and it's never going to change. It's angle is such that you cannot accurately judge how far your weapon is going to hit, or how far the enemy is away from you. It's not high enough to see forward past your character, and it isn't zoomed out enough to keep track of what is going on. It also isn't reliable for actually locking on to the enemy. Sometimes they'll be in view, but you cannot lock onto the enemy, because some invisible hitbox is making them untrackable. You'll hit the camera lock key, and then the camera faces whichever direction your character is facing, which could very well be the opposite direction from the enemy. Add to this the enemy becoming aware of your presence, and you'll be getting attacked with no knowledge of the attack incoming.

The circling of enemies is a place where the camera should be zoomed back, so the camera isn't as disorienting, especially when the enemies are mobile and jumping around. I honestly feel like what makes this game difficult at all, is because of the camera.

In addition to this, multiple enemies are extraordinarily difficult to take on, because the camera locks on to one, and all your weapon strikes go in that direction. You have to keep changing the lock on to deal with enemies as they come at you, but naturally with such a close camera, you really can't keep track of what's going on. The difficulty should be in facing multiple opponents, but the camera plays the biggest opponent of all.

Then there are hitboxes that lock you in place. So many objects, and obstacles to make sure you can't move freely. Some terrain is easy to go over, and some just stops you in place. However you can always move freely when a large drop is nearby. It's like they designed this stuff to be artificially difficult. You get trapped in these hitboxes, and combined with the awful camera, you have no escape available. It feels awful and terribly designed. Maybe you wouldn't fall off cliffs as often during combat if the camera zoomed out more, but they refuse to do this.

Enemies have tracking attacks that you cannot get away from. You must dodge at the exact perfect moment, or you have zero chance. Enemies chain together attacks where if you dodge one, you get hit by the second strike before you can dodge again. They also have defenses, so if you ever attack the guy, before he attacks you and opens themselves up, they can counter your attack, and return with a follow up strike that you cannot dodge out of. This is a pain when opening up the enemy requires dealing with numerous tracking strikes. You'll have to get dodging down to a tenth of a second accuracy.

Then there are the ambushes that are set up to make sure if you are new at all, you will die a lot. Given the death mechanic of dropping all your money/experience, you'll have to put yourself back in the ambush to get your money back. I feel like a better designer wouldn't need to add cheap ambushes and what are essentially jump scares to add difficulty.

In fact, this game could be called Dark Souls 4, and I'd be okay with it, because that's what it is: Dark Souls with mods.

Btw, I know Demon's Souls came first, but the same lineage is there: Demon's Souls, Bloodborne, Dark Souls, and now Elden Ring. The only game that really escaped this pattern is Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, which actually changed things.

If you look at FromSoftware's games over time, you can see a pattern. They take what they already did, adjust it, and try to perfect the formula, but they don't create enough new things. Look at Armored Core and Frame Gride, for example. It's the same idea, trying to perfect the formula, and then they continue with Armored Core and Another Century's Episode.

I don't care if they reuse elements from past games, but do you know who does this too? Activision with Call of Duty.

And look, Elden Ring is fun, but there are a lot of things that feel like Bandai Namco the publisher, not the developer put its hands on parts of the game. I remember playing Code Vein, the typical Souls like that tries to be unique but ends up feeling like, "Hey, look, I'm Dark Souls too." It was disappointing, with its vague story and some parts like The Depths: Tower of Trials, where the enemy damage made no sense.

Elden Ring also starts with static images instead of the kind of cinematics that gave context at the beginning of Dark Souls, Sekiro, or Bloodborne. I remember thinking, "Wow, wait a second." There are things in Elden Ring that feel like they were just written into the script because yes.

The Fire Giant is a good example. You're close to the end of the game, there is no cinematic and barely any context, and when you reach him, the fight doesn't feel special. Remember Dark Souls III and Yhorm the Giant? If you did Siegward of Catarina's quest, he appeared there, and suddenly the fight had more context and feeling. It felt like you had to finish something.

In Elden Ring, the Fire Giant feels like a boss placed there just to fill an empty, soulless scenario.

The game also has too many bosses. You enter a cave, explore for a while, suddenly a health bar appears, "epic" music starts, and you fight another boss. Then you do it again. Because it happens so often, bosses stop feeling special.

Even the main bosses were a disappointing experience for me. There is so much recycling. Look at Margit, the Fell Omen. I saw that guy like three times, or maybe it was Morgott, the Omen King, because they all look the same. Down in Leyndell, Royal Capital, there is also an illusion that is basically a copy of Margit or Morgott. Even Godrick the Grafted didn't feel that unique to me.

Radahn was also disappointing. Only in the DLC do you really see his power. I understand that the version we fight in the base game is weakened, but still, we're fighting this legendary warrior while he's riding a skinny, scrawny horse.

Malenia, however, actually felt special. She was fun. And the final Marika/Radagon encounter was cool because it felt like the game was telling me, "I'm the Elden Ring." Not me saying it the boss itself felt like it was saying that.

Godfrey was also disappointing. I expected a real version of the Elden Lord, something like when you fight Gwyn or even the Soul of Cinder. Not because I wanted a harder fight, but because of the feeling you get when you fight them for the first time. Godfrey didn't give me that feeling. He felt weak.

And then there is co-op. I bought this game expecting to play with friends, but if you want to play with friends, forget it or at least, that's how it felt to me. You get invaded constantly, and it becomes annoying when you're just trying to explore.

In past games, invasions had a purpose. You could farm items for the covenant you joined and get special rewards, like Darkmoon Blade from the Blade of the Darkmoon. In Elden Ring, that doesn't exist in the same way. Invading other players often feels like PvP for no reason.

And you already have THREE different arenas for PvP. Some people prefer invading because they enjoy it, and that's fine, but from my experience, getting invaded while trying to explore with friends made no sense.

So don't expect to easily play through the whole game with friends. I ended up playing almost the entire game alone, even though I bought it expecting to play with them, and eventually they just left the game because of things like this.

I'm also worried about the direction FromSoftware is taking. This "new DLC" attitude of "it's just $5" makes me worry that in the future the company could become like Activision, Bethesda, or Ubisoft. I really hope that never happens.

And then you see the new FromSoftware game coming to Nintendo Switch another Souls game, or basically Bloodborne with jumps. Do you see the pattern? The direction they're taking? Maybe I'm wrong. I hope I am.

So, who is Elden Ring for?

If you've never played a FromSoftware game: play it. It's fun, huge, challenging, and has an incredible amount of content.

If you've already played their previous games and you want more of the same formula, you'll probably like it.

But if you've played them all and you're hoping to find something genuinely new, think about it before buying. Maybe you won't care that it's the same formula. Maybe you'll love it anyway. But maybe, like me, you'll regret the purchase.

When I watched the trailers and gameplay, I had this feeling in the back of my head saying, "Hey, this is the same game as the past FromSoftware games." And literally, it was.

I wasn't wrong.

I don't expect this to be seen by someone legitimately wondering if this game is worth picking up or not. I don't even expect this to be seen by anyone really but to begin: Elden Ring is at best a mid game and at worst a terrible one.

You will frequently be put in situations where you have to hope for RNG that the enemies don't move in a way that locks you into unavoidable death, bosses that deal ridiculous damage while you deal nothing, enemies that have ridiculous stats despite what they are (e,g, archers with large health pools and ridiculous damage reduction on top of that). You will get to experience the constant cycle of having to guess when an attack is going to happen because the enemy has 3 different versions of the same attack that are all identical in start-up but come out at different speeds that deal high damage. Not to mention the FromSoft special of lingering hitboxes or hitboxes that just plain make no sense, almost always to the detriment of you! Another FromSoft classic too of enemies having grabs that inflict bleed so they will 99% of the time kill you. On top of all that, enemies just plain do not follow the same rules you do, they will not run out of FP, they do not have to stop their combos at any fixed point and can string as many attacks together as they want (this is mild hyperbole, they genuinely can string together their hardest to avoid moves in one combo and I've had enemies that forced me to wait dodging through 7 attacks before I could even attempt to poke them) and speaking of stats:

Poise does next to nothing relevant in this game. It will help your attack not get interrupted if you get hit by something while charging a heavy attack but god forbid you don't want to be staggered by every pebble that hits you regardless of what you're wearing.

Level design where traps, hidden doors, and enemies are just thrown at you in ways where you'd think you'd get a grace after running low on healing despite having 10 flasks and, oops no sorry. Did you die? Make that entire slog again, bud. Oh that hole you need to dodge a trap? It's a small enemy that you're going to end up either dying to the trap trying to hit the enemy or die from the enemy somehow almost instantly proccing bleed or some other status effect on you. The Haligtree is a perfect example of another issue with the level design: Elden Ring does not do platforming well, at all. You will be put in situations where you will wonder if it's even what the devs intended before realizing, yes, they did in fact and- oh sorry you stood on the wrong part of the branch bud you will not be punished for the bad game design with death.

I think FromSoft games were what made me fully realize there is nothing more infuriating than a game over that takes way too long to get you back in the game. Ironically, for as quick as your health drains it's actually fairly long to die in this game. You get your choice of a quick death where the game still sits before finally going to the loading screen or on the opposite end: an animation that takes what feels like a full minute before you even get to the 5 second needless linger part that boots you to the loading screen.

TL;DR Elden Ring is mid at best and bad at worst. Play Dragon's Dogma or Hollow Knight for games that do the "challenging but fair" approach (in Hollow Knight's case) or the open-world medieval approach in DD's case

Elden Ring, along with just about everything else FromSoftware has created, is a solid entry in the canon. There is no denying this. This review has nothing to do with the base game. Yes, I think you know what this is actually about. The ugly little elephant which consistently plagues the gaming industry as well as the many aspects of modern life, I'm afraid. Consolidation of power, income inequality, the end of individual ownership. You see these phenomena play out in all walks of life. And yes, it's infected even the most beloved studios of our day. Perhaps this is inevitable, but this is no reason to give in to mediocrity and extortion.

The implications of "horse armor" need no introduction. Once implemented, they tend to signal a decline in the equitable partnership between player and developer. Bethesda, Ubisoft, EA, Activision, to name the obvious ones. Oh microtransactions. Oh gated content. Oh Pre-order bonuses. "They are totally optional. They are purely cosmetic." "Content" of this kind is completely overwhelming in the space today, so commonplace that few even seem to notice or remember a time before their coercive ubiquity, but those of us who do remember, we are still out here, and we still care. I know whoever decides to read this cares too. And you can do something about it.

You don't have as much freedom to do the things you want to do anymore, and as more of life gets behind you, the equation will never pencil out in your favor again. Elden Ring is genuinely one of the best games I've ever played.

The exploration is incredible. You can pick a direction, wander off, and somehow end up finding an entire castle, underground city, or boss that you had absolutely no idea existed. The combat is satisfying, the build variety is ridiculous, and the feeling of finally beating a boss that's been kicking your ass for an hour is something very few games can replicate.

It's not perfect. Some bosses can be frustrating as hell, the PC performance has had its issues, and occasionally the game seems determined to remind you that you are, in fact, terrible at it.

But overall? Elden Ring is an incredible game and absolutely deserves the praise it gets.

Unfortunately, the Tarnished Pack is where FromSoftware and Bandai Namco completely lost me.

$5 for two starting classes, a handful of armor and weapons, some NPC invasions, and three cosmetic skins for Torrent is already pushing it. But the fact that some of the equipment can be obtained in-game anyway makes charging for this feel even more ridiculous.

And then they bundle this content with the new Switch 2 version while turning around and telling the people who already bought and supported the game on other platforms to pay extra for it.

Seriously?

This isn't a real expansion. This isn't Shadow of the Erdtree. Shadow of the Erdtree gave us an entire new world to explore, bosses, weapons, enemies, and dozens of hours of content. That was DLC worth paying for.

The Tarnished Pack feels like they looked at a small amount of bonus content that could have been a free update and decided, "Nah, let's charge them for it."

And before someone says, "It's only $5," I genuinely do not care. The price does not magically make bad DLC practices okay. If anything, it's the principle of it. Elden Ring has sold millions of copies. People have supported this game for years, bought Shadow of the Erdtree, and helped make it one of the biggest games of the last decade.

So rewarding those players by making them pay extra for a couple of starting classes and horse cosmetics while giving the content to new Switch 2 buyers as part of their edition is just insulting.

I still love Elden Ring. The actual game is phenomenal.

But I'm not going to pretend the Tarnished Pack isn't a blatant attempt to squeeze more money out of an already massively successful game.

Pros: Beautiful art design, particularly character and monster design. Architectural design can be a bit generic and repetitive but it fits the setting. Incredible world design. 

Cons: Combat is, at its heart, a knife fight simulator. Not a true RPG and would not recommend to other RPG gamers. The magic system is shallow and underbaked and fundamentally doesn't fit a combat system that wants to be a rhythm game. If you like casters, stay away.

The game occasionally stops being an RPG and confiscates your build. As an egregious example: Rykard gives my pure-Intelligence sorcerer a twelve-weight Strength weapon that ignores Intelligence entirely, then balances two enormous health bars around using a weapon you'll never touch again. 

Other complaints: 

1. The sorcerer's principal progression region, Raya Lucaria, heavily resists magic. If you rely purely on exploration and refuse to metagame and explore Caelid early to get Rock Sling you will suffer. 

2. Casting speed is governed by Dexterity, making magic the playstyle with the most awkward stat distribution and imposing an archetypally incoherent stat tax.

3. The already lackluster spell variety collapses under the FP economy. The first spells you get will likely remain among the most efficient throughout the game. Many of the spells are situational, redundant or boring, larger version of a previous one.  

4.  Weapon skills and Ashes of War frequently deliver the feel and look of 'magic' with far fewer downsides. Moonveil and Dark Moon Greatsword as the obvious examples here. 

5. The summoning system is heavily restricted by geography but is also the only broadly reliable way for casters to create the uninterrupted openings required by the game's longer and more elaborate spells. Where summoning is disabled, the caster is pushed back toward quick, close-range attacks like Carian Slicer. In practice you'll often spend a good chunk of your game outside boss arenas as a spellblade by necessity, whether that was your intended playstyle or not. 

6. Summoning is also so poorly balanced that roughly 90% of its enormous roster is not worth upgrading. A handful of durable generalists and exceptional group ashes are almost never the wrong choice, reducing most specialized summons to self-imposed novelty picks. 

7. Damage-type adaptation is locked behind obscure spell acquisition, hybrid stat requirements, or entirely different casting traditions. To “adapt” here often means abandoning the mage you built. Even respec is gated by play-time and a somewhat rare consumable so it's not an encounter-level solution here either. 

8. Bosses frequently erase the strategic advantage of range. There's no real magic, in an RPG sense, without it. 

The standard Souls player rebuttal “but mages can melt bosses” doesn’t counter any of this. Sorcery has enormous optimized peaks when the enemy stays still and the player stacks Terra Magica, a Physick, specialized headgear, talismans and a summon. But that does not show that it consistently supports experiencing the world as a caster. 

Given that I had to ask an AI model to heavily rewrite the magic system into something resembling an actual RPG, I can't in good conscience recommend this game to other RPG players in spite of hundreds of hours of playtime.

[h1]Probably the biggest letdown of a game.[/h1]

I have to preface this and say that this is my first soulslike experience. Elden ring videos and players promise hard gameplay, great story, and cinematic experience. In reality? It's [b]unmeasurable disappointment[/b] on several fronts.

My first issue is that this game was supposed to be made for controllers. You'd think with controllers your movement would be optimized with omnidirectional movement, variable speed, etc. No. No it is not. Too simple of concepts for these simple devs. In order to sprint in this game you have to hold the same button you dodge with (B as I'm on Xbox controller). So if you were to do something as simple as dodge while running, you have to hold the direction and quickly release and tap your dodge button again. This is already awkard of a movement and you'd think it'd be fixed in early builds of the game. Nada. On top of this awkward movement, your dodge actually only starts once the dodge button is released. This wonderfully stupid idea of a mechanic makes reactive playstyles (what'd you'd expect to play as a game centered around boss fights) useless. The amount of time it takes for you to actually do what you inputed is elongated by dumb design. This leads to another problem later on. [i]I'm just gonna forego the horrible auto-lock and let other players tell you about that dumpster fire.[/i]

My second issue is FPS being locked. 60hz is stone age. People have to spend $60 to get this game (crazy ik). When you can get a 60+fps monitor for $80. Let's think here, are your customers going to say "God I hope this cinematic game is locked at 60fps". Seriously unless you're a foot in the grave you can see the slop that is 60 fps. Did you buy a actual monitor? Something beyond 60fps? Yikes you're going to see some stuttering if your hz isn't divisible by 60 f*cking fps or has freesync. Now in the defense of this game, I understand that the game is based around the 60fps for engine reasons and for console players. Yet, WHY is it 60 fps when ported to PC. I'm writing this review 4 years later and there is still no support for higher framerates. Dollar per frame game.

My third issue, difficulty. This game isn't "hard", it's tedious. I started playing this game in hopes of dodging bosses last second, paying attention to a flurry of attacks as they came out, and getting bested because I lacked the mechanical skill to beat a boss. Reality? This game has THE MOST BORING BOSS FIGHTS. Let me explain. Every boss has movepools.  Which when learned make the boss easier, but Elden Ring makes it BORING. However, the fun should lie in going against new bosses right? Maybe getting lucky and beating them first try? Well unless it's one of the billion copy print dungeons with bosses that might as well be 2D for the lack of depth to them, you're going to die (probably in those dungeons too). You'll be hit with a move you can't properly dodge because well you've never seen it before.Or even worse, you have yet the timing is slightly different, with extensions of range or attack(s). Some people may not have a problem with this whole "see a new move, die and come back pattern". And to those people I say, "Keep flipping those burgers." The allure in bossfighting games is making yourself a betterplayer. One able to become better in any situation as you progress. Not dying 2-3, 4 times before you get the boss to a next phase where you'll have to repeat the same steps. This loop? It's not skillful dodges, parrying, or anything cool like that. It's just dying, learning, and coming back. That is profoundly boring. If all your bosses can just simply be put into a youtube video devolving strategies to counter every situation, you didn't make a skillfull game, you made a knowledge gap. [u]Seriously the bosses might as well be a quizlet looking at each boss's attacks like flashcards and memorizing.[/u]

And you'd know I'd take it all back if the story was redeeming. Stories can carry bad gameplay after all. But truth be told you won't really even learn the story in this game. You have to go OUT of your way to find what this game is about. Other RPGs I've played such as Fallout 4, Cyberpunk 2077, Pokémon, all find ways to sprinkle in story if you just go a little bit off the game's main course. This game? You pretty much need a guide to get a inkling of it at all. You will have many questions when the game starts and as it progresses, you'll just have more and more. It's hard to find motivation to do quests with characters you know nothing about. This game doesn't motivate you to do anything, you pop in the world, you look around a bit, and you're confused. I understand that it is a game for adults, so make the story a bit complex. However at the start of the game, you as a protagonist get the sole goal of becoming the Elden Lord from a good cutscene. Now it may just be me, but [u]why does it sound like we're setting up a tv show?[/u] Could it be that it just said a bunch of characters nobody knows, gave the tiniest amount of backstory that you don't really understand, and had a vague direction? Maybe...maybe. But surely this is a good story. It will tell you a bit more as you start the game... Yeah no, this game has bad storytelling. Not necessarily a bad story I hear if you have thousands of hours to waste reading every item, replaying for minute things you missed because the game [b] Doesn't Have Story Direction [/b]. My advice F-Soft, narrow the guage just a little bit more so people can know why they should give a crap. Then the whole discover the lore thing works. 

But hey, if all that sounds appealing to you, go ahead and pay your $60 for 60fps. Have fun wasting your time memorizing an interactive textbook everyone else has already read, memorized, condensed, and posted the results of online.

Edit 1: I've since beat Elden Ring and it was unfulfilling. I have yet to play the DLC (got a gamekey bundle for cheap). At this point in time everything still stands. Play modded if you can. But unless you're an achievement hunter like me, better steer clear, there's some enjoyable moments in this game, but the bad camera control, crappy controls, and 60fps still make this game hard to enjoy. It's sad that unpaid modders make the fixes that paid devs couldn't. That said, if you have a fit girl you know, go there. Don't buy.

Elden Ring is hands down the most forgettable game I ever played.

World building and exploration: 4/5
Few games have locales and lore as evocative as this game, but the From formula for half-baked lore might be beginning to wear thin. The world is often also too large, and the level design of the open world is... lacking.
Visuals and art direction: 5/5
Every frame a painting. The DLC especially is amazing, visually.
Build variety: 5/5
Never has a From game offered such variety, and it's hard to think of many other games that offer this much, either. Tens of weapon classes, spell schools, lots of armor and talismans, different buffs and synergies to build on - it's great. It's too bad that so much isn't viable in the late game without cheese, but it's difficult to balance so many options.
Dungeons: 3/5
Some legacy dungeons are very good, like Stormveil and Leyndell. But many are incredibly linear, like Farum Azula, and devolve into straight lines.
Enemy variety and quality: 3/5
Enemies are recycled ad-nauseum to fill out the large world, and enemies are often poorly balanced and the over-use of delayed attacks where an enemy (misbegotten, I'm looking at you) will hold their weapons up for 6-7 seconds before finally attacking is just comical, the only way to know what to anticipate is to be subjected to it a few times first. Game design in general is very akin to arcades, where you would have to memorize a pattern, not hone your pattern recoginition and reactions, so that you would die as much as possible and put another coin in. More on this on the bosses.
Bosses: 2/5
Most bosses are bad. Margit, Morgot, Mohg, Godrick, Rellana, Messmer are examples of good bosses that are worth your time to learn, but in a roster with 100+ that's a very poor crop. Input reading is rampant, delayed attacks and 10-hit combos that can only be avoided by failing over and over until you memorize them (or looking up guides) feature in every boss, bosses in general do massive damage, especially towards the end of the game, and their health pools balloon. The end result is that you will spend 90% of the boss fights just watching the boss have fun, before you might be able to get a hit or two in, rinse and repeat. A boss like Malenia is actually really well designed besides two moves, but the moves are telegraphed really poorly and can come out at any time, and if the player's positioning isn't optimal when she decides to do it a non-streamer without 1k hours learning the fight will die and have to try again. But she could also just never do those attacks, you could be lucky. Then you'll beat her since the rest of the toolset is very fair and managable. And Malenia is not alone in this. Radagon is not a particularly fun fight, Elden Beast outright sucks, Fire Giant is absolute bottom tier of From's bosses ever, PCR phase 1 is too basic and phase 2 turns your screen into a white smear where you can't see what he does, Malekith phase 2 spends 80% of his time airborne and untouchable, Metyr is garbage tier, bosses are recycled again and again - even remembrance bosses like the Ancient Spirit, Godrick and Astel. In short it's difficult to say much positive about the bosses as a whole. In previous games, like Bloodborne and DS3, bosses were difficult but fair. There were few gotcha mechanics. The developers did not try to waste your time. Here you should probably look up boss guides before you touch the golden walls since that's a much better use of your time. There's gigantic crutches that a player can whip out to avoid all of the above, like strong spirit ashes or the mimic tear, but they trivialize the boss encounters so much that saying that it is intended to fight them that way just can't be true.

Overall, a good game brought down very low by what has been the highlight of From's previous work: The bosses. They are mostly very bad. Considering how much of the game is centred around overcoming bosses and how much time you will spend fighting them, it's difficult to recommend the game on its merits as a whole. Many players will build their character around a fun use of weaponry and spells they discover as they explore, only to find their build useless against a big chunk of bosses, demanding either a respec or the use of spirit ashes.

Most likely, a new player going in with the viewpoint of bosses as necessary speed bumps filled with visual spectacle that should be overcome with spirit ashes, rather than the absolute highlights of their journey, will have a much better time than most.

I could write a long video essay on why I do not think this is a good follow up to the amazing souls trilogy. I'll break it down in a summary with bullet points.

The Good:
-The Story. Its fantastic. Far more fleshed out and more interesting than even an entire three games of Dark Souls story.
-The Views. There are some stunning sights in this game. Seeing Raya Lucaria across the Lakes is astonishing.

The Bad:
-Enemies. It feels basic enemies no longer have any real function in the game anymore except to be run past. They're so copy and pasted without consideration that it feels a chore to kill them. There's also usually no reward for the vast majority of them. A boss will give you more Runes than a thousand standard enemies can give.

-The Open World. Despite the sights being fantastic, the Open World kinda doesn't add anything. There's so many extra dungeons with random, copypasted bosses that the Open World feels more like it took away from development time that could have been put towards certain fight mechanics and enemies.

-Fight Mechanics. Look up Zullie the Witch's video on how the heal punishing is not technically input reading but is just as bad because of how poorly they designed it. Its one of many very disappointing combat decisions in this game that makes it feel much worse than many other Souls games including those that came before. 

Overall, alot of people like this game, I get I'm in the minority. I don't blame others for liking this game but after playing several Souls and Souls-likes, this one so doesn't click with me its made me not want to buy any other Fromsoft productions on release anymore. Now, I'll be looking elsewhere for Souls-like experiences like Lies of P.
