The first maybe 40 or so hours was some of the most fun I've ever had in any video game, and I realize I've been chasing that high ever since, and somehow it only got worse. 

Firstly, the most blatant weakness for me is the storytelling: it's a joke. I can tell there's some interesting lore and characters somewhere in there, but it's presented in a completely incomprehensible manner. 

"You must seek the Elden Ring and become Elden lord!" okay, cool. Why? You are given the vaguest of the vaguest motivations to do *anything* in this game. I meet random characters with absolutely no context or build-up, that apparently I'm supposed to care for.  I have no idea who am I fighting and why. There's barely any RP in this supposed RPG, as joining 'factions' and completing side-quests is completely inconsequential. Not to mention those aforementioned side-quests have incredibly obscure requirements to complete, some feel almost impossible without the wiki.

I understand FromSoft is known for indirect storytelling, but when you want to tell a classic, multilayered fantasy epic, this style simply does not work. It's a completely ridiculous proposition that I'm supposed to rely on vague item descriptions to understand major plot points. Again, this would be fine on some other game that wasn't heavily touted as "having a great narrative written by George RR Martin!!"

Once I realized the story was pretty much non-existent, my open world immersion and suspension of disbelief was irrecoverably shattered. I began to see cool ruins as nothing more than simple repeated 3D assets thrown randomly across the landscape. It's absolutely clear that the devs had no idea what the story behind most places in this game really was, they just expect the players to fill in the blanks. That is not even mentioning the INSANE amount of recycled areas, enemies and bosses in this game. 

Well, the story is kind of bad, at least the game can redeem itself with its gameplay right? Eh, sort of. Like I said in the beginning, I thoroughly enjoyed the early/midgame. The enemy variety was great, and I had tons of fun fighting the early bosses.

However, that's where much of my enjoyment ended. What I started realizing, is that the open world aspect of the game doesn't really work. Here's what happens in Elden Ring all the time: you stumble across a boss or a difficult area which feels way too hard and you think "okay, I'll just explore and come back later." You come back after some hours, realize you've grown vastly more powerful, and the fight becomes an unsatisfying cakewalk. It's such a shame too, because some of the coolest bosses visually were the exact ones I beat in one try. There were some bosses that I  didn't have to engage with, because I could just brute-force it by chugging down health potions. 

The other category of bosses and enemies is those that are wholly anti-fun, attacking so rapidly that you can't play in a proactive manner. There are bosses that legitimately feel like I was playing a turn-based game, since I could get in a hit safely once in a blue moon. There's so many cool skills and playstyles in this game, but it feels like you aren't allowed to experiment with any of them. My complaint has nothing to do with the difficulty, it's about the forced defensive and reactive playstyle.  

That is, if you don't use spirit summons, which are one of the most baffling design choices in this game. The spirits summons turn most fights into a joke, as they draw aggro from enemies and allow you to freely act as you wish. This is clearly meant to be an accessibility mechanic, but it almost feel like the devs designed certain encounters around them. It almost feels like the devs are constantly whispering my ears like "oh geez, this encounter sure is a bit difficult, are you sure you don't want to use the summons bro?"  

This all leads to an extremely unbalanced experience. If I died, it felt I got cheesed out. If I beat a difficult enemy, I felt I cheesed them, as opposed to feeling like a hero who has slain an epic monster. It all feels very...mechanical in nature, which is the absolute killer of my immersion.

This game was incredibly disappointing to play.
For starters, this game is absolutely beautiful. The set pieces, the enemies, the backgrounds, the game is gorgeous to an unbelievable degree. What I find a bit lacking, however, is that a lot of the enemies and levels can feel overdesigned and clunky to a degree where the deeper thoughts of the design are unreadable. While high gothic architecture is always appreciated, it can definitely feel eye glazing at times when the developers obviously didn't care as much about a location as others. The biggest problems I found with this being the numerous catacombs, caves, forts, and mines that are present throughout the game. Although they are at numerous locations, with very distinct landscapes, there's never anything visually interesting about them that wasn't done before. It makes it feel very video-gamey and copy and paste, when I felt that the worldbuilding of this game was incredibly interesting originally.

The difficulty of the game is far higher than previous souls titles, which in itself is not bad. However, there is a clear distinction between boss encounters. There's Margit, who feel very intentionally designed, while remaining difficult in a fair way, maintaining the "I died, what did I do wrong" mindset that many of the previous games seem to hold. Then there's Knight Ordovis, which is a boss encounter stapling two mini-bosses you have already fought, then taking to precautions to make it feel like a well-made duo boss. The first knight will always cover the second's punish windows, and if you're unlucky, they will attack at such intervals where it is impossible to not take damage. The vast majority of this game is a good boss fight, followed by 2 or 3 boring to bad ones (Some of these being repeat bosses that you have already fought plenty of times before). The difficulty, then, feels less like a natural result of the game attempting to challenge you in an interesting way, but devolves into feeling like it is overly punishing and unfair because they didn't take the extra second to ensure the encounter played smoothly. It doesn't help that your rune gain is decreased if you summon additional players, so it makes single bosses crammed into a duo fight feel even worse, since you are discouraged to summon others to help even the fight out (See gargoyles and godskin duo). 

The game itself and its grandness seems impressive at first, since the selling point of over 100 bosses appears incredible, but you soon realize that the game only has over 100 boss encounters because of how much they reuse and repurpose the same enemy over and over again. I personally would have preferred a smaller world, if it meant having less repeat encounters, but the game insists on reusing things that don't make sense. For example, the tree sentinel being a returning encounter makes sense. But having an Ancient Hero of Zamor be in a catacomb makes it feel very repetitive. Why is the boss here? Because you reached the end of the dungeon. Erdtree Avatars guarding the Minor Erdtrees makes sense. Having a named magma wyrm followed by a nameless magma wyrm in another unrelated cave is boring and repetitive. Ancient Dragon Lansseax was extremely cool to find, but now, one of the later game areas throws an identical copy of the fight, thus making it less impactful. The critique here is not that the individual encounter was bad, it's moreso that the individual encounter's overall effect and impact in the game is weakened since now there are just more enemies that act exactly like the boss.

I would suggest playing this game with an open mind and a guide. Playing guideless will cause you to miss many things that the game, and most players, would deem as "important" and "required." Do not be surprised if the open world leads you to having a weapon lacking upgrades for where you're supposed to be. Perhaps, had I started the game with a guide in hand, I would not have struggled as much, but I also deem myself to be a pretty experienced souls-like player and have always enjoyed the problem solving and natural progression of the game. Sadly, it seems that this game tried to be too big, but didn't have enough things to fill the huge map.

This review is NOT how I would rate the game. If it was, I'd give it a 11/10. Great gameplay, story, art, everything! This review is if I would recommend this game to other people who are looking through Elden Ring steam reviews, and If you aren't sure on whether to get this game or not, please listen to what I have to say.

If you are looking for a game with amazing... Everything... get this game. It is allows thousands of different playstyles with thousands of great weapons and armor. Even better with the DLC! HOWEVER... this game does not hold your hand whatsoever, and that is partially why I don't recommend it to newer souls players or people who want to have a laid back time. Before you flame me or tell me I'm wrong, I beat the game with 120 hours with no guide or help whatsoever, so although some things might be wrong, I have a good amount of experience with this game. Regarding this "hand holding" issue, I have two major concerns. 

1. This game is extremely vague with where you are supposed to go.
Sights of Graces are helpful and tell you where to be to some extent, but in some instances, it doesn't help you outright and you are forced to look up where to go or what to do. There is a great example around 1/4-1/3 of the way into the game that I constantly find people looking up where to go.

2. Quest and Items can be extremely hard to find and are locked behind dialogue options, choices, bosses killed etc. Which gets rid of the desire to pursue it in the first place.
This kinda goes with my first reason, but this is such a large issue that it should be mentioned. All of my friends who have played this game struggled to level up or find items, which led them to look up where to go, defeating basically the entire purpose of this game of discovery. I know this game is supposed to be extremely difficult, (I have played other fromsoftware games like sekiro) but for a game as large and expansive as Elden ring, I feel that there should be some sort of way to at least track quests or give you a hint of where to go.

In conclusion, if you skipped everything else, If you are a die hard FromSoftware fan 100% get this game, it is peak. But if you are not familiar with how FromSoftware does it, Elden Ring should not be the first game you play. It overwhelms many beginners and causes them to quit early.

After having played and 100%ed Dark Souls Remastered, instead of going to play Dark Souls 2, I chose to buy Elden Ring at full price while waiting for a discount that never came during this Summer Sale. Regardless, I bought it, played it, and 100%ed it.

At first, the game was amazing. Big map, lots of weapons, and so many things to explore. I wanted to put in as many hours as possible. Up until the end of the early game, I was having a great time. But eventually, the game started feeling very repetitive, and it only became good again at the very end, when I was already bored and underwhelmed.

One of my biggest issues is how often content gets reused. The same bosses appear multiple times under different names, many enemies feel copied from previous Dark Souls games, and the dungeons quickly start blending together. As time went on, it became more and more evident to me that the developers created a huge map without always knowing how to fill it in a meaningful way. At times, I genuinely felt like I was fighting the same boss for the fourth time in a different location.

That isn't to say the world doesn't have great areas. Limgrave is amazing, Caelid is memorable, and several of the endgame locations are excellent. But areas like the Mountaintops of the Giants, Altus Plateau, and much of the underground felt tedious to explore. Also, because the world is so diverse, it doesn't give you one specific vibe. One moment you are in a dark cave and the next in a flower field, it doesn't feel like the world is corrupted and dying, unlike Dark Souls.

The same applies to the bosses. Some are absolutely fantastic. Malenia, Godrick, and the Elden Beast are obvious highlights. The problem is that they're surrounded by so many repeated encounters that they lose some of their impact. The standout bosses are great, but they're buried beneath a mountain of recycled content.

To be fair, the world is packed with locations and things to discover. The map rarely feels empty. My issue is that much of that content follows the same formula: enter a dungeon, loot a corpse, get ambushed by a group of enemies, fight a familiar boss, and move on. After dozens of hours, it became very tedious.

Another problem I had was the difficulty balance. Groups of small enemies were more dangerous than the actual bosses most of the time. Most bosses that were supposed to be major challenges got destroyed within seconds by my max-level Mimic Tear and Bloodhound's Fang. What's funny is that I wasn't even trying to make an overpowered build. A friend simply told me Bloodhound's Fang was a great beginner weapon, and I liked the concept of the Mimic Tear. Apparently that was enough to beat Malenia, supposedly the hardest boss in the game, on my first try, as well as a lot of other bosses. The only challenges I had were Starscourge Radahn, Valiant Gargoyles, Elden Beast and Dragonlord Placidusax.

I never wanted to avoid using the Mimic Tear because it's part of the game. The developers put it there. But that's exactly why I think Spirit Ashes hurt the balance. It feels like they were added to make sure bad players could finish the game without quitting, but in the process they ruined many boss encounters.

Also, fall damage was my true nemesis. I probably died to it at least ten times more than I died to actual enemies, and I'm not exaggerating. It's not funny, it's just annoying.

Beyond gameplay, I think Elden Ring exposes some of FromSoftware's outdated design philosophies. Back in 2011, when the PS3 era was at its peak, those design choices felt innovative because the games achieved so much within relatively small worlds. The map of Dark Souls 1 remains my favorite map in any video game. Not because it's massive or packed with content, but because it's so cleverly interconnected and thoughtfully designed.

The storytelling is another area where I think Dark Souls 1 handled things better, the characters too. I still miss Siegmeyer and Solaire... And you would always come across them because there was only one or two ways to go. Here the NPCs (if you manage to locate them), feel passive-aggressive towards you, and they are not even memorable (bar Alexander). 

DS1's lore complemented the atmosphere and world design, while in Elden Ring it often feels like important story details are hidden inside item descriptions simply for the sake of being hidden. The story itself is actually very interesting, but I had to Google large parts of it to understand what was happening.

Personally, I think the game would have benefited from clearer storytelling: more cutscenes, more meaningful dialogue, more explanations, and NPCs who play a larger role throughout the adventure. I wish they wouldn't just spawn outside the boss gate to help you, but actually followed you or something, or made an actual epic entrance. It feels so outdated and 2010-coded. The storytelling actually got even worse for me with all the similarities between names... Godfrey, Godrick, Godwyn and other examples, some of which are fought more than once under different aliases or forms. This is not lore or worldbuilding, it just makes the player discombobulated, like reading a Dostoyevsky novel.

Furthermore, all questlines and even major bosses feel intentionally hidden to the point where a guide becomes absolutely necessary. To me, that doesn't feel rewarding but pretentious. And yes, I absolutely hate Ubisoft games and dislike Bethesda's too, but this is the other far end of the spectrum, which is almost as bad...

That's what frustrates me most about Elden Ring. Beneath all of my criticisms, it is a game I kinda enjoyed. The gameplay is excellent, many locations are memorable, and several bosses are very well designed too. The story is also surprisingly good once you actually understand it.

But despite all of that, I don't understand why so many people call it the greatest game ever made. It's a good game, but I don't think it deserves that level of praise. If the world had been smaller and more tightly designed, if the storytelling had been more direct, and if the enemy variety had been more original, I honestly think the game would have been far better than what we got.

And yeah I didn't even mention the poor performance, locked 60fps with no DLSS, bad camera, and subpar hitboxes.

Elden Ring is obviously not a bad game. With such an overwhelmingly positive reception, it is clear that it works incredibly well for a lot of people.

But taste is subjective, and after 73 hours and several attempts to get properly into it, I think I can fairly say that this game is not for me.

I enjoyed the Dark Souls games in the past, but at some point I think I grew tired of this style of gameplay. Elden Ring takes that formula and expands it into a huge open world, which is both its greatest strength and one of its biggest weaknesses for me. If you love difficult exploration, environmental storytelling, build experimentation, and discovering things with minimal guidance, this could be an amazing experience. If you enjoy using interactive maps, wikis, and progression guides on a second monitor, it may also fit you well.

For me though, I prefer games where the story, characters, and quests actively pulls me forward. My biggest issue with FromSoftware’s Souls-style games has always been that they do not feel like RPGs in the way I personally enjoy RPGs. There is lore, atmosphere, and worldbuilding, but the storytelling is very indirect and cryptic. If you mainly want a character-driven RPG with story choices and clear quest progression, Elden Ring may disappoint you.

There are absolutely things I like about the game. The atmosphere is excellent, the world feels oppressive, and defeating a difficult boss after learning its patterns can be very satisfying. I also understand why the lack of difficulty settings appeals to many players, because it makes those victories feel more earned.

But many of the same things that make the game rewarding for others make it frustrating for me. The game often feels like it does not respect my time: there is no normal pause function, death can mean losing resources, some runbacks are tedious, and questlines can be so obscure that I often felt pushed toward using a wiki. I do not mind difficulty, but I do mind feeling like I need external guides just to understand how to follow certain quests or avoid missing major content.

The game has lore and atmosphere, but very little of what I personally consider satisfying storytelling: proper dialogue, clear character motivations, narrative agency, and quests that are understandable without a guide.

Ultimately, every time I try to play Elden Ring, I end up feeling bored, frustrated, or like I have to push myself to continue. I can admire parts of it, and I understand why so many people love it, but I do not personally enjoy the overall experience.

If you are an exploration-first or gameplay-first player, this may be one of the best games ever made for you. But if you are like me and prefer structured quests, stronger narrative direction, character-driven storytelling, actual roleplaying and narrative agency, I would advise skipping it.

I know, for many people, there are so many good things about this game and I can see the reasons why its regarded so highly, but maybe souls games just aren't for me so I'm giving this review from that perspective (as someone who wanted to dip my feet into this genre). 

This has nothing to do with the difficulty of the game. I couldn't wait to "git gud" at this game or grind my way to victory if I needed to. I just had a really hard time trying to get over:

The various menus/interfaces are clunky. 

The controls: The controls feel really bad to me. I get you don't dodge until you release the button and all that stuff but just mechanically it feels clunky to me. I much prefer the layouts and more responsive action of fighting Valkyries in God of War or Stellar Blade. I first tried with KB+M and it felt clunky trying to dodge, parry, etc. People told me to try a controller so I grabbed a PS Dual Sense and it's clunky to use potions etc especially in the heat of battle. With KB+M and Controller I'm struggling to control the camera and actually see what I'm fighting properly. 

The controls again: How are there no native PS glyphs for this game? Tell me to press triangle instead of Y. Yes, I can get over it but this is basic requirement of a game this big. 

The graphics: Nearly everyone seems to say this game has amazing graphics. I'll admit the art direction is great, but graphically this game does not look great. Yes, graphics aren't everything but I expect better graphical fidelity than this. When I bumped up things to 4k it started to look decent (but like on par with Tainted Grail or some other AA game). Never was I ever thinking "woah this is impressive graphically". It messed with my immersion. Too much fog. Low textures all over the place. When you kill enemies they just sort of ethereally fade away in an uninteresting way. I tried turning on HDR and after a few computer restarts it was finally working and that did help, but why does this game have so many technical problems still? 

I've been on plenty of corpse runs in various MMOs over the years. This is a boring/time-wasting mechanic for me in a single player game at this point. 

Lore/Atmosphere/Exploration/Mystery: This was very good/interesting. I just couldn't get over the clunky controls, bad camera, and lackluster graphics.

TLDR: This game is probably great for lots of people, but if you care about tight controls and good graphics this might not be it.

Now that I finally got to really playing through Elden Ring, I must sadly say that my initial opinion did not change. I know it is a hot take and contrary to the overall opinion, but this has to be the worst FromSoft game I've played (granted I've never played Bloodborne or any of the Armored Core games so those are out of the count). For me, soulslikes are closer to dungeon crawlers than the anime boss rush that they've become. That's why I think that even though Dark Souls 3 is my favorite overall, none of the games have come close to the feeling of DS1.

While the base combat still feels good and far more fluent than any Dark Souls has ever done, the issue is that they've gone head first into the idea that you wait for a combo, then hit once or twice, rinse and repeat. To me, that has become a tedious way to fight, considering how well games like Monster Hunter have perfected the idea that you can take control of the fight and play more aggressive. Yeah, I know that you can do that in most soulslikes too but the difference is that even when I've learned a boss so well that I know almost all the spots, it never feels like I am in control. The only FromSoft game that made me feel like that is Sekiro. The reason this wasn't an issue in DS1 for example is because bosses actually died after a reasonable amount of hits.

And that's the key point, these games focus too much on bosses and with Elden Ring, the idea of visual clutter to make things look cool instead of engaging to fight has been overutilized. There is so many flashy moves that are 100% dodged only with iframes, which to me signals incredibly lazy boss design. When I practically have to analyze the moves like I go through some SDVX charts, I just feel like rather focusing on a game where studying things on paper is actually fun. In my entire playthrough, the only boss I actually felt was fun and I'd like to go through again was Placidusax. Maybe Maliketh too, if we exclude the first phase. Not a huge fan of it but that's mostly just because I suck at it. Radahn was nice as a concept with all the summons and it being a sort of a brawl but the fight itself was pretty meh. Other than that, the bosses were pretty lame.

As for story, I can't help but feel like they just took the original story of Dark Souls, gave it to Martin and told him to just reimagine it with them and then they called it a day. This is almost a carbon-copy clone. And with most NPC's dying and that being a trend of FromSoft's games, I feel far more surprised when someone lives but I find it hard to care for the questlines when they're just "go talk to someone, quit to menu or sit at site of grace, go talk to them again + maybe a summon/invade at the end." It just feels lazy that this formula is still repeated for almost every quest, even after all these years. FromSoft should really come up with something new.

The world design was great though. Places like Stormveil and Leyndell felt really fun to explore. But the open areas and the open world was bad. For me it just doesn't work in a soulslike setting. It is too open and when everything respawns, there's no permanent impact on your actions, which to me is a key point of open world games. Plus when the entire world is practically dead and almost everyone is hostile, I feel like the sense of exploration is pretty watered down.

It just doesn't feel like there's really a need for the open world setup, especially when you realize how linear the game actually is. It's not like you can approach Leyndell from several areas, since the map is extremely linear and there are places blocking your progress further. It is a good thing in this game but makes the open world feel pointless. I feel like it only exists for the same reason that Monster Hunter Wilds is "open world", which is just to fill a marketing tickbox because open world games are trending. You need to sell the concept of the game being massive, not so much the actual amount of unique content being there, so what's an easier way to do that than making your game open world.

All that being said, it is not necessarily a bad game. I just think that it is mediocre when compared to FromSoft's previous products. I started with DS2 then DS3 > DS1 > Sekiro > Nightreign > Elden Ring and before playing Elden Ring, I considered DS2 the worst FromSoft game, which is why I find it hard to believe it would be just nostalgia talking.

Before getting into what I don't like about this game, I will say a few positive things. The game looks beautiful and runs pretty well all things considered. The voice acting, characters, verity of enemies, locations, etc... are also all well done, and even though I don't like open world games because they are usually slop filled with nothing, Elden Ring somehow manages to make it feel more alive and actually have things to discover and do. Thats about all the compliments I can give it though. 

For the things I don't like, for starters, its a painfully easy game. I have no idea how people are saying its the hardest souls like game or harder than Sekiro, both I hear quite a bit in the spaces I am in online or the videos I watch. Granted I have not yet finished the game yet, I cannot bring myself to do so, it feels like im forcing myself to play this game. But I still do have (I think) enough playtime to form some sort of opinion based on what I have played. From the bosses and enemies I have had to fight, none of them were difficult, and most only took 1-2 tries. I know there are probably harder enemies and bosses in the rest of the base game, and DLC (from what ive heard) but thats not the main problem I have with this game. I do plan on eventually completing the game and DLC, but until I do that my review will stay as is and I doubt it will change. 

The main issue I have with this game is that for most of my time playing its straight up riding on horseback going from one castle or cave to the next while having to fight pathetically easy ass enemies in between. At first it was really cool riding a horse and exploring the world, but eventually it got boring and tedious. I know one of my compliments was that there were things to discover and explore, and that is true, once you found a new castle or cave or whatever to get into THAT was fun, but for the other majority of the game, you are just left riding on a horse until you get to those fun parts, and even then they don't last very long sadly. Maybe I just prefer the more "linear" (I don't think Dark Souls 1 is linear) Dark Souls games, but for most of the time, it never felt dull, repetitive, or felt like I was simply waiting for there to be a fun moment like I do with this game. I get its an open world game, but its still. The reason I don't have this issue with RDR or RDR2 is because the combat while on your horse in those games is actually fun, and there's more you can do with your companion, even having a bonding level with the horse and various other mechanics. I think they dropped the ball not making the 1 animal your around for 99% of the game have more mechanics than just feeding them when they have low HP. 

Another thing is that at least for me there was almost nothing rememberable about this game compared to the other ones. I can think of several moments, enemies, characters, etc... from the other souls games, sekiro, bloodborne, that have stuck with me off the top of my head. The only cool thing I can remember is when you are about to fight Radahn you can see other characters in the game at the Castle ready to be summoned and fight alongside you. As far as im aware its the first time you could summon this many people and it felt very cinematic and cool. Again, something really cool that happens because its a main boss / castle. Another L for the rest of the open world area. I just find it extremely funny that even though its an open world game, the best parts is when you aren't in the open world, like in a castle, cave, etc... 

I think this game would have benefited from being not open world, or at the very least having a smaller world. Again, I do plan to finish this game eventually, and change my review accordingly, but until then all I can say is that as a game itself it is fun somewhat, but compared to the other Souls games or From Soft games, its the weakest one. 

I do expect alot of criticism / hate and I suppose theres nothing I can do about that, but these are just my opinions and if you enjoyed the game I'm happy that you did.

Elden Ring was a disappointment for me because it tries to combine an open world with the soulslike formula, yet never fully excels at either.

As a soulslike, it relies too heavily on systems and ideas that FromSoftware has been using since Dark Souls 1. After dozens of hours, I often felt like I was playing another variation of familiar mechanics rather than a true evolution of the genre. The combat lacks enough fresh ideas to justify the massive time investment the game demands.

As an open-world game, it also falls short of the best examples of the genre. The world is huge, but much of the content feels repetitive. Similar enemies, repeated dungeon layouts, recycled bosses, and familiar activities create the impression that quantity often takes priority over quality. Instead of being excited to explore, I frequently felt like I was simply crossing another section of the map to find a slightly different version of something I had already seen before.

My biggest issue is that the combination of an open world and a soulslike structure does not work particularly well. What I love most about soulslike games is focused level design, interconnected areas, meaningful shortcuts, and a strong sense of progression through carefully crafted environments. Elden Ring sacrifices much of that focus in favor of scale, and the result is a game that often feels diluted compared to the tighter experiences that came before it.

I cannot say that Elden Ring is a bad game. Its production values, scope, and ambition are impressive. However, as a long-time soulslike fan, it failed to deliver what I personally look for in the genre. It did not meet my standards as a soulslike, and it did not meet my standards as an open-world RPG either.

For that reason, I would not recommend it to players who prefer more focused and replayable experiences such as Bloodborne, Mortal Shell, or Lies of P.

A beautiful, open-world Souls Like that most will probably enjoy, especially if they are new to the genre. Technically it's the entry with the most new gameplay mechanics and stunning graphics as well as amount of bosses and areas to explore/clear out, however, aside from that it doesn't have much else better from previous titles.

I played through DS2 and all the DLCs as well as NG+, it's my only experience with the series but it was a really good one. So when I entered the world of Elden Ring I had similar expectations of the bosses and enemies and general ideea of exploration, except they couldn't be applied. ER takes such a inbetween position of gameplay that it utterly annoys me how disrespectful it is to the player, it tries to stay on two stools, one which is Dark Soul's movement/dodge based wait out with punishment to the boss after their combo, and to the Sekiro's/Bloodborne aggressiveness of the enemies/the player...? 

Most notably the only real mobility change the player gets in combat is jumping, which would have been a nice addition if it wasn't for how ridiculously inertialess it feels. Finding the actual gap where you can attack the enemies and bosses freely or at least even just trade with them - is extremely tiring. The recovery time for the combo's are so short your gameplay will be 95% of the time just seeing someone's body and a bunch of metal sounds and bright flashes while constantly spamming dodge. Dark Souls at least had you use your actual positioning/walking/running and not just dodge rolling at the correct time so you had  a more balanced type of gameplay between the boss and yourself.

Horseback fighting is also extremely clunky and unsatisfying, most enemies that were designed around it are really not entertaining to fight against because they are so much easier when using the horse. It should have stayed as a mode of transportation since the springstream mechanic is quite fun and the world is already pretty big. To continue - the world being big doesnt necessarily mean it's shallow as a puddle, but I would have definetely preffered if they condensed the world by 2x and not made the curious player feel like they waste time 90% of the time. Dark Souls while linear would always reward curious players, so when i came over to ER and started looking over each nook and cranny only to get useless crafting materials - well it's just discouraging and feels like the developer trying to take out as much time out of you as possible.

Ashes of War are perhaps the only good mechanic that came out of this entry and even then from the little use that I did have with them, it seems most are extremely niche and likely to never be used in favor of other objectively better ones leaving 90% of them to never be used and be clutter. Take this with a grain of salt as I didn't use them all that much.

Overall, while the game is good and many new players will enjoy it - I wouldn't buy it if you are self respecting Dark Souls fan. The game caters rather hardly to the hardcore players and I say this as a DS2 fan which had the same allegations thrown against it. Elden Ring is through and through made to break your patience and test just how much are you ready to adapt to it's bosses and new mechanics constantly. God forbid you are a UGS user in this game, good-fucking-luck, you will need it.

First off, Elden Ring is not a bad game. The boss fights, visuals and world building are all cool, and while I finished the game and then some, its just... a drag.

What is not fun, is the absurd scale of the game combined with a complete lack of non-filler content. Useless crafting materials, random ashes (another whole topic on its own) and grave glovewort being treated like "rewards" for exploring far off corners of the world, same one enemies in every dungeon, and half of the boss fights being "what if we did it again... but now there's two of them". Same one tree sentinel. Same one tree spirit.

With enemies scattered all over with nothing to gain from killing them, the game heavily encourages you to not fight, and just explore in the open world. What's that? John Knight patroling a random road drops a unique item, but you ignored him as he's literally a generic enemy found all over elsewhere? Oh well, thats unfortunate. Better luck next time. 

Souls games inherently will never be possible to mostly complete on a first run without some sort of guide, and quest chains even more so as they're intended to be done over multiple playthroughs, but the insane amount of NOTHING in this game that is just recycled over and over and over that you CANNOT skip without a guide because guess what, that one dungeon you chose to skip, missed or forgot was the one dungeon that didnt just have useless ashes in them. That one hill over there might have a key item for your build or quest chain, so you better go explore it thoroughly, but wait... there was nothing. Again.

As I started with, the game isnt bad. The game is mostly enjoyable. It has some crazy fights, its weapons and various forms of incantations/sorceries are very cool, but there's just too much in this game that has no place, or is recycled adding nothing but filler, for me to reccomend it before literally any other fromsoft souls game. If part of the enjoyment in these games for you is trying to explore and find as much as possible without help, the world is filled with far too much nothing, but hey, at least it will look pretty and the main boss fights will be cool.

I was excited to try this game because of the 10/10 reviews and George RR Martin's involvement. But sadly the world just feels so...empty and forlorn. I get that its supposed to be post apocalyptic dark fantasy, but you'd think there would be at least be some kind of narrative and more than a handful of NPCs that only babble nonsense. 

The game is absolutely mind-blowing in its visuals. Even in the spell animations. They're some of the best I've ever seen, in fact. The world is gorgeous and the art direction team deserves some heavy praise. But this illusion of immersion shatters the moment you realize there isn't much to do while exploring that beautiful world aside from randomly killing things to grind XP. 

It actually baffled me quite a bit. I'm not the biggest fan of Game of Thrones, but Martin obviously knows how to write fantasy lore. But I didn't see any of that in my nearly 10 hours of play. I was lost and confused and wondering what my motivation was, what I was supposed to do and why I should care about this world. 

So I did some research, and it turns out that he didn't write any dialogue or narrative for the actual game, but just the lore that happened 5,000 years before the game started, which the player has no way of accessing. I don't really see the point in this. If they were going to hire someone to create an elaborate fantasy world, why didn't we get to play in that world, instead wandering around randomly fighting stuff in an empty world of nothing?

Perhaps the gameplay could have supported the experience, but I found it quite lacking in that department as well. I elected to play a mage, and the only useful spell I could find was the generic magic missile starting spell. There were others, but the selection was very limited, I had to grind runes to get them, and even then I could only access them after fighting a secret boss that could only find by looking it up on a wiki. (Seriously, there was no clue about this in the actual game itself.) After going to all this trouble, what did I get? A handful of useless garbage spells that were worse than what I started with. 

So yeah, my impression of this game is probably tainted by the poor implementation of magic. But I don't think I would have enjoyed playing a martial-type character either. The melee combat is slow and sluggish. It doesn't feel quick and responsive at all, more like moving through a layer of mud, and evasion is awkward. 

Character progression is likewise pretty lackluster. All you get on level up is 1 point of stat assignment that barely changes your numbers. No feats, skill trees, talent points, anything like that. It didn't feel like I was making a build or learning new abilities that changed how I played, more like just grinding to make numbers go up. 

All of this only got worse when I ran into the first major boss. I wasn't strong enough to beat him despite being almost level 30. I'm not sure how much more I would have had to grind to get past it, but I was already bored by that point. 

The kicker, though, was when the game randomly deleted all my save files. I might have been halfway tempted to keep going, but not if I have to start over now on top of all of that. 

I honestly don't understand the positive reviews for this game. Even 15 year old games full of jank like Oblivion and Morrowind have better worlds, more complex magic systems, and are more creative than this.

I was pressured into playing this by many people. I loved it for the first 12 hours, then I tolerated it for the other 12 I put into it, trying to be open-minded about playing an official soulslite for the first time even when I was starting to realize it wasn't for me. I was holding off on posting this review as I KNOW there will be fans out there prepared to counter any points I could make before I'm actually understood. Regardless of the backlash I'm sure I'll face for daring to downvote Elden Ring, I feel like there are multiple elephants in the room around this game that are still critical to one's enjoyment of it. If you like Elden Ring / FromSoft games, I don't intend on changing your opinion, I just ask that you respect mine.

I'll get the positives out of the way first:

-The exploration is gorgeous, the map is big and adversity is around every corner; it reminds me of the original Legend of Zelda, where you (mostly) have access to everything the game has to offer from the beginning and it entirely lets you dictate the pacing of it. Combat is accessible, you don't need to be good at mashing buttons or remember complex combos to learn this game's controls; it's really easy to pick up where you left off.

Now for all of the negatives:
-Enemy placement and design in Elden Ring consistently resorts to what would be considered cheap in any other game; enemies killing you from around corners / off-screen, inflated damage and health bars, unexplained debuffs, mechanics and attack patterns that're literally impossible for even the top 1% of eSports players to react to.
-The open-world and the stealth mechanics are a necessary waste of time to eventually overcome boss battles. Some bosses are literally impossible unless you grind for stats in a game about hacking-and-slashing.
-The 60fps lock is a design choice to prevent you from ever having the ability to react to particular fatal hits from bosses. It is not even theoretically possible for a fresh player to complete this game without some kind of memory or knowledge of the bosses patterns.
-Dying boots you to a really long loading screen, even on a gen 4 SSD, that reloads every enemy back into the map. I'm sitting on the loading screen of this game about as often as I am actually playing the game and then wasting further time, fighting the same enemies again, to get back to where I was before.
-Class variety can change your experience of the game from a brutally difficult experience trying to fight with sticks and stones to a breeze with purely ranged magic attacks that bosses are completely helpless to.
-The general design of this game is very hostile and manipulative. Playing Elden Ring is like being a young person trying to survive in America; you need experience you can't get and you need money / runes you can't earn; choosing the wrong career path / class will ruin your life / game. When you beat a boss, you can't tell if it's because you actually mastered it's pattern or if you just didn't die that time. You don't get to fight all of them again to know for sure, at least not within the same save file. A game that provides enough content as-is doesn't need all of this fluff to justify it's usually $60 price tag; playing Elden Ring became a chore, whether you repeatedly fight the same boss or you spend hours farming for runes you could very easily lose.

I'm going to list some games that Elden Ring reminds me of and why I like them over this:

Castlevania (1 and 3 on the NES) Fights are hard, but not drawn-out. You don't need a memory of patterns / where good stuff is to progress, but they do help. it's all entirely possible with what your character starts out with. No save points, but it's quick to get back to where you were before you had to shut off the game.

Zelda BOTW: The exploration, side-quests and puzzles are guaranteed to help you progress through the game even if they're not what you primarily play BOTW for. You don't bend over backwards for a weapon / move that's weaker than what you already have and enemy variety is much more interesting than "hehe bird with a barrel haha look at this loading screen some more." Upgrading your character and farming Rupies isn't contingent on you keeping your character alive, you're permitted to make mistakes while you're still learning the game.

DOOM (2016, Eternal and TDA): Brutal difficulty you can always dial back or shut-off and come back to as you please. No bloated leveling system or big world designed to waste your time, progression is consistent; if you get past a hard part, you have confidence that you could pull it off again. The game doesn't let you just barely survive; enemies you fight come back and are compounded by newer enemies and patterns, so progression is made clear to you through demonstration, even if it's harder that way. Boss fights are not drawn out to the point where you die because of human error, but they're challenging enough to where you still have to learn them.

If all I have to do is git gud to enjoy any video game, then what responsibility do developers have in designing it? Why is $60 no longer a good enough accommodation to know you'll enjoy the game? If I just want to understand the world of Elden Ring and experience the story, if I just wanna see what the other 200+ bosses look like, why do I have to commit a bunch of time into the ones I'll see only once, maybe twice?

Why am I not allowed to pause in a singleplayer game? Yet another hostile design choice against those who may not have the option to play the game uninterrupted. I don't want every game I play to be super difficult and demand more out of me than my own work does; If you're a master Elden Ring player, yeah this game brings you clout, but it brings you clout by making others regret buying something that apparently wasn't for them

186 hours played.

And I still don't understand why people talk about this game like it reinvented the wheel.

The exploration is fine. The map is huge, there's plenty to find, and for a while it does a good job of keeping your curiosity alive. But it's nowhere near the life-changing masterpiece the internet keeps insisting it is.

My problem has always been the bosses.

Not because they're difficult.

Because they're tedious.

I have no interest in spending hours memorizing attack patterns. I have no interest in fighting the same boss twenty times. I have no interest in chipping away at a ridiculous health bar while my mistakes are punished far more severely than theirs.

Every time I reached a boss, it felt like the game was putting a wall between what I wanted to do and what FromSoftware wanted me to do.

I wanted to keep exploring.

The game wanted to test me.

This game is nothing but hard. Yes that's a skill issue, HOWEVER that's not the complaint. A stupidly hard game can be fun. Elden Ring is not.

Even if you like vague storytelling, it doesn't change the fact that it's told in a really boring way. Cutscenes made from a few still images with voiceover, clicking a button at a specific site of grace for 2 minutes of Monologue (and yes it's ALWAYS Monologue, because the MC has either pulled the Kimiko move or forgotten how to talk, leaving you with only an occasional grunt or scream of pain).

So yeah, the story sucks, the storytelling sucks as well. Lets move on to the world you move around in.
It feels empty and dead even though there are enemies everywhere. These enemies however are completely silent, stand around until they die of dehydration or walk their set path. Over and over and over... Which wouldn't be so bad if there were other things that made the world interesting. So let's see... There are a few NPCs, that are ALL COMPLETELY stationary (unless you try to kill them, then they remember they have arms and legs) and remain - just like the enemies - completely silent. They don't react to you, they don't talk to you unless you talk to them first and when they talk, they all sound the same. Boring monotone voices, that make listening to these NPCs more of a chore than an enjoyable part of the game.

With a boring story, a dead world and badly designed interactions there is progression.
You basically follow the "guidance of grace", which is just a beam of light pointing towards the next lost grace. You can do some side bosses, which mostly awards you with mid items. You can also do quests. Which brings me to the part i hate most about Elden Ring
There is NO WAY to keep track of progression. There is NOTHING that help you find your next point of interest. If you get a "quest" from an NPC, you gotta do some sometimes really complicated stuff (or find some item in some cave after killing some random boss) which is explained so vaguely or not at all by whoever you talk to, that even on your first playthrough you kind of NEED guides to help you understand what you gotta do. And if you take a longer break from the game GOOD LUCK finding out what quest you were on, what you had to do next and so on. The game provides ZERO Info which makes progression a tedious act of walking and scouring every part of the map just so you could complete one assignment. And after you do that you don't get your reward, because the NPC has moved to a completely arbitrary spot on the Map, which means you gotta go look for them. Again. No indicators, no Info on anything. I'm not asking for a Quest Marker that tells you where to go at all times, but at least SOME Info would be nice. I wanna do my quest, win hard fights against many enemies or a strong boss, not backtrack to every part of the map looking for a chest i might have missed or an NPC that moved. I also don't wanna play a game that needs guides for every Interaction you have. I wanna figure stuff out myself, but doing so shouldn't involve 16 hours of walking around playing hide and seek.

Last thing I wanna mention is the Co-op. Calling it that is kind of an Insult to every other Co-op system out there. The so called "Co-op" let's you call your buddy into your world, where you fight together, get invaded constantly. You can't turn these Invasions off. Sometimes you get lucky and your invaders aren't too strong. But usually you get hardsweats, that kill you and you friend in a few hits so you gotta re-summon them. Your buddy is extremely weakened while fighting alongside you, and if they die, they return to their own world, meaning you gotta call them again. If you beat a boss, they auto-leave, so you gotta call them again. There is no cross progression, meaning if you beat the boss in your own world, you gotta do the same shit in your buddies world. I genuinely only enjoy this game when I'm playing with friends, which needs a mod, because the base-game Co-op is a mix of bad ideas and worse concepts.

First of all: I bought ELDEN RING expecting another great Dark Souls-title or successor. I was disappointed. That is not to say ELDEN RING is an objectively bad game - it just didn't click for me, coming from the Dark Souls-series.

It really pains me to give a thumbs down for ELDEN RING. I really wanted to like this game, so at first I tried it alone, but found myself aimlessly wandering around, wondering: "Where do I go?" - "What do I do?" - "Why is what and where is who?" and so on.

Then I played together with my girlfriend so we could at least experience the chaos and wonder together... But I was constantly checking the wiki, looking at game-progression-routes, stumbled into dead-ends. That took the fun away quick - having a to look at another screen, just to find out, you've skipped or passed an important part of the map or must do this and that before doing that and this.

Where Dark Souls succeeded in taking me into its world by doing exactly that - developing lore by showing, not telling - ELDEN RING just falls short for me with its ambitious, yet chaotic and not well thought-out attempt to lead and pace you.

Where Dark Souls left you wondering, who the NPCs were, but still had a game-route for you, that you could follow even withput completing any NPC-quests - ELDEN RING throws you into this world, gives you NPCs, that are cryptic as always, which is fine for Dark Souls, but are your (only) way to get information where to go and what to do.

Where Dark Souls paced you by offering you 2, 3 or maybe even 4 paths, that you could, based on skill/items/knowledge/... , take - ELDEN RING just throws this massive open world at you, that you can wander around.

Where Dark Souls Bosses were built up, felt unique and rewarding to beat, so you could continue the path - ELDEN RING Bosses were sometimes like "Oh... Apparently I'm in a Boss-Fight now...". Some Bosses seemed all too similar and I had the feeling they locked onto you, no matter their orientation and it was all just a "Dodge at the perfect time, then attack - rinse and repeat"-game. Which Dark Souls kinda is, but it just felt too repetitive and non-rewarding.

Where Dark Souls gave you weapons, armor, spells and many more items to explore and try out - ELDEN RING gave us 3 maybe 4 armors after hours and hours of playing.

For some this "open-world Breath of the WIld-inspired hype-train" might be something to enjoy - For me it was (just as Zelda) trying to be too much: An RPG, an Open-World-Game, a Dark-Souls-Game and so much more. But in trying to be everything (or at least more than before) it fell short and became nothing for me.

Timings are carefully crafted so, that you often cannot heal in "attack" window and one mistimed roll leads to eating all the combo (almost all attacks stagger character). I played until completion to leave this review, finishing through spite rather than enjoyment. My playthrough was late and apart from knowing about Ranni and Rykard through memes, I went in completely blind as a big Dark Souls 1 and 2 fan. The game wasn't what I expected and for the first few days of playing, I went where I thought I was supposed to go and just hit wall after wall after wall. Whether through the luck of it being open world, but I roamed around until going north and just felt powerless against everything. I'd tough it out against what I thought were boss looking enemies in the overworld only for them to not drop anything after trying to kill them for an hour. Or randomly get ambushed by a pack of something, which I learned is the games favourite thing to do. It took a long time to realize enemies were meant to be avoided unless progression was blocked.

My intent to not look anything up and play a dex build was tossed when I genuinely felt like stopping, because I was endlessly frustrated at nothing being consistent and the general gameplay. Enemy poise and my ability to parry was completely up in the air, I'd break poise against soldiers in armour but an emaciated ghoul with a knife could have super armour in or outside attack animations. Enemies I thought I could parry, were unparriable so I'd end up dying trying to get a pattern down and thinking I was failing. Even when successful, it was just too risky for the fact that from start to finish the game is a one-two hit kill fest if you're not specifically built for each threat, which I wasn't. This is made even worse from the fact that so many enemies in the game have multiple moves with 3-8 hit strings, whether a knight or some sort of boss. It felt so oppressively designed, not in a fun to overcome but sheer irritation to perfect dodging one attack only to be hit by a follow up attack designed to hit if you did. Then if you do manage to avoid getting hit, the enemy immediate acts again with no delay, no breathing room whatsoever. Shield the attacks instead, you get staggered and killed first combo.

This is why despite really liking all the different weapon arts and weapons themselves, there was little point. Mobs tended to die easily to anything yet anything a stage higher only let you hit once between combos or leaping away to do a ranged attack or summoning 8 of its mates to swarm you to death. Unless you use a Greatsword, then a few more enemies than normal can be staggered easily. I assume that's why I saw to many shadows use them and why enemies with them were so strong. I grew to hate the open world and the endless one note ambushes and beginners traps that were no different to each other just so frequent you got numb to it. Spirit Ashes being a requirement annoyed me at the start because I wanted to have that 1 on 1 challenge. Then they annoyed me even more when it regularly became a 2v2 race to try and kill one enemy before the spirit was killed. I can't honestly tell you a boss I liked fighting, for the first half of the game as a dual thrust wielding/twinblade dex build, to the Dark Moon Greatsword INT build I switched to at the end because I couldn't deal damage anymore. I didn't feel like I overcame a challenge, only kept trying till I got a pattern each time that let me succeed. I only stuck it through to the end because I paid for this and wanted to see Ranni's ending for myself. I assumed this game would be like Dark Souls, slow, consistent and methodical. Complete unfairness would be kept minimal and bosses were fair but challenging once you understood. Exploration would be rewarded, not met with 1000 ambushes to a crafting item. No, it's an action game with an open world and no leniency. I felt like I was in Devil May Cry but I wasn't Dante, I was the random mob he styled on. If you like that sort of thing, good for you. This isn't the souls gameplay I was looking for.

First of all, I did not like the game, I loved it!

I am writing this review as someone who has played Skyrim for quite a long time. I will also compare the game to Skyrim from time to time. Of course, they are structurally very different games, but in terms of open-world exploration, atmosphere, and the feeling of making the player wander around the map with curiosity, I could not help but compare it to Skyrim.

I finished the game without using Mimic even once, relying completely on my own hands, reflexes, learning process, and gameplay. This made me feel the difficulty of the game in a more naked way. My comments about the boss loop, build progression, and the challenging sides of the game mostly come from this experience.

Elden Ring is truly a great game. But it is NOT FOR EVERYONE! This needs to be understood.


MY POSITIVE THOUGHTS

I do not want to go on and on about the positive sides everyone keeps repeating, but to put it briefly: the open-world design, graphics, sense of exploration, music, and atmosphere are top-tier. Very few games can compete with Skyrim. In my eyes, Elden Ring is one of them.


-The boss loop is incredibly satisfying.

Dying to bosses, understanding their moves, reading when they are going to attack, learning to react better, looking for a talisman suitable for the damage they deal, coming back a little stronger, and finally beating that boss that once seemed impossible… It is an incredibly satisfying loop. The game is really strong in this regard.


-The map constantly keeps your sense of curiosity alive.

The exploration side works just as well. You see a ruined structure ahead and think, “I wonder what is there?” You go and check it out. Suddenly, an NPC there gives you a critical quest, or you open up an area you never expected. In this sense, the game flows like butter. There is something in almost every corner of the map that makes you curious.



MY NEGATIVE / INFURIATING THOUGHTS


-The interface is really clunky.

Despite loving the game this much, parts need improvement and seriously drove me crazy.

Skyrim had a similar problem, too, but at least it could be made great with mods. Elden Ring needs improvement in terms of interface, and it definitely does not feel like a game meant to be played with a keyboard and mouse.

Item switching is torture. Pressing "I" does not open the inventory. You must press Esc, then go into Equipment, and change things from there. You cannot change items from the Inventory section. You have to scroll in the equipment menu, find the new item you dropped, and only then compare its stats.

Not being able to set favorite weapons is another problem. When you want to switch a weapon, you have to search through all your weapons.

Another missing feature is a list of bosses you have not killed yet. In a game this huge, with so many optional bosses and hidden areas, not having a checklist feels like a big omission.

Esc not working properly is another problem. It does not take you back in many places. Even after 60 hours, I noticed myself instinctively spamming Esc, which does nothing. You have to use E and Backspace. Getting used to this is really hard. At some point, it feels like you are not fighting the game’s difficulty, but the stubbornness of the interface.


-There is build variety, but in practice some weapons stand out too much.

When it comes to build variety, there is definitely variety in the game. In fact, on paper it offers quite a wide build space. But in my experience, this variety does not fully feel noticeable until you reach the later parts of the game.

Especially weapons like Bloodhound’s Fang feel so efficient that the player naturally stays with the same weapon for a long time. It is also possible to sense a similar tendency from the ghost-like silhouettes of other players around me. Of course, there are different weapons, different build paths, and different playstyles, but in practice some weapons feel so strong and useful that at some point you start thinking, “Why would I even drop this?”


-The armor system and variety did not satisfy me much.

Armors cannot be upgraded, and most of them feel very close to each other. Some armors have meh-level differences in poise, weight, resistance, and appearance, but for someone expecting a clear Skyrim-style armor progression or feeling of getting stronger, the system is not satisfying.

There is no clear sense of difference at the level I expected between the armor I had at the start of the game and one of the heaviest armor sets I wore at the end. I can even say that if you finish the game with your starting armor, you do not really feel a serious difference.

In Skyrim, this was very different. There were many different levels of weapons and armor, you could make different combinations with the enchantment system, and you could upgrade sets. Whether you were a mage or a warrior, whatever job you played, there was a feeling of almost endless combinations. Elden Ring has build variety, I do not deny that, but especially the armor system does not give the same progression satisfaction.


-No offense, but: THERE IS NO QUEST MARKER!

The thing I generally dislike in Souls games is here as well. There is no quest marker. This looks like a very cool feature and is defended like crazy, but at some points you get stuck and then have to Alt+Tab to check documentation, wiki, videos, etc. Unless you are part of the top 1% elite gamer crowd, of course.

In my eyes, this is a big immersion killer. Hold my hand a little, man. In Skyrim, there is even a special skill just to show the direction of the active quest. In Elden Ring, following the progression of some quests without looking at an outside source is seriously difficult.

I think the quest marker issue should be left completely to the player. Put the markers in, make them off by default. Let us see what percentage of players will go and manually activate them. Let us choose whether to turn them on or off. There is no need to act cool.


-The input reading issue is not fair at all in my opinion.

Another serious criticism I have is the input reading issue in the game. I definitely think input reading is happening, and I do not find this ethical from a game design standpoint. Some enemies and bosses react early depending on which key you are spamming on the keyboard. There are way too many moments where it feels like bosses are directly reading your input and acting accordingly.

You use a flask, an attack comes instantly. You cast a spell, and you get punished before the animation even properly starts. Of course, I have no objection to the game being hard. In fact, I respect this difficulty. But in my opinion, there is a serious difference between difficulty and reading the player’s input to punish them.

The first gives a feeling of learning and mastery, while the second sometimes creates the feeling that the game is straight-up cheating. Challenging the player is one thing. Reacting reflexively according to the button the player presses is another.


-Some normal mobs feel way stronger than they should.

The damage balance of normal enemies is also exaggerated in some places. I am not saying bosses should hit harder or be turned into damage sponges. The problem is that some regular mobs feel way too strong for what they are.

A random bird, dog, or normal enemy on the map can sometimes tear you apart in two hits, even when you have solid armor, talismans, and buffs. The infamous rune farm bird is a good example of this kind of absurd scaling. These are supposed to be regular enemies, but some of them end up feeling more threatening than they reasonably should.

This does not make the game feel more balanced or more fair. It just makes certain mobs feel overtuned.


-So

Elden Ring is special to me. Its flaws annoyed me, and I still disagree with some choices, but its exploration, boss loop, atmosphere, and world are unforgettable. Not for everyone, but an amazing game.

Would prefer if I could give this a "meh", but there are so many frustrations honestly so far. I'll possibly update once finishing, but wanted to produce some thoughts on the game at this point in my playthrough.

I'm going to start with just some things about Elden Ring, and then some issues with FromSoftware in general.

I'd not played a mage/sorcerer in any previous Souls games, so wanted to try it here, and basically the literal level 1 spell you start with is just better than basically 99% of anything you'll encounter in the game. Who tf designed that? It's ludicrously bad. You'd think "oh cool, I just spent 5-10k on this new spell, surely it must be better than the literal starter spell!" Yeah, unfortunately you'd be wrong about that.

This game feels very empty a lot of the time. Most of the game is just running around through fields, trying to guess at where the game wants you to go. 
Finding the areas suitable for your level is also pretty bad, as you can literally walk for 10 seconds out of somewhere massively underlevel for you, straight into massively overlevelled enemies. Most FromSoftware games do this, which again feels pretty stupid. I like that you *can* get to higher level areas in these games, but it shouldn't be just a case of "oh I turned right instead of left and now I have to grind away 10 minutes to try to get my souls back without getting 1 shot lol".

Most actual buildings that you'll find (like the whole, massive sunken town area in the West side of the map) are inaccessible. What's the point in making a massive area with all these buildings etc., and just... None of them serve literally any purpose whatsoever.

I also feel like this specifically does not work very well when they just try to rehash the same FromSoftware formula over and over, because whereas in previous Souls games, you will naturally encounter an NPC that is crucial to the story or to being able to buy certain items for certain builds, this game does the same thing except over SO much empty space.

For example, they put the primary mage trader in a random hole in a random ruin in the middle of nowhere behind a miniboss. How does that make any sense gameplay-wise? You're not going to naturally encounter them like you would in other Souls games so putting random NPCs in random places makes way less sense than in any previous games. If you don't literally look that up to start with (i.e. remove your own immersion), you're likely to not encounter them for ages if you don't happen to go in that direction early on.

I'm 15 hours in so far, and have found 0 pairs of gloves, and no real usable armour or shields lol. I imagine if you want to actually get some, it's again going to be a case of "yes, we designed this so you have to look up a guide!" Very engaging, immersive and fun.

They literally self sabotage the atmosphere in their own game by doing stuff like this. I love the Souls themes for the most part, but it's impossible you immerse yourself when your only option in these games is you HAVE to look up a guide in order to have any sort of gameplay enjoyment (more on that later).

The whole collecting/crafting stuff in this game feels very un-thought through, very much like it was shoehorned in without much direction at all. You just end up picking up stuff most of the game that you never use, never need to use and that has almost no value. It doesn't feel like a main feature for you to utilise, it doesn't feel rewarding, and it pretty much exclusively used for stuff like making arrows.

The controls feel worse in some cases and a step backwards (again). No idea why, but FromSoftware simply is incapable of making good decisions with controls, or from ever actually just building on their previous game(s). 
This game for example, unlike in several of their previous games, they have decided to remove being able to move the camera slightly when locked onto an enemy. Why? You want to look around slightly whilst fighting an enemy you're locked onto? Not possible. Changing targets when locked on also doesn't work half the time, and even actually just locking on can often be a struggle. 

They add a horse, so you're often moving faster whilst fighting in bigger, more open areas, and yet you have no way to quickly look around you a little bit whilst travelling? Just no thought behind it honestly, the number of times I'm stuck locked onto an enemy and because you're covering more area, you just run into more enemies that you can't easily just look around at.

I've also had so many times when I've been running away whilst my camera is facing an enemy, pressing to lock my camera, and it just spins my camera to face the front instead of locking onto the enemy that is in the open, central in my camera to begin with. This then causes your movement to completely change, and feels awful. Getting stuck on a candelabra in a dungeon because you tried to lock onto an enemy and the camera spun round instead of locking, or running off of a bridge you're traversing because you tried to actually play the game and fight an enemy, very fun...

The game looks very good, but there are many, many reused assets & enemies which kind of detracts a bit from how good the game looks. Make a few really great looking buildings/areas/enemies and then just reuse the living shit out of them.

###

Moving onto FromSoftware in general:

My biggest issue with the Souls games is the developers just never really seem to know why they're doing things, or they never really have the motivation of making something actually fun to play, more just to make it difficult/frustrating to deal with just for the sake of it. 

Take weapon damage for example: for those who are unaware, there are so many hidden elements that determine how much damage you do. It seems like a completely arbitrary system that punishes being intelligent or creative and having ideas, and kind of lazy to be honest; basically, adding hidden crutches that prevent you from actually being able to utilise things like your stats in any real sensical way, and saving them having to actually try to balance things properly because the hidden crutches just add hidden limits to everything you want to do.

You'd think "hey, I want to play as a mage, I'm going to focus mainly Int at the start". Wrong, you just fucked your experience. "I want to put some points in dexterity to-" WRONG, start again. It's really does reduce the fun when the game actively punishes you for not going and trawling through 100 guides and documents (not provided by FromSoftware, of course) to find exactly the right stuff to do.

Why do players need to go and look through a spreadsheet and plugin 10 different numbers in order to actually know whether a weapon is better to use? And even then, there are then a dozen more elements like swing speed, animations etc. that can still mean a weapon is better/worse, that there is literally no information for within the game. It honestly makes these games so unimmersive and takes away a lot of the joy of playing them, because you literally have to go and *research* every single thing to know whether it's actually not just going to be miserable to use.

They can never just decide on a reasonable list of useful stats to include in the games, they seem to change it EVERY single different Souls game, and most of them are literally just useless and a waste of precious levels, and this game is absolutely no different.

Where do I begin? By the time I was done with it, the game left me completely disappointed. Most of the negative reviews have captured all the significant problems with this game so I'll keep it (relatively) short.

My favorite games in the Fromsoft catalogue are Dark Souls and Sekiro (also among my favorite games of all time). These games feel deliberately designed; Dark Souls made you feel like exploring a dangerous land, and Sekiro's combat system is truly one of a kind. But Elden Ring? It's a video game ass video game. 

Everything in this game exists for the player's benefit. Side dungeons almost always end in boss fights with a treasure chest to reward the player. Stakes of Marika make it convenient to fight bosses. Sites of Grace abound so that you never feel the tension of exploration (also free fast travel). Every single death in this game will only be due to bosses, or sometimes gravity. Don't wanna fight overworld enemies? Get on Torrent and ride away.

The open world is simply a collection of all the dungeons they made spread horizontally. Is the open world truly open then? Nope, there's a strictly linear progression with some side stuff along the way, with arbitrary progression gates like Morgott's Seal and Great rune requirements. Balance is literally non-existent. 

Is the combat good then? It's basically Dark Souls combat again. There's a gazillion weapons, but they all mostly play the same, you know how it is. Boss fights are now true shonen anime style affairs, wait for your turn and dodge while the boss does his wombo combo and then poke. Repeat all over again for a 100 bosses, and the nail in the coffin is that a significant portion of them are repeats. Not even remembrance bosses are spared.

Don't even get me started on the DLC.

I was genuinely excited to play this game, and sadly, this made me question the future of Soulslikes from Fromsoft. I guess we'll have to wait and see.

The problem is clearly with the game itself.

What makes this especially frustrating is that this is not a new or obscure bug. Players have been reporting this freezing issue for a long time, and FromSoftware has done little to nothing to address it. When a problem is this widespread and this well known, leaving it unresolved is not an oversight, it is a choice. Selling a product you know is broken for a significant portion of your playerbase and doing nothing about it is simply not acceptable. At some point, the developer and the platform that profits from selling it share responsibility for that.

Of my 2 hours and 57 minutes of playtime, the vast majority was spent attempting to debug the freezing issue, not actually playing the game. I requested a refund, not because I didn't want to play it, but because I couldn't. Steam denied it, citing their 2-hour/14-day policy without any acknowledgment of the circumstances.

The support experience was worse than the technical issue. Three different agents gave me copy-paste responses. One assured me refunds are considered "case by case" but offered zero explanation of what factors were actually weighed. When I asked them to consider that I only launched the game for the first time days ago, or that nearly 3 hours on a 100+ hour game hardly constitutes taking advantage of their policy, I got silence. As a software engineer, I'd never tell my customers to debug my product on their own time. Steam apparently has no such qualms. The platform I trusted to protect my purchases hid behind a rigid policy to retain a modest amount of money from a customer with a completely legitimate complaint about a broken product.

If you're thinking about buying a game and playing it at your own pace, the way gaming used to work, think twice. Steam's refund policy doesn't protect that. Buy it, launch it immediately, and decide within 2 hours or you're on your own.
