Elden Ring / S.O.T.E – FromSoftware’s False Messiah 

166 hours played – completed main game and DLC - Elden Lord ending

Rating: 6/10

Elden Ring presents itself as a once-in-a-generation masterpiece. At first, it really feels like that’s true. The world is huge, the atmosphere is incredible, and moments like seeing the Scadutree for the first time genuinely feel unforgettable. 

But the longer you play, the more that image breaks down. What is sold as a perfect masterpiece slowly reveals itself as a messy, inconsistent experience built on frustration and unclear design. 

What starts as awe quickly turns into frustration. Exploration often feels unclear or pointless, progression can feel like aimless wandering, and the game frequently fails to guide the player in any meaningful way. Instead of leading you through its world, it often leaves you lost in it. 

Pros

Elden Ring does have strong build variety. There are many weapons, spells, and playstyles, letting you customize your character in different ways. 

The world and art design are also impressive, especially in the DLC. Areas like the Gravesite Plain and Cerulean Coast look beautiful and atmospheric, even if they sometimes feel like the only consistently strong part of the experience. 

Boss designs also look great visually. Rennala, Radahn, Maliketh, and Malenia all stand out in appearance, even when their gameplay design is heavily flawed. 

Cons 

This is where the illusion completely falls apart. 

Boss fights are often overly aggressive, filled with heavily delayed attacks that deal inconsistent but extreme damage. Instead of learning through fair repetition, many fights feel like trial-and-error until you survive a messy attempt. Even with high HP, you often feel like you never have enough; Artificial difficulty makes boss fights feel poorly balanced rather than challenging. 

Malenia is the clearest example—visually incredible, but completely undermined by mechanics like her two Scarlet Aeonia attacks(one-shots), Waterfowl Dance, grab, and healing on hit and block, which can erase progress instantly and make fights feel unfair rather than rewarding. 

Consort Radahn continues this problem with overwhelming pressure, visual clutter, and attacks that feel difficult to read rather than difficult to master. Messmer stands out only because he is one of the few bosses that actually feels fair, readable, and well-paced in comparison. 

Most other bosses devolve into waiting simulator gameplay—dodging long, repetitive combos just to get a single hit in. Strength builds feel unnecessarily punished, while faster builds like bleed or magic often outperform them significantly. Wins don’t feel earned—they feel like relief that the fight is finally over. 

Reused Content

A large portion of the game also suffers from heavy reuse of bosses, enemies, and dungeon layouts. Many encounters feel copied and pasted with minor variations, which makes exploration feel repetitive rather than fresh over time.

Open World & Direction 

The open world suffers from a serious lack of direction. 

Exploration is often not rewarding, but confusing and time-wasting. You can easily spend hours in areas that do not clearly contribute to progression, with very little guidance on where you should go or why. 

Compared to structured open-world games like Breath of the Wild, Elden Ring feels less like a guided experience and more like a massive pile of content with no clear structure holding it together. 

Even Melina, who is supposed to guide the player, feels poorly implemented. She disappears for long stretches, returns inconsistently, and ultimately her death happens so randomly, making her character fail to provide meaningful direction or emotional weight. Her role feels underdeveloped and almost irrelevant to the actual experience. 

Story & Endgame 

The story is extremely unclear unless you look outside the game. Most of it is hidden behind item descriptions or external lore explanations instead of being properly told in-game. 

By the end—especially in the DLC—you’re left with major moments like Consort Radahn and Miquella cutscenes that look important but feel confusing and underdeveloped in context. 

The base game ending also suffers. Radagon is a solid fight, but the Elden Beast immediately after feels like a drawn-out, frustrating fight filled with delayed attacks, constant running, no room to get damage in, and magic attacks that feel unfair, making the entire fight a huge disappointment rather than a meaningful conclusion. 

Overall, the Elden Lord ending feels more tedious and boring than satisfying, making it feel more like “oh, that’s it, I guess I beat the game” rather than an impactful, worthwhile journey. 

Conclusion 

Elden Ring (including SOTE) is not a well-made game and is heavily overrated for what it actually delivers for its price tag. It presents itself as a flawless masterpiece, but that image does not hold up under real time spent playing the game and calling out poorly made game design. The more you engage with it, the more its flaws become obvious—unclear direction, inconsistent boss design, and storytelling that feels too vague to be satisfying. While it does have strong moments in world design, atmosphere, and build variety, these highs are constantly undermined by frustrating gameplay systems and poor pacing decisions. In reality, Elden Ring is a 6/10 experience rather than a 10/10 experience—a game with massive ambition and beautiful presentation that is consistently dragged down by flawed execution. 

A false messiah: impressive on the surface, but deeply inconsistent underneath.

Man... I really wanted to like this game, I love other souls-likes and was so hyped to play this, but it just felt so disrespectfull of player's time. The open world was overambitious and it lead to most of the game feeling empty and many many enemies even bosses being recycled.
Despite what people say about fast-paced combat, a huge portion of the experience is spent riding around on your horse wondering where to go next.
I put 132 hours into this game, and honestly, it didn’t feel worthwhile. I kept expecting it to get better or deliver some kind of payoff that justified the time investment, but it never really did.
The boss design felt excessive towards the end of the game, where it's just one brutal bossfight after another all of which felt like a chore. Usually in games like this there's a satisfaction from beating a tough boss, and you look back fondly on the fight. But the last few bosses I'd finish and just feel that my time had been wasted.
By the end, this felt like something I had to finish rather than something I wanted to finish. Instead of improving on the Souls formula, it felt like it watered it down and soured it.

After 130 hours of Elden Ring, I dropped the game right at the final boss, Radagon and the Elden Beast. The fight had already taken me four hours, and it was beyond my patience. I knew I could beat it if I put in more time, but what was the point? At that point, it was only the sunk cost keeping me playing. There was no more enjoyment from discovering new things or making progress. All that was left was frustration and tedium.

Actually, that feeling had been there throughout the entire game. I haven't played another game that was so successful at creating frustration instead of enjoyment.

There are some good parts to this game. Otherwise, I wouldn't have played it for so long. The strongest part is exploration. The distinctive areas, landscapes, and architecture you can see in the distance make you curious to explore.

However, the exploration is constantly undermined by everything else: the meaningless repetitive runbacks, because you will constantly die to blind-spot ambushes and stupid platforming; sluggish controls and unintuitive, delayed enemy attacks; and enemies that can kill you in just two hits. When you have to die multiple times just to travel along a route, there is no curiosity left. There is only annoyance.

Another thing I can't stand is that you almost have to use a game guide. A good game should teach players its mechanics naturally, and I do think natural, minimal guidance is good game design. Elden Ring wanted to do this and failed, and it is made even worse by other aspects of the game: NPCs talk in pretentious nonsense, enemies can kill you in just a few hits in the early game so finding a strong build quickly can feel almost necessary just to keep playing.

The game even has a ridiculous built-in system where players can leave messages and recommendations for one another. It almost feels as though the developers recognize how difficult and ambiguous the game can be to understand without outside assistance.

I'm the kind of gamer who almost never looks up game guides. I finished Hollow Knight and Silksong without any guides, along with many puzzle games. But in Elden Ring, I had to look up guides several times.

The first time was after I had arduously explored Stormveil Castle and defeated the final boss there using only my two starting spells as a squishy Astrologer. At that point, I seriously wondered whether I should continue playing if the rest of the game was going to be like this. Then I watched some guides that recommended finding a specific piece of equipment and a specific spell in a very well-hidden place in a dangerous area. Once I got them, the game's difficulty was significantly reduced. I would never have found those things by myself, and I probably wouldn't have continued playing for this long if I hadn't watched that guide.

Then there was the entrance to the Plateau. I reached the lift but couldn't use it. I knew I had missed something, but there was no hint about what I had missed. All I could do was stare at the huge open-world map without knowing where I was supposed to go next.

I know that the things I consider downsides may be irrelevant to some players, or even what they enjoy about the game. Some people may not think looking up a game guide is a big issue. Some may even find communicating with other players about hidden objects interesting. And some people may genuinely enjoy defeating a boss after dying 50 times over two hours. (sometimes much longer)

But I don't fool myself into believing that the relief after a multi-hour boss fight is accomplishment.

Many times, what keeps you playing isn't the "what's in that castle over the hill?" kind of curiosity, or the "I invented a strong build from what I have in hand" kind of accomplishment. It's the sunk cost, loss aversion, anger, and competition that keep you engaged, myself included.

This game design philosophy feels more like that of online PvP competition games than a handcrafted single-player experience. The repetitive runbacks and loading screens only add more meaningless time, making the problem even worse.

And that's why I don't think it's a good game even though I played for 130 hours. Much of the experience was frustrating and tedious. I simply happened to have a lot of free time recently and nothing better to do, and only in such a situation could I spend so much time on this game.

Elden Ring could have been a good niche game, but the Game of the Year title made it so overhyped that I almost felt scammed for paying a AAA price only to get such a negative experience.

I wouldn't recommend it to anyone. It has also used up whatever patience I had for the Soulslike genre. Perhaps I won't buy another game from FromSoftware, or any game with the Soulslike tag - which has spawned so many copycats after FromSoftware's commercial success.

Planning on coming back and updating this review at some point because I know its a bit unfair of me to rate it negatively after having only scratching the surface of the game (from what I've heard/seen) and only having played it for 4 hours BUT: within those 4 hours I barely got to play the actual game. I don't have much experience with souls-likes but I have played my fair share of RPGs. In fact, one of the things I hate the most about most modern RPGs is the amount of hints and 'recommended paths' they do. I don't need a hint to pop up when I can't solve a puzzle within the first 30 seconds of encountering it and I don't need NPCs to use no-so-subtle dialogue to tell me which path may be harder or which path will have more dire consequences. At this point if you're a fan of souls-like games you might be thinking "Oh Elden ring would be perfect for you! There's no hand holding at all." Except no hand holding doesn't have to mean no tutorial/unrepeatable tutorials and bad interface design, but it does in this game. I don't know if that's because this game may not have been originally intended for PC and therefore may have been poorly adapted for mouse and keyboard players but in my experience so far, it's really sucked. Boxes that should be clickable aren't, you can't use the escape key to exit out of some menus, you can't pause the game even though its just you playing, among other pains. Now I know some players bask in the brutality of it but the reality is that its a primarily single player game, meaning if players deviate from the intended way to play, who cares? They're enjoying the game the way they want to. I personally have never 'pause-buffered' or used menu shortcuts to give me an advantage against difficult enemies in any game, nor do I intend to, but not being able to pause a single player game when some sort of IRL circumstance calls is quite frustrating. Additionally, the tutorial sucks and returning to the game is incredibly difficult. I have tried returning to this game twice now since I first played it, each time giving it roughly an hour to an hour and a half. Both times I have spent nearly 30 minutes trying to understand the combat mechanics and the equipment menu. It's not that either is incredibly difficult to use, it's that they are poorly explained and difficult to learn. I've played several other games that have the formula of 'dodge roll' 'heavy attack' 'light attack' 'block/parry' but in all of them all I have to do to learn what buttons do what is hit the pause menu and look at controls. In Elden Ring, even when I do that it simply lists 'dodge roll' 'strafe' 'backstep' as one button. And on top of that  that same button is used to turn light attacks into heavy attacks. Sure I can adapt, figure out what conditions need to be met for my character to perform a 'strafe' instead of a 'dodge roll' or a 'backstep', but I don't want to relearn every single time I return. And if you're thinking "Huh, what kinda guy only plays a game for an hour or two then doesn't come back to it for a month??" I'd agree with you because normally I do enjoy a game for a full playthrough, however many hours that may take, but with Elden ring, every time I've given it a try, I've experienced more frustration than I have had fun. So when I come back to my computer for the next session a day later, I decide not to play it. And games are meant to be fun. So maybe your personal takeaway can be that you need to give it more time to transition from frustration to fun than I did.

I really want to like Elden Ring as I loved the Souls series and I have tried many times to like it but it has so many issues that I personally have with it that make it not click with me like Demon's Souls or Dark Souls did.

I think my biggest problems are that the open world while it seems cool just doesnt work with Elden Ring so well, if you explore it with no direction, you can end up in areas that feel just straight up unfair and it can be really frustrating to find where you are supposed to go at whatever level you may be at and sometimes you just have to wonder if its a skill issue or if you are genuinely in the wrong place. Ontop of this, if you are a completionist like I am with souls games then it can be really hard to find bosses or areas that you may have missed without needing to pull up a guide every 5 minutes which just feels annoying and tedious for no reason.

Another big problem I have with the game is that the boss designs are just horrid. It feels like they upped the speed of the bosses since Dark Souls 3 to match how quick they were in Sekiro, but the problem with that is that in Sekiro, players were given a parry to avoid damage and tools to exploit any bosses weaknesses, in Elden Ring, you are given nothing to help and while majority of the bosses arent too bad with how spammy they are, they have other issues. Some are way too overused, some are just straight up stupid gimmick fights and some are just straight up boring. Its hard to find bosses in Elden Ring where I sat there and thought to myself "okay this was actually good"

Another issue I have with Elden Ring is the fact that base game co-op is straight up just unplayable and takes away many features without using the seamless co-op mod, they disable your horse in base game and block off a lot of areas so that open world that was a big selling point of the game is just completely gone if you are like me and are someone who loves exploring open world games with others.

Its not all bad though, Elden Ring has some very gorgeous places and backdrops and I genuinely think that the amount of content you get is wholeheartedly worth the full price of the game even if you just played it once. Some of the characters have some very interesting storylines and the replayability is really high with how many weapons, builds and ending you can get. And thats not even counting the DLC.

All and all, I think that Elden Ring is a DECENT game, but I will NEVER understand how people glaze it and say its the best game of all time or anything like that, and if I could I would leave a maybe review but I cant and I personally dont like the game and don't think it lives up to the scores it has or the hype around it.

This is an excellent game for players of a particular sort: 
A. You like a game with a rich open world feel. The landscape is sumptuously rendered and can be interesting to explore.
B.  You do not want what fans call "hand holding" your way through the adventure. There is little intuitive about what the player is to do next other than a general cardinal direction.  ("Hand holding" also applies to understanding the interface of the game which is not especially intuitive unless you have played other Dark Souls games.)
C. You like pointlessly hacking and slashing your way through enemies for the only reward to level up" so you can defeat more challenging enemies until there are no more enemies to defeat.


As for A, Elden Ring is in the class with the very best games of the sort, Skyrim, BG3, Dragon Age, etc.

Regarding B, there can be much appeal to this philosophy.  However, unless one has countless hours to devote to exploration and experimentation, the feature can be frustrating. This is especially true regarding the interface and menu systems if one is new to the Dark Souls way of doing things. For example, multiple icons appear on the screen announcing some aspect of the gameplay, but with zero tutorials, there is no way of knowing what these mean or how to take advantage of them. HP, Mana, Stamina, are pretty commonly understood for anyone who has ever played a video game. Of the dozen or so other indicators, there is little intuitive about how to interpret them. In addition, Menu items and inventory control is vast.  That could be a good thing. Knowing how to manipulate and change items in your inventory, it will take you awhile.  Of course, the player always has the option to consult the various player guides and walkthroughs for help, but: 1. That defeats the purpose of no "hand holding: in the first place. 2. The interfaces are so complicated the guides are sometimes hard to follow even still.

As for C, my personal taste is that progress in the game only by killing virtually everything that moves is an unimaginative approach to game design. It lacks subtlety that better games employ to create an intriguing storyline. There is never any banter that gives the fights scenes emotional value - leveling up is pretty much the one and only point. There is never any negotiating with an adversary to obtain your reward without a fight.  95% of the living characters are out to kill you on sight. The other 5% only provide you information or an item of need, but rarely with any condition or side quest. There is virtually no subtlety here.  The closest to subtlety is that when you are underpowered, you can sometimes sneak past the bad guy to obtain the reward. For my preference, the Cardinal Sin of Elden Ring is it takes itself so seriously. There is a dearth of whimsy or humor. Out of thousands of NPCs with which I have interacted, only one made me laugh. 15 seconds out of 58 hours provides a really grim world and experience.

When it first came out, Skyrim was much like this. However, fans developed mods to add some entertaining NPCs and side-quests. Over the the years, Skyrim became a much better game. but Elden Ring makes modding cumbersome, as opposed to BG3 which incorporates modding into the interface, and Skyrim which incorporated fan mods into the later editions.

One final aspect of the game bears noting. Leveling up requires the player to collect "souls," hence all the killing. However, if you die in a battle, you lose the soul point you have collected.  On the plus side, this requires to player to plan strategically, especially since you cannot save before entering a fight as with so many other games.  It creates a unique challenge to gameplay. However, the downside is it promotes a "use it or lose it" approach to resource management and  an excess of passivity and reluctance to experiment in gameplay.  This appeal to some because it gives each battle higher stakes, but is also frustrating when player  has worked an hour to build up enough resources to level up and then loses it all.   Add to this, that the game is glitchy.  I have had it freeze up in the middle of a battle in which I was doing well to find on rebooting, I had "lost" the battle and my resource along with it.

BOTTOM LINE.  Very pretty game. The kinds of frustration it creates will appeal to some, but turn off others.  It lacks any motivation that appeals to human emotion other than self aggrandizement of killing others to get to the top. It engages no human emotion other than simplistic greed. Ironically for a game dependent on the collection of souls for advancement, the game itself lacks soul in its design.  I will continue to play it for a time if for no other reason than to get my money's worth out of it, but I cannot recommend it to anyone who seeks joy in their role play gaming. I will add, I thoroughly object to this game being listed as an "RPG."  There is NO role to play other than Executioner. It should be listed as a first person shooter. I have made this mistake with Steam before and will not do so again.

However, there are so many lows to average aspects (repeated bosses and dungeons, some bosses you fight them later as lesser enemies, performance till today isn’t optimized even with strong PC, meaningless open world design that simply doesn’t work with souls-like formula, boring combat and weapons,  artificial difficulty, and it feels like riding a horse simulator.

I really think if this game was developed by Ubisoft or Bethesda, we would have seen completely different reaction.

In short, this is 7/10 game due to the high highs of it, but considering all the flaws and the unjustified long length, I don’t recommend it. It is a great piece of art but not fun game.

Elden Ring is a disappointing experience. I recently completed both Dark Souls 1 and 3 (I'm not an expert by any means) and went on excitedly to play Elden Ring but it ended up being a huge mistake. This game is pretty and the story is at least interesting and I understand why the masses would like this game but having played it myself I think it's not a bad game per say but it is not a good Souls game. The open world structure actually feels detrimental to the game and sometimes the exploration can be very confusing (especially the Rauh Ruins in the dlc that are easily the worst offender in that regard). The enemies drop very little runes which ended up being a problem as it meant this game was the first Souls where I ended up having to farm levels to progress. The difficulty feels very artificial as well, from the midgame onward the enemies feel very spongy, have a ton of poise and deal a huge amount of damage, so much so that it's common to get two shotted in the end game. As for the bosses, they usually have a very cheap attack pattern where they attack a lot very fast and deal a truckload of damage, so it's not really a matter of skill issue and more a matter of luck in the latter bosses. There's also a lot of things that feel re-used and areas that feel samey wich is a shame because Dark Souls 1 for instance had some pretty nice diversity in areas in my opinion (granted not all of them). In the end, in my opinion, I feel like you should pass up on this game. It is simply not a good Souls game and the difficulty is way too high for very little reward; in the end, the only real regret I have is that I played too much of this game and I can't get a refund anymore.

I want to preface this review by saying that I have not played Dark Souls or any similar boss-focused fight games, and I am guessing this genre is just not for me, which may color my strong dislike of this game.  I played for 45 minutes before requesting a refund (which I have never done before on a game).

Positives: This game is very beautiful in its environmental production with some stellar fight mechanics.  I can also see how people would get an adrenaline-boost when faced with battling the monster bosses as well as the intellectual challenge of finding ways to overcome their overwhelming power over you.

Negatives: The story is basically Lord of the Rings (which I love) but void of any heart or soul or character ambitions.  The playable character lacks motivation and I do not know what I am trying to accomplish by seeking the Elden Ring.  The game is also extremely difficult, which is fine except that it forces the player to grind hours trying to beat a boss who I don't even understand why I should be trying to defeat.  I could see a scenario where I dedicated hundreds of hours into this game only to achieve nothing, which is why I decided not to waste my time with it.  It is basically fan-fiction for Lord of the Rings where you play as a nameless Easterling (evil man) fighting in Sauron's army and have to defeat all the big-bads of the franchise without even knowing who they are besides their names or what the One Ring does or why you are trying to wield power over it in the first place.

The gameplay is also very repetitive: basically you go and attack something, try to kill it, and then go onto something else to kill, then heal, then often re-kill all of these monsters again and again and again.  And your reward for these battles?  Some random loot that is so difficult to understand it is like getting paid for farm work with NFTs.

If you like hack and slash games without story or purpose, this may be a great time suck for you.  Otherwise, it is truly a waste of your life.

I *DIDN'T* use any Rune exploits to increase my level to over level the bosses. I played this game with all the tools that this game deigned to convey to me...which isn't a lot. No matter your spacing, your timing, your judgement- this game throws all of that away in favor of over-leveling, and using cheap tricks to kill bosses. I'm sorry, but if you have to cheat the system to progress- then that's bad game design. And let's be fucking real, here. Using an outside source for information, over leveling, abusing terrain, having to completely ABANDON your playstyle for a "more optimal build" (choose a different weapon, spend hours grinding for runes to artificially inflate your stats, stack a bunch of buffs that a new character wouldn't have any way of naturally obtaining) that's fucking cheating- at least, that is in my book.

Frankly, this game is highly overrated. The weapon movesets are incredibly unrealistic and add unnatural end lag to attacks that, frankly, shouldn't be problematic or have high recovery times. The boss attacks are incredibly anti-player, being slower than Christmas on the windup- then swinging faster than lightning, is fucking cheap as Hell. That is a gross disrespect of my time and effort- for fucking NOTHING.

Maybe this is where I officially become the old guy yelling at games. Because somewhere along the way, “bigger” replaced “better,” and nobody seems to question it anymore. Elden Ring is what happens when you take every questionable idea during development and decide not only to keep it but double down on it. The real difficulty is genuinely in your effort to remember that you’re playing something critically acclaimed, because so much of the experience feels confused, stretched thin, or undercooked.

I forced over 40 hours into this. Having played every mainline Souls game, I had to see it through. I wanted to know what the “final form” of this formula looked like.

Now I know.

The disappointment is as vast as the empty landscape, and the confusion is immeasurable. This isn’t a case of “you need a break from the game.” This is a case of needing a break because of the game because of its design, its systems, its world, and the constant feeling of randomness pretending to be depth. It’s not challenging in a meaningful way, it’s not rewarding in a satisfying way it just slowly drains you. Not from difficulty, but from repetition, confusion, and the sense that everything is just slightly off. You’re not playing a game anymore, you’re enduring one. And my patience ran out around the 40-hour mark.

To put it front and center:

The big selling point here is the open world. And like most open worlds, it proves a simple rule: scale does not equal quality. What you get isn’t a carefully crafted experience, but something closer to an “MMO from 2008 but with better lighting.” Vast, empty landscapes filled with enemies awkwardly standing around like they’re waiting for their shift to start. Half of them look like they spawned in five seconds ago, the other half like they forgot to despawn.

Instead of the tight, interconnected level design that made earlier Souls games work, you now roam what feels like the Scottish highlands populated by idle mobs, copy-pasted assets, and the occasional enemy placed on a hill or in a ditch for dramatic effect. Not because it makes sense, just because.

I can sense the confusion in the mobs themselves. Hollow soldiers guarding a broken cart. Patrols defending a handful of rocks in the middle of nowhere. Entire camps built around absolutely nothing of value. It feels less like worldbuilding and more like someone forgot to remove placeholder assets. Whatever themes were intended are completely lost, overwritten by sheer randomness. At times it feels less like exploring a world and more like wandering through a very expensive early-onset dementia simulator.

To make this scale even remotely playable, the game introduces a mount. And this is where the domino effect really kicks in. The world is too big → you get a mount → encounters lose structure → enemies become filler → combat turns into drive-by hits or stamina management on horseback. What used to be deliberate level design is now replaced with wide open killing fields and loosely scattered content.

Combat has also gone in a direction I personally can’t stand. After Dark Souls II, things have been getting faster and more “spectacle-driven,” but here it hits rock bottom. What used to be methodical combat is now closer to button mashing with extra steps. Most fights boil down to abusing dodge invincibility frames and hammering heavy attacks until something breaks (guard or poise). Repeat from start to finish.

If that’s “skill,” then sure. To me, it feels more like exploiting a system than mastering one.

Then there’s crafting, which might be the most pointless system in the game. Enemies rarely drop anything meaningful, materials are scattered everywhere with little thought for what, where, or why, and the whole system feels like it exists just to justify itself. You end up running around committing wildlife genocide deers, turtles, birds, rabbits just to craft items that could have easily been sold by a vendor. It adds nothing but menu clutter and busywork.

And even when the game does give you loot, it quietly undercuts it somewhere else. Rune (souls) gain from regular enemies is so low that it might as well not exist. Your actual income comes almost entirely from bosses. Everything else either gives too little or takes too long to be worth the effort.

So the usual gameplay loop “farm a bit, get stronger, try again” barely functions. There’s no real incentive to clear areas, no satisfying buildup of progress. If you’re underleveled, you’re not grinding your way up you’re waiting for the next boss payout. At times it feels like you’re more likely to grow bored than actually progress through effort.

The core issue with the game: it constantly adds systems without improving the experience. More space, more mechanics, more items but less purpose.

There are moments where you can see what the game could have been. But its dead and buried under repetition, filler, and design decisions that work against each other. Honestly, it’s almost worth playing just to witness how all these pieces somehow fit together into something so mediocre, so confused, so boring.

For a game that has received such high praise I did not expect to become so dissapointed. The game is praised for breaking the curse of bloated open world games, yet falls into the same pitfalls. Every hour feels more boring than the last.

Open world and progression
The first hours of this game feels fresh and exciting. There is lots to explore and the scenery is stunning, yet this feels like the most the game has to offer. Past a certain point the world loses its appeal, due to the insane amount of repeat bosses, dungeons and ruins. This is a shame, because there is a good amount of unique and fun bosses and dungeons, but the amount of trash I have to wade through the get there is painful. This is made worse by the fact that bosses who feel unique and powerful are casually thrown back into the game when the devs feel the need to fill their massive open world. Not only does the game bore me with repeat dungeons, but they actively shit on any good experience I just had. 

The progression system in this game seems to actively contradict what it means to be an "open world". In Dark Souls 3 the progression was pretty straight forward. You complete an area, you get stronger, you get to the next area and the enemies have also gotten stronger. It is a linear game, so thats what you would expect. Yet elden ring copies this formula with little concern for how this would affect the open world experience. Early on it is established that the player has to explore the world. Both the Iron Sentinel and Margitt teaches this to the player as if you go fight them as early as possible you'll be massively underleveled. This does not reward exploration, this punishes the player for not doing so. Whatever I'll level up. I explore some stuff, get stronger, complete stormveil castle. After this the game takes a weird turn for me. I go to  Liurna of the lakes, but by doing so Caelid becomes massively underleved. Atleast games like the witcher 3 tell the player what the recomended level is when such an artifical barrier is set up.

There is fun to be had in the world, yet that is only when the game feels like dark souls 3. The so called legacy dungeons are fun, precisely because they took what fromsoftware had mastered from previous releases. It is almost like this is because the game becomes more linear, the enemies are more tighly packed, healing becomes restricted creating tension and consequences, and because the map becomes both interesting to traverse and look at. Oh wait, that is what every other fromsoft game is known for. 

Combat
This franchise has become synonymous with difficulty. It is dissapointing to see fromsoftware forget why that difficulty was interesting in games like ds3. The whole reason is that the difficulty felt fair and that the player could overcome it by reasonable means. Fundamentally this game still feels like ds3. The same core mechanics are still here yet the bosses have become more agile, more dyanmic, they have more delayed attacks, more aoe attacks and overall more bullshit. The whole point of the game is that I can take all that to the face and learn something, yet on every new run the boss decides that it can chain another combo in a series of absolute tomfoolery, where if I even dare try to get a light attack in, I get a stick shoved straight up my ass. The fact that the AI can chain up attacks like this promotes a passive style of play, where I am left up eating scraps when the boss eats a 9 course dinner. 

Then there are attacks that are just completely ridicuouls. Rykard's earthquake, Malenia's waterfowl and tons of other aoes or grab attacks. Their timings range from delayed, arbitrary or non existant. This game is incredibly insistent upon difficulty for difficulty's sake. 

The game has tons of gimmicky ways to offset difficulty, but I find them to be just that, a gimmick. Summons are at the core of this, yet the game fails to convince me that it was balanced around them. Bosses becomme laughably easy when using them, since they can usually only target one at a time.  Gimmicks only push the problem back. Why are they needed? Are fights too hard or just not rewarding enough when using the core mechanics? 

Story and narrative
Despite the harsh words above, this has to be weakest part of the game. There are some fun moments to be had exploring and there are fun bosses to be fought, however the answer as to why the player is doing this seems non existant. This game borrows the same principles from soft have worked with. That is to tell a vague story with item descriptions. In elden ring it works less than ever. In dark souls 3 the vague story could be tied to the very themes themselves. The world felt hollow, because it literally was. Humanity was fading away and that was the motivation for the whole journey. Elden Ring shares this same broken world premise, yet struggles to captivate me. Why does the player blindly follow the path to become elden lord when no one else does? Even when this game wants to pretend that it is a good rpg, every quest follows the same trends: blindly gain persons trust, go fetch item, npc dies or you kill them. This is made worse by the fact that I need a wiki glued to my ass to find the npcs in this vast world. Every quest feels impersonal, becuase they are. Joining volcano manor and killing other tarnished holds no weight. Killing demigod after demigod changes nothing, nothing happens to the world and no one acknowledges my effort. There is no change troughout the plot, the story is still the same. Kill boss, collect the rune. If I had not played the first half and was put into the game, there wouldn't be much I missed in terms of the main story. 

People often state that this game isn't trying to tell a regular story. It wants to be vague and doesn't want to "handhold" you throughout. This feels strange when in the first 10 minutes I meet 4-5 npcs, who i will continue to see throughout their sidequests. The game wants to tell a obscure story, yet still wants to use npcs and dialogue in a traditional sense. This ends up being boring, because of the aforementioned tropes. The ingenuity of fromsoft storytelling, seems to lie in the item descriptions. They tell the lore of various parts of the world, but I couldn't bother. 1 Why should I care when the lore so often depicts random "fun facts"; Why should I care about the backstory of some random enemies when the narrative is still the same? Kill, loot and move on. 2 The act of stopping to read is a lazy way to utilize the video game medium. If read dead 2 and the like get critique for being too much like a movie, then elden ring wants to be too much like a book. I feel like just observing the community is a great affirmation of item descriptions being bad: Why do people watch lore videos, when you can play the game?

A game that supposedly fixed open world gaming still commits the same mistakes. A game that wanted a rawer experience with less map markers outsourced the problem to the wikis. A game that was supposed to be the newest iteration of souls combat feels derivative and cheap. In the end this game struggles from wanting to cater to as many as possible: Being open world to challenge the AAA market and being more difficult to cater to the loudest fromsoft fans, but to make the game feel fair it is offset with gimmick summons.

I would not recommend this game simply because there are better fromsoft games.

Then there are large spectacle pseudo cutscene moves that are cool the first couple times and then just become boring and ruin the pace of the fight. I can appreciate the difficulty of it, but it ruins any kind of immersion or world-building for me.

Elden ring is a game that you cannot pause, even in offline mode. Every other aspect of the game is permeated with this same sort of smug, sickeningly arrogant design philosophy. It's a game that totally realizes its vision, but this vision is so far beyond awful it is genuine difficult to describe how bad it is. It's central thesis is that what is obscure, cumbersome, or difficult is good. And that's it, there are no other design considerations. 

The game is terrible at explaining itself. Towards the end of it there is an area with invisible enemies. You can't see them without an item that is found very, very far from this area. No one so much as hints to the player where the item is, or even that it exists. If you do stumble on it, the default stats display for the item tells you nothing about it being special. Buried in a different menu page that normally just contains item related lore is a brief message telling you the item lets you see invisible enemies. Just awful design.

Staggering and being staggered by enemies is a *huge* part of the game. A weapon's stagger stat is probably more important than its ability to deal direct damage. Luckily, the equip menu displays this stat where it is easily viewable. Just kidding, there is no where in the game you can see this stat at all, for any piece of equipment, ever. At least you can see a stagger bar that shows you how close enemies are to having their stance broken. Just kidding, there's nothing like that anywhere in the game. But at least you can see a stagger bar for the player character. Just kidding...Well, you get it by now.

Elden ring just feels so, so sickeningly bad to play. Player movement is ponderously slow, and there is a noticeable delay before the player executes any attacks. I just can't overemphasize enough how *unmotivated* the player character behaves as they lethargically, limply swing their weapon. And that's not even taking into account the restrictive stamina system. 

But, if you spend enough time leveling up endurance, you can eventually circumvent this problem. Just kidding, welcome to "soft caps". Far before you can increase your stamina to the point the game doesn't feel like a slog, you start getting massively reduced returns. Like, you can still put more points into endurance, but it only increases stamina by one measly point per level.

In fact, Elden Ring mostly robs the player of feeling stronger as they level up. You can definitely find a lot of weapons, and those weapons can definitely be upgraded, but I've never seen a better example of illusory progression than the effect player attribures have in this game. Even endgame weapons that scale "well" with dexterity give something like a 0.33 percent increase in damage for every level of dexterity. There is also not even a remote semblance of different character attributes being balanced, the best build, for every type of character, is always one that emphasizes vigor to gain HP. Focusing on any other attribute instead is playing a challenge game. 

The worst thing about the game is how it generates difficulty. Remember how I told you that the player lacks any sort of agility? Well, the developers decided that meshed well with a lot of platforming and (usually lethal) fall damage. Enemies also have every movement related advantage that the player doesn't. In addition to turning invisible, they can charge, sprint, dodge quickly and energetically, teleport, and don't seem to care about stamina or MP. Another thing enemies do so often it I consider it to be the game's trademark, is attack the player from across the level with devastating ranged abilities. I'm talking about what basically amounts to artillery, and does tons of damage and knock the player down. And when I say "across the level" I don't just mean they aren't super nearby, I mean it is often genuinely difficult to figure out where these attacks are coming from because they originate so far away.

My favorite terrible thing the game does is this: player attacks terminate when weapon swing arcs hit an obstacle. The game *meticulously* checks for these collisions when the player attacks. And so, when I ended up in combat with an enemy on the other side of a wall, I thought "ah, I'm safe, the game is super careful to check if obstacles block swings." And then the enemy attack totally ignored the wall and hit me anyway.

Generating difficulty in games is both very easy and very hard. It's easy to put obstacles in front of the player, but hard to do it in a way that feels fair. Elden Ring feels like a game where the developers didn't come remotely close to understanding this, and instead generated challenge in the most lazy and uncreative way possible. It feels like the work of a self-absorbed amateur. 

There are so, so many more terrible things I could say about this game, but unfortunately I only have limited space.

Three times, I've tried to like this game. The internet makes such a big deal of it. Every time, I fail. 

The mechanics feel like they push back. And in some games, that works for it, forces you to wonder, to jiggle the handles, to test and begin picking a mystery apart. Here, it feels less like a mystery, and more like they're manufacturing confusion. Some of the arbitrary rules don't seem like they're grounded in the world, but in game balance, and there doesn't feel like there's more depth to some of them than that.

The character gets clear signals that the player can't interpret without a lot of experimenting, and we don't know what that signal is. NPCs that should PROBABLY warn you that you'll die if you mishandle the stuff they give you, don't. And why? Because mystery, I guess. Corrupting the narrative to make it more mysterious, like a sitcom where the main character turns stupid when the plot needs him to misunderstand.

I know it's probably a good game for the right kind of player. It's too popular not to have captured its own niche with skill. But I can't recommend.

This is a good game. Yes a good game not an excellent one. It certainly doesn't live up to its hype and one of its biggest flaw, actually being its open world.

But first lets get to the good parts of the game:
- combat: still works great, with a lot of different enemies and movesets to keep you busy experementing.
- legacy dungeons: these are smaller areas that kinda work as the level-like areas in former Dark Souls entries and they are most of the time very good, like you are used to, with shortcuts great enemy placement etc. Some of them are very short, but most of them are really great and are parts  where Elden Ring shines and shows that FromSoft is still capable of pulling that sort of quality out.
- enemy design: again one thine I really enjoy much also in former entries and here in Elden Ring the enemy designs show a great variety and range from standard soldiers to intersting fantasy species to creepy horror apperances. A little caveat come already here, when enemy types pop up at areas where they seemingly dont belong
- Mechanics: Overall I admire how much depths of mechanics is put into the game. You have upgrading, can change affinity of weapons, can calll Spirits to help, which you can also upgrade, you can mix your own potion, use great runes, make your own signs into the map etc.. - if you got runes you always find a way to spend them 
- variety of weapons: this is also sth I want to point out: you are faced with a huge amount of a great choice of weapons. There are over 300 weapons spread across 32 categories. Not all of them are useful and ofc most of them are useful more or less to a certain build, but you can pretty easily respec your char (which is limited) to try out different builds. I had a lot of fun experimenting with it, until I reached the point where every build I tested came to more or less the same dmg output just in different colors.

So far that all sounds very fun you might say and wonder where that negative criticism derives from. Well, now I will share the drawbacks of that game and they will become more and more significant the longer the game lasts:

- first of all the open world: this is an empty and hollow world with no real background living behind it or living behind the inhabitants of the world. It´s more like you travel from one diorama to the next. When you reach a certain trigger point that diorama sets in motion. This becomes even worse since the two first areas are very similiar to each other and very boring. The way you uncover this world is better than in most open world games, yes, since you dont have your map cluttered with items, but still its a shallow world
- Questdesign: this is also a huge problem. FromSoft stayed with their established formular of stumbling into NPCs which then give you cryptic instructions (well a bit less cryptic than in former games, but still very cryptic). Then you are left up with trying to figure out where to find this NPC next. Only problem is, since this game is open world and these NPCs sometimes travel to locations you already have been, you might never find them again. Also if you reach certain areas before you met this NPC you will miss the entire questline. Since I want to see as much content as possible and not that guy who plays a huge open world game a second time, I was lot reading where to find all these NPCs, which I think is not fun anymore at a certain point. Also the quests also lead to the same fate for their protagonists.
- Dungeons: and here I am not speaking of these level-like dungeons but of the smaller dungeons which are all around in this world. There are four or five types of dungeons which are all build very similiar and follow the same formular. At the end you will always find a boss or chest with some loot. They get boring very quickly and feel like a classical filler of a too big open world. In most dungeons you also find the same enemy types which even more make them boring. 
- enemy variety: yes you read it right. I praised the variety further above, but its just the overall variety. So here are more dffetnt types then i.e. Dark Souls 3. But the longer the game lasts the lesser the variation gets, since in new areas are all the same enemies just in different combninations. They also just have more dmg output and a higher healt bar, which make progress seem pale because you wonder why this enemy takes so much more hits than he needed two areas before. Also, some stroy-unique bosses get reused, which make them feel less unique. I dont have a problem with mini-boss reusage if it fits the scenario, but story important characters reused breaks the immersion and the meaning.
- Bosss-fights: Speaking of bosses, the boss-fights are some of the weakest parts of the game. Either you are most of the time overpowered for the average mini or dungeon bosses or you run into annoying boss fights which have the following problems: the bosses spam aggressively their attacks with no stamina constraints. They use input reading which means they don't react to what you do, they react the moment you press a button, before your action has even started. This also becomes relevant when they use their huge wind up to delay their attacks. If you cant stand the tensions and press the dodge button they turn towards you and strike their attack just in that moment. These wind-ups mess up dodge timing and ruins the rythm of the fight, which also becomes very unnatural since you dont react to what the enemy does but more try to guess when his delayed will finally come down to react.
- Upgrading: I said I had a lot of fun experimenting with weapons, which is true, but there is also a caveat to the system. Upgrading material is scarce, you can find items which allow you to buy these materials at a special merchant, but grinding for upgrade material can become tedious. But its neccassary, since if you change your build you will need your new weapons at the same level as your weapons you had before, because otherwise you wont deal enough damage.
- Bonfires: this is one of the biggest problems, which is a result of an open world. There are bonfires everywhere. The problem that encompasses this design is, that there is no real tension if you die, no real meaning for shortcuts. The amount here is ridiculous. There are some areas where bonfire placement is scarce and they are great for that, but overall it breaks the mechanics  for a soulslike.
- Music: the music is lackluster. Music playing in different area is just some annoying ambience rattle, which gets nerve-racking pretty quickly. The music of boss-fights is mostly very uninspired and just gets better towards the end. Only good titel here is the main screen music in my opinion. If you wanna here good background music which is fitting for each area you should try out Tainted Grail: Fall of Avalon, which does a formidable work in this aspect.
- PVP: this is a double-edged sowrd, but as so many of these criticims it becomes worse the longer the game lasts: you cant play in a relaxing coop, because if you do, you will always almost instantly get invaded. Either you fight some hardcore-super-pros which will kill you instantly, what will be almost the best outcome, because there is a bonfre nearby and you can go on. But often you get invaders which will hide somewhere or runaway if they realize they cant win. Thats a problem because invading closes the area and you cant leave until invader or you is deafeated. From my almost 200 hrs you can easily discount 40-50 hrs of being invaded and need to find or follow invader and then regroup with teammember. Because if you die you have to summon your friend again, which often doesnt work to disconnects, then you need to restart the game - so after hundreds of invasions where you actually dont fight - no fun!

So after all I would not recommend the game to anyone who has the inner commitment to fully complete a game (as I do) because it becomes more and more a chore. 78 / 100

To preface this, I put over 120 hours into this game in 2022 on console. I love this game.

However, I don't recommend this game on PC. It was not designed for PC. The game/animations are max 60 frames (or it will break the combat systems, a massive pitfall of FromSoftware game design), and the game has limited settings available to configure the game correctly for a PC level of experience. The default vsync function does not work, the game resolution breaks completely if you try to play it while you have more than one monitor connected, and you can't click off the game screen even when it's in windowed mode. There are so many issues with the PC port of this game it genuinely ruins the experience. I paid good money for both the base game and the DLC, I should not have to be troubleshooting workarounds to fix basic functions of the game. 

This is a souls game, therefore it has a level of difficulty that's unmatched by any other game. BUT, on top of the actual gameplay difficulty, the developers couldn't be bothered to finish certain functions of the game so that they work properly. The lock on system is a prime example of this. It is nearly impossible to lock on to the target you want to hit. You'll be locked onto an enemy, and another will attack you from another direction that you can clearly see coming, but you can't do anything about it because you're frantically cycling through locking on all other enemies before you reach the one that you need to hit in that moment. Game difficulty is a lazy excuse for an incomplete game. It should be difficult but feel good to play. This is not the case for this game on PC.

A complete game should never be at a point where you have to do actual research before your every move to make sure you are not breaking questlines. Unfortunately, you can break questlines permanently in this game. You can't just save the game manually before doing something and reload if it destroys your whole playthrough. The only way to save the game is by saving AND exiting. This is not a game you should play for the story, but the rewards earned by completing quests warrant a complete and functional questline system.

This game's exploration, content quantity, and graphics are incredible. That being said, this game is incredibly overrated. I sincerely hope FromSoftware fixes this PC port, even if they have to re-configure their game engine. That will likely never happen. Do not buy this on PC if you want the proper Elden Ring experience.

Problem pojawia się jednak w trakcie rozgrywki. Dość często okazuje się, że build, który wcześniej działał bardzo dobrze, nagle przestaje być skuteczny. W pewnym momencie trafiamy na ścianę i przeciwnicy lub bossowie zaczynają być wyraźnie trudniejsi dla konkretnego stylu gry. W efekcie gracz zamiast rozwijać postać według własnej wizji zaczyna dostosowywać się do wymagań konkretnych walk.

Oprawa wizualna i świat gry

Pod względem artystycznym gra prezentuje się znakomicie. Świat jest ogromny, różnorodny i pełen charakterystycznych lokacji, a każdy region ma swój klimat i wizualną tożsamość.

Na uwagę zasługuje również historia świata współtworzona przez George R. R. Martin. Lore jest ciekawy i intrygujący, choć duża część fabuły pozostaje ukryta w opisach przedmiotów i fragmentach dialogów. Dla jednych jest to element budujący tajemnicę świata, dla innych bariera w odbiorze historii.

Problemy z kamerą

Największą wadą gry jest kamera. To właśnie tutaj pojawia się najwięcej sytuacji prowadzących do frustracji.

Podczas walki z przeciwnikiem można zablokować kamerę na celu. W teorii ma to pomagać w śledzeniu przeciwnika, ale w praktyce często prowadzi do chaosu. Kamera potrafi się gubić, nagle zmieniać pozycję albo ustawiać pod dziwnym kątem. W efekcie gracz nie widzi ani ataków przeciwnika, ani czasami nawet własnej postaci.

Problem szczególnie nasila się przy dużych przeciwnikach. Kamera potrafi wtedy ustawić się tak blisko modelu bossa, że trudno ocenić sytuację na ekranie. Próba grania bez blokady celu również nie rozwiązuje problemu, ponieważ kamera nadal potrafi poruszać się samoczynnie i nie zawsze pozostaje tam, gdzie gracz chciałby ją ustawić. W praktyce oznacza to, że część zgonów nie wynika z błędu gracza ani z poziomu trudności walki, lecz z problemów technicznych i projektowych.

Powtarzalność przeciwników i bossów

Kolejną wadą jest design przeciwników oraz powtarzalność wielu walk. W wielu miejscach widać wyraźne użycie metody kopiuj i wklej. Boss, z którym wcześniej stoczyliśmy efektowną walkę, później pojawia się jako zwykły przeciwnik w innej lokacji.

Osłabia to poczucie wyjątkowości starć i sprawia, że niektóre momenty przestają być tak znaczące, jak powinny. Walki bywają widowiskowe, ale to nie zawsze oznacza, że są dobrze zaprojektowane. Niektóre starcia sprawiają wrażenie mocno oskryptowanych. Czasami wygląda to tak, jakby można je było przejść sensownie tylko jednym konkretnym stylem gry, ponieważ inne podejścia są znacznie trudniejsze.

Podejście do nowych graczy

Gra nie szanuje również graczy, którzy wcześniej nie mieli styczności z tytułami typu Souls. W wielu momentach zakłada się, że gracz już zna mechaniki charakterystyczne dla tego gatunku. Systemy gry są słabo tłumaczone i wiele rzeczy trzeba odkrywać metodą prób i błędów.

Popularność marki w dużej mierze opiera się na opinii o jej wyjątkowej trudności. W praktyce jednak spora część tej trudności wynika z problemów projektowych. Nieczytelność walki, problemy z kamerą czy niespójne decyzje designerskie sprawiają, że gra bywa wymagająca nie dlatego, że przeciwnicy są świetnie zaprojektowani, ale dlatego, że niektóre elementy gry utrudniają komfortowe granie.

System punktów odrodzenia

Dobrym przykładem niespójnego designu jest system punktów odrodzenia. Czasami ognisko znajduje się dosłownie przed areną bossa, a dodatkowo mamy jeszcze statuę, która pozwala odrodzić się jeszcze bliżej. W innych sytuacjach po każdej śmierci trzeba pokonywać długą drogę z ogniska do bramy bossa.

Przy trudniejszych przeciwnikach, takich jak Malenia, Blade of Miquella, oznacza to, że spora część czasu nie jest poświęcona samej walce. Zamiast tego gracz biegnie z powrotem do areny i ponownie nakłada buffy przed starciem. W efekcie nawet jedna czwarta czasu spędzonego przy bossie może polegać po prostu na powtarzaniu tej samej drogi.

Podsumowanie

Elden Ring jest produkcją pełną kontrastów. Z jednej strony oferuje piękny świat, ciekawy lore i ogromne możliwości budowania postaci. Z drugiej strony cierpi na wyraźne problemy projektowe, takie jak praca kamery, powtarzalność przeciwników czy niespójne rozwiązania w designie walk.

Nie jest to zła gra, ale zdecydowanie nie jest też tak bezbłędna, jak sugerują niektóre opinie. Część graczy wynosi ją na piedestał głównie ze względu na renomę studia FromSoftware, a niekoniecznie przez faktyczną jakość wszystkich elementów gry. To tytuł, który potrafi zachwycić wizją świata, ale jednocześnie momentami potrafi też bardzo frustrować.

An amazing artistic work with cool exploration, but the worst gameplay ever put in a AAA game.

1.  There's no pause button.  Immediately that's just unacceptable to not have a basic game feature such as pausing.  Also you can't open an check your map if there's an enemy nearby.  Why?  I'm trying to navigate and there are basically always enemies nearby.  This is just annoying and there's no reason for it.

2.  Multiplayer system requires in-game resources which need to be repeatedly used if someone dies.  This is pointless.

3.  Combat is slow, clunky, unresponsive, insufferable, and unfortunately a big part of the game.  Playing as a mage, your character takes so long to cast a spell you're just going to get hit doing it.  Your spells rely on guzzling infinite potions, but your character also takes so long to drink a potion that you're also going to get hit doing that.  There's also a lock-on feature since there's no actual cross-hairs to aim spells, but your character can't actually aim straight.  You can "lock on" to an enemy, and your character will just miss anyway, burning more of your magic meter in the process through no control of your own.  I swear, Skyrim of all games had better magic use than this because you could actually just aim magic yourself.  On top of this, your spells have an absolutely pitiful range.  You could throw a rock farther than you could cast a spell.  Also the spells don't aim where you're aiming, they aim where your body direction is pointing.

Speaking of guzzling potions.  You can get away with not having to drink health potions if you're good enough since you can mostly dodge damage outside of some attacks that just fill the whole screen, however for magic you just need to.  You will also need to select spells to use.  Both of these require you to use the game's cycling menu.  Normal games would have some sort of wheel you pull up to select an item or spell.  Instead, the developers make you cycle through spells and potions in a one-way selection scroll by pressing up or down on your D-Pad.  So you also have to frantically manage an unintuitive and clunky spell and potions selection system amidst the slow and clumsy character gameplay.

Your character can "dodge", but is so slothful even with a lighter load that it's a good second between pressing the button and him rolling as if you're playing a laggy online game.  This is fairly integral to the game, and so having so central a mechanic be so slow, and also not actionable if you're drinking a potion for example, is completely insane and against any sort of common sense.  You would think if the character had any sense of self-preservation whatsoever they would supercede drinking a potion with rolling and moving out of the way of an incoming attack.  Not so.  Our stupid hero has an IQ of a lemming and zero regard for his own life, and so if you try to hit that dodge button while drinking a potion or performing an action, nothing will happen.  The devs programmed the character to simply be stupid and you have little control over what he does moment to moment.  You almost need to think of it as a turn based game rather than an action game, and lock in your actions in a queue far ahead of time, like playing chess by mail.

Compare this to something like DOOM.  You have fast attack power, intuitive aiming, responsive movement.  Combat actions are entirely in your hands in other better games, not arguing with an in-game avatar to do what it's told.  Playing this game and its controls feel so disconnected it's as if I'm yelling at the character what to do and he's a bit hard of hearing so only registers it a second or so after.  This is just what we'd call basic unresponsive controls in any other game and it's not really charming or excusable here just because the art is nice.

4.  The game's "difficulty" is pretty much just based on levelling and enemies having bigger numbers than your numbers, and the above described incompetent controls.  The "action" of the "action RPG" is better served if you're running melee, because with magic you are hard locked to the amount of meter you have to trade into damage dealt.  It's a math equation more than any sort of action.

5.  I swear, I thought we were done with garbage cameras in games, but this one if you use the targeting system (there is no other way to actually aim) the camera absolutely freaks out so you can't see anything if you're close to the enemy you're targeting in many cases, especially with big bosses.

6.  The final boss is pathetic.  The first stage is easy, the second just runs away from you the entire time.  It's not even really a boss fight so much as a marathon simulator.  Doesn't matter if you're magic or melee, your magic has no range so you'll have to be running after it either way.  It's extremely anticlimactic, especially after there were a couple of cool bosses right before leading up to it.  The boss you fight right before the final boss should have been the final boss, felt like a much more intense battle.

Overall it's like a beautiful woman with a nightmare personality.  The game is gorgeous to look at, and then absolutely unbearable to actually interact with.  At best combat just becomes boring and repetitive while having to slog through the controls.  Instead the game shines most when exploring, and is like pulling teeth when you have to actually play it.

Good game in general, but the difficulty is all artificial. The actual mechanics are not hard whatsoever, the only difficulty that they put in the game is delayed attacks in an attempt to throw you off, but every single enemy has delayed attacks that look completely unnatural and buggy at times. And it's not just an enemy holding their stance until they can reach you with their weapon, they run up to you and don't swing until they literally touch your body so you can't accurately predict the attack, which in turn makes the enemy roll-catch you 9/10 times. That does not take skill to learn, that takes luck and legit immediate reaction. There are corner enemies everywhere that you cannot do anything to bait out, they are hard coded to not react unless you pass in front of them, making throwables absolutely useless for distractions/flushing them out (which in turn, makes throwables completely useless in the overall game because they suck for damage). The only way you can do anything against enemies that are super tucked into a corner without having to risk the buggy AI is having an AOE spell that goes through walls, and you hope it reaches while their weapons go through the wall to hit you somehow. It's also an open world game that punishes you for exploring by way of locking you out of countless quests and items with no prior warning or even interaction whatsoever, which in my opinion is just a way to inflate the amount of people who continue into NG+ so they can go back and get stuff that shouldn't have been locked in the first place. There is barely a quest system, and it's extremely barebones and lazy, not to mention buggy at times, which again, in turn inflates NG+ numbers so that people can hopefully do the quest that bugged out on them. This game runs on hype and depends on fans who dismiss any kind of criticism as "you're bad". Those people are the reason the DLC was as shallow as it was, and why FromSoft has such an awful relationship with their community. They change what they want, when they want with no regard for the community. For example, they changed the menus to be sluggish and slower and refused to revert it despite community-wide backlash all in the name of fixing an unrelated bug. They pigeonhole players into going with a magic or bleed build, because any other build is mid at best and they nerf any other weapon that is even remotely good into complete uselessness. The only good bosses in the DLC that actually have cool mechanics and no bullshit delayed attacks are killed in a minute or two because they have so little health, all while providing absolutely no story whatsoever. We went through the entire expansion just to be told something that we have known since the game's release. The only well-made boss in the game is Bayle, his attacks aren't delayed, you can tell when he's charging up an attack, you can differentiate between his attacks, and his fight is difficult enough to be satisfying to learn and he has enough health for the fight to actually feel like a fight. Compare that to a buggy fight like Godskin Duo, which FromSoft has of course refused to address the awful geometry of the room, which makes a mechanic completely unavoidable at times whenever the boss feels like rolling over the broken pillars. The scariest and most toe-curling part of the game is hiding behind a broken pillar and hoping the Noble doesn't run you over. Them endlessly reusing bosses and movesets aside, the fact that the Godskin Duo fight even made it into the game in the first place shows they are just constantly searching for ways to make the game difficult and bullshit instead of just designing a fight properly and incorporating the difficulty into the mechanics themselves. Make the mechanics harder, fix bugs in the fights and the geometry of multiple fights, and give players freedom to make their own viable build without having to resort to mods to buff certain things to be useable in the first place. That cool looking spell that you get for killing Radahn and Miquella? Complete trash, because it's holy damage and holy has always been trash. It hurts your eyes more than the enemies. I would love to make a build surrounding such a visually appealing spell, but it would become a challenge run just by using the spell. Divine power channeled into a mini nuke will tickle a wolf, but if you kill some vulgar shrimp lover in the middle of a swamp, you get one of the best weapons in the game, which is just a downgraded version of another best weapon in the game, which you find off a random corpse in a dark corner.
All that being said, I would say the game overall is fun. For me, the fun is exploring and getting overpowered so that I don't have to deal with all the bullshit, though some of it is just unavoidable. I would say that I wish they would make armor better and more of a help than a hinderance, but it is widely agreed that Fashion Souls is more important than stats, and I completely agree. I'm a moon mage dressed in black with the hat and mask of someone who turned people into puppets. I look badass. Another prop I will give FromSoft is that they made a LOT of different ways to do stuff. Challenge runs will open your eyes to this. Can't jump? Use one of the ashes of war that makes you jump. There are multiple ways to get to certain important locations, many of which let you get to the locations earlier than you usually would which is extremely important in my eyes in order to prevent doing the same thing. The bell bearings are really nice so that you don't have to waste time grinding most of the materials in the game. All I can hope is that FromSoft takes the good from this game, and then builds even more good on top of it while keeping in touch with their community.

Pros
This game offers a huge variety of weapon builds, making it great for players who love playing with different weapons.

Cons
Many legendary weapons are hidden in corners of the world. Without a guide, they’re very hard to be found.

The game’s guidance is quite poor. In the starting area, you basically have no idea what you’re supposed to do. If you just follow the Sites of Grace, it becomes a typical Souls-like experience. But if you use a guide such as reddit or youtube to quickly locate legendary weapons, then it stops being a Souls-like exploration game and becomes more of a “power trip” game. However, with a guide, you’ll also get spoiled a lot, which takes away the joy of discovery. BTW, many of the town/city maps and dungeons in this game are extremely confusing, and without video walkthroughs, it’s easy to get lost.

Summary
This game is best suited for players who have plenty of time and enjoy exploring on their own;
or for players who have limit time or don’t care about the story, use reddit/youtube guides to quickly grab your ideal weapons, and experience all the content.

I wish I could like this game more, God knows I tried. It is very reminiscent of the way Morrowind made me feel many moons ago. It doesn't hold your hard, it encourages exploration, it encourages experimentation, the open world and world building are absolutely incredible, and it is overall extremely interesting. That said, just about everything else is insanely underwhelming. Obviously the game is insanely unfair towards the player. It isn't a hard game, it is an unfair game. Some people really like the feeling of accomplishment from beating their head against the wall for hours until it finally breaks, and I'm definitely not against a challenge, but what doesn't feel rewarding is defeating a boss because you got lucky. And sure, some things are worth suffering through for the reward, except there really isn't any reward other than saying you did it. There is clearly lore and some semblance of a story here, but there is absolutely no coherent storyline or characters for me to feel invested in whatsoever, which makes the idea of working through yet another insanely cheap and unfair boss encounter all the more uninteresting. I've played for over 65 hours this point and couldn't tell you why I'm doing anything in the game other than I guess because it's my destiny to do so or something? The insane thing is I'm actually the kind of player to go and explore and try to read and interact with everything I can. I will interact with every NPC and exhaust every dialogue trying to learn more about worlds like this that are very interesting, but there quite literally isn't a narrative at all. The combat feels pretty generic and uninteresting, like a more hardcore version of Skyrim.

What is disappointing is I felt this way around 5 hours into the game but decided I would give it the good ole college try, but here I am at 65+ hours feeling the exact same. If you like the genre, you'll probably enjoy this. If you're okay with an insanely unfair challenge, give it a go. If you're looking for a truly wonderful open world experience with interesting boss fights, you'll easily get dozens of hours out of this game. If you're looking for a game with depth to really draw you into its world and immerse you, then this isn't it. It was fun working through some castles while watching videos on my second monitor. Definitely feels insanely overhyped. 

I'd probably give it a 6.5/10. If you like open worlds, RPG games, and aren't averse to challenge, maybe give it a try especially if its on sale. The real crime is if you don't play the game, you really aren't missing out on anything. No one is ever going to say "Whaaat, you didn't play Elden Ring!?"
