I’ve been at conflict with myself on whenever to rate this game as positive or negative.
But considering this is AAA title and GOTY holder - Based on my experience with the game I’ve decided to be a little bit more harsh in reviewing this based on the title of the game, and thus it’s negative.

It will be a little lengthy - to put a negative stick into what a lot of people treasure i’ll need to describe it properly.
I’ve beat the game like the other 22% of players lol.

Elden ring is not my first souls like experience, I have played Code Vein and Lords of the fallen before,  but it’s my first experience with From Software games - as a pioneer in the genre, and widely praised for their design - I expected a lot. You might say a shit eater only knows how shit tastes like, well if Elden Ring is a donut, then it might look like Donut but it still tastes like shit.

I know the game does not really have any difficulty settings officially - but my friend who is a fan of the series provided me with feedback that magic is basically what you call easy mode in this game, and so I’ve ventured on the adventure with this game as a warrior. 

The game start harsh for a new player you being lore dumped with new lore about new world and then thrown into tutorial area where you can experience for the first time horrible control design of FromSoftware - I’ve been told it was even worse in their first games, but what retard though it’s good idea to put sprint on holding B on pad, and jump on A - sprint jump requires you to bend your thumb to some weird angles and then hope you are doing it correct - there are countless other examples in gaming where this was done better - you can’t rebind - like the friend said - “get used to it” - and that seems like the motto of this game tbh.

Anyway, the tutorial is to smash or get smashed - I was smashed.



The first time you see the world - it is truly magical - I can see the care and attention put into the world design - you are instantly encouraged to explore the world. Too bad the world does not have much to offer. Let me explain.

The Elden Ring story is a main quest which involves 13 bosses, every other boss is optional and the story is tied to main bosses. Dialogues, lore dumps, interesting bits - all tied to the main story. Now what about side content - There are some side quests in a old school type where you don’t have a marker of where to go or what to do - which are something you do for npc you find in the world, for example carrying a message to the father of daughter to the fort he is stationed at, you get some lore bits for that - that’s nice. But what about the rest of the world? Dungeons? Smaller bosses - like Erdtree Avatars? - Nah, not even fucking notes. Don’t get me wrong - the main quest is great - I enjoyed it - It was great - I don’t have anything wrong to slap there - but the main story is not the whole game, and that’s what I am essentially reviewing.

Almost every dungeon is the same thing - enter, avoid traps, find levers, unlock doors - kill the boss and leave. No story about why this boss is here, is this a prison? Who was held here? Who was the boss, why was he here? There is literally nothing about it - almost every location is just a location with no ties to the massive canvas of beautiful world you are in. I am sucker for good story, and I love discovering bits about lore - when they are presented to me in an enjoyable way - I don’t want to bother with navigating this dogshit UI of an inventory that they didn’t bother to change since DS1 to view description of items and read the lore about items - that’s moronic design. To understand the world of Elden RIng you either need to know someone who loves the world and spend time getting to know it a little better like my friend, watch a youtube lore videos or maybe read a book - anything other than main story quest - I dunno maybe if you look hard enough you will find some.

Speaking of DS1 - combat is ass.
Now the boss fights are amazing, I love design, the animations are flashy and visual, they are dancing on the field - no complaints - other than Dragons - but nobody likes dragon fights from what I heard.

You, the player, have the most wooden animation possible - I have cross referenced the animations and they are exactly the same animations they’ve used in DS1 - no changes at all, every class dodges the same, every class attacks the same. One handed animation looks like it's from Minecraft. The special skills have some flash - some work done - I can see those apart from previous games - that means developers actually worked on them instead of coping and pasting it from previous games like movement, dodges and basic attacks. Most games I played when they used previous animations they were used as a base and then refined upon, not in Elden Ring - GOTY btw. The magic looks cool, the magic weapons look cool - but I was told it's an easy mode - Don’t use magic I was told - You will get bored quick, well I am bored anyways.

Combat gets so fucking dull after a while, that you are hoping that at least story will prevent you from falling asleep. But like I’ve mentioned before when you are exploring - forget about the story you won’t get anything.

While the world is amazingly pretty, for the most part it’s empty - Hey is that ruined tower atop of the cliff? I wonder what’s there, a bunch of trash mobs, 1 elite and a few golden runes scattered on the ground and few plants. So just some ruins like most of the ruins and locations you find in the world - there is nothing special about it, definitely not a story that would set it apart, or I dunno a small dialogue for the present Monster when they idle. Nah.

The RNG loot in Single Player experience is just retarded - Hey that Cuckoo Knight looks cool I wonder if I can get his armor, you can after 50 kills or more if your RNG is shit. At the very fucking least the inventory weight is only counted on what you are wearing not the stash you are hoarding, that would get annoying pretty quick to teleport to round table to sell another 10 pair of boots because you are over-encumbered.

Now the PVP - I wouldn’t review if it wasn’t forced on you.
I know it is some kind of tradition from FromSoftware games, that you can invade other players' worlds and kill them for trash loot. I been told by my friend that it operates on vengeance basic, a new player is invaded by heavy sweat that puts 3000 hours in this game, is easily outskilled and killed, and when they eventually get good stuff and level they proceed to do the same to another new player, and circle of vengeance is closed. I saw there is an arena for the players to PVP in, but most of the players apparently do not want to be matched against same level players - they could lose, that’s not as fun as bullying low levels. There is no cool loot for these encounters for either invader or the one being invaded, so they just do it for pure pleasure of bullying the weak. You cannot out-yourself from PVP, it's hard locked as enabled, the only way to avoid it is to play offline. Also another fun note - If you disable anti-cheat and start cheating, the game is too retarded to detect that the client has disabled anti-cheat and will still allow players to invade you. So the anti-cheat is so retarded that it will prevent you from cheating, but it won’t prevent you from matching with a cheater without anti-cheat. I am just leaving it here as another fun point on why PVP is pointless in this game.

The Game of The Year - I expected such a game to be set apart from the competition - after all it claimed the title at the top - but me it’s 5/10 or 6/10 if being generous, It’s really mediocre, and there are rip-offs who offer more condensed package rather than pretty open and empty world. The art, music, visuals might be GOTY worthy but the actual content - definitely not.

It's a From Software game which as a result inherits many of the good mechanics from the Dark Souls series and forms a great base for gameplay however it is ruined by the addition of the needless open world design. The world feels empty and did not make new game plus enjoyable through its repetitive dungeons and reuse of bosses as common enemies. The disuse of previous linear and interconnected design of Dark Souls negatively impacted the game's travelling and discourages normal traversal of the world in favour of the fast travel system. 

The PvP scene is very lively albeit highly over tuned, power-stancing certain weapons such as great spears deals far too much damage, in addition, many spells and weapons seem far too powerful comparatively to the rest of the roster leading to fights being repetitive. Whilst some weapon such as rivers of blood received a rightful nerf, it seems to have inherent balance issues. 

The boss fights in this game whilst visually stunning, relies heavily on delayed attacks intertwined with normal attacks or attacks requiring the player to stay in a safe zone or risk an instant death, an example being Malenia. Not every boss displays these attack types however it seems that, from the base roster, and the new DLC, that From Software has favoured such boss designs over the conventional ones found in previous games such as Bloodborne or Dark Souls. The community's common response of "Git Gud" focuses on the difficulty rather than inherent boss design, ignoring that memorising attack patterns can be done by anyone and a person who did successfully beat a boss may have criticisms of its design nonetheless.

I noticed there was a lack of genuine criticism, so here is everything I don't like about Elden Ring

I have sunk so so many hours in Elden Ring on both console and PC. I first bought the game when it came out and played it day one. I enjoyed Elden Ring during my first playthrough, but given time and multiple replays my opinion has drifted greatly since then. The world in Elden Ring is disgustingly empty or full of not so rewarding challenges and it doesn't get enough slack. I huge talking point near launch was the 100 bosses and that sounds great on paper, however 80% if not more are just repeats of usually not even good bosses to begin with. One experience I remember in particular is Morne Castle. Morne Castle is one of the legacy Dungeons in the game (areas which are more linear) probably one of my favorites in the game too. You work your way through this castle and fight a fairly cool boss at the end, only to fight the same boss again, and again... and then as a common enemy. It really takes away from the first experience on top of feeling lazy. The enemy variety gets very weak not even halfway through the game, and starts to make little sense as to why they are placed where they are. And don't forget the endless amount of copy and paste catacombs, caves, and encampments. On a new playthrough I would skip all side content and only do the essentials unless there was a specific item/weapon I wanted to use. One more final point is the lack of interesting NPCs in Elden Ring when compared to the other Souls games that Fromsoft has created. All of the endings for NPCs are usually very underwhelming/they end abruptly. Near the end game enemies and bosses alike do so much damage that if you want to avoid getting one shot, you need 60 Vigor. In DS3 about 27 vigor is all you need for both the base game and DLC.

To put it short (and add some tiny mentions)

1. Too many junk/repeat of junk bosses (82% of base game is repeats, 73% if you buy DLC)
2. Unrewarding exploration
3. Boring/Repetitive points of interests (Caves, Catacombs etc.)
4. Too much walking/riding to point A to B with not enough interesting AND rewarding points on the way
5. Crafting is either pointless or too annoying to farm resources for
6. Endgame enemies/bosses do too much damage while being spongy
7. Builds don't feel very different from one another
8. AOE attacks/hitboxes way bigger than they should be
(Side note, Online has and has had a huge hacking problem)

I've been playing the game through a mod called "Reforged" and have been enjoying it the game that way. Reforged alters combat greatly, changes balancing of weapons, adds many QoL changes, and so much more that I could never go back to base game. All of this isn't to say the base game is terrible. If you are the type to only do one run of a game and are not a completionist then you will probably finish this game and write it off as a solid experience. But too many people refuse to criticize the game and the community of Fromsoft doesn't take kindly to anything that isn't glaze. I've seen people get clowned on for simply saying "I wish this boss was a little different" or "Anyone else think the open world is kind of empty?". It is one of the most hostile fan bases I have ever seen.

[h1] The Great Disappointment [/h1]
Game that was supposed to be great was shattered, but by whom? and why?
 Elden Ring, from all the fanfare and praise I heard about this game, I truly expected something special, one of best games of all time was finally in front of me, although I'm few years late to the party, and if it wasn't so hyped this would probably be a positive review. The patented FromSoft gameplay still works, you roll and then you hit(in second phase you cant hit on that timing anymore, find a new one bro), base of gameplay is as engaging as ever, but seemingly nobody bothered to fix issues that were already present in Dark Souls before, instead prioritizing adding new ones.
[h2] The Open Nothing [/h2]
One of the biggest changes from this title to previous ones FromSoft made is the inclusion of open world. So what did this bring to old formula? There's some stunning views in game, landmarks, like Eldentree on majority of land or Mohgwyn Palace from down below under second sky of Siofra River are very beautiful and stand out through your exploration. Thats about all pluses of it. One of things i realized after playing Elden Ring for about 20 hours is how extremely dull the exploration is. Main content might as well been a better linear game with better area transitions than ones that we sometimes have in open world. To punish you for exploring there's quite a few giant archers/catapults/other ranged bullshit that gets old after two encounters, with archers being by far the worst. Locations that you can stumble upon randomly that supposed to reward you for exploring are three main things - ruins, catacombs and mines. All of them are an exercise in ctrl+c and ctrl+v pressing in editor, you did one of them - you pretty much know rest of them:
 - Ruins are mostly small and just different placements of same textures with some staircase downwards leading to a chest, only differential is enemies of region.  
 - Mines are an exercise in moving same assets around and pretending you did something new, with mini-boss you probably already fought at end as a "reward", maybe if you're lucky you will get loot useful for your build from that. Even worse is that sometimes u actually NEED to go to mines to collect stones to upgrade your weapon, and they are certainly not good enough to ever go there more than once.
 - Especially offensive for me were catacombs, FromSoft wanted players to see them so much they even put statues lighting the way towards them scattered around the map, after you follow the blue light you will find... something similar to Ayleid Ruins from Oblivion(yes your main exploration target is about same as in RPG from 2006 that ran on xbox 360). Not only they all look the same and only difference is layout, but they also feature traps-cliche galore just like Todd wanted it. 
[h2] The sparce good and the vast ugly [/h2]
The standout of Miyazaki's modus operandi always was and will be one thing - boss fights. Elden Ring has about 200 bosses, and that roster also suffers heavily from disease of copypastetonis. Dragons are the worst of that world by far - not only are they all basically same, they are also plan and simple unfun, with AOE attacks either right under boss while you're trying to fight it, or after a little bit of flying in air always aiming at one side. These flying critters are mostly just waste of time, defeat one on your horseback and forget about them for rest of game(or until game forces you to fight more).
Around 30 out of 200 bosses are even worth actually talking about, and its truly a mixed bag. From heights of well designed fights like Godfrey, Godwyn and Godrick that make you realize that it was worth paying George R. R. Martin big bucks to come up with these names or first ever FromSoft gimmick boss that actually works brilliantly - God-Devouring Serpent. To straight up piles of hot garbage like ALL DRAGONS, Valiant Gargoyle, Godskin Duo and Crucible Knights, hopefully one day they will realize that putting two enemies that don't work together at all is not the best idea, and circling around them for 2 minutes to isolate one is not a fun challenge at all.
  However that's not what pained me most, the worst bosses of Elden Ring are the almost great bosses that for some reason got worse. Hardest challenge of game is Malenia(Blade of Miquella btw), with her smooth and interesting combos making a thrilling experience... up to the point she uses Waterfowl and you don't want to see that fight again. Or you can spend hours on boss just to learn one attack and realize that you're trying to dodge camera circling around, not attack itself. 
Or the long awaited and teased battle on top of Pantheon against Mohg, where just when you start having fun with it, up to point he randomly covers entire arena with AOE attack from sky, that stays on ground to fuck you over for quite a while, until you learn that for some reason you're supposed to dodge it into attack and stay next to boss that is doing AOE splatter damage from sky, not away from it, which visually and logically makes 0 sense.
 Or you fight against also very nice and dynamic Radagon, and awaiting to experience second phase you are greeted by one of worst bosses of the game. Elden Beast is glorified dragon-like boss, a boss that you need constantly run towards and get right under, just to get hit by attack you couldn't even see... because you need to be right under boss to hit it in first place, sadly FromSoft haven't figured out a way to zoom out camera for these fights just yet.
[h2] The everso bad [/h2]
While we're at camera, why is locking in still randomly breaking when boss is behind some column or other piece of geometry, just like it used to from way back in first Dark Souls? And when you try to lock in again you randomly look forward and get hit by attack you can't see anymore cause you're looking at nearby scenery for some reason.
Why there's random pieces of geometry scattered around boss arena to begin with, that will randomly fuck up your movement?
Why bosses and mobs attacks still go through walls like they exist only for player character?
Why can't game remember that i used to two hand this weapon when i switch back to it?
Why I can remember only two tracks from entire game's OST?
Why I'm forced to single-hand weapon near blacksmith where I'd actually like to see what upgrades I'm spending resources is doing, making numbers in UI entirely useless if I'm two-handing said weapon?
Why are all grab attacks getting a random 1m of extra range of animation even thought visually it looks like they shouldn't get you. Visual clarity and just general logic of some rolls is iffy sometimes, only way to understand which direction game actually wants you to roll is trial and error, not your eyes quite a few times.
Why are poison swamps and their alternatives still in game? How exactly standing around for minutes to wait for status effect meter to empty is fun or interesting?
Why are some bosses(especially Malenia) not doing anything for 40 seconds and if you try to attack them first you get punished? Surely you can use same code that makes them attack you after input reading your heal to speed it up a bit.

This is my first Souls-like game, so I’m leaving comments open in case someone wants to share their perspective or maybe spark my interest in the genre again. That said, I genuinely don’t see the appeal.

I played fairly deep into the game, far enough to defeat major bosses, slay something massive, and set something important on fire (no spoilers). So this isn’t a surface level take.

Story:
There barely is a story. What’s there feels vague and disconnected, more like a sequence of boss fights than a narrative. Lore exists, sure, but it’s buried so deeply that it never felt engaging or motivating to me. I never felt invested in what I was doing or why. Is it the genre? Like racing games where lore and story is not the point? 

Combat:
It’s… fine. Rarely exciting. The biggest issue is rewards: you’re showered with an overwhelming number of weapons, most of which feel completely pointless. Beating around 95% of bosses gives you nothing meaningful, which is a big problem when the game is essentially a boss-rush experience. Progress often feels hollow.

Setting:
The world is technically open, but it feels lifeless. There are almost no people, no real villages, no towns just ruins and enemies. Exploration didn’t feel rewarding or immersive, it felt empty. An open world should invite curiosity, not make you feel alone in a dead museum.

Overall I don’t understand the obsession. For me, Elden Ring feels more like endurance than enjoyment and I will not be returning to the genre again... Maybe for that Napoleon era game.

Great Game, Bad PC Experience

Elden Ring is an incredible game held back by a frustratingly outdated PC implementation. Despite running on powerful modern hardware, the game is hard-locked to 60 FPS with no official option to uncap it. In modern PC gaming, this feels unacceptable.

On high-refresh monitors, the game feels sluggish, heavy, and choppy, especially compared to newer soulslike titles such as Lords of the Fallen or Lies of P, which fully support uncapped framerates and modern display technology. Camera movement lacks fluidity, input feels delayed, and traversal never feels as smooth as it should—none of which are limitations of my hardware, but rather the game’s design choices.

What makes this worse is that the 60 FPS cap isn’t just a technical limitation, it’s a deliberate decision tied to FromSoftware’s aging engine. Players who want smoother gameplay must resort to unofficial mods, disable anti-cheat, and play offline, which is ridiculous for a premium AAA title.

Yes, the art direction, world design, and combat depth are outstanding. But great design doesn’t excuse poor PC optimization. A modern PC game should respect modern PC standards, and Elden Ring simply doesn’t.

If you’re used to 120-144Hz (or higher) gameplay, be prepared: Elden Ring will feel slow and dated no matter how strong your system is.

I fully acknowledge Elden Ring's popularity and wide appeal, unfortunately I have no desire to continue putting any more time into it, nor have I enjoyed the vast majority of my time playing. My lack of enjoyment comes from two sources, the setting and the gameplay.

Simple explanation first, my issues with the setting. I find it purposefully niche. Maybe if I was more interested in the overall aesthetic, I would be able to push through my disinterest in the plot or characters, unfortunately almost every boss, enemy, and NPC is ugly as sin. Yes, it is supposed to feel depressing and like you're up against larger-than-life enemies, but instead of feeling inspired to pick up my sword and fight until my last breath, I am completely uninterested, checked out, and bored. Nothing about Elden Ring's setting, characters, or enemies inspire or immerse me, and I will fully accept that this is not a fault of the game itself and simply a misalignment of my interests and the games inspiration. 

Next in my major concerns is gameplay. I find the combat in Elden Ring feels slow, sloppy, and difficult to navigate. I've fought enemies at high level, low level, for hours before beating them and beaten some before reading their name. While the time spent mastering my dodges is satisfying in some respects, I barely felt any level of enjoyment in beating enemies. What I did often feel was the relief of never having to fight them again, and the dread of having to fight something else.

Between my disinterest in the setting and the gameplay I struggled to have any enjoyment, regardless of the method or approach. I envy those who find this gameplay engaging. From the stories I've heard it FromSoftware games have been lifechanging for some and I don't doubt their effect on most, but for me this was time I wish I could get back.

Elden Ring is what happens when a studio mistakes inconvenience for artistic vision and then refuses to fix it out of sheer stubbornness.

The game advertises freedom and exploration, yet punishes curiosity at every turn. Stray too far and you’re either deleted by enemies clearly not meant for your level, or rewarded with empty ruins, recycled mobs, and loot that exists purely to waste your time. The open world isn’t deep — it’s stretched thin, padded with repetition, and held together by vague mysticism and fan excuses.

Combat, once a FromSoftware strength, now feels bloated and erratic. Bosses rely heavily on delayed attacks, input-reading, and absurd damage spikes that test patience more than skill. Winning often feels less like mastery and more like surviving questionable balancing decisions.

Then there’s the technical embarrassment: no proper ultrawide support. In 2022 and beyond, Elden Ring proudly greets ultrawide users with black bars, as if modern displays are some kind of experimental luxury. Want to actually use your screen? Enjoy third-party fixes — and the delightful knowledge that using them can break online functionality.

Which brings us to the punchline: to play comfortably, you’re better off offline. Mods and fixes that make the game tolerable force you out of online mode, turning a supposedly shared world into a mandatory single-player exile. Messages, invasions, co-op — all sacrificed on the altar of FromSoftware’s rigid anti-cheat philosophy. The result? A game where the best experience requires disconnecting from half of its advertised features.

The narrative hides behind obscurity like a legal disclaimer. Critical story beats are fragmented, whispered, or buried in item descriptions, daring players to call it “deep lore” instead of what it often is: incomplete storytelling dressed as mystery.

In the end, Elden Ring is not a bold evolution — it’s an indulgent self-parody. A massive world that doesn’t respect your time, a technical design that doesn’t respect your hardware, and an experience that actively improves once you turn features off.

A masterpiece — as long as you squint, unplug, and lower your expectations.

Elden Ring is actually a good game. The world is beautiful, the sense of scale is undeniable, and when combat clicks, it really clicks. I don’t dislike this game because it’s bad. I don’t recommend it because it’s not a game for someone like me.

The single biggest issue, and the thing that actively works against my enjoyment, is the lack of direction.

I don’t need hand-holding, but I do need orientation. I constantly found myself asking what I should be doing right now. Should I be leveling my character? Is there a boss I’m supposed to defeat? Is progression hidden behind some obscure item or location that I’m only meant to discover by pure chance?

Playing Elden Ring often felt like being told to figure out my entire life path on my own without modeling, guidance, or feedback, and then being judged by the outcome anyway. Maybe that comparison hits something personal for me, but I need to know that I’m on the right path. I don’t want to dump ten or more hours into dying repeatedly in the same cave or region with no idea whether I’m even supposed to be there.

The open world is impressive, but also confusing to the point of frustration. You can be farming enemies to level up while standing right next to a massive enemy that you are clearly dozens of levels away from defeating, with no indication which content is appropriate and which is not. Progress is learned almost entirely through trial and error or by using guides online.

That is where the game lost me.

I don’t mind difficulty. I do mind ambiguity that wastes time. Elden Ring offers very little feedback or reassurance that you are making meaningful progress. Combat is decent but clunky and punishing, which compounds the stress when you are unsure whether repeated failure is part of learning or simply a sign that you are in the wrong place.

Ultimately, the game felt disrespectful of my time. I don’t have a hundred plus hours to burn on trial and error just to discover whether I am progressing correctly. If I wanted that kind of experience, I would go outside.

The challenge itself does not bother me. What bothers me is constantly thinking, am I supposed to be here, for how long, and where do I go next?

Elden Ring is clearly beloved, and I understand why. But if you value clarity, structure, and knowing that your effort is actually moving you forward, this game may push you away rather than pull you in.

[b]A Disheartening Discourse on Elden Ring[/b]

Crippled controls with evade and sprint bound to one button by the devs, just to make the game look difficult. It’s not, trust me. It’s positively tedious—162 lazily designed, reskinned bosses sprinkled all over the map. I’ve vanquished a knightly foe with the same visage no fewer than three times. What a cheap game, eh? Try to defend that—you can’t. There exists no cogent argument for such shoddy design, period.

With these impediments enforced by the developers' hands, one cannot help but lament the dire state of a looting and crafting system directly lifted from the Resident Evil franchise. This raises an egregious question: does Elden Ring proffer anything remotely fresh upon the gaming table? The answer, it seems, is a resounding no.

Moreover, the relentless grind of battling clone adversaries becomes an exercise in monotony, robbing the player of any semblance of satisfaction. Instead of a cornucopia of engaging encounters, one is left with an insipid array of repetitive skirmishes that entirely lack innovation.

The emergent frustrations of attempting to navigate a vast yet empty world, rife with spawn points for these insipid bosses, turns what should be an exhilarating journey into a dreary slog. Add in the paltry semblance of narrative coherence and one could easily conclude that this is merely a cacophony of contradictions masquerading as a cohesive universe.

I shudder at the notion that the developers may soon return with yet another instalment, likely a hapless mishmash of AI-generated drivel destined to be branded as “fresh.” Mayhap it is a forewarning that the once-esteemed FromSoftware has succumbed to a malaise of creative ennui, cycling through the same tired tropes whilst failing to imbue the world with genuine depth or intrigue.

In summary, Elden Ring stands as a testament to the perils of overhype and lazy design—an experience to be forgotten rather than cherished.

Since I had some unfinished business in the DLC, I came back to this game after a long hiatus. Taking that break made the issues in this game even more glaring. I'm giving this game a 10/10 for lore, exploration, and world design, though the latter feels a bit empty for its size. But gameplay-wise, FromSoftware took their games in the wrong direction ever since Dark Souls 3, with its super aggressive and fast enemies, only to dial this up to 11 in Elden Ring.

I think having more consistency would do the next game some good. Meaning:

* A working poise system (again).
* Clear attack patterns without those long-winded combo streaks.
* Reaction-based dodging instead of instant attacks that come out of drawn-out wind-ups.
* Clear punish windows.

The late game also turns into a slog. Having bosses you've fought before and some new ones only this time they deal a ton of damage and have massive health pools. This is not challenging; it is exhausting to fight.

And of course there is a wide selection of weapons and consumables, especially spirit ashes (summons you can call into a boss fight or certain areas) that trivialize some fights massively. But what was the point of making boss fights artificially difficult in the first place then? Meaning: almost undodgeable attacks, massive damage, massive health pools, endless combos, high mobility that leaves very little time for the player to punish the boss, if they can even get to them in the first place, that is. It's like there is no middle ground here anymore, which could have been achieved with fine-tuning all boss encounters. But it's clear what they did here instead: go mass over substance.

It is still a great game, just not the best souls-like they've made so far. And as you can see by my hours played, I still got a massive amount of enjoyment in return for the money spent. But Steams rating system has no stars so I'll go with the negative one. If the FromSoftware games are more about the lore and the exploration for you (just like me), then I'd still recommend this game. If it is challenge you seek, then the other FromSoftware titles will be more enjoyable, in my opinion.

I will never understand the Souls-like genre. Everybody seems to love it. I get recommended these games multiple times a year and yet every time I try one, it feels like the same experience all over again.

When Dark Souls 1 and 2 were still a novelty I actually UNDERSTOOD the appeal. “The point is that it doesn’t handhold you” great. That made sense at the time. But this genre has been run into the ground. Over and over it’s the same setting, the same tone, the same "mythic past" or "bleak dark future" where the bloodied, tarnished, vanquished whatever must fight Eli the All-Mighty Executioner to prove their worth. The genre is also an oxymoron. Souls-likes are constantly framed as niche, hardcore experiences, yet they are massively popular. They sell millions, dominate charts and dozens of them release every MONTH. That isn’t niche. The appeal often seems less about fun or creativity and more about being able to say “I did it or something.”

I’m not here to trash THIS specific game. Elden Ring is clearly well-made and crafted by the original architects of the genre. But Souls-like games have been mythologised to such an extreme degree that they can never realistically deliver what people claim they do. They don’t meaningfully prove skill, they don’t offer an especially interesting challenge and for me, they’re rarely fun.

Elden Ring: A Giant That Lost Its Way

Ok, let's keep this short and substantial - exactly where Elden Ring failed (ha-ha).

Elden Ring is better than Dark Souls II, but it falls short of Sekiro, Dark Souls, and Dark Souls III. The game is ambitious (perhaps too ambitious) - mistaking sheer scale for depth, and quantity for meaning.

Open world. It is not a strength here — it’s a burden. Elden Ring is simply too large. At first, exploration feels exciting, but that excitement quickly fades into obligation. The world often feels stretched far beyond what the core gameplay can support.

Bosses. Most of them feel insignificant, uninspired, and disposable. Many are recycled, mechanically shallow, and too easy, undermining what used to be the studio’s greatest strength. Boss fights no longer feel like tests of skill — they feel like tasks placed there for the sake of justifying the world’s size.

Dragons. Dragon fights are perhaps the clearest example of this problem. They were already cancer of the series, and Elden Ring not only does not fix the problem, but multiplies it. These encounters are easy, repetitive, and absurdly long. With huge health pools and high defense, dragons feel more like endurance tests than battles that challenge the player.

And yet, there are moments of brilliance. The lore is deep and compelling, surpassed only by Bloodborne. The characters are genuinely memorable, and their side quests are often more engaging than the main path — quiet, tragic, and emotionally resonant in a way the rest of the game often isn’t.

At the time of writing, I’ve played about 145 hours, with roughly 60 hours still remaining. There is simply no reason for ANY game to be this long. Length is not depth. Excess is not ambition. Elden Ring reminds us that FromSoftware shines brightest when it is restrained, focused, and disciplined — not when it inflates its world into a sprawling, self-indulgent marathon.

With all that’s been said, Elden Ring is the first game in the series that I’m  leaving unfinished. After over a hundred of hours invested, the thought of continuing feels more like a chore than a challenge or a thrill. For a series that has always demanded and rewarded dedication, this is a telling sign of how the game has overextended itself. It’s not a bad game. But compared to the studio’s finest work, it feels overextended, unfocused, and bloated — a game that forgot what made FromSoftware great in the first place.

Simply put, the game is too big and too long for me, it just gets tiring and cumbersome, I seriously just wanted it to be over by the time I was 75% of the way through.

I'm also not a fan of a lot of the boss fights. It takes a problem that started in Dark Souls 3 and cranks it up even further, which is the design idea of, "If we just put a bonfire right outside the boss arena, we can make it a 3-phase clusterjam with movement cancelling and 69 different attacks for the player to memorize, and it won't matter if the player dies 20+ times because they can immediately retry!" Too me, this is so much less fun than the classic Dark Souls 1/2 challenge of battling your way through a gauntlet of enemies and traps and then fighting a challenging, but not overloaded boss as the cherry on top. It used to feel like a boss fight was your opportunity to prove that you have mastered an area and are ready to move on. In Elden Ring, a lot of boss fights feel like a tacked-on reflex and memorization challenge that is separate from the challenge of the area itself.

While I can appreciate that FromSoft tried going bigger and grander, I ultimately feel like they lost some of the old magic along the way, and Elden Ring ended up being annoying and fatiguing in a way that their previous titles never were for me. What a shame, as this is clearly their biggest hit, so I guess I'm in the minority. I can squint and see a 10/10 life-changing game in it, but ultimately the size and length of the game, some of the ridiculously complex bosses, and the copy-pasted open world elements distract from the solid core and drag the experience down. I can confidently say I won't be replaying this game, unlike Dark Souls 1 and 2, Bloodborne, and Armored Core 6, which all sound very enticing to return to.

[h1]Review[/h1]
[h3]Mostly for those halfway familiar with the specific ARPG, Hack & Slash brand of FromSoftware's entries[/h3]
Elden Ring fixed a grand total of one of FromSoftware's decades old design flaws: it gives you saves in front of most bosses (but still not all of them, there are still terrible runbacks here, just less terrible than their older games). Other than that one thing I mentioned, it still suffers from all of the same FromSoft flaws that are unlikely to ever get fixed, because the games have developed a cult around them, which doesn't understand anything about game design and just echoes "git gud" at everything, even technical bugs and none of them have probably played an indie game, because they all think their enjoyment of FromSoftware's products somehow means they're really niche, underground and cool, when these games are all just AAA games, that don't have predatory monetization practices (save for maybe a season pass here and there).

These games do, however, also take all of the archaic difficulty design from oldschool games where the only way to succeed was: die one million times to things you couldn't have seen coming until you learn it all and hopefully don't have that one enemy do that one seemingly not playested attack too many times, with the poor telegraph and bad hitbox that takes half your health bar at once. And the actual times the difficulty of these games is fair, like in some of the better fights of the series (i.e. Slave Knight Gael, Dancer of The Boreal Valley)? It ends up being just slightly above average in terms of difficulty (except for Nameless King, idk what I was doing there, that guy crushed my nuts back in the day for hours)

The parkour is also just as bad as in all of the other FromSoft offerings that have it. 50% of your deaths will also still be due to the terrible camera, which has become a signature of this franchise at this point. The game also features the exact same, carbon copy combat system, that only works halfway decently in 1v1 scenarios, while the incompetent devs still insist on trolling every five steps with 2-5 enemy ganks that come out of a corner you couldn't have seen around and stun-lock you, while either not staggering or only entirely inconsistently staggering themselves.

The game also introduces a new issue, or exacerbates an old one (I'm not entirely sure) where the bosses will have the most unrealistic, bullshit windups and fake wind-ups for their attacks, which is really fun, especially paired with the aforementioned horrible hitboxes for some attacks (which, again, have become a staple of these games).

I 100%ed this out of spite like a year or two ago, because of crippling mental health issues (which is as funny and pathetic as it is true). I also have 100% in Bloodborne and many indie games that would make Souls fanatics, who only ever insist on playing these games and nothing else, pee themselves and uninstall. This review (not just for ELDEN RING, but serving as a general review for all of FromSoftware's games) is not based on a lack of skill, but based on an understanding of game design, built through playing hundreds of games a year and 100%ing a fair amount of them, while critically analyizing almost everything about these titles along the way. FromSoftware makes cookie cutter, cryptic, fake deep experiences, whose difficulty design is less Hi-Fi Rush or Expedition 33 and more I Wanna Be The Guy and The Impossible Quiz: cheap, artificial, time-wasting.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Do you love FromSoft? You'll likely love this! Are you jaded by playing more games than the average consumer and don't enjoy your time being wasted and being actively trolled by devs? Play something else, preferably something AA or Indie, as those are the only two categories worth playing these days, and have been for more than a decade (barring the exceptions to the rule that only come around every few years at best, like the God of War games).

P.S. I know it's super cringe to keep mentioning how seemingly above average I am at video games, and I would never do it in any other scenario, with any other community of gamers, but some of the people who will inevitably stumble upon this are... a special breed (emphasis on "special").

we don't need another rehash of a combat system that has already been milked dry.
As usual FromSoft treads new ground by removing all the fun game and seeing if you can still git gud?
The game was designed like a mathematical limit, where the closer you get to the end of the game,
the more the game strives to erode your motivation to keep playing it.
Out with rewarding skill development and mastery, in with the boredom and frustration maximization.
Playing the game feels like working on a job you have already long grown tired of.
Where in dark souls you lose your humanity in-game, in elden ring you lose your soul in real life.
They took the novel approach of not playtesting the last 20% of the game.
And that's what makes it so great!

Maybe fromsoft just got tired of all of the players that keep yelling:
"I've platinumed every single FromSoft game"
and used that as an argument of validity to their criticsm.
Here's Malenia, platinum that!

FromSoft truly opened my eyes to a wider world.
I now believe that the pinnacle of game design is adding a boss to the game so difficult,
that so many players summon another player to do it for them instead,
that the player that others summon actually becomes famous for it.
I never would have thought of game design from that angle before Elden Ring.

Other innovations include Elden ring's increasing emphasis on verticality,
but still having the controls of a game where the world is flat.
Running into the smallest step known to man stops you dead in your tracks.
You can see your foot going higher than the step, yet you stay stuck dancing the running man.
When rolling backwards these ledges will teach you brand new insights into physics.

Some of the design choices are refreshingly devious.
Smithing stones are sold all the way on the other side of the round table hold as the smith.
You can't put a currently equiped weapon into the stash,
so every time you try out a new weapon and put it in the stash you get to curse at the developers.

Grab attacks are amongst the most hated mechanics in souls likes.
So FromSoft made sure to use the mechanic exhaustively and even the weakest of mobs now have grab attacks.
In fact, how about sending huge armies of gank at the player, all of which execute grab attacks?
FromSoft brilliantly builds upon that by making the animation for getting up the slowest one ever to sit through.
Even I don't take that long to get up in the morning, but this chad takes his time in the middle of combat.

By the time you get to the end of the game, you will start dreaming about fromsoft.
I still remember vividly seeing Miyazaki and his clan dancing around me in circles wiggling their middle fingers.

Jokes aside, I've never been this bored and frustrated while playing a game, but I still worked through it.
I beat every single boss in the game once and I platinumed the game.
And the most rewarding part of it all is that I never have to play this game again.

Bloodborne has aged a little bit, like a fine wine but also maybe like it wasn't kept fully corked shut.

Sekiro is... still sitting on my shelf unplayed. Unfortunately.

Elden Ring is more technically impressive, visually, thematically, and in its grandiose nature, but it lost a lot of the intrigue and morbid curiosity that the originals had, despite their limitations by today's standards. It is a more new-player-friendly experience, and finally explains some of its systems well. For me personally, I harbor the same disappointments as I did with Breath of the Wild as a Zelda game. The moment-to-moment stuff just wasn't always there. The open world made it into a mile-wide/inch-deep feeling for a lot of the experience, which is a shame because there still ARE locations in this game that are so freaking cool to explore, and have a lot of great enemy experiences and player rewards. It's just all the stuff in between that, beautiful as it may be to look at, which I find so forgettable after I'm done with it. I'm not saying you should never play this game, but I don't feel that the lightning in a bottle from From's earlier games is on display as much here. It's more lightning as a spectacle; still beautiful but less contained, less magical, and less unique. The DLC unfortunately brought more of the same feeling to me, and that really sucks! Because I historically really love From's DLCs.

This review is a bunch of nitpicking but the more I go back and play the older From games the more I'm disappointed with this game:

The open world itself is forgettable since it poses zero challenge to the player.  You can just turn your brain off and run past every enemy with zero punishment. People still reminisce about their first time in Blight Town or facing those two guys down the well in Bloodborne. There is literally nothing of sort in Elden Ring.

The small dungeons spread out in the open world sometimes have interesting gimmicks but usually end with you killing a reused boss and being rewarded something you'll never end up using. Bloodborne chalices had random layouts, a decent amount of  enemies/bosses not in the regular game and gave you a reason to do them in Blood gems. All that and most people still skipped them. Ubisoft level bloat for people who don't realize more playtime doesn't make a game better. 

Legacy dungeons, you don't even want to explore because after doing a few you realize the only decent content the game has are the bosses. DS1 was praised for the inteconnected world, DS2 and 3 still had shortcuts you could discover by exploring.  The level design once again devolved with ER, with a grace around every corner the shortcuts and the relief from finally finding one are mostly gone. 

Bosses, I've died to Malenia, Messmer and Radahn dozens of times yet none of them gave me the same dopamine hit from killing Gael or Orphan in maybe one fifth of the tries. It feels like 90% of the challenge with all these big bad bosses are their one or two crazy moves. You'll die over and over to Waterfowl or the big snake combo Messmer has until you figure out when and which way to roll or run. You'll never get that adrenaline rush from getting a boss to 5-10% your first try because these moves solely exist to make older players not whine about everything else by giving the illusion of difficulty while still letting the new "broader audience" tank half the combos with their summon. This contrast in difficulty between the world and the bosses also makes the game feel like a boss rush rather than an adventure like the older games.

Narrative, they don't leave things to imagination much compared to the older games. Ranni probably blogs more about the story than the entirety of DS1 dialogue. Around the same amount of NPC questlines in a much bigger world makes the world feel even more barren. Through 3 playthroughs I haven't noticed a Solaire, Lucatiel or Anri. Someone on a similar journey, living their own life you come across multiple times. Maybe they exist but the world isn't interesting enough for me to go find them.

Multiplayer, covenants are gone, invasions are opt-in. All the fun sucked out of it because god forbid the people who already look up everything online would have to look up how to turn invasions off too.

It's still an okay game but I'm worried where FromSoft is heading. I don't care if some guy who didn't have the dedication to beat the older games now gets to have fun beating bosses with spells/summons/weapon arts as long as it doesn't end up making the game a worse experience but the multiple steps backwards taken in level/world design, narrative, multiplayer are clearly an attempt to make the game more appealing to them, and it affects everyone.
Even the content people create has gone downhill, from meme videos, challenges and invasions to weapon/spell/x rankings, how to cheese x boss and loreslop (FUCK VAATI)

Let me be clear: I don’t mind difficulty. In fact, I’ve loved challenging games since childhood. I enjoy learning from my mistakes, improving, dying, trying again, and beating bosses. I defeated 30–40 bosses in Elden Ring without giving up, raging, or complaining about the difficulty.

My issue is not difficulty, it’s everything else.

Story & Worldbuilding

Yes, the world of Elden Ring can be huge, rich, and deep. But a world that big shouldn’t be this vague. The “story” basically consists of a guy shouting at the beginning and a handful of cryptic NPCs who talk like they’re solving riddles. That’s simply not for me.

I want to engage with a story.
I want an actual script, a main quest that makes sense, something to pull me into the world.
I shouldn’t have to check item descriptions or chase random weird NPCs across a massive map just to understand the basics of the lore. (Lore of the world, not the story)

Some players enjoy that style and that’s completely fine, but I don’t.

Gameplay.....

This is where the game completely loses me.

Elden Ring still uses the same old formula from 2007: slow, clunky, roll–dodge–hit combat that becomes extremely repetitive after a while. After a masterpiece like Sekiro, I genuinely thought FromSoftware would push their combat systems forward. Instead, they went backward.

Sure, there are tons of builds and creative options. But at the end of the day, every boss fight ends up feeling like you're just a rolling Pokémon waiting for openings. It’s uninteresting and dull.

Visuals & Exploration

I’ll give credit where it’s due: visually and structurally, the world is stunning. I normally hate getting lost in video games, but Elden Ring’s worldbuilding makes exploration rewarding, every corner has something to discover, and that’s a huge positive.

But in the end, amazing exploration doesn’t mean much when:

1)The story gives you nothing to hold onto, and

2)The combat system feels boring and outdated.

Conclusion

I respect people who love this game, everyone has different tastes. But I genuinely cannot see the appeal. After 42 hours of boredom, I have to drop it midway.

A generous 5/10.

I beat Elden Ring, and I think this game is just exhausting.

I've played Dark Souls 1-3 and I think, comparatively, Elden Ring is just not a similar enough experience. 
Boss design feels too fast for responding to, leaving you to just gamble on dodging correctly or leaning into just blocking most of the fight. The attacks aren't big OR fast, they're big AND fast.
Navigating detracts from combat. I ended up just racing around with my horse and getting all of the possible waypoints around the map, which seems to be par for the course, but it felt like a waste of my time. Same for walking into a level 40 area at the start, grinding there for a while, and then coming back to all of the bosses dying in 4 hits. Not to mention mounted combat, which has been interesting in concept, and frustrating in practice.
Speaking of which, the balance is suboptimal. As a Strength Barbarian, I was fascinated by the stun/knockdown system, but it didn't feel rewarding because you have to keep attacking for so long back-to-back. This incentivized   just gambling on charged heavy attacks and being rewarded for the boss to by chance just use the worst attack on you. It felt gross. I bet other builds like Magic are a lot faster and feel better to play, but I definitely didn't play that build so that's moot to me.
So yeah, I can't really recommend it. I wish I could. The game just left me feeling pretty empty and regretful. I think FromSoftware made an okay game, I just don't think it can be justified to recommend others for spending the hours to beat it. If you do end up getting it though, maybe don't play a Strength build like I did.

I want to preface this review by saying that I've played Dark Souls 1 and 3 which I thought were pretty good, and I also played Sekiro, which I enjoyed very much. I also enjoyed playing Elden Ring, at least for around the first 75% of the game. The problem is what came after.

Once you reach a certain point, level design, enemy design, and just game design more broadly starts to go downhill very quickly. Late-game regions (especially one in particular) start to just become enemy spam, throwing a bunch of things you've already seen together in a room, but with way over-tuned health and damage. Bosses become a mess of AOE, janky hitboxes, janky attack timings, and extremely long combos, making the game more about memorizing the input sequences to avoid each boss' attacks rather than actually applying the skills you've developed over the course of the game. It turns into pure trial-and-error, or into a lottery where you just hope you get enough favorable patterns in a row to eke out a win.

It's really disappointing, because if I could just review the early- and mid-game, I would absolutely recommend Elden Ring. The exploration is fantastic and the boss fights are generally tuned appropriately so that you can either fight them as you are, or go off and do some other stuff so you can come back later better equipped. But to get so close to the end only for the game to suddenly devolve into an un-fun mess that you have to spend at least another dozen hours to slog through is just a horrible experience, and not one I would wish on others. If you're the kind of person who is happy to play a game while it's fun and then drop it once it's not fun anymore, Elden Ring is a great game to choose. However, if you're like me and you want to play games through to completion, it's sadly really hard to recommend it.

Bosses have too long combos, too fast tracking, and too many unnaturally delayed attacks.  At least for melee builds.

I believe boss fights are the single most important aspect in the FromSoft formula, so it brings the rest of the game down when the crescendo of an area is more fun than the climax. It pushes players to rely on defensive and "cheap" tactics like cheese, summons, or overlevelling. I like that the latter two are still viable options, but they shouldn't be the only ones outside of spending 10 hours memorizing tedious and unintuitive attack patterns for one boss. If I want fast paced combat (ie not ds1) then I much preferred learning the movesets of bosses from games like DS3 and Sekiro, where aggression is the key to winning and there is less visual trickery to "gotcha!" the player. Admittedly DS3 has many of these same issues, just not cranked up to 11 like in ER.

It comes off like FromSoft making each successive game faster paced and with less margin for error in order to keep up with returning players' ever-increasing skills, and adding "easy mode" options for more accessibility to new players. But as someone who likes to beat challenging yet balanced bosses while solo and at a reasonable level, neither option is a fun way to play.

The rest of the game is fine, although after playing every Soulsborne game besides King's Field, I think I prefer when the maps are more linear and curated than a vast open world. The points of interest themselves like dungeons and forts are good at least. It's also great that you can go grab more variety of weapons right at the start of the game. But ironically I get tired of exploring the open maps more quickly than I do exploring the linear ones. It's the difference between scouring a carefully designed and fleshed-out highlight reel versus aimlessly wandering the wilderness looking for something to do. The whole mounted combat thing and crafting using foraged reagents are really cool but not quite enough to justify the map design and size I think.

The atmosphere and lore are also inferior to DeS/DS/Sekiro/Bloodborne. It's not a dealbreaker for me, but I found it disappointing and less inspired. It's just more of the same recycled ideas from the Dark Souls trilogy. Sekiro and Bloodborne impressed me with the range FromSoft has with lore, settings, and levels of technology, so I know they can do better.

In terms of visuals the game is beautiful. Probably the best visuals out of all their games so far. Nothing more to say, other than mentioning that it sometimes causes frame loss. Thankfully this lag seems to (usually) vanish when entering boss arenas where it would be the most disruptive. But it's all hardware dependent so take that with a grain of salt.

TLDR: Get this game for the lore and world-building if it's on sale, avoid because of jank combat system.

I really wish steam had an in-between option for recommendations because that is exactly how I feel about Elden Ring.

Of all the souls-like games I've played, Elden Ring has given me the most enjoyment. Adapting the dark souls formula into an open-world where exploration, story-building, and combat are all up to the player is such a fantastic idea and the amount of effort that the devs put into that concept shows! I really felt like I was experiencing the world through my Tarnished's eyes, and learning to choose for myself the direction that I felt the story needed to go. The characters have as much depth or shallowness as you give them, and despite my worries, I had no problem figuring out where to go to progress the story.

Unfortunately, there's one major flaw that keeps me from recommending this game: the combat system. 

1) The system shows its age. It clearly hasn't been seriously re-worked since dark souls 3. If it has, it wasn't enough. How do I know? Well, play any other Fromsoft game and you'll see that standard Souls jank. Stuff like enemies hitting through solid objects, enemies phasing in and out of things, and physics glitches that I can only imagine are left to irritate the player. These issues have persisted ever since the original Demon's Souls, and for some reason Fromsoft has never fixed any of them.

2) Input queing. For those unaware, input quieing is a way for games to prevent you from spamming items and attacks. When a button is pressed, it enters the que, and after a certain period of time has passed, the game allows that action to occur. Unfortunately, Fromsoft's implementation here is just... broken. There are times where I will press a button to do anything, say attack, roll, or heal, and my character just... stands there. I've checked my controller multiple times and tested it with other games, but no. Elden Ring just sometimes eats my inputs, which can be all the difference between beating a boss or starting the whole thing over. The opposite is also true in that action canceling is also inconsistent. Often times I'll press a button to attack, then roll to dodge, only for my character to come out of the roll swinging. While that sounds cool, if I needed to dodge repeatedly this usually means I'm now stuck in a stun-lock combo.

3) Enemy AI. I'm not a big fan of the whole "wait for an eternity while the boss holds their sword over their head" shtick, but I can concede that it can be overcome by learning to time things properly. What I can't excuse, however are:
- Overabundance of seeking projectiles, including normal arrows. Wood and stone do not make heat seeking missiles.
- Enemies winding up for an attack in one direction and then instantly pivoting 180 degrees to smack you on the head. I hate to be that guy, but physics still does exist in-game, and I double anyone can spin while one-handing a heavy club.
- Aforementioned stun lock combos that provide no opportunity to counter or dodge out.
- Attacks that hit mid-roll, completely trivializing its role as a survival method. Also, inconsistent hitboxes for enemies and weapons.
- Input reading. Look, it's fine if the enemy AI needs to know what I'm doing in order to attack. However, the AI should NOT be able to instantly react to one of my button presses, especially if they react before the qued action even begins. That's like if a cowboy was able to shoot a man in a duel the moment their opponent even started thinking about drawing their revolver.

I understand and accept that this is a game in a fantasy setting. But if you set some rules for the player, it seems reasonable that other entities in the world should somewhat follow those rules as well. This is not that game.

Overall, I think this is a game everyone should play for the experience, but not at full price. I honestly wish a little more time had been spent on reworking the combat, even if that meant a little less lore. 

Get this game, but only on sale.

I tried. I really tried to enjoy this game. Buckle up. I have some thoughts. No story spoilers here.

Let's start with basic ratings that I can give a number.
Pros: | Graphics 8/10 | Visual Design 10/10 | World-building 10/10 | Music 10/10 |
Cons: | Audio Design 4/10 |

Elden Ring does not reward progression or skill (in the normal gaming way). Every game has obstacles that can be bested either with some progression or skill-based learning of the game mechanics. Yet, as I’ve progressed and defeated various non-boss enemies, explored, retrieved armor and weapons, and leveled significantly, no skill or progression has prepared me for the first boss (if you follow the guided path). There is no enemy like this one leading up to this obstacle, and the attacks are so designed to be unrelenting and difficult that no amount of traditional gaming skill could allow the player to beat this boss without knowledge of the attacks. In fact, the only thing that will get you past the obstacle is memorization. Not skill. Not levels. Not anything enjoyable (imo). Just memorization of the attacks, animations, exact timings, and eventually executing this idealistically after many attempts. This is the uniqueness of FromSoftware games; the development of a niche "skill" to pass an obstacle, never to be used again in any other instance. Allow suffering to consume you and master it to move forward. It can be a great life lesson... or a source of unneeded stress for those who've learned this lesson time and time again, only to repeat it and suffer more.

For that reason, despite the beauty of the world, the incredible monster designs, and world building, Elden Ring is not a masterpiece in my eyes, and I find no satisfaction in playing. I simply do not have the level of masochism required to mistake the end of suffering with true joy and mastery. Back when I beat Bloodborne, I was happy to confuse the two. However, I am no longer one who avoids reprieve in their limited free time dedicated to a game they bought to, in one way or another, escape suffering. If I wanted to spend my time memorizing to progress, I would do so outside of a video game that breathes more stress and anxiety into a sleepless, loud world, echoing the oppression of peace of mind and creativity that has invaded the entertainment industry.

And, look, this may be a masterpiece for others. I have no doubt that if you have the willingness to endure, and the persistence to recognize patterns, memorize them, and engage in patient execution, you will beat this game, and perhaps you will love it. But, for me, it is the illusion of skill and the gate-keeping of beauty behind intense suffering that, after beating the first boss 12 hours in, only brings me relief from my self-prescribed suffering in the form of a game titled Elden Ring.

Game has absolutely painfully incompetent combat mechanics. It is not a matter of "this was meant to be challenging." It's the case of input buffering being wildly inconsistent with one of the worst camera systems I've ever had the displeasure of encountering. Sprint will frequently not work and need to be attempted again.

The world building is gorgeous and the graphics are stellar. The game has a compelling story-line and you are able to carve your own path at your own cadence. It has some outstanding "HOLY SH*T" moments and satisfying upgrade paths.

I love the idea of tackling the same boss repeatedly, learning their move set until I can perfect the dance of the fight and beat them with flawless execution. It feels like a rewarding accomplishment.

However, melee combat is tediously inconsistent, almost exclusively due to this disgusting input buffering (cannot speak for sorcery or ranged combat - perhaps those do not suffer the same fate). Sometimes your move will buffer to complete immediately after your current one, other times it won't, despite being cast at identical times. Another deeply flawed issue is you may attempt to dodge roll backwards, to the south, let's say. But, if you are camera locked onto an enemy, and they've quickly sidestepped or dodged behind you, your dodge will already be queued up in the original direction and send you somersaulting towards them to your death. But, the fun part is, sometimes it won't queue either! It's thrilling not knowing if my dodge will behave the same way moment to moment.

The camera control is also atrocious. I turned off all optional settings in an attempt to have full camera control and it feels like I'm fighting the camera to go where I intend. I have fallen off countless ledges because as you are running around a corner, precariously perched on a tower ledge, the camera will arbitrarily flip 180 degrees and send you running head first off to your death. It's a shame you NEED to have locked camera on to keep up with the speed of some bosses, since they don't allow your sens to be adjusted very high, but bosses will frequently go over your ahead making attacking or dodging nigh impossible.

You frequently CANNOT swap to an intended target. You can try every single angle with your right stick to change to a different target, yet certain ones will be excluded from selection, even though they are right in front of you, or directly between two other targets you can easily swap between. 

Or, you may simply miss a completely stationary target, despite being in range with your weapon. I've slain 3 demigods but suddenly I'm incapable of hitting a target dummy!

I would not recommend subjecting yourself to this game, at least as a melee. Too inconsistent in the core mechanics of the game to be enjoyable.

Dark Souls I, 10/10, is the greatest game of all time. Dark Souls II was almost as good, 9/10. Elden Ring: 4/10. 99% of the map needs to be removed. Everything after Stormveil Castle is boring and the enemies all suck (but are not hard). The weapon arts are underwhelming. The level design, the absolute best thing imo about Dark Souls I and II, leaves you either spending more time searching and getting frustrated or looking things up than actually playing the game. Within instances, level design is decent, but the instances don't cleverly chain together, instead you have to travel MASSIVE distances of worthless, sparse content just so they can force the "open world" concept (which is DOGSH*T in EVERY game I've ever played) wasting 90% of your time. Unlike Dark Souls I and II where you actually spend the time playing the game, Elden Ring feels more like doing research so you can write a paper than an actual game. In previous Dark Souls games, it was super fun hunting for hidden content due to the brilliance of their level design. Elden Ring is just the same level of fun combat but feel as if you get 1/10th of it, despite the game being massively larger. It's overall more content, but every piece of the map is nauseatingly unsatisfying and takes all the nerves you should spend stuck against enemies instead spent on finding what in the hell you are supposed to do. I don't want to spend half my day to find where I need to go unless I look it up, both options ruining the game, just to spend an hour crushing the bosses and monsters, which, if you are a veteran of the souls series, aren't tough, but are sometimes annoying due to poor design. Game would honestly be better if it contained 4 total bosses and they just ended it after Stormveil. Can't start with such a beautiful and then followup it a hundred hours after of garbage content. Would actually be fun if it stopped constantly peppering the player with cheap shots, and sometimes it does stop. It's also as vague and poorly communicated as humanly possible so that the only way you'll understand some of the most fundamentally important mechanics in the game are wiki-crawling or spending dozens of hours on rote trial and error. 

Ignore the reddit hivemind trying to gaslight people into thinking this is a perfect experience. I got 'good'. I understood the design language, parried and dodged bosses, beat Malenia, Elden Beast, Maliketh, etc with a melee strength build and a colossal weapon. There's potential here but it squanders those possibilities so it can pretend that it's difficult with unintuitive memorization-based gameplay, boss combos that cannot be interrupted even during extended pauses with badly telegraphed switch-ups and lackluster RPG mechanics. 

You can tell a lot about a game's design by examining where the most effective tactics leave you, and the most effective tactic in elden ring is to run past enemies to grab a bunch of items, stack up a ton of buffs and effects so you deal a ton of damage, and then kill the bosses as fast as mathematically possible before they start any kind of attack sequence to minimize the time spent interfacing with boss and foe mechanics as much as possible. That's not a good sign, but it can be excusable if a game has more to it beyond the core mechanical gameplay. Elden ring does not have a whole lot more to it than the core mechanical gameplay.

Compare that with the most effective tactics available in something like Doom Eternal on Nightmare difficulty - move, shoot, dodge, swap, combo, chainsaw, stagger foes you can't kill, and so on. The most effective way to play that game is to interface with all it's mechanics as much as possible and do so constantly. It's not a perfect game, but it doesn't bury it's own strengths.

There's a good game buried in Elden Ring somewhere, where combat is a mad dance of risk, retreat, aggression and dynamic play, but the game almost never lets it come to the surface. A damn shame.

I want to start this review by saying I don't hate elden ring, i've played through the game plenty of times, unmodded, modded, challenges, etc, and i've had my fair share of fun (at times) throughout my time with this game.

However, Elden ring has introduced some new issues to the fromsoft series that, at least for me, are too significant for me to ignore as a long-time fan of their games.

For starters, i would like to talk about what Elden ring did well.

Elden ring marked the first souls/souls adjacent game to shift to a full open-world format, allowing the player much more freedom than their other games.

Elden ring also introduced a ton of incredibly helpful new combat mechanics like the return of powerstancing, guard counters, a dedicated jump button, and multiple new weapon types.

However, all of these new features came with their fair share of issues. Powerstancing is more limited than what it was in ds2 (and I'm not someone who will tell you that was a good game, mind you), guard counters are useful but can often become useless in the face of most bosses unless you use a spear and shield, and although new weapon types are a good addition, elden ring suffers from a lack of weapon variety if you care about the stats or weapon art as there are a few that dominate their weapon class heavily. (Moonveil,RoB for katanas, Messmer's spear for greatspears, blasphemous blade for greatswords, rellana's for light greatswords, and other similar weapons) and other weapons that have every right to be good just suck because the devs didn't give them good stats or scalings (Hand of malenia, for example)

However, the largest issue elden ring suffers from is power creep. over the years fromsoft's bosses have gotten harder, but elden ring marks a point for me where it strays from the "tough but fair" style of design i've come to know from previous games and starts to feel oppressive and unfair. Bosses give you far less time to attack, push you aggressively, punish you any time you heal by reading the animation the moment it starts, and often fall into incredibly long attack strings that prevent you from doing anything but dodge repeatedly and wait until the boss decides it's your turn to play the game. these issues only got significantly worse in the DLC and turned what should have been the best and most enjoyable dlc in fromsoft's history into an exercise in masochism and "how long can i bang my head on this brick wall before i get irreparable brain damage" Compare this to DS3 where no boss was particularly egregious and always gave you fair options to punish them.

Consort Radahn is the pinnacle of this powercreep, having all of these issues dialed up to 11, i have a review on SoTE if you'd like to hear my thoughts on that, but there's little for me to say that hasn't been said already by most in the community. the boss design they've shifted to is not fun nor fair, and i hope they can find a balance between this and their older titles when the next game rolls around.

The way i've come to describe this game is that it's a good game, just one that doesn't want you to enjoy it or experience as much of it as you may want. there are many optional areas of the game that require a lot of work to get to with steps often so complicated it'd be almost impossible to figure out how without looking it up first. this alongside the open world making fromsoft's classic linear character questlines incredibly easy to fail without realizing and the world can often feel empty unless you go out of your way to play the way the game wants you to without deviation, at least DS3 made it easy to follow questlines comparatively.
