I am going into this stating that while I have played "souls-like" games before, I have never actually played a game made by FROMSOFT games.

TL;DR Version: If you are not a masochist, don't play this game. It will torture you, test your sanity, and make you incredibly stressed out. This game isn't actually 'difficult', it's rigged against you, and takes pleasure from your pain.

....
My Rating: 6 of 10
....

The game ultimately has a very uninteresting story, despite how deep the lore is for the world. You are Tarnished, your goal is to become Elden Lord, and you must slaughter everyone and their mother (literally) to achieve it. Unsurprisingly, with George R. R. Martin helping in world building, the game ends up feeling like an episode of Game of Thrones, leaving you wondering what character, that you might even have a sliver of emotional attachment to, will die next and in what horrible context.

Possibly the main reason why everyone plays this game, the emphasis on frantic combat, would be less jarring if the more complex enemy mechanics were introduced gradually over time, to allow a player to become better accustomed to what is expected to them. Admittedly this does happen to a degree, because enemies in later zones do gain access to a greater array of skills and spells, however, it's all rather unforgiving for first time players trying to learn how this game works. 

Enemies, especially of the tarnished/human variety, can literally just dodge most of what you do anyways (with infinite stamina to boot), can cast however much and as far as they might like (there is a fall off, but it's waaaaaaay longer than the tarnished), and they also have an greater attack and retaliation speed than the player. 

While the player is forced into a particular set of rules and limitations, the NPC's freely break those, creating an uneven playing field almost perpetually during combat, leaving the player at a constant disadvantage.

Despite environments and NPCs being a graphically beautiful, the character, and customization is left wanting. Personally, I spent about an hour trying to make a normal looking face, only to change another slider ever so slightly and end up with an abomination. Outfits are neat, but... cosmetically I cannot wear one set, and gain the bonuses of another that I'm looking for. It's kind of a minor thing, but it'd be nice.

Finally the perception that you have a choice when it comes to spells/incantations/skills/weapons, is that you actually don't have a choice. That is to say, you can make a choice about what spell/incantation/skill/weapon you wish to use, but it's likely wrong. When enemies (especially bosses, looking at you Malenia) can dodge even Night Comet (a spell that cannot be 'seen' by NPCs), then what's the point of being a spell caster. The long wind-up spells leave you vulnerable in a game where you cannot stop moving, being dodged despite having spent an enormous amount of FP to cast a spell, and being forced to use a melee weapon over a spell, because that is the only way you'll actually do damage, is, in not so many words, bullcrap.

So look, I get it. To all those who love this game, love this genre, I understand. You like putting your balls in a vice and crushing them. That is so cool. But for casual players, this game is not one I can recommend. It's incredibly stressful, the rewards are not rewarding, and while you may end up sinking 170+ hours into the game to actually get somewhere, it's not really that good of a game, and you can spend that time better elsewhere.

Best of Luck!

Elden Ring is a massive and epic game with so much to see and do, so many choices, and so many possibilities, that every experience will be different. If you get on and play as if it is a solo Dark Souls style experience, then Elden Ring is almost perfect. That being said, one thing that makes you think about the quality of a game is whether it succeeds at what it sets out do. In that sense, Elden Ring stumbles. One large component of the Elden Ring experience is it's online multiplayer. I got this wanting to play it in a co-op style with my brother. I had an idea of what I was in for, having played Dark Souls type games before, so I knew that summoning an ally would also create the potential for an enemy player to invade my world. This is where the game faltered for me. 80% of the time when I want to fight my way through the areas and bosses with my brother, our game gets invaded. If the invader being a much higher level than us and having a build specifically for PvP weren't bad enough, the game is not good at stopping players who willfully cheat. Many times between my myself, my brother, and a "hunter" player character summoned to help surrounding our enemy and throwing all sorts of attacks at them, they manage to pull off impossible dodges, but more often all of our attacks from all sides simply go through them with no effect, and then they soundly defeat all of us as if completely impervious to all damage. Some of this could have been the unfortunate result of poor netcode and lag; but more often than not it was pure cheating. Something about being forced into involuntary PvP, in which there is no matchmaking based on skill or level, where most opponents obviously cheat  greatly ruined much of the enjoyment.

The last straw came when we realized that people can "hack" your game. We noticed something strange happen after getting killed by yet another invader. Afterwards certain, key bosses would not spawn in my brother's game. And we realized there was a problem when after fighting two other bosses, he would not receive key items or equipment drops. So we put in some 400 hours into this game only to have a majority of it spent dealing with one-sided, forced PvP with opponents who are clearly cheating, only to end up with a corrupted, hacked game. Seriously, how do you enjoy it after that? The GM's/ customer service is not particularly speedy or helpful if you make a claim.

In that sense the game itself is great, my only criticism is some of the generic repetition that you run into with regards to lesser bosses and dungeons. Outside of that the biggest let down has been the multiplayer which has led to my brother's game being hacked. It is just weird how what was supposed to be a great feature about ruins an otherwise epic game.

The game is visually quite impressive; the landscapes and environment designs are striking. It has an intriguing lore and an unconventional presentation. The music is rarely effective and mostly consists of repetitive melodies, which doesn’t fully support the atmosphere.

In terms of gameplay, the variety of weapons is satisfying and the mechanics are smooth. However, the fall damage system is quite inconsistent; sometimes you survive high falls, but other times even small drops can be fatal, which momentarily disrupts the fun. Also, there are many collectible items in the game, but most are unnecessary; it’s frustrating to overcome tough enemies only to have these efforts go unrewarded.

When picking up items, notifications appear that block some controls; if there are enemies nearby, this can easily lead to death. The co-op system is a major issue; despite a large player base, matchmaking and team formation are quite difficult, making a proper co-op experience nearly impossible.

Despite some minor issues, the optimization is generally good and the performance remains mostly stable.

A significant downside is the lack of Turkish language support. For native Turkish speakers, understanding dialogues and the story is challenging, especially with item descriptions. There are many great items and mechanics, but not fully understanding them negatively affects gameplay. Perhaps they offered useful advantages that I missed.

Overall, the game offers an enjoyable and good experience. However, the lack of language support is a major downside, and because of that, I’m leaving a negative review.

Elden Slop aka. Dark Souls 3.5, the Ubisoft quality open-world spinoff.

(+)

- Best weapons, spells, and armor in the series.
- The new Ash of War system is well-made and very much welcome, streamlining the weapon arts and affinities.
- NPC fights are much more tolerable.
- Most of the unique bosses are awesome, but there aren't as many of them as there should be.

(-)

- Enemy variety is not good. No way near as good as it should be, coming from a company that's been making action games for 2 decades. If you are around 2 hours into the game, you've almost seen the whole enemy cast, because even in end-game areas, 70+ hours later, you'll be fighting the same enemies, but recolored! How exciting! Oh, and they also throw magic rocks at you now. Did you like the basic soldiers or the troll giants you fight at Limgrave? Well, you'll fight the same guys recolored 3 or 4 times. Hell, maybe even 5. All around the game, you'll find bats, octopi, crabs, runebears, etc, all of which are mind-numbingly boring to fight after the first couple of times, but we have to fill space in our huge open-world game, am I right?
- Many reused enemies, models, and movesets from previous Souls games. Lazy and immersion-breaking. Approaching an Erdtree Avatar for the first time only to see it's just an Asylum Demon WITH THE SAME MOVES AND MODEL. Same with Imps. Somehow, From Slop took the Thrall moveset from DS3 and made it even more cancerous. Crabs, slimes, basilisks, dogs and wolves, man-serpents. All reused enemies.
- The open-world is full of copy-paste catacombs, mines, and caves. Pay a little attention and you'll spot all the set pieces, taking away the chance of having a unique experience. These places mostly have new weapons, spells, and talismans, but they are boring to clear. Give AI the tools, and it would create more unique-looking dungeons. At the end of all these is a common enemy with a boss health bar, bringing us to the next point.
- The term "boss" has lost its meaning. Elden Ring gives normal enemies boss health bars left and right. As said before, you'll have the most memorable moments against "Legends and demigods", the "main" bosses of the game, per se, but you'll also have to fight a lot of slop that don't deserve a boss health bar. You might encounter your first dragon fight early in the game. Cool, right? Now, try getting hyped for the next 5 field dragons with different colors and damage types. Night's Cavalries, Deathbirds, and Magma Wyrms are all on the same boat. Even worse are the end-of-tunnel enemies, a common enemy (Runebear, Demi-human, Pumpkin Head, etc.) with a boss health bar. You'll find dozens, if not hundreds, of these guys out in the open-world.
- Gaols, teleporters, chest-traps, and crafting are totally redundant. They don't have a place in a Souls game.
- The Great Rune system is disappointing. They took the humanity/ember system from the older games and tried to put an extra spin on it, but realistically, you don't have a reason to switch from Godrick or Radahn, giving you an illusion of choice. Mind you, on your first playthrough, it takes a long time to get new Great Runes, so you're always anticipating the next one, only to get disappointed. Also, you don't get Great Rune activation after killing a boss, which was a mechanic in DS3. Why would you remove that?
- The game looks OK at best. It looks dated. The horizon is constantly obscured by mist and fog, so you can't enjoy the little beauty the game has to offer. You can also constantly see textures popping in. 2022 game, btw. God bless PlayStation and their game engines.
- Same cryptic and stale lore as the other games. No, this game does not introduce a new universe. Names and places are different, but it's the same old sh*t, along with the NPC quests.
- Locked to 60 FPS, even on modern hardware, and even gets below that in some cases.
- Laggy multiplayer since DS1. They haven't improved in that regard at all.

Notice how most of these problems stem from the game being open-world? Elden Ring doesn't gain anything from being open-world. This would have been a better game if it was a more linear experience, like its predecessors.

I really fell in love with the Dark Souls series and had high hopes for this game, but now I sincerely regret spending money on it.
The open world is implemented as poorly as possible. 80% of it is completely empty. There are no settlements or anything else to give it life — it’s just a vast space with small groups of enemies placed randomly here and there, simply walking in circles.
Enemy behavior is completely inadequate — they often don’t react to the player's presence unless you step directly into their path. This is acceptable for corridor-style maps, and in classic Dark Souls it wasn’t noticeable — due to narrow passages, enemies would detect the player anyway. In an open world, however, this mechanic completely breaks any challenge — you can walk five meters away from an enemy and they'll just ignore you. Enemy AI wasn't adjusted at all and was just carried over from the corridor-style games into an open world setting.
The map itself is as repetitive as it can possibly be. Yes, there are a few different biomes — swamps, forests, etc. But within these biomes, everything looks exactly the same. After a few hours of playing, you’ll start to notice that even large objects like buildings or mountains repeat in other places. The game focuses on the size of the world rather than filling it with meaningful content.
As for the difficulty, it’s completely broken — to defeat many bosses you just need to spend hours farming to level up your character. On the surface, this might look like encouragement to explore the world, but in reality, you’ll just wander through repetitive areas fighting the same enemies over and over just to get a higher level — or, if you’re lucky, find an NPC who gives you a useful item. Considering the typical Dark Souls storytelling style, which only provides a background, these activities become incredibly boring.
There are many optional bosses in the game, but defeating them mostly rewards you with useless junk — after five or six such "rewards", you completely lose any desire to explore optional areas. Not only do they look very similar to each other, but the exploration also gives you nothing in return.
In conclusion: this game is 90% old Dark Souls with no changes to key mechanics or character behavior. The problem is that classic Dark Souls is a corridor game, and its mechanics were tuned specifically for corridor-style maps, not open worlds.
Despite the game’s popularity and my personal love for the genre, I strongly do not recommend buying it — not even at a discount.

Edit: After several more hours into the game, its time to really review the latest soulsborne game.

This game all in all is just dark souls but open-world. Lots of players love it because of this but there are tons of problem gameplay wise. FromSoft took the worst parts of Dark souls 2 and ramp it up ten fold. I played all soulsborne games and prior to elden ring, all but one are great. Dark Souls 2 was a very bad game because there are tons of artificial difficulty which was brought back to Elden Ring. 

[b]1. Enemy placements:[/b]
- Big or Giant enemies in extremely small space with half a screen of AoE attacks.
- Gangs of enemies in very small space.
- Gangs of large enemies in one area in an open world. i.e Giant bears, Giant crabs, Giant you name it.
- Gangs of large enemies in very small space. That's right.
- In dark souls 2, every single range enemies have homing projectiles. Obviously this is one of the worst thing in a souls game, in elden ring, these were replaced with gangs of range enemies shooting at you with lightning speed projectile. 

[b]2. Bosses with minions:[/b] Some boss fights, you will be facing multiple smaller enemies.

[b]3. Delayed attacks:[/b] There are way more delayed attacks you will have to deal with compare to DS2. This is to punish dodge rollers. DS1 and 3 rewards you for timing your dodge rolling. DS2 punishes you for it. Elden ring makes it 10 times worse. 

[b][u]Now moving onto non DS2 comparison.[/u][/b]

[b]4. Repetition:[/b] Lots of copy paste bosses. Also lots of copy paste double bosses.

[b]5. Enemy attack chain and animation cancel:[/b] Some enemies have a near infinite attack combo where they don't stop attacking because they follow up with an animation cancel attack. This is not exaggeration, its real. You cant do shyt. There is no window for attack, cant dodge roll, cant block, cant avoid. Literal definition of artificial difficulty. The primary culprit of this is a boss called Margit then later on Morgot.

[b]6. Horseback combat:[/b] The horse riding itself is a new and good implementation to Elden Ring, but binding the dismount button to your Left Analog is the worst thing the devs can do. Sometimes you will accidentally press the left analog which makes you dismount and possibly F you over.

[b]7. Parry and riposte bug[/b]. Sometimes riposte doesnt work, don't know if its an intentional design or bug. How it works supposedly is after you parry an attack successfully, you will hear the parry sound cue like a typical souls game, then you will get an opening to riposte the enemy. Sometimes it works and sometimes it doesnt and no, its not your positioning. I was in the same exact position to riposte an enemy (i.e in front of their face) and on many occasion, the game decides that it is not a riposte state despite the enemy is still in that state. So on top of dodge rolling, you can't rely on parry either. Dodge rolling due to hundreds of delay attacks and parry due to riposte being buggy as hell. You are left with relying on Blocking, that is pretty much it.

[b]7. Grace placement[/b]. The placement of the grace in this open world game are fine until you reach the late game area where grace are place extremely far away, either that or you wont find any grace at all so if you die, you are gonna have to travel another 20km distance. 

[b][u]TLDR[/u][/b] There is no fairness in this game. There are OP builds that allow you to 3-5 shot bosses and if you want fairness, then this is the route to go for.

TLDR:TLDR; breadcrumb storytelling does not work with big open world with filler content

In a vacuum it is a great game. But I feel compelled to leave a negative review to highlight the shortcomings.

My main gripe with it is in comparison to the earlier Fromsoft games, Elden Ring is just too damn big. It is a great thing for replayability and in general a good thing for a game, but it clashes with the core philosophy that Fromsoft games have in regards of lore and story. I love these games, and my passion is the reason why I am so harsh on Elden Ring. This game has way too many different places, items and the map is enormous, which means the meaningful places and items are very far and between and there is a lot of just items without any or barely any significance to the story and lore of the game. 

They wanted to make a big open world game with horseback traversal and comat, its great gameplay, but Elden Ring is not Breath of the Wild, it is not light on important places, lore and story. It is devastating for the  Fromsoft game to be like that. It is so easy to get lost in meaningless story wise content and it is way easier to miss the really important places and items just from the sheer size of the game map and abundance of filler or repetitive content. 

The story is buried in heaps of empty nooks and repetitive dungeons, and by the time that I realized how meaningless they are they already consumed about 50 hours that In any other Fromsoft game would naturally take me through all of the real juice.

My core problem with Elden Ring is that it is not the game that I wanted, and I fully realize it is a "me problem". But I did want to experience a dense world where every item, every enemy and place has meaning and unravels the story and lore of the game. The gameplay challenge is great and fun, but this game absolutely does not respect your time investment, exploring everything in the world, killing every enemy and reading every item description is rewarding in every other Fromsoft game, but it is punishing in Elden Ring. I often found myself thinking while playing this game "I could have had played through the entirety of dark souls 2 with all of the dlc in this time twice and discover more story that I missed previously instead of doing this". Why do we need 10 different crafting ingredient variants that have same item description, different cookbooks that are separate items that have same item description etc.

TLDR; I hope their next game will be more concentrated with meaningful content, like they used to be, or at least that they will clearly explain what content is there for grind and gameplay and irrelevant to the lore. This game is a step forward in gameplay and audio-visual art, but a massive misstep in overall direction. True open world like that does not mix well with meaningful breadcrumbs style of storytelling. Atmosphere suffers, lore suffers and it is a massive shame that I have to either go through hours of chaff to discover something or go watch VaatiVidya lore videos and get spoiled everything robing myself of discovering things on my own.

Most will have already made up their minds about this game, but those like me that decided to give it an honest try after enjoying Nightreign with friends, this may be pertinent to you. 

The game is clearly lovingly crafted with intent and an admiration for crafting a world with beauty all around. I never could be bothered to try prior souls titles because of the sheer bleakness permeating every aspect of them. Unfortunately, this game is still bleeding that bleakness in every aspect of it, just with a prettier coat of paint over it. 

Core gameplay - the controls of the game are certainly better than past souls titles, but still relatively clunky to other fantasy combat titles. I'm not talking about the intended design being that every action you take must be fully committed to, though I have problems with that as well (why can't my character feint an attack in an input reading medieval style combat game?). Targeting, camera, movement, sprinting, rolling, all of it is just not as smooth as other titles have managed over the years. The introduction of guard counters and a stance bar is a dramatic improvement over prior souls titles, so combat is more than just rolling like an idiot until you can plink the enemy once or twice. But because of the amount of stamina blocking takes, it's still the least optimal option for taking on your larger enemies and bosses. You will likely find yourself switching to two handing your weapon. The actual dungeoneering of the game is relatively shallow, and relies on griefing style mechanics more than interesting exploration mechanics. I do sincerely appreciate that the game re-popularized old game design such as Metroidvanias, and I think that is a major saving grace of it. But like much of modern gaming had started a trend I dislike of being too hand holdy, this one runs too far in the opposite direction and is designed to be miserable at every available opportunity. 

Game Introduction - This game has one of the most miserable introductions to a new player I've seen in a modern game. It's clearly designed for those that are familiar with the franchise. If this is your first time, you will be lost as the game tells you next to nothing about how to get started. You will wander around aimlessly dying needlessly and get nothing out of it until a handful of things click for you. If you enjoy beating your head against a wall until you find a way to break through the wall, you will likely still enjoy the game. If that feels as much of a waste of time to you as it did to me, my counter recommendation stands. The game did pick up for me after the first 10 hours or so maybe. But "getting" it didn't make me fall in love with it the way most of the community clearly did. 

Buildcrafting - in my humble opinion, the build craffting opportunites are relatively shallow and you get virtually zero chances to experiment. You have to fully commit to builds because of the way weapon ranks and stat based leveling work. You can respec a limited number of times, but most of the new gear you get will going to a vault pit never to be thought about again because to try it requires such an enormous investment. If you aren't a caster, your non-basic attack options are limited to what Ashes of War you can attach to your weapons. There is a good variety of interesting ashes in the game that let you start to lean toward certain kinds of class fantasies. But you will only have access to a small handful of these abilities at any one time in the middle of combat unless you are casting spells or incantations. 

Open World - As mentioned previously, there is a tremendous amount of stunning scenery around the map as you explore it. But the game is not improved by being made open world. Most of it is wasted space, serving only to have you waste more time in the chance there there is something hidden there, but more times than not, there won't be. I recall solidifying my position on this when I found a small madness village on a mountain. After clearing it and finding minimal loot, I spent some time jumping my way up onto the roofs of the houses and then around atop all the houses. And there was nothing there to find. That's fine, but Legend of Zelda was providing interesting things to find atop houses 3 decades ago. This little village only served as a way to deliver you your first madness incantation. 

Lore - The opinion I would for sure be most crucified over. I think the game's lore is shallow and un-engaging, and I wonder if most people that love it have simply not yet experienced lore and worldbuilding from other franchises. It serves its purpose, it give you a base reason for why the world sucks and you have an apocalyptic world with more green than usual to go around killing a bunch of strong bosses in. But it's a practical waste of time to explore much more beyond the opening cutscene, because the game will give you no answers. To be clear, I don't like it when lore or story gives you all of the answers definitively and obtusely, but this game gives you nothing. I don't think it struck the right balance for me. A lot of people enjoy speculating about what the lore could be saying, but I'm not interested in baseless speculation. Most of it is a waste of time to me if there is literally no basis for it. Not to mention, the game play design conflicts with what the lore's core message seems to want to say - that power is bad no matter who wields it. But that's a strange message to host in a world inhabited by the influence of outer world powers that would make the world significantly worse than anything the core powers have done. 

Online/Multiplayer - It just isn't worth it. Running through a dungeon or a castle with friends sounds fun and it can be. But it opens you up to being invaded and there is no way to turn this off. The player messages seriously degrade the magic of the world as you explore it. The overwhelming majority of them are a waste of time. I genuinely haven't the slightest idea why anybody would find the PvP engaging whatsoever. The combat is pure griefing, and designed to be so. If you get invaded, the mobs near you will not engage the invader but will engage you. So 90% of invaders are just there to make your experience miserable by running to mobs and camping there, harassing you if you try to ignore them then running if you turn to face them. There are no limits on their ability to run, no timers or arenas. And PvP combat is mostly just dodging, which I think is the core flaw of the gameplay overall. Rolling constantly is bad design, in my opinion. So if you want to play through the game with friends in the limited capactiy the game allows, the game will severely punish you for that and try to make you miserable. 

And I think that is the core flaw of the game. It is suffused with intent of design to make you miserable, to add friction to the game, and to grief you. This is called difficulty, but I did not find the bosses particularly difficult and swept through almost all of them in 1-3 attempts. People online tend to believe that reactions to this kind of game are binary, that you either suck it up and deal with it and "git gud" or you "rage quit" and "lol mad". But that was rarely my reaction to 4chan trolling just like it wasn't my reaction to this game. I didn't want to throw my controller, I just resigned myself to feeling like the game was trying to waste my time. And so eventually, I decided I would not waste my time on it any further. 

If you are the kind of person that enjoys pushing yourself through grueling experiences designed to be miserable (not difficult generally, just miserable), and feel great about getting through to the other side, this game is for you. But then, you've likely already played it. If you're like me, and don't care to spend your your spare free time being griefed by game designers when you could be doing literally anything else, then I don't recommend the game.

I initially heavily disliked the way they designed the boss fights and was hoping there would be better designed bosses later on.

But it only got worse, having beaten the elden beast and some optional remembrance bosses, i have not seen a single enjoyable boss fight. They weren't even that difficult, I'd say Khazan bosses are quite a bit harder, but unlike in Khazan, not a single one was a fun fight. And the game went even further many times - taking the bosses you hate and putting 2 in 1 fight. They are not designed as a single fight, but are quite literally just 2 individual bosses doing their own thing - being relentlessly aggressive.

Even at 50 Vigor w/ Radhan's armor set, the bosses and some elites will consistently 2-shot you with stronger attacks, or combo 3-shot you with weaker ones. They are constantly either attacking or running away from you making it very hard and annoying to land damage. But the real misery starts when you get hit once. For many bosses they are so aggressive and fast in closing the distance, trying to heal off the hit to avoid death from the next one becomes an absolutely miserable experience. The healing animation in this game is very slow. So chances are you'll either die before you get a flask off, or lose all the hp you've just healed off by eating a hit right after. And many of the bosses that do have some chill in terms of spamming attacks - have special range attacks that they input the moment you try to flask, rendering your healing null, which is cheap af.

Some bosses also have attacks which are basically guaranteed damage if they start them when you're point blank. They either have a very long duration or are a sequence of very fast hits, so dodging the 1st one makes you get hit by the 2nd one.

The hp of the bosses is also largely arbitrary, using a +10 Somber weapon, in later game I could go from a boss that takes 15min to poke to death or one that dies in like 10 hits or less.

And the old classic of spamming giant bosses, or even mid-sized bosses on uneven terrain - you get hit by attacks that are not on your screen, it's awful and miserable.

To conclude the bosses part, it feels like the main criteria in their design was to make them as obnoxiously annoying and difficult as possible rather than making the fight a spectacle or mechanically fair and fun, and later on to counterbalance it they gave many of the most aggressive bosses paper HP pools, which is a terrible way to do it imo. Khazan, Sekiro and Wukong did bosses significantly better while keeping the difficulty.

Now onto exploration, it was initially fun to ride around looting camps and crawling through caves and dungeons, but 30hours in the novelty wore off. Most of the caves/dungeon are the same-ish thing, making the process boring. And the conclusion was even worse once I realised that the rewards are completely worthless. Once you pick your preferred weapon/playstyle (and you will have to, due to how stingy the weapon mats can be), the only drop you'll care about are the somber stones, literally 99% of everything else becomes worthless garbage. So closer to the end of the game, there was little to no incentive to explore said dungeons since the dopamine pay-off wasn't there anymore.

They killed my boy. I'm a lover of the whole "souls" franchise and related games. Dark Souls 1-3, Sekiro, Bloodborne, Demon's souls. They're all amazing and unique games that reward the player in ways no other game has. So needless to say I was excited to see what was next for the franchise. And what I got was a very pretty open world game that absolutely destroyed the core of what made those previus "soulslike" games so unique and rewarding, seemingly in the name of adding features that a focus group said would make things better. Those previous games gave you a narrow path with a direction to go and an obstacle to overcome. They were difficult, but you had a focus and direction and the one way through was to get good and overcome. Elden Ring gives you an open world, and suddenly the pacing is gone. You have a cluttered map where you explore and hope to stumble on your next appropriate content. I encountered a boss early in the game that was an easy fight, except that he was overtuned to my level so I was only able to do 1 damage per swing at it. After 20 minutes of successfully dodging the boss attacks and responding with my own bursts of damage, I realized that I had hardly made a dent in his health bar. So I quit and realized I had to find a new direction to go in and hope it is where I'm supposed to be. Those tense roads to the boss that created tension and forced the player to plan and learn to overcome? Elden ring has horse. Go wherever you want, these slow ass enemies won't be able to catch up. The lore of the games is no longer tight and cohesive. There are arbitrary dungeons littered all over that have a boss and a treasure at the end. Not because it makes sense for the enemy to be there, or that there's a story behind the dungeon's existence. But because there's a big map now, gotta fill it with something. And players expect a fight and a boss when they stumble on a new place. The experience is so watered down, it might as well be a checklist style game a la Far Cry. Every single other souls game was an addiction to me, games that got their claws in me and didn't relent until I conquered the challenge of the game. Elden ring is easy and directionless in some ways, but also arbitrarily frustrating in other ways. But because open worlds have mass appeal, the winning magical formula of the previous games might mean the death of the reals Soulslike experience going forward. And that's a real shame. Wish I could give a mixed review here because the game suffers from so many flaws but is also pretty fun at the same time (especially for JUST the first time playing). 

Originally played at launch on PS4 and the game was horribly balanced and I didnt enjoy it much, honestly hated how much glazing it was getting when it just did nothing for me (i still ended up 100%ing it). Coming back 3 years later, the game has changed A LOT since launch, so many NEEDED QOL and balance changes. The current state is a fairly polished game that you can sink endless hours into. However, it misses the mark a lot. 

The replayability is incredibly reduced by the fact that its a massive slow (near walking sim even with torrent) open world game with the heavily reused assets. A lot of times you spend more time just travelling rather than playing the game. Compare this to previous titles made by fromsoft and the game is non-stop action that feels atleast well paced with the bonfire system, the open world only degrades the quality of the game here as a lot of the time you are purely returning to the legacy dungeons or bosses anyway. The area of the game which highlights this the absolute WORST is liurnia, a flat never ending boring lake thats the biggest area on the entire map.

Boss design is also MASSIVELY inferior to previous games. The game throws bosses at you that have incredibly long combos, delayed attacks, aoes and insane movement; and thats the cookie cutter template for all of them. With the open world, you can level a bit, tank some of the undodgeable attacks and outdamage the health you lose. THAT aside, bosses are also balanced around spirit summons too. The long annoying combos are basically "balanced" by the fact that the aggression can be diverted from you, meaning you usually have to wait for a long combo to end or risk getting hit with a charge or jump attack during their windups (which usually are tracked to hit as soon as you make an action - dodge, hit, jump whatever). Obviously the problems I have listed vary with every boss, some have it worse than others (big offenders are morgott, radahn, malenia and the final boss). The worst designed boss in the game by far is malenia and I was honestly shocked how it was still the same as it was at launch. I dont even need to go in detail here, the healing, hyper armour and water dance being mentioned is enough - a poorly designed and easy to cheese boss. Side note, but if you had some sort of defensive counter to actually match most bosses aggression itd be more fun. It feels like youre fighting sekiro bosses with the speed of an over-encumbered dark souls 1 character.

If you want to see how bad boss design is, just look at level 1 or no hit runs - you have to spend ages waiting for an actual opening and not a faked out one that damages you anyway. Playing the dark souls games at level 1 is so fun and challenges your knowledge of the game and skill but the bosses here are just so poorly designed im not interested in even trying.

Despite the flaws this game has, its a very easy (given you play the game how it wants you to, exploring everything and getting overleveled/op gear) open world game that was incredibly satisfying usually with discovering stuff. There are still quite a few times where you get useless crafting materials (who tf uses this) instead of something actually worth the effort you put into finding it. Regardless, since this was a lot of peoples first soulslike game, its understandable how crazy the hype it got was. Personally id play any souls game over this, but its still a solid game and probably a good entry into fromsoft games in general. 6.5/10

Playing this game is like being in a toxic relationship. Most of the time it’s frustrating and punishing, but just when you’re ready to walk away, it throws you an intense but fleeting burst of satisfaction. Just enough to make you think, “Maybe if I just try harder… maybe I can be better.”

Pros:
The environment art and atmosphere are a 10/10 absolutely stunning. It’s one of the most visually inspiring games I’ve ever played, and I frequently reference it in my own work. The enemy AI and animations are top-notch as well, with fluidity and responsiveness that make each encounter feel dynamic.

Cons:
Just about everything else.
Controls and movement are clunky. Bosses are absurdly overtuned, and the challenge is often amplified by mechanics that feel intentionally punishing like how drinking a health potion slows you to a crawl, or how bosses can knock you down and chain-combo you before you even stand up.
Cluttered arenas make fights chaotic in the worst ways I’ve tripped over scenery more times than I can count. The soft-lock system is unreliable, constantly snapping to irrelevant targets (rabbits, for example). Enemies like Glinstone Sorcerers spam attacks to an irritating degree. 

It’s not just that the game is difficult it’s that the difficulty often comes from handicapping the player rather than presenting fair challenges. You’re punished for every mistake in a game designed to make mistakes inevitable. Losing all your runes after a minor misstep is maddening. Success feels more about brute-forcing repetition than skill surviving an encounter often comes down to running it enough times until you finally don’t screw up.

On top of that, the skills and modifier systems are unintuitive, and if you’re coming from more traditional RPGs, the NPCs will likely feel flat and lifeless by comparison.

I constantly flip between “I love this game” and “I hate this game,” and I think that says something. There’s brilliance here something truly special but it’s buried under layers of unnecessary tedium. It’s an experience I admire more than I enjoy.

I've changed my review after beating Dark Souls 1.

I actually think that the quest system here is fine. There's no need for a quest/NPC log. And I really appreciate that there's no handholding.

The late/end-game balance is still problematic. Making summons really powerful means that Elden Ring is more accessible for new players. But that also means that balancing bosses becomes much harder. So that's why the end/late-game balance is so bad. Getting killed in 2-3 hits with over 40 vigor is just artificial difficulty. This was never a problem in Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 3, or Sekiro.

Unfortunately, this is yet another one of those mid games that's only praised because it introduced a concept that other games have done 10x better to the masses. Can I seriously have an opinion on a game as large as Elden Ring after only spending 8 hours with it? Yes, because actually playing the game is only a small part of this title's intended experience.

Firstly, let's get the positives out of the way:

This game is gorgeous. While most modern games, while high-rez, are ugly to look at because what the developers made high-rez looks like crap. (Like seriously, would you people who praise those games because they're high-rez say an 8k picture of a moldy dog turd looks better than a 4k picture of the Mona Lisa just because it's higher rez?) But Elden Ring is like exploring a beautiful painting.

There are a few good parts in this game that hold the expected FromSoft level of quality.

...And that's about all the positives I have to mention.

My hands-on experience with this game is as follows: I listened to what the game told me to do and went to face the first boss, but after he was way harder than a first boss should be, even a first FromSoft boss, I got the hint that the game was telling me to go level up first. So, I went exploring...and quickly learned that despite this being advertised as a revolution on open-world games, this is yet another empty field and copy-pasted mini dungeon simulator that I'm frankly tired of at this point. I decided to lessen the pain of this by looking up some starter tips for this game, then I fell down the rabbit hole...

What I knew Souls games for was their brutal difficulty that forced you to keep learning from your mistakes and trying again, but Elden Ring is not difficult, it's a game that's basically impossible without a guide, and easy with a guide. If you don't follow the meta and look up obtuse weaknesses bosses possess that you could never realistically figure out on your own, this game is so hard that some of the later bosses have periods between their attack cues and actual attacks that exceed the average human reaction time. There's no "getting good" around hard biological limits, and that's why all the players insist on following a strict meta that makes the gameplay less varied and more tedious. To me, the experience being outlined for me seems more like following an instruction manual than playing a game. Like assembling ikea furniture or something, and beyond that, the game becomes stupidly easy.

Furthermore, given the nature of this game, it completely kills any fun that could be had with it being open world, since if you don't follow a guide on where to go in sequence, your open world adventuring will be an obnoxious mix of not getting to explore because the encounters are beyond your level and kill you too often, and cheesing enemies that are a way lower level than you the whole time. This could be partially eliminated if this game did a good job of hinting where to go so that there was at least an illusion of both freedom and fun, but it doesn't.

I get that there are great parts in this game, especially the "traditional" segments, but there is nothing of value you will get out of playing Elden Ring that you won't get out of playing earlier FromSoft titles, which are nothing but these "good parts."

And no, this is not a more "accessible" Souls game for newbies either, since the game flirts with literally impossible territory if you don't follow the meta and the guides, and becomes cozy game levels of easy if you do. Sure, you can pick and choose what to limit yourself to to try creating a good difficulty level, but the game wasn't balanced with this in mind, so it will suck compared to games that simply have a good difficulty level.

Now go play a real Souls game and stop giving money to modern AAA developers.

Elden Ring – A Critique of the Overhyped Giant
Despite being widely acclaimed, Elden Ring is far from a universally loved masterpiece. For many players, it’s an exhausting, bloated, and inaccessible experience masked by mystique and hype. Here's a breakdown of the most common complaints and frustrations:

1. Obnoxiously Difficult & Not Newcomer-Friendly
The game refuses to explain core mechanics, builds, or progression.

Enemy difficulty spikes wildly, making early areas manageable but later ones frustratingly punishing.

Bosses are often designed with delayed attacks, excessive tracking, and overwhelming AoE moves.

There’s no scalable difficulty—“Git Gud” is still the only option, alienating casual players.

2. Terrible Quest Design
Quests are cryptic and easily missable, with no journal, no quest log, and zero guidance.

NPCs disappear or die without explanation, locking players out of storylines they didn’t even know existed.

Many players are forced to follow external wikis just to understand what’s going on.

3. Janky Combat
Hitboxes are inconsistent and unfair at times, with enemies hitting through walls or dodges.

The camera becomes a nightmare during large boss fights or enclosed spaces.

Lock-on system struggles with verticality and fast enemies, constantly targeting the wrong thing.

4. Repetitive Content
Overuse of the same bosses (Tree Spirits, Crucible Knights, Erdtree Avatars, etc.) across the map.

Dungeons often feel copy-pasted with slight variations, making exploration less rewarding.

Many side areas exist solely to pad game time without offering meaningful content.

5. Bloated Open World
The world is massive for the sake of being massive, leading to long stretches of emptiness.

Horseback traversal becomes tedious after a while, with no real fast-paced travel options.

Too many minor dungeons and locations feel like filler rather than genuine discoveries.

6. Poor UX and UI
Clunky inventory management and convoluted menu navigation.

Multiplayer summoning and co-op are overly complex and unintuitive.

No pause button—even in single-player—which many view as outdated and needlessly punishing.

7. Vague Storytelling
The plot is vague to the point of being nonexistent without YouTube or lore deep dives.

Players who enjoy story-rich games are left confused, with unclear motivations and disjointed narrative progression.

8. Technical Issues
PC performance was a disaster at launch: stuttering, crashes, and frame rate drops.

Texture pop-in, janky animations, and poor frame pacing are still issues on some setups.

Controls can feel floaty or delayed, particularly with mouse and keyboard.

9. Overrated by Critics and Fans
The game is often praised as a “masterpiece” even by those who admit they didn’t finish it.

Fanbase toxicity: any criticism is often met with hostility or dismissed as a skill issue.

The constant comparison to other open-world games ignores the genre's evolution toward accessibility and player respect.

10. Unbalanced PvP
PvP is full of cheese tactics, one-shot builds, and poorly designed invasions.

Balance is inconsistent across weapons and spells.

Anti-cheat is weak on PC, allowing hackers to ruin the online experience.

11. Poor Build Balance
Some classes and builds are hilariously underpowered or obsolete.

Magic was broken at launch; bleed builds trivialized bosses; and faith builds often feel underwhelming.

Respeccing is limited and tied to boss progression, discouraging experimentation.

12. Unclear Progression Path
Players can easily wander into high-level zones too early with no in-game indication.

Multiple progression paths and NPC interactions are poorly communicated or hidden behind obscure triggers.

Conclusion
For all its artistic ambition and scope, Elden Ring is not for everyone. Its inaccessibility, janky mechanics, repetitive design, and refusal to explain itself create a game that many consider more frustrating than fun. If you’re not already a FromSoftware fan, this game may feel more like an overhyped endurance test than a rewarding adventure.

Three years after its release, I finally decided to drop a review of Elden Ring. I’m absolutely not interested in debating this game, so this review is for people who’ve heard about the “legendary game from Miyazaki” and are wondering whether it’s actually worth playing.

Just to clarify: I’ve sunk 163 hours into it and got the platinum trophy, so I guess I’ve figured out at least some of what’s going on.

Let me start with what completely killed my first impression—literally from the second I created my character. The engine in Elden Ring is just straight-up copy-pasted from Dark Souls 3. I liked DS3, it played well—but that was back in 2016. Just for comparison, The Witcher 3 came out in 2015. Can you imagine the outrage if CDPR released a new Witcher game in 2025 with the exact same combat from a decade-old title? And combat in The Witcher isn’t even the main focus

Next up—the bosses. One of the main selling points of Elden Ring is the sheer number of bosses. And yeah, there are 165 of them in total. The catch? Only 8 are actually original. You only have to beat 12 to complete the story. The rest are repeated bosses—at best reused twice, and in reality, much more often. And yeah, fighting the same boss over and over again is just as exciting as it sounds. Some “bosses” are literally regular enemies with buffed HP bars.

Oh, and let’s not forget the ones that are recycled straight from older FromSoftware games—sometimes just with a texture swap and a couple new moves. For example:

Omenkiller – Capra Demon (DS1)

Erdtree Avatar – Asylum Demon (DS1)

Raya Lucaria Sorcerers – Grand Archives scholars (DS3)

Red Wolf of Radagon – Sif (DS1)

Aging Untouchable – Winter Lantern (Bloodborne)

All kinds of slugs and basilisks? Let’s just say they're “classic staples.”

And that’s probably not even all the recycled stuff. Got this info from a Reddit post, which is now slightly outdated since DLC added Radagon and Dragonlord Placidusax again)
https://www.reddit.com/r/Eldenring/comments/t7uht1/the_number_of_truly_unique_bosses_in_elden_ring/?tl=

Now about the open world… I mean, what’s even left to say? People have covered this already, but in short: it sucks. Your choices are:

Clear a bunch of generic copy-paste dungeons to maybe get a summon or a smithing stone +1.
Loot some ctrl+C ctrl+V ruined houses with a miniboss/stat-check enemy inside.
That’s pretty much it. Sure, there are NPC questlines, but they’re so forgettable I literally couldn’t recall a single one without Googling.

Let’s talk balance: There isn’t any. On my first playthrough, I followed the glowing path to Margit (like the game suggests). I was playing as a Prisoner, and Margit kicked my ass hard. I struggled, beat him, and then checked online—turns out the game expects you to go in a different direction first, level up somewhere else, and then come back.

Later in the game, I was so overleveled for some areas that it just became boring. I tried to rationalize it like “maybe everyone’s meant to have their own unique experience,” but it just ended up being a mess. I’d get stuck on some random mob boss, then nuke a “main” boss like Radahn in 2 tries. First try I even got to the end of the fight and realized I had no idea what the hell just happened. Restarted just so I could at least try dodging his attacks.

Basically, if you want a smooth experience, you have to follow some player-made route online. Maybe even look up recommended weapons—because, yes, some weapons are objectively stronger than others. It’s just such a lazy design that it’s honestly depressing. I played at launch and didn’t really want to rely on guides. And yeah, my experience was kinda garbage.

I could go on, but I won’t. I’ll just say this: if you’ve already played FromSoft games before, Elden Ring is probably not for you. And if you’re new to the genre—there are better places to start.

I got into Soulslikes with Bloodborne and played most of FromSoft’s catalog. But Elden Ring might honestly be my last game in the genre. I only went for the platinum to figure out what exactly didn’t sit right with me—and in the end, I realized it’s just time to walk away from FromSoftware. It’s only gonna get worse from here.

Big open hostile world with a story sparsely sprinkled around as an afterthought. Bosses can kill you in 2-3 hits, and so can the trash mobs. It is challenging at the start, but later just feels like a tedious grind.

When you kill stuff, you get 'runes' (cash), which you use to buy stuff and level-up. When you die, cash falls out your pocket but you can run back and collect it after you respawn. There are checkpoints scattered all over the place which can be used for basically resting and fast travel, but mobs will also respawn. You have a map that shows discovered dungeons etc, but it doesn't indicate what has been completed.

Combat mechanics are realistically sluggish and weight restricted. I dislike that you cannot block attacks quickly with a shield. If you swing a sword, the animation doesn't cancel out, so you need to dodge attacks constantly instead. Need a drink from a health/mana potion? it slows you down to walking speed which is very convenient for the mob chasing you. Annoyingly you cannot quickly check your map when in combat/near enemies.

There are hundreds of weapons and outfits in this game which is nice, but most weapons have stat restrictions before they can be used efficiently. The stats page is an ugly complicated mess. It is difficult to tell what is good or not.  Upgrading weapons sucks - the components you need are either hard to find or very expensive.

It is actually almost impossible to complete this game without a guide. Your journey progress will likely grind to a halt at various points due to bad game design. For example, I and literally millions of other players had to look up a youtube video on how to cross a lift/bridge. 

The main story events are disappointingly short, forgettable and often nonsensical. There are side characters to add more lore, but they are very easy to miss. The game has one ending with slight variations depending on which npcs you encountered along the way. If your goal in life is to be a lord of some zombie rat infested city, I think you need to see a psychiatrist. 

On a final note, I wish game publishers stop taking clips from the ending cutscenes to put in game trailers.

I have a lot of respect for Elden Ring and everything it achieves — it's a massive, rich, and ambitious game. But after spending quite a few hours with it, I’ve realized that I clearly prefer the Dark Souls series.
Everything in Elden Ring is bigger, more open, more free... but for me, that freedom comes at a cost: I find the game less tense, less dense, and less impactful. Where Dark Souls offered a tight, interconnected, oppressive world, here I often feel like I’m getting lost in a world that’s too big, with a lot of side content that doesn’t leave much of an impression.
Combat is great, no doubt, but the faster pace, the horse, the frequent checkpoints and fast travel all lessen that constant sense of danger that made Dark Souls so gripping. In Dark Souls, every bonfire felt like a hard-earned relief. In Elden Ring, it’s just another stop.
Artistically, Elden Ring is stunning, but I’m more drawn to the heavy, quiet, almost suffocating atmosphere of Souls. That world still haunts me. Elden Ring feels more distant by comparison.
It's an excellent game, no question. But for me, it’s less intense, less personal than Dark Souls. And sometimes, less… unforgettable.

I have tried so hard to love this game.
Sometimes it feels like everybody it the world gets it but me.
Look, I get that it's hard. It's supposed to be. Maybe I shouldn't have gotten it as one of my first games on PC getting just used to new controls. But I don't have a problem with hard games. I beat Hollow Knight and it was my favourite game of all time. I beat Genocide Route in Undertale easily and had as close to fun as you can have in Genocide Route without being psychopathic. The difference between Elden Ring and Hollow Knight however is in Hollow Knight the bosses only have a handful of attacks, the graphics are much cleaner (there were ocassions in Elden Ring where I could hear but not see NPCs no matter how hard I looked) so I can see the attacks better, and the attacks don't consist of what is practically a dance across the battlefield (in Malenia's case quite literally). I simply don't have the time to invest in memorising the signals for all 200 bosses' attacks. 
'Well have you tried levelling up?' It's time to talk about world design. It makes no sense. I start off in an area surrounded by all sorts of difficult hazards, but if I push through them, I can get to an area with easier challenges? The system for weapons is awful as well. You are supposed to level up around your weapons, which is great and all, but then when you collect enough weapons you also have to choose your weapon around your stats. Which one do I do? 
Then there is the story. People talk at great lengths about how great the story is. I looked up a summary of the 'story' because the opening made no sense to me even after the third attempt at restarting. The game basically doesn't have a story, it has a mythology. And an incredibly convoluted mythology at that. How am I supposed to tell the difference between Godrick, Godfrey, and Godwyn, or Radahn, Ranni, and Radagon? And remember their family tree which is the size of the giant tree in the middle of the world. While the game is perfectly happy to elaborate on the familial disputes of the various demigods, it gives almost no plausible reason for me, the Tarnished of no renown, to be suffering through all of these challenges other than 'it's your God-given fate.' Which is pretty Medieval logic so I guess that increases the immersion, but if I am pushing through all of those punishing bosses I should at least be given some motivation. Having recently finished Undertale it reminds me of Sans' dying words at the end of the game when describing the player's motivation; 'and because you 'can', you 'must.' The game's story doesn't have to be Final Fantasy VII, it just has to provide me with some reason to keep playing.
Sure the graphics are beautiful, so as long as you don't look too hard at it. Sure the bosses are super cool, but there is only so long something can be cool for before it starts being annoying. And sure the devs worked really hard on the game, and I would hate for their hard work to be in vain. And playing the game feels good too. It's never boring, unlike so many other games. It never cuts corners. It was a labour of love. 
And I still don't know how I can possibly keep playing after 200 hours and 3 retries and I still can't beat MARGIT THE FELL OMEN, the first main story boss in the game! Maybe I should take his advice and put my foolish ambitions to rest.
This doesn't mean I've given up on soulslikes. Sekiro looks pretty good in that any death is your own fault and not because you missed some item. let me know what you think in the comments.

Elden Ring, developed by FromSoftware, has received overwhelming praise from both critics and gamers alike. Touted as a masterpiece in open-world design and gameplay, it won numerous Game of the Year awards and became a cultural phenomenon in the gaming world. However, despite its popularity, Elden Ring is often overrated. Its widespread acclaim can sometimes overshadow significant flaws in its design, accessibility, and storytelling.

One major criticism is the game’s lack of accessibility. Elden Ring, like other FromSoftware titles, is notoriously difficult, and while some players enjoy the challenge, it can alienate a large portion of the gaming community. There are minimal in-game tutorials, and the game offers very little guidance, which leads to frustration rather than fun for many newcomers. This steep learning curve can feel more punishing than rewarding, especially for players who don’t have the time or patience to “learn by dying” repeatedly.

In addition, the game’s open-world design, while massive and detailed, can feel overwhelming and empty at times. Players often find themselves wandering through huge areas without clear objectives or meaningful rewards. While the exploration is meant to feel organic, the lack of direction can result in aimless gameplay, where progress is more about luck than skill or strategy. This design choice, although praised for its freedom, can also be interpreted as a lack of structure or thoughtful pacing.

Lastly, Elden Ring’s story is hard to follow and not delivered in a conventional or engaging way. Much of the narrative is hidden behind cryptic item descriptions and vague dialogue, which makes it difficult for players to grasp the full scope of the plot without looking up lore videos or fan interpretations online. While this approach might appeal to hardcore fans of the Souls series, it leaves casual players confused and disconnected from the story. In short, while Elden Ring is impressive in many ways, its flaws are often overlooked, making it a highly overrated game for the general audience.

TLDR; 5 / 10

This game is an artistic masterpiece, both visually and audibly. If you really are into Souslike games or want to play the game just to explore the open world for it's artistic style you will probably not regrett purchasing the game.

There are however, too many issues that I have with the game to generally recommend it. If Steam had a "mixed" option I would probably pick that.

My main issues in no particular order:

Depending on how you play the game you will a) find the game too easy b) think it's alright or c) not enjoy most of the combat. All of it just depends on whether the weapon and playstyle you choose are (either intentionally by looking up guides or by accident) "the meta way to play" or not.

The bosses can be quite annoying to fight. They will constantly do the most crazy over the top anime main character moves you have ever seen while you get to play the game maybe once every 20 seconds ([spoiler]having to dodge Malenia for 3 full stamina bars without pause gets tiresome really quick when you are only allowed one attack afterwards[/spoiler]).
Additionally they will spam AoE all over the place and have some of the most ridiculusly delayed attacks imaginable. It is so bad that some of them are straight up immersion breaking. All that just so you don't beat them too quickly (unless you use a meta build, that is) and to throw a "gotcha" at you every third attack.

The input lag is the worst in any FS game that I've played (DS 1-3, Sekiro and ER) and while the input queue is not as ridiculus as it was in DS1 (no, I don't want to do my queued attack after an 8 second grab animation) it will still cause you to perform inputs you didn't want to after a stagger.

This game is the least replayable of the soulsborne games. I'd really like to play through the game another 2 or 3 times, but I'm dreading the thought of how long it would take just to reach the interesting parts.

The optional dungeons are straight up lazy design. You have a handful of "themes" that are copy-pasted over the entire map. It's so bad that even some major bosses are reused as additional fights.


Overall the game is pretty alright when compared to games in general, but when compared to earlier FS titles it is a bit of a let-down.

Great game for the type of people who like "souls" games, unfortunately I am not one. I did give it a fair shot I would say. Played twice, once with summons then again without summons as a lot of people suggested it might be ruining the experience. After thoroughly experiencing it and wanting to like it, I just can't.

Things I don't like (about the genre as a whole), If you enjoy "souls" games skip over to the next part -
* The attack commitment makes the combat "not-fun" for me. I like to play aggressive and not having any attack-cancel window just removes any fun form the combat. Sekiro, for example, hits the sweet spot for me - you can't arbitrary cancel an attack but there is a tiny window at the start where you can cancel an attack.
* Not being able to pause was another bummer, now I understand that with PvP component it might be tricky. As someone who does not care about the online part and PvP having to forgo pausing just plain sucked. Like mate I need to open the door for people coming into my house, attend the phone, take a leak, etc. Having to pause life for a game seems like a tall order.
* Not having a journal as another thing I am not a fan of. I play the game when I can spare the time and sometimes I have to go weeks (or even months) before I can get back to it, not having track of all the stuff that is going on to refresh my memory is stupid.
* Camera was the hardest boss in this game a lot of the times, specially on larger enemies. And for some reason there are these ancient dragons for which the locking on is different from other dragons. I couldn't really understand the point of that. Was the point to make the fights difficult my not being able to lock-on to easily approachable targets like hands/feet, well it was indeed successful, but wasn't really fun for me.
* Non-immersive world - The world is empty, too empty. No (friendly) settlements of people, barely any NPCs you can talk to. Now as there are no settlements these fair few NPCs, you can talk to feels even more weird and overall that just takes away from the any sense of immersion form this world. Another aspect that adds to it is that the world does not react at all to your actions. e.g. the Nephelli-Haiget combined questline.

Things I did not like which I feel like someone who enjoys "souls" games might agree with -
* In my first playthrough I came across a lot of same-y feeling dungeons and a lot of recycled bosses, which wasn't the case in the second playthrough. The difference in playthroughs was that the first one was quite through and second one I just ignored fair bit of caves/catacombs. So, it felt like the game was punishing me for exploring too much.
* Questline progression felt non-obvious. I think it a staple of the genre, I have played Sekiro and Lies of P in addition to Elden ring and there I did not face this issue. As I was progressing I met the NPCs along the way and they were hard to miss because of the linear nature of the games. Same "quest design philosophy" leaves much to be desired in an open world as there are plenty of ways to miss these NPCs.

Things I am unsure where to put -
* Waterfowl dance - This felt like a crutch used by devs to inflate the difficulty of a certain fight. There are ways to counter it, sure. But for someone with a two handed cold damaging build the only option was to change the build as the cold pot throwing might not work to apply status effect as Melinia might already have that status. Dodging is achievable but takes ages to master. Switching to shields was a viable alternative (but, as I said, kind goes against the build I was going for). Some people will enjoy such a challenge I, for one, did not at all.
* Difficulty settings - This is pretty odd. I saw an interview of the person behind these games and his claim was they want people to reach a level like everyone and enjoy the sense of accomplishment. I was like cool that makes sense and this is how Sekiro is. But then ER has summons which trivialize encounters and Miyazaki admitted to using them himself. So, then the whole point about "sense of accomplishment" just feels like lip service. It's like they are saying we are ok with an easy mode we just don't want to call it that.

Now if you are a "souls" enjoyer, the problems with this game are pretty much non-existant and there are loads of positives. This is a no brainier for you to get. If, however, like me, you are not, I have listed out things that try to segregate the "problems" of the genre from the game and you can take a call for yourself.

"I enjoy challenge." Sure you do. That’s why you’re dodging job applications, ignoring that book you said you’d read, and can’t sit through a 30-minute lecture on something real without alt-tabbing.

This game sells you the illusion of growth. You bash your head against a boss for 3 hours, memorize its moves like a dance, and feel like you’ve accomplished something. But what exactly did you learn? How to parry a demon dog with perfect timing. Cool. Meanwhile, the real world is full of challenges that actually matter—learning a language, building something, fixing your life. No checkpoint saves there.

FromSoftware is great at manipulating your dopamine system. But don’t kid yourself: this isn’t "enjoying challenge." This is choosing controlled, aesthetic frustration over meaningful struggle. It’s fast food for people who want to feel like they’re growing without actually stepping outside their comfort zone.

I'm not a huge gamer, and I don't have sixteen hours a day to spend playing video games; this game doesn't appeal to that much, as it's pretty difficult to take in bite-sized pieces, especially when you haven't mastered the controls. It leaves each playthrough feeling frustrating and unrewarding, save for the few times you finally beat the boss.

I understand the appeal of the difficulty, but it's frustrating to get anything productive done in a 30 minute playthrough; I wanna spend my free time having fun and goofing off, not spending it farming runes, dying, then running back to pick up my runes again, all so I can level up enough to make a boss fight a bit easier. Yes, it's a skill issue...but one I wish I didn't have to sink tens of hours into playing to vanquish, especially since majority of the game is hack-and-slash grinding. I just don't find that fun.

This game was made to be played on controller, which is great...for controller players. I've played mouse & keyboard almost exclusively for most of my life, so trying to play this game on the controller felt pretty unnatural for me. I tried, but later switched to mouse and keyboard, but it's very clear the game wasn't made for that format; the keybinds are janky, and it's difficult to customize something when there isn't even a setting for it. I was in a VC with 3 other people, and none of us could figure out the keybind to quickly summon the horse.
There were other weird issues as well, like how the locking on mechanic works. I would be fighting something in front of me, and suddenly it would lock onto a random entity in the background and I'd die.
Another frustration is that you can't customize things like FOV—it's pretty dang hard to fight a boss when it's big toe takes up the entire screen.

The game has some super in-depth lore, and some pretty good visuals; the cut scenes are excellently made. I can understand why people adore this game so much, but like any other game out there, I don't think it's for everyone.

If you take the whole gamedev, then the game is excellent, it stands out against the background of other projects of other studios. But if you take Miyazaki's games, then this is the best game, but for me personally it turned out to be a failure. Previously, the challenge was partly thrown by bosses and situations in which Miyazaki puts you with his game design, in Elden Ring only the numbers throw a challenge (This cannot be called bad, because we ourselves, the players, were striving only for complexity, and not for an interesting process)

Elden Ring is just a huge daub of repetitions and boring bosses, locations, with small grains of content. The only thing that the huge world gave was a huge number of weapons that can be changed several times during the game. But the problem is in the balance of this weapon, if you play without blood, freezing, without GDS in both hands, then the game turns into hell, and going through something like this is terrible for me, in the previous parts you could take any weapon and comfortably go through the game, even screwing up with the pumping and still get a pleasant experience, without bothering with the most boring farm. In the ring, you have to press only with pumping, vacuuming empty, absolutely not beautiful locations (my personal taste) with the most terrible motivation for exploration, where you are rewarded with rowan or stone, it looks like Dark Souls 3, where the locations are castles, castles, castles.

DLC is a special case, the studio followed the players and made absolutely all mobs comparable to bosses (in damage and resistance). In FromSoftware DLC games, there was always work on errors, in Shadow they only bothered to fix the dungeons and made an incredibly beautiful landscape, which is interesting to travel and explore the nooks and crannies, but the problem is that except for consumables there is essentially nothing in it, as a result, the DLC world is beautiful, but it is boring to study, the mobs are pumped up.

In conclusion, I want to say that the game is good, you can call it the best of the creations, but not for the genius Miyazaki. The situation with Ring can be described by one phrase: "You want to make a game for everyone, but you make it for no one." Fans of the open world in the original game did not receive the proper motivation and meaning to vacuum locations and study the structure of the world (since it is monotonous and primitive). In the DLC, the situation was corrected, but the motivation to study... Fans of interesting bosses received well-written characters, but most of them are absolutely boring in terms of gameplay (10,000 hp 10 mouset). Fans of intricate locations have the same situation as fans of the open world. Fans of weapons received, but playing with regular guns is hell. Fans of interesting game situations and adrenaline from overcoming, a small supply of heal and many valuable souls that can be lost, received bonfires every 2 meters and many consumables that negate the value of souls (since you have a million sealed souls in one location).

All of the above is my schizophrenia and my vision of the game. If you do not agree, sit on the erd tree and be happy.

While acknowledging all the time and technical effort that has gone into the production of this game:
There is just too much of two ingredients. You go either with difficulty or vastness. When you have both in this amount it just becomes a waste of time. And especially if you come to need to watch walkthroughs or tutorials on where to go, what to get or in which order, then there is no freedom or excitement in that, because you're letting someone else spoil the story for you while having to follow their strict path in order to proceed, so the whole open-world thing loses its purpose. In dark souls you had an idea of roughly where to go next and you made new discoveries along the path and just fought your way through and got good till you accomplished the objective or killed the boss, you didn't have to run around like a headless worm hat got smacked around all the time. 

Difficulty:
After having leveled up my character and my weapons to max using a cheat engine, I tried beating some of the smaller human looking bosses that were the same size as me with similar looking weapons without God-mode, and they still killed me with a few hits while I did maybe 10 heavey attacks and didn't even bring them close to half of their health. So I turned on God-mode and one-hit kill and danced my way through the game while enjoying the landscapes view. The game isn't necessarily hard, it just takes a stupid amount of time to get good at. And the difficulty is not spread evenly, while the bosses and enemies have tons of health and damage points, getting to places and platforming is like child's play.

The lore: its probably decent. But its not really worth being curious about as its all incomplete and fragmented, and obscured away behind either NPC-dialogs or item descriptions. so you have the vastness, the difficulty, plus you have to be a detective to find out all the clues about what is going on and why. I maybe watch a short version of the lore of this game one day, for now I don't really care.

Here is what I did:
I played through the game blind with a cheat-engine and used god-mode, infinite-items, stealth-mode, infinite-runes, one-hit-kill and flying, just so that I could get through the game and the DLC, explore most of its world and make new discoveries. IT STILL TOOK ME 60 HOURS TO GO THROUGH IT! It felt like playing a somewhat balanced game because I only had the vastness to struggle against.

Also, what's up with all creatures wanting to kill me specifically??? It just doesn't make any sense??!! There is so much misery, pain, and evil in these realms and they are all in in one another's approximation, but they become aggressive as soon as they see me?! Why is that??? Having enabled stealth-mode on the cheat engine it felt much more natural to explore the areas, and creatures only attacked me when I attacked them first.

Maybe one day I play this game without a cheat-engine but for now its a big thumbs down.

The only thing worth the money was the technical efforts that has gone into the production of the game, such as sound, music, vocals, cinematography, visuals, coding, animation, character design, mechanics etc. This game is truly a work of visual and sonic art!
