There's so much to enjoy in this game, after 40+ hours of playing it is very clear that the attention to the visual aesthetic, and musical score are exceptional. Like any FromSoft game the action can be very tense and satisfying. This alone was almost enough to keep me playing but, despite my previous experiences of absolutely loving Bloodborne and DS3 from start to finish, I found this game to be exhausting and a little disappointing. 

The world is massive but lacks the variety of gaming experience to  fill it, the bosses can be entertaining but more often than not I found myself either overleveled and bored or underleveled and horribly frustrated. Obviously no-hitting is still possible on most of these fights but the attack speed and movesets, combined with minute punishable windows of opportunity, made them feel unreasonable. The only solution for a player like me, who can handle other FromSoftware titles quite happily, is apparently to grind levels and weapon upgrades. However I just couldn't stay interested in the very pretty but rather empty feeling world the game provides. I get that various spells and summons can soften this challenge substantially but they just don't give me the same sense of fun and satisfaction. If the game created more engagement from interesting traversal mechanics then this might compensate for it, but riding round big empty fields on a horse doesn't stay exciting for very long.

The legacy dungeons I explored are fantastic but so much of what surrounds them feels like filler, the vast majority of the loot I found in the game was not relevant to my play-through making repetitive Catacombs and recycled bosses feel particularly underwhelming. If the quest lines had more story and weren't so easily missed then I might have had a different perspective.

FromSoftware are an incredible developer and I will definitely keep playing their games in the future, but this has left a bitter aftertaste considering how much goodwill I had for them before bouncing off of this title. Who knows, perhaps I'll come back and change my mind, I hear the DLC is pretty damn good.

[b]A few hours of engaging combat and exploration, but gets boring quickly.[/b]

The Good:

+ The combat is exactly the same as your Dark Souls games, maybe even a bit more streamlined. If you just want hours and hours of tense combat and a bunch of big bosses, Elden Ring delivers. 
+ There's some nice vistas.

The Bad:

- Most everything else, unfortunately.
- FromSoft continues to substitute hints of lore in place of actually having an interesting story or characters. That was a novel approach 15 years ago in Dark Souls 1. By now the novelty has worn off. Everyone is as vague, unrelatable, and unhelpful as possible, providing absolutely no in-universe motivation or context for your actions.
- Combat, exploration, and balance are at odds with each other. The combat is hard, punishing you for experimenting or being a jack of all trades. You [i]have[/i] to optimise. This means that 99% of the items you find are useless for your build. This, in turn, renders exploration useless - you can spend hours clearing copy-pasted dungeons and not find anything useful, so why bother?
- The game is basically Dark Souls but with a whole bunch of empty open areas and identical mini-dungeons to add padding between the main dungeons. Problem is, all this new content is far less interesting than the actual dungeons. It just dilutes the experience, rather than enhancing it.
- Once again, summoning other players to help is extremely janky. Most new players will need a guide to figure it out. Then the game goes and makes summoning an even more central part of the experience by giving you NPC allies you can always summon for boss fights. And yet, the boss AI [i]still[/i] falls apart the moment it tries to handle multiple opponents.

[b]Overall, doesn't improve the Dark Souls formula in any meaningful way, and the series' ongoing flaws are only becoming more grating with each entry. There's enough content that FromSoft fans will probably get their money's worth, but I wouldn't recommend it to newcomers.[/b]

Update: Allez, c'est parti, rentrons dans les détails!

Elden Ring:

Bons points:

Réalisation: XL, presque top niveau: 1 petit cran en dessous de ce que j'appelle époustouflant, mais on est quand même très haut.

Musique du menu: J'aime les bonnes BOs, et la musique du menu principal est top. 

Bel univers: Un très grand soin a été apporté pour développer l'univers du jeu, qui plaira beaucoup à ceux qui y sont réceptifs.

Build: J'ai l'impression qu'il y a quelque chose de très intéressant au niveau des builds possibles pour les différentes "classes". Mais...

Mauvais points:

Pseudo multi: Cette volonté de te caser des fonctionnalités multi dans un jeu qui devrait être solo... Tout ça pour justifier la connexion internet permanente anti-piratage. (N'essayez pas de me prendre pour une bille)

Contrôles du personnage: On dirait qu'il flotte sans être en contact avec le sol, comme dans certains vieux jeux 3D de la fin des années 90. De plus, le personnage est très lent dans ses actions (il faut augmenter certaines stats pour qu'il soit plus rapide).
Et comme la plupart des actions ne sont pas interruptibles, il faut être extrèmement précis. Vous voulez boire une potion, mais vous n'en avez plus? le personnage fait une animation dédiée (il cherche la potion dans sa poche, montre sa surprise de ne pas la trouver, etc), que vous ne pouvez pas interrompre pour parer ou esquiver, vous laissant bien bien vulnérable.

Ergonomie clavier: on s'emmèle dans les boutons pour utiliser une potion, changer d'arme, de sort, invoquer sa monture...
Je veux dire, le gameplay de base, c'est se déplacer, attaquer, sauter, esquiver, parer. Ces actions ont chacune leur bouton, mais pour le reste, faut faire des combinaisons, sélectionner une potion ou un sort pour l'utiliser. Sérieusement, 50% de mes défaites sur les boss sont dûes à un moment ou à un autre à une confusion de bouton. "Ha merde je voulais changer de potion", "oups, mauvais sort", etc
Apparement, le jeu a été prévu pour être joué au pad.

Ergonomie pad: Un peu mieux. Je suis pas fan des manettes à 11 boutons, mais ça c'est moi. J'imagine qu'il faut ça, mais le côté "toujours plus" est un peu énervant. Vous aviez pas accès à une manette jaguar, c'est ça?

Menus: On dirait que les gens qui ont fait les menus se sont dit "on va tout réinventer de zéro pour pas faire ce qui marche chez la concurrence". Je crois que l'expérience des menus de ce jeu est parmi les pires que j'ai pu voir de ma vie.

Pas de minimap: Et si vous me dites que c'est pour renforcer l'immersion, je vous emmerde. C'est ouvrir la grande map qui me sort du jeu. Et qui a (encore) une ergonomie frapadingue.

This is a good game, however there are some jarring design issues that cannot be overlooked. Some of thesse issues also existed in Dark Souls 3.

The difficulty in Elden Ring is a bit controversial, since the tools at our disposal can make the boss fights either far too easy (free summons, bleed, Bloodhound's Step etc.) or too hard (pure melee, low vigor etc.). You should never have to respect in order to win a fight.

Compared to DS1, I found that DS3’s more challenging boss fights were not suited to a game where you could be either a glass canon mage or a melee tank. The second Gundyr fight was too hard without parry, Deacons of the Deep were very easy with melee and hard as a mage, I managed to kill Pontiff Sulyvahn very quickly on my first try by spamming pyromancer spells (it ruined the fight…).

Bloodborne is a response to DS1 players hiding behind their shield. It was a better idea than tampering with the game mechanics like Hidetaka Miyazaki did in DS3. For example, DS3 has weaker heavy armor compared to the DS1 ones in order to make the game less easy. But what’s the point of having heavy armor if they are useless ? Sorcery and shields are also weaker. Why make some playstyles less viable in a damn RPG ? But now in Elden Ring, having unviable playstyles against some bosses should be OK because you can summon ?!

I thought that Sekiro was hard while being balanced. There are no summons, no builds, you have all the tools that you need.

It seems that in order to have interesting, balanced and challenging fights, FromSoftware should either make action games with no builds (Sekiro) or limited builds (Bloodborne, Lies of P) focused on a specific playstyle. I’d love to play a Miyazaki game focused on magic. But he didn't do any of that with Elden Ring.

The main upgrade since DS3 is the open world. Elden Ring’s open world feels like an experiment because it is still kinda linear, the map looks like a crooked finger, and there is no level scaling. The already obscure quests are now much easier to miss.

An open world game shouldn’t be played like a Dark Souls game. In Skyrim, I never felt compelled to tediously comb the map. If I wanted more spells, I knew that I should do the mage guild quests. In Elden Ring, the rewards are too random, and because you don’t want to miss anything like in Dark Souls, you will waste more than 100 hours to completely finish the game. And it kills the replayability. Elden Ring suffers a rhythm issue which wasn’t the case in either Skyrim and Dark Souls.

Also, Elden Rings lacks many features suited to an open world. In Morrowind, a game that doesn’t hold your hand like in Skyrim (no quest marker), you still have a damn journal to track the far less obscure quests. Also, there is no bestiary in Elden Ring, and enemies’ weaknesses are not always obvious. Why no bestiary like in The Witcher 3, or any in-game way to learn their weaknesses beside dying experimenting ? I’m tired of checking the wiki again in 2025. Why no hub on the damn map ? Why no civilization, no friendly town ? Why only a handful NPC ? I’m not asking for a narrative game, but I was shocked to see how barely you interact with Melina and Ranni, yet they got their own figure toys IRL.

Elden Ring’s open world is too diluted with its useless cookie-cutter dungeons and its overlong world. It feels like a missed opportunity. You can’t just stick Dark Souls’ gameplay into an open world and expect it to work.

In conclusion, I think that Miyazaki should just make new games with their own formula that works. He knows how to balance difficulty, but he doesn’t know how to properly balance it around very different playstyles. Maybe no one can, and RPGs’ fights shouldn’t be that difficult and fast. He knows how to design linear games, but for now he doesn’t know how to design a good gameplay loop in an open world.

Ironically, I believe that Miyazaki should let the Dark Souls flame die.

If you're a casual gamer, don't play this game. It's too much. It's not fun, in the end.

I'm writing this as a somewhat casual gamer, I look for a thrilling, interesting experience with games. I don't mind a difficult challenge, but not when absolutely everything is stacked against you, from sparse lore, to ambiguous and barely motivating story, to insanely tough enemies and absolutely no objectives to help you forward, to basically being tested for your motor skills as if I'm qualifying for an Astronaut programme... it's just too much.

Elden Ring is beautiful, intriguing, fairly amazing... but ultimately a very unsatisfying experience for a gamer like me.

The two main issues for me are:

1. the incredibly sparse instructions and objectives, and basically zero story. And what story there is makes no sense and is also not very motivating or intriguing. I spent as much time on google trying to figure out what to do. The most fun I had was following a speedrun as it actually helped me get around and understand the game a little better, I actually got very far. But after having followed the speedrun, I honestly wouldn't know how I would have figured ANYTHING out myself, unless I would have committed WEEKS into this game. I don't have that kind of time. A whole session just figuring out where ONE smithing stone is? Sheesh.

That all wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't for the next problem:

2. FromSoft's chosen controls (lumping dodge/roll/dash under one conditional button) made the game entirely impenetrable for me. The bosses are actually not even that hard, it's the controls that make it an immensely awkward task. I'm not used to that style of control, especially if you have to also time it to within half a second or less. 

'Getting gud' is not about difficult bosses, it's about learning FromSoft's awkward control system. 

Even with my own keybinds, I'd basically have to re-learn how to play games, and with how sparse and ambiguous this game is, with no satisfying goal to look forward to, no rescues, no villages to save, and with literally everything trying to kill you with incredible accuracy and timing, with a non-sensical level of aggression, purely designed to get under your skin, it's just not worth the hassle. It's a beautiful, but ultimately an incredibly unsatisfying slog of a game.

If in your free time you enjoy time-consuming punishment, being humiliated by your computer over and over, testing your motor-skills to the max (like NASA level max), fighting and dying over and over to a boss to learn their exact moves, and wasting entire nights on one enemy when you could be chilling having fun with a more intriguing game with a story and lots of enemies in one night... then Elden Ring might be your poison.

If not, then please do yourself a favor and avoid this infernal game at all costs.

Maybe I might enjoy the game a bit more if I mod it, which I might do... because it is still a very beautiful game.

Overall, I'm binning the game and moving on because I'm simply not enjoying it enough. I understand that a lot of my complaints apply to the Soulsborne series as a whole, so it seems pretty clear that the series is not for me.

I really like that just about every mob can be a real threat and should be treated as such, and that you really have to be conscious about not letting yourself get surrounded. Some of the special weapon moves can feel really satisfying if pulled off. But that's about the last good thing I have to say about the combat.

Ultimately, I think the controls just feel too jank for what the game demands of you, especially against the bosses. Dodge rolling feels VERY inconsistent, as does whether or not my character will decide to drink their health potion when I press the button. I really hated getting stunlocked by bosses too. I get that part of the challenge is avoiding the initial hit that leads to the combo, but it made me feel helpless, rather than motivating me to improve.

The jank also extends to the exploration. The platforming feels absolutely awful, whether on foot or on horseback. The amount of times where it was literally the intended path to take a risky-looking jump off an innocuous-looking ledge bordered on absurd. It's crazy to me that a game that advertises its open world as including an interesting amount of verticality would contain no climbing mechanics or ways to interact with ledges besides awkwardly running off them. It was equally crazy to me that fast travel was the only way out of the Leonine Misbegotten arena. Actively requiring fast travel because there's no other way to exit an area feels like a violation of the open world promise.

The runes/souls system for levelling up and shopping is of course excellent, though the corpse running mechanic feels like it makes a lot less sense in an open world game as opposed to earlier, linear entries. Nothing discourages exploration like returning to the same area over and over again. First and foremost, this game is a beautiful artistic work. That's about the only positive I can give it.
The artists completely carried the experience. Now let's go on to the actual gameplay.

This game sucks. I don't care what every From Software cock sucker has to say. It is a boring slog, comprised 90% of running around to pick up things, and 10% fighting bosses. You'd think that for an open world, exploration would typically be a fun or interesting experience, right?

No. Quests are intentionally vague, misleading, and otherwise unintuitive. For instance, in Sellen's questline, you're suspposed to find someone called Master Lusat. Sellen tells you he should be cooped up somewhere near Selia, the town of sorcery. Turns out that couldn't be further from the case. The fucking guy is behind an illusionary wall, that you'd NEVER discover unless you just so happen to be running around hitting walls. He isn't even close to Selia. He's by Fort Faroth.

The story is a simplistic wash. Almost nothing you do has lasting consenquences. 90% of the endings result in your dude sitting on a fucking chair with some VFX that looks a little different. The quests stink. Most of them wind up with NPC dead or suffering some horrible fate, which I get it, isn't new for From Soft. But it isn't interesting. It's just boring, and makes the only point in doing them a possible reward for a build.

The bosses also suck fucking dick. DS1 was a masterpiece because it was hard punishing combat, but it was learnable. You had windows inbetween attacks, as well as opportunities to counterattack so long as you understood the timing. In Elden Ring? Good fucking luck. Most late game bosses are usually always attacking. They have combos which can change based on RNG, they can read player inputs to result in unavoidable attacks, and they NEVER. STOP. ATTACKING. It's insane. In DS1, you had clearly defined windows. In Bloodborne, you have windows and utilities to create windows. In Sekiro, you can parry, and you have tools at your disposal to create openings. In Elden Ring, good fucking luck. Your only hope is Spirit Ashes, to alleviate boss aggro. And guess what? If you use those, evidently the sweaty showerless nerds think you're not a true gamer.

The thing that really stinks is I WANT to enjoy these fights. The bosses are beautifully made models by 3D artists, have epic voice acting, and are themetically the tits. I can't fucking do that if I'm too busy getting raped because the dipshit programmers very purposely overtuned these things to the fucking gills.

What are your options build wise to deal with this if you don't have an inhuman reaction speed?

Shield build right? Nope, some bosses have split second AOEs, or just ATTACK STRAIGHT THROUGH THE SHIELD (aka Malekith). If that wasn't enough, Miyazaki nerfed this shit into the ground so that you don't even have enough stamina to block and attack after another 15 second long combo. Good fucking luck.

Blaster caster. Most bosses will now just fucking sidestep magic abilities. It is still a very potent way to deal damage, however, it feels cheesy. You don't really learn most mechanics in a meaningful manner. Most just use comet azur alongside a billion buffs to deal health bars of damage. Any boss fight with Torrent is pretty much invalidated.

Poise breaking. This relies on either using a big fucking sword or fist weapons to poise break. It can be very effective, however, the main issue with this is From Soft's targeting system. In my case, when using Lion Claw , many of my attacks missed because of the insane mobility of the bosses. It would lock on to where they USED to be. I haven't tried fist weapons yet, perhaps that's better, but I see it as unreliable. They could also attack through the lionclaw, dealing massive damage. Even though Lion Claw is a relatively quick attack, the boss combos are so quick, sometimes they'd just attack me anyways. As well, they have such high poise, that it'd frequently take me at least three strikes to poise break them. Fist weapons are probably superior, but I am willing to wager there'd be similar issues, where they'd have the possibility to smack you while you charge a R2.

Finally, buffing cheese. This is self explanatory. Oneshots bosses. Criminally unfun in my opinion. 

This game advertises itself as having many different ways to play the game. This is pretty much a lie. If you play it in a way where you're not watching guides, get ready to not be able to complete a large majority of quests due to vagueness or gamebreaking bugs due to programming issues. Get ready to fucking hate your existence, because the upgrade system is a laughable easter egg hunt unless you discover where the bellbearings are. If you're a masochist, this is the perfect game for you. The bosses past Rennala are combo spammers with input reading.

I wish they had focused on making a quality game instead of just trying to hop on the open world train most developers did.

Elden Ring is From Soft’s worst game. I don’t say this from a place of wanting to hate this game. I love From Soft and their titles, and I wanted to love Elden Ring. I’ve beaten the game twice, once with summons and once without, and quit halfway through the DLC. 

So why? 

Let’s start with the positives. The level design of the legacy dungeons are immaculate. The best of From’s work by far. Leyndell and Scadukeep are tied for best From level ever in my opinion. 

The lore is fascinating and deeply engrossing. While the Story remains simple, there are simply so many interwoven parts of this game’s lore. I would read it as a book. 

The music is great. The visuals are not technixally impressive, but the art design is incredible. From the Erdtree to individual bosses, this game is gorgeous. 

Elden Ring also has the best build variety of any From game. There are a million ways to play the game and most of them are valid. 

Now, negatives. The enemy design in Elden Ring is awful. It seems From heard that its players liked difficulty and so turned every boss into an utter slog. Enemies attack fast, with hard to read patterns and unnaturally delayed attacks, and combos that can be extended at random. Enemies also input read (or can react so fast they might as wll be input reading) using a fast projectile whenever you try to use your very slow estus flask (if you get hit while healing, your healing is cancelled). And, their damage is scaled obscenely high, to the point most bosses can two shot you with heavy investment in health. 

The world, while gorgeous, is empty. Like, actually empty. There is very little to see or do out there except fight enemies with low rune drops or fught a boss you’ve seen a half dozen times before for an item you likely can’t use. While the exploration is great the first time through, by your second run you realize that much of your playtime is just spent running to where you want to go. 

I cannot stress enough how bad Elden Ring’s open world is. It’s a lie. Areas are scaled for certain player power levels, and trying to do them out of order is a mistake. So the map only appears open, and by the end game Elden Ring abandons any concept of being open world, with the final area being extra empty and very linear. 

I had hoped Shadow of the Erdtree would fix this, but no. While SotE does improve on the open world, as all enemies are scaled to the same difficulty and you truly grow more powerful as you explore, the bosses double down on what makes Elden Ring’s enemy design bad. Outside of Rellana, who is my new favorite From boss, every boss in SotE is wither a base game repeat, an annoying fake PvP fight, or the worst parts of Elden Ring’s boss design made worse somehow. 

Elden Ring was not made for the casual gamer. Elden Ring wasn’t even made for me, and I play games as 90% of my free time. It was made for the streamers who can beat dark souls 3 at soul level 1 in 2 hours. 

I tried very hard to love this game. But ultimately I don’t think anyone should play it, and I have no intention of playing any future From Soft games having seen the design trend of Elden Ring and its DLC.

Friends recommended I play Elden Ring a few years ago, sending me a clip of the opening cutscene. Needless to say, it was pretty hype. A promise of a rich storyline and lore to sink your teeth into. Fast-forward a few years, I start my gaming era with strong recommendations for me to play Baldur's Gate 3. 
Going into that, I wasn't so sure I'd like the turn-based style, but having given it a due shot, to say I was impressed would be an understatement. I've played a dozen or so games since starting this arc and I'd say I have a sense for what I like. I'm attracted to visuals and story more or less equally > followed by gameplay, so my review will break it down as such.
Elden Ring has good to decent visuals. The first thing I appreciated as I started was the character creator, which is even more comprehensive and detail oriented than I was expecting. The customisation is IMMACULATE. Compulsory two or three days in the creator and I started the game. The open world is pretty well designed, and while there's nothing overtly WRONG with it, there's also nothing particularly eye-drawing in its beauty. Nothing "bad" =/= nothing particularly good. I will say the character designs themselves, along with some weapons, are pretty great, though these would be stand out exceptions to the overall "okay" rule.
Story/character: I've racked up some 70 hours of the game, and if I had to eyeball it, I'd say I've likely covered about as much (60-70%) of the map, been in a bunch of dungeons, met a ton of NPCs... I am not impressed with the world-building in this game. Like I said, when you start the game, the opening cutscene to me felt like a PROMISE, a prelude for great stories to be filled in. You enter the world and everyone and thing that sees you wants to kill you on sight...even other humans? Why? What is a Tarnished? Why did Marika take their grace...am i even understanding that correctly? So there's different species of humans? Is the only difference between Tarnished and regular humans the grace? Also why are there monsters everywhere? It feels like you've fallen into a world that's got a lot of lore, but you missed it all and only get to understand it from a barebones POV. The quests and NPCs are bland and uninteresting. Varre is literally the only NPC I like and he's not even that in it either. Some friends have advised me to play the game a few times and I'd get the hang of the lore, but I'm not interested in that. Story is important to my enjoyment of a game. Even games as basic as Tekken and Street Fighter, which aren't high on lore priorities and are geared towards PVP than PVE have a better presentation of story to me, and that's kind of crazy. So yeah, the cutscene was 11/10 but the game thus far is easily a 5/10. Not horrible, but a massive disappointment in his delivery of the aforementioned promise. 
Gameplay: one thing I truly appreciate about Elden Ring is the gameplay. Whether it's with the sword, flail, or magic staff, it's pretty fun. Anyone who knows me, knows I LOVE a challenge. Whatever the game is, it needs to present a certain degree of challenge for me. I can't stop myself from selecting the hardest difficulty, though I'm not so proud as to select perma-death options since I do a TON of intuitive trial and error. So I appreciated that this game is just made to be BEATEN, no difficulty selector, this is how it is and everyone has to do it lol. It's my first Soulslike game and I'd categorise it as something sort of like Witcher 3 except more polished, with a lot more options for customising your style of play whether you're a mage or hand to hand kind of person. It'd be perfect if the levelling system wasnt so gruelling and I wouldnt even mind that if the story wasn't so awful. Grinding to level up in this game is not fun, not at all. Farming resources for crafting and such is relatively simple though. 
In summary, I'm not dazzled by the visuals of this world, though I love some designs. I went into this story thinking it would be something it wasn't and am left disappointed. Gameplay is challenging and great on a technical level, but coupled with weak lore presentation, makes playing the game more than a tad bit tedious. This is my first soulslike and I intend to see it through to the end, but if all are like this, it's definitely my last.

[h1] An honest review for who never played souslike games [/h1]

Look: now I've finally beaten and got more than 100 hours. It's been pretty close to completion in terms of bosses. I don't know if I'll have any reason to download this shit again.

[h3] Disclaimer [/h3]

If you're here to complain or disagree or you really like soulslike, I get it - totally. This is not an attack on the game. Don't even bother. 

If you're here to have a honest opinion before getting a game you're not so sure you should, you're in the right place. That's where I was before buying it.

Don't fall for this "it's the easiest souslike, everyone will enjoy" crap. I'm up for any type of challenge, this isn't a challenge, it's a nutjob product.

[h2] Good points [/h2] 
• The game is completely gorgeous. The scenery is really well built. 
• You feel the aggression and hostility intended on the game, not only on bosses but on the environment. Mosnters will jumpscare you. You'll have to take risky jumps. All of that.
• Boss fights are engaging - [b] not well made, but engaging. [/b]
• You have good options on builds. Some of them are fun but you'll not complete the game with them, unfortunately.

[h2] • Bad points [/h2] 
• The game is a complete mistery. That's my main complaint.
• If you wanna know what each attribute does, [b]Google it.[/b]
• If you wanna know about the lore, [b]Google it.[/b]
• If you wanna know where the quest npc is hinting you (they'll never tell you, rest assured), [b]Google it.[/b]
• If you wanna know how to get to some boss [spoiler] I'm looking at you, Malenia and your "hidden" medallion for an elevator [/spoiler], [b]Google it.[/b]
• If you wanna know how can you be stronger, [b]Google it.[/b]
• If you wanna know how to get to the next region, [b]Google it.[/b]
• New symbol on your screen? [b]Google it.[/b]
• New symbol under your character? [b]Google it.[/b]
• Vaguely written quest dialogue with important answer? [b]Google it.[/b]
• New debuff of 10% HP reduction? [b]Google it.[/b] [spoiler] Spoiler: it was because you rested your head on a woman in the only safe place of the game. [/spoiler]
• Got a new item who says it functions just like another item - except you don't fucking know what the other item do? [b]Google it.[/b]
• If you're not careful, some random lv 200 dude will invade you and kick the shit out of your character in the early zones.

Nothing will ever be HINTED to you. You'll have to just explore the shit out of a ginomoursly big game until you forget what you're doing and hopefully gets something else to do. 

tldr; [b] You'll have no sense of progression, no way to know any single shit of this game. [/b]

[h2] Neutral (?) points [/h2] 
• In online mode, you'll get several tips from players. This is 60% useful. Most of the time they're hinting something the game should've explained to you.
• Invocations are helpful but won't get you so far as people say. They aren't an "easy mode". Don't fall for that too.
• Most people will tell you to play as an Int/Arc build if you're looking for an easy way. This isn't an easy way. You'll feel better playing what type you like.
• Game is full with easter eggs - but they get boring since everything is a easteregg in the game.
• It's a nice place to hang around if you got no intention of acomplishing something.

[h2] Final Thoughts [/h2] 

The game have everything to be good. If you have a long term relationship with soulslike, you'll probably love it.

But if you're looking on what should be a hard RPG and thinking you should spend $60, think twice. This isn't a hard RPG. This is a game intended to be played without any kind of helpful content. Not even explaining mechanics. And you won't find any help in the community explaining. Afterall every soulslike and mostly Elden Ring communities are a circlejerk who will shit in anyone trying to understand something the game should've explained.

If you're fine no understanding a single thing or having to reach for google every two hours for something that is a "Hidden item" or a "Mystery quest" or "Enigma" and it's just some item you have to progress or how the fuck did you get instakilled - you'll be fine playing it.

If not, you'll be just like me: you'll wanna beat the game so bad just to be able to break the circlejerk and say it's one of the worse gaming experiences you had. 

Pro player tip: there's a mod for an "easy game mode" That's probably the best way to enjoy the game if you don't care about achievements.

If you enjoy visual spectacle, grandiose architecture and an emphasis on really, really challenging and cinematic boss fights then Elden Ring has it in spades.

However, I personally found the open world and exploration based gameplay and constant emphasis on character progression where level and world design exist to push and empower the player to be really exhausting and not at all immersive. What makes dark souls, dark souls is a question that if you ask 10 people you'll get 10 different answers. There has been a deliberate focus on bosses with complex attack patterns, with respawn points directly outside many of them.

It is shackled mechanically by previous entries by insisting on keeping consistent with them in despite runes still dropping on death, in that healing is limited which only really matters in the context of bosses and that areas have to have enemies in them as not keep things utterly devoid. And yet, enemy placement doesn't feel like they're encounters with relationship with the world. If anything they exist to be something your character and weapon choices to be vanquished by. Whilst many soul veterans simply rush through areas, there is an art to it in ds1 and ds2 with how claustrophobic the level design can be. It all strikes me as formality, even more so when the final stretch of the game has no actual dungeon or level and is simply a boss rush, which is right after another boss rush segment with completely optional enemy design in a open world.

It is dark souls, whilst not being dark souls. It carries a lot of the vestigal and narrative designs of those games to supplement the two big things they wanted to focus on the game. Big, open world and big fucking hard as nail bosses with spectacle and lore implications.

Personally, I found most if not all the challenging bosses simply "Keep doing it until you get lucky enough that the bosses don't do their worst attacks constantly back to back." They are so fast, and in many cases you'll be fighting the camera to see them. I didn't find it fun. Nor did I care to explore the open world when it felt so empty and void and that all the optional areas are just a mixture of mines and castles that exist to let you get runes and materials so you can fight the next boss.

EDIT: Came back to the game after a long break for a fresh run. If anything, traversing the open world with boring open swathes of emptiness and design catered to the player as being a theme park has only made it even more boring to traverse in a game as large as Elden Ring. My second try at writing a review for this beautiful, complicated, deeply flawed game, because the first sounded like an insecure mess. (because it was.)

Elden Ring was my first souls game. While I'd played many titles inspired by Fromsoft's work, I'd yet to taste the main dish itself. While I did ultimately end up appreciating my time with the game, I don't know that I'd recommend it to anyone else new to souls titles. 

An overwhelming majority of my first playthrough was defined by mind-numbing frustration and confusion alike. This is down to what I believe are the game's two biggest flaws; It fails to communicate what you did wrong, and, maybe more at fault, it fails to communicate what was done right.

This is probably best shown in Elden Ring's best and worst aspect; the boss fights. As a souls newbie, I found myself quickly overwhelmed and bewildered by the insane difficulty of the fights. By itself, not a bad thing. In fact, I'd say that difficulty is one of the most enticing pieces of the experience. The problem lies in how the game uses that difficulty. Traditionally, high difficulty in games is used to build mountains for the player to climb. Slowly, they mount it's insane skill requirements, and at the end, present the player of a view of how far they've come, rewarding the player both in-game and out of it with loot and the satisfaction of the skill it took to master the challenge. 

This only works if a player understands what it took to climb that mountain. I usually didn't. Boss patterns are often so overwhelmingly complex and nuanced that first-time players just simply are not going to fully understand what the game is asking of them in order to avoid it, and will stumble into band-aid solutions with finnicky reliability in consistently dealing with said attacks. To be clear; there ARE solutions to the challenges the game presents. They are often even very cool and skillful expressions of player movesets. They are also completely unacknowledged by the game and oft passed via word of mouth online from fans who figured it out to another. Beyond combat, some features are so obscure that some amount of presence in the community might as well be required in order to enjoy them. This approach has its pros and cons.

The other issue is that when players start to test out solutions to the problems the game poses, the game struggles to indicate that you are on the right train of thought, or approaching a solution. In fact, it delights in punishing players with movesets designed to follow the exact train of thought a player might have in experimenting, with input reading or reactive boss attacks that become harder to punish the more you attempt to punish them. It's not that the solution isn't there, it's that the game wants you to repeat that process of experimentation several times over before you land on viable strategies to counter all of a boss's tricks. I'm sure for many series veterans this style of boss design is immensely rewarding and exciting. I can only speak for myself however, and for me it felt like I'd try something new, encounter a uniquely devastating style of punishment, and give up on anything other than the most basic level of engaging with the fight. I ran a split spear/spell build, switching between one and two-handed as needed, and often felt like I'd cheesed fights when I did anything other than indulge in very slow, taxing, hit and run-tactics with my stick.  Likewise, fighting bosses in a 'fun' manner with summons and spells and whatnot was more often than not equally unrewarding and made me regret not attempting to learn the fight in greater detail. As a result, especially towards the midgame, every major challenge devolved into hitting things with my big stick with little variance. I didn't find this style of gameplay very fun, and why would I? That wasn't what the developers were asking of me. I just had no way of knowing.

The end result is a game with brutally difficult and challenging enemies that felt unfun and unrewarding to learn, (with some exceptions) and a payoff to those challenges that usually felt like the game congratulating me for work I had not and could not even comprehend how to put in. In short, a mountain not worth climbing. The endgame, thankfully, especially with DLC, addressed this problem somewhat with a few genuinely complex fights that felt rewarding to learn, but, was this worth the 100+ hours I put in to get there? Your mileage may vary. For my money, I don't think it was.

Frustrations aside however, there is a lot to love here.

I don't need to tell you the lore and story is good. I don't need to tell you the game is gorgeous. I don't need to tell you the music and character design is unmatched. But I will, because all of the above is true. These were the things that kept me exploring the lands between, beyond my own stubborn, insecure pride to scale this mountain, no matter how frustrating and unfulfiling the adventure became.

On subsequent playthroughs and by engaging with the community's advice, I found myself vastly enjoying elden ring more the more I played past that rocky first playthrough. The frustration stayed, however, just reborn. Why wasn't all this complicated, interesting boss combat communicated the first time around? Why did I need to turn to outside resources if I wanted to engage with the boss fights on any other level than bash head in wall for several hours, and then move on when the stars aligned for a perfect, unrewarding run? Why did I feel like, having done as much side content as I could muster, having beaten the DLC in full, staring at the body of the final boss, that I knew no more than when I started?

It was, in fact, a skill issue. I just wish the game was willing to teach me. 

Is the game good? Yes. Is it a once-in-a-lifetime videogame? Probably. Would I recommend it to anyone besides the people that already know they're going to enjoy it? In my experience, no.

From the 76 hours I've played the game, you can see Elden Ring has held my attention and I do feel like I've gotten my money's worth. The game has stunning art direction, engaging combat and scenic exploration.

That being said, the game is an exercise in frustration. The open world is huge and utterly breathtaking at times, but without a clear sense of progress or compelling rewards, there is nothing to counteract the endless supply of bang-your-head-against-the-wall moments. The world is full of life, but none of it meaningful. It's all just mindless enemy NPC's who will only attack you when you get too close.

I don't mind a challenging game or even a very long, but this one feels like the developers don't want me to play it. A lot of the game-play is terribly inconvenient or punishing. Upgrades cost a fortune and all your progress can be lost very quickly. There is virtually no plot. No decision making or consequences. I often stream a Netflix series on my second browser to keep me entertained while I play the game. It feels like it took all the wrong lessons from grindy MMO games and brought them into a single-player RPG. To top it off, It seems like the ending is probably another 70+ hours away.

There is a small part of me that would like to finish this game, but really, it's a chore to play -- and I already have too many chores to do.

You have to be a special kind of self-loathing masochist weep to enjoy this. This was my first souls-like and also my last. Tedious! Monotonous! Grindy! It's satisfying in the same way when, you're hitting yourself with a hammer and then stop hitting yourself.

The Good:

-The World: Exploring was enjoyable. The sense of scale is incredible.
-Graphics: Everything looks amazing.
-Weapons and Spells: There are tons of them to choose from.

The Bad:

-The Bosses: I liked maybe three of them—all dragons. Lichdragon Fortissax was a highlight. The bosses were actually the worst part of the game for me. Every time I encountered a new one, I thought, "Oh no, here we go again... sigh."* Their attacks often feel random, and most of them take you out in one or two hits. Sometimes, you survive the first hit, only to get staggered and finished off by the second. You spend more time dodging than actually fighting. After a while, you notice a pattern with the bosses: different skins, but very similar movesets. I had an okay time until the Fire Giant—after that, I just wanted it to be over. I made it to the Elden Beast, died countless times, and quit.

-The Story: You have to defeat [Fancy Name] [Grand Title] of [Dramatic Something] to become a god? Why? What’s actually going on? The presentation is confusing, and the writing can feel overly dramatic. "Go here and defeat the mighty ruler of the Wetwipe Clan to claim his strength." It tries to sound deep but comes across as unnecessarily cryptic.

-The UI and Controls: A nightmare on PC. Clearly not designed for mouse and keyboard. Who puts a frequently used action on Shift? (I changed that immediately.) Also, try sprinting, jumping, and doing a power attack—hold down Alt + Ctrl, then press Space and click the mouse. That’s painful. The menu is clunky, and some explanations don’t make much sense.

-The Game’s Presentation: I had to Google things constantly. No quest log, no way to track what you’re doing or why. It feels like the game assumes you’ve played Dark Souls before and already understand everything.

Final Thoughts:

Difficult does not always mean fun. I feel like the developers may not even play their own game. Through sheer stubbornness, I reached level 200-something, maxed out a weapon, a +25 incantation offhand, and a +10 mimic summon, and still found myself frustrated. Every step of the way, the game felt like it was actively working against me. I usually believe game developers want players to enjoy their games—in this case, it felt like they wanted players to struggle.

I kind of enjoyed the first 20 hours. Kind of. The last 30? I was just pushing through to finish it, but I eventually gave up. Not worth more of my time.

Elden Ring: The Most Overrated Game of the Decade

Let’s just get this out of the way: Elden Ring is not a masterpiece. It’s not even good. It's a glorified walking simulator

“Open World”
Dark Souls II had interconnecting zones, secret areas, and real progression. In Elden Ring, you wander a giant field like a lost dog, picking flowers and praying the next cave isn’t just another recycled “Putrid Tree Spirit” reskin. If DS2 is a tightly woven tapestry, Elden Ring is a toddler’s finger painting stretched across 100 hours.

Where’s the Depth?

DS2 let you build wild hybrid characters. Hexes, dual-wielding power stance, adaptable poise systems, and NG+ that actually changed enemy placements. Elden Ring? Here’s a bleed build. And another bleed build. Oh, and you can summon a Pokémon to fight for you so you don’t have to actually play the game.

Bosses With Personality? Nah, Just Copy-Paste Giants

Remember Fume Knight, Sir Alonne, or Burnt Ivory King? Bosses that felt like duels, with music and arenas that hit your soul?

Now compare that to Elden Ring’s 27 reskins of the same knight in different lighting. There's more emotional depth in a DS2 hollow’s sigh than in the entire Radahn Festival.
Dark Souls II Had Real World-Building

Majula had atmosphere, a haunting melody, and a cast of broken, tragic characters. Elden Ring has… what, an abandoned shack every 10 minutes and an NPC who dies off-screen after giving you a Talisman you’ll never use?

Difficulty for People Who Know How to Play

DS2 punished you intelligently. It had real consequences (hollowing), reduced health, enemies that stopped respawning. It respected your time and skill. Elden Ring’s idea of challenge is throwing three enemies at once and praying you forget how to roll.

And don’t even get me started on the map. Why am I playing an open-world Souls game with a map? What’s next, quest markers and a minimap?
Elden Ring: 4/10 (and that's generous)

While Elden Ring has an impressively large world, it unfortunately falls into the trap of repetition—far more so than even the most newer entries in the Assassin’s Creed series. The sheer scale of the map is admirable, but the enemy variety fails to keep up, making encounters feel redundant over time.

The story is decent, and I particularly enjoyed the Ranni questline, as it was a highlight of the game for me. However, it doesn’t quite reach the narrative impact of Dark Souls 3’s Lord of Hollows ending, which felt far more meaningful and thematically rich.

Boss design is a mixed bag. While some encounters are well-crafted and engaging, the sheer number of bosses leads to fatigue. Many fights devolve into a repetitive cycle of dodging overly long combos and waiting for a small opening to strike. In contrast, Dark Souls 3 maintained a consistently high standard, with around 90% of its bosses being memorable and enjoyable. Elden Ring, on the other hand, delivers only a handful of truly unique boss fights, with the rest relying heavily on reskins and minor variations.

I've owned this game since release, but didn't feel like leaving a negative review at the time. But even after giving it several chances to win me over, it failed to meet expectations. 

At launch, the game was extremely buggy, and had the worst optimization I've ever seen. The game was literally unplayable for the first week or so due to how poorly it performed. I'm talking 5-23 FPS on minimum settings and 2-4 second long hitches every 7-15 seconds. The game also, unfortunately, has this orange smear filter over everything if you try to play below native resolution. The bugs were numerous: random crashes, getting frozen in midair until the game auto killed you, spirit springs not functioning at all, Torrent movement in every possible way, multiplayer connection issues, etc, etc.

Unfortunately, it didn't really improve much. It's 3 years later and the game barely runs. The hitches are still present, and you're lucky to maintain a choppy 45 FPS. It still doesn't really matter which settings you use, as the game will run the same whether in 4k or 720p. They did fix most of the Torrent related bugs, but the horse can still randomly hyper accelerate in a different direction than you are moving the joystick.

The combat is the worst I've seen in any FromSoft title. Coming directly after Sekiro, this was the ultimate disappointment. It's slow, clunky, and predictable. All the bosses act so similar there's virtually nothing to really separate them. Some of them are literally copy/pasted around the map. The difficulty was insanely watered down to the point where nearly every boss was defeated in the first or second attempt. The DLC was promising for exactly one fight... then it quickly went back to the slog that the base game had.

This is the only game I've played where upon finishing the game... I felt disappointed. There was no feeling of triumph or satisfaction in any way... I merely pondered why I'd bothered walking around for so long hoping it'd get better.

Edit: Perhaps I was too harsh on this game. I decided to give it a 6th chance, and decided to stop treating the game like something it was not. Elden Ring is an exploration game. At its core, Elden Ring is a walking simulator. The enemies are not really meant to be a challenge, but a small inconvenience as you wander around. Most of them will drop in a hit or two, with some taking a little bit extra. But you only need to bother with them if they are blocking you from picking up your thousandth Arteria Leaf or Mushroom. You won't do anything with the things you collect, as there is no need, all that matters is you've found it. You press on, watching the scenery change around you, with billboards and trees reminiscent of a PS1 port. The textures pop in and out, the lighting spazzes, but every so often things will look absolutely beautiful. You stop for a moment to take a screenshot as 3 enemies blow themselves up behind you. You could almost feel it that time. But alas, nothing can actually harm you on your peaceful walk in this wretched place.

I have a lot of thoughts about the game, but to keep things  simple i'll start with a pro/con list

Pros: 
Decent Artstyle
Some interesting Boss Designs
The Musical Score

Subjective Pros/Cons:
Few Cutscenes (mostly Boss Introductions)
LORE (Insert Markiplier Face)
Open World 

Cons:
Balancing (Late game)
The Camera
Boss One hit Kills
Many Enemies are Damage Sponges

Personal Thoughts (Mostly just a rant on poor design, feel free to ignore):

While soulslikes are difficult on principle, the game feels difficult not by design but by poor implementation of concepts and artificial difficulty .  

The open world is the biggest example of this, as with most open world games you are rewarded for exploration, however because a lot of enemies in Elden Ring are... dark souls enemies, one wrong step in any direction could result in a complete loss of leveling progress (as you lose all leveling xp/in game currency on death) though no fault of your own, aside from not constantly checking the wiki every five seconds to know that deadnor the immortal spawns in this random corner of the world. In smaller dungeons and more traditional dark souls linear gameplay this can work, but in the open world, this creates difficulty through being tedious rather than being hard. Add to that that most side dungeons reward you with summons or weapons that require specific stats, meaning you could clear a dungeon and get something your character can't really use without grinding for x stats/re-doing stats that you have no way of knowing you need until you've beat the dungeon and get the thing.  And this punish the player for playing the game the way most game are supposed to be played (and the lackluster exploration rewards) makes it feel more artificial difficulty rather than a well designed challenge, given that the game does this constantly with most of its game design choices.

[spoiler] Honorable mentions for worst Boss mechanics: Any Grab move, Malenia sword of Miquella, Scarlet rot, and of course Nihil, Nihil, Nihil [/spoiler]

Of course, this is just my opinion, and given most people seem to enjoy it, feel free to ignore my opinion, or call me wrong about my subjective feeling on a game.

The principle of "armor is useless" was never really true in Souls games until Elden Ring, the same goes for health. It comes down to a game of trying to make sure you never take a hit while hoping your positioning is good enough to get one strike in. This in turn, limits your options for builds to high speed weapons which will minimize the amount of punishment you receive for trying to squeeze an attack into the brief window you're given. It feels like if it were up to them, bosses would be attacking non stop. Other bosses are capable of simply dealing damage to the player freely, unless certain steps or research is performed on the player's end. If and when you do defeat these bosses, one often feels empty, like a large inconvenience has been waited out, rather than the triumph we used to receive in older titles. 
Overall, Elden Ring is something that could have been perfect, but cannot let go of this difficulty escalation principle.

Elden Ring may not be a bad game, but it's certainly not for everyone. 

There is an intriguing world to explore, with an art direction that makes you want to find out what's in the distance. 

This was my first FromSoft game - I had always avoided these games in the past because my skill level is quite low and FromSoft games are notorious for their difficulty. But I heard so many incredible things about this game that I wanted to give it a go. 

My takeaway is that if you kinda suck at video games like I do, the positives of this game do not compensate for spending hours upon hours upon hours smashing your head against a wall. With almost 40 hours in I have only defeated the first major boss, and there are plenty of areas in the starting area I have yet to properly explore. So I am experiencing the game *very* slowly compared to what's normal I imagine. There is a level of satisfaction and intrigue of exploring somewhere new, but re-exploring that same area for the 20th time to try to kill something or just retrieve the currency you spent hours building up for the next (mostly useless) level up does not carry that satisfaction or intrigue. 

Elden Ring is a combat game first and foremost. Everything else about it is supplementary, at least in my experience. So if you're not a fan of combat-focused games, don't be fooled into thinking that the exploration or world design will carry the game for you. It probably won't. There is also essentially no story to speak of and a near-complete lack of NPCs, so that won't engage you either. Elden Ring is a game about trying to kill tough bosses and everything else is window dressing. If "trying to kill tough bosses" isn't that exciting for you, feel free to ignore all the massive hype surrounding the game and give it a miss.

This isn’t a review that I wanted to make as I hold a deep respect for Fromsoft and their works. They have superior artistic vision compared to just about everybody else in the industry; aesthetic mastery par excellence. I would also consider some of their older works to be some of the most fun and fulfilling games I’ve ever played. If I were to compare this game to anything it would be Skyrim. Both games showed a grandiosity in vision relative to their time of release and an inability to fully realise the potential of their worlds and both games were uncritically lauded by contemporaries as “the best game of all time”. Elden Ring is by no means a bad game and it certainly does a lot right. I could ramble on and on about how beautiful the Lands Between are and how fascinating the lore and worldbuilding of this game is, the new innovations to the combat system, and the stellar sound design and soundtrack (with a minor issue being the use of AI generated vocals in many of the tracks) but that is not what I want the emphasis of this review to be about. Having already completed a full playthrough of this game on my Xbox Series X and encountering no issues, I was shocked to see just how badly unoptimised this game is on PC. Even with many patches, this is still an utterly abominable PC port and especially for such a high profile game! You would think that the developers setting out to make the Hardest Game Ever would prioritise performance but nope! The performance of the game is especially bad during the game’s more notable boss fights with all of the visual clutter you are constantly being bombarded with. This is why I can’t in good faith recommend anyone play this port of the game. My PC is fairly capable too and I don’t consider “just buy a $2000 graphics card” to be a valid counter-argument but instead mindless boot licking. Just stating this as I have seen examples of Fromsoft fanboys telling inanimate objects to “git gud”.

Coming back to this game in 2025 after a PC upgrade, only to find the same performance problems and lack of modern PC enhancements, “inspired” me to leave this review.

The gameplay and world are wonderful - great art direction, combat feels good, and an open world with plenty to find if you explore without forcing you to. Unfortunately, it’s all buried under a game that is complete shit from a technical standpoint.

No 21:9 support. 60fps cap. Really Fromsoft? Was an embarrassment in 2022 and simply inexcusable in 2025, especially where there is a mod that fixes both. But having to use that means giving up online features. Simply a joke for a developer that’s been around this long and a game this profitable.

And the performance is absolute shit. Playing with a 9800X3D, 64GB RAM, and a 5080 at 3440x1440, I get frequent drops below 60fps in the starting area near the Tree Sentinel. How is this still a problem years later? Having stutters makes it nearly impossible to play or enjoy the game.

Cannot recommend this game on PC due to a developer that’s is either incompetent or just doesn’t care. Not sure which is worse.

Ultimately, my frustration isn’t with Elden Ring as a game but with its PC port, which is, frankly, unacceptable. For a game of this scale and reputation I was expecting more.

I was genuinely excited to finally dive into Elden Ring. After years of relentless hype, I thought it was time to experience the game that so many people assured me I would love. Souls games are known for their difficulty and challenge, but I never expected my greatest struggle to come from the FPS cap, FPS Drops, Stuttering and clunky mostly uncustomizable control scheme rather than the in-game enemies.

Perhaps Elden Ring is an incredible game—I honestly wouldn't know. I simply couldn’t push past my first hour of gameplay because it felt like I was fighting against the game itself rather than engaging with its world. Some might argue that mods can fix these issues, but if I need to rely on third-party fixes just to make a game playable, that’s a dealbreaker for me.

the combat itself is pretty boring to me, a critique i have with all of the souls games, it's just dodge roll dodge roll dodge roll swing maybe once or twice, sekiro had WAY more interesting gameplay with all the different ways you could respond to attacks and how aggressive it encouraged you to play vs how passive the others are, i'm a big fan of parry mechanics but the attacks that you can and can't parry aren't clear at all here, i DO however like the guard counter mechanic, i think that's a pretty neat way to buff more tanky playstyles, another thing i always gravitate towards. 
while i play it i feel lost 24/7, i don't know what's going on, if i'm in a level appropriate area (doesn't help that it's easy to get thrown in a late game area right out the gate of the tutorial), the stats on everything are just overwhelming, and god help you if you take a break for a while, then come back and forget where you were in the story.

the exploration aspect is definitely a/the strong suit of the game, but it's really not enough to keep me playing for long. that said, i do believe i'm gonna probably complete this game eventually, if not just to say i didn't waste 60 dollars.

I purchased this game after MANY reviews about how great the story was (written by George RR Martin) and it was one the best games to play.
My son and I both played different saves and at 100 hours and beating everything in the capital we both are done with the game.  
This has to be the worst storyline game as there really isn't one.  You have to rely on youtube or other sources to try to understand the scant info you are given that really tell you nothing.
The thing that capped off my frustration with the lack of substance was that I wanted to feel purpose so instead of just exploring until you find something new, I followed just one NPC storyline.  I liked Sellen, so I followed a IGN walkthrough of sellen's quest.  You meet her early in the game, she is a magic merchant and doesn't give you much guidance.  Luckily the walkthough tells you what you need.  SOOOooooo, I had to go halfway to the other side of the world, find a guy huddled up in a off the way nook, he doesn't talk, is half crystal so is easy to miss.  When you try to talk to him he just slowly raises his hand and gives you a spell.  Somehow THIS is the trigger for Sellen (again all the way in the early area) to do something other than sell you stuff.  She then, at least, gives you some guidance of where you are to look for the next master Lusat. BUTTTTTTTtt, the place you have to look is a normal looking part of a mountain just like the next 20 miles of mountain boundary (this happens be behind something, but nothing else tells you you anything) and if you hit it, it disappears.  Deep inside the dungeon you will find the guy you are looking for (also huddled up and just raises his hand to give you something, no speaking, doesn't do...anything..else).
When you give sellen this and then do her next quest you meet her at the academy.  Things are progressing goodish, but when you return (after meeting her at the academy the first time) she is no longer there, just a ball of magi-helms that you've seen a few time before that now mumbles with her voice like she is having trouble speaking, but still will sell you the same things.  WHAT?!!?  So, what happened, what do you do now, should you have done things differently?  You'll never know, you have to to to youtube/reddit for theories.  THIS IS GREAT STORY TELLING?  Saddly this was one of the more full conversation quests I found.  My son and I have been trying to find what makes this game so highly rated.  But the negatives outweigh the postives and I'm not getting much enjoyment out the the timesuck this game is.
Positives:  Beautiful landscapes, varied, fun to explore surface/dungeons/underworld.  Varied weapons/armor/trinkets.  Varied NPCs/beasts/bosses.
Negatives:  lack of direction for non-souls players: the first grace you go to (that is supposed to guide you to your next objective) points you to the tree sentinel that you try 1000x to beat but keep getting crushed, when you look it up - oh, no, that guy is for latter in the game, matter of fact don't follow the grace until you level up a bunch.  WHat? you think there should be a NPC to tell you that or something instead of a NPC that tell you to follow the grace?   Then you grind forever to get stronger while no real direction what each stat is for and how they work with different weapons/armor/trinkets (unless you again go to youtube/reddit to findout.  Grind some more...rinse and repeat.  The game is very frustrating (apparently that is what makes this game so good is how punishing it is?) but even when I was stronger than most things I faced and would wipe them out with one death poker use, I wasn't having fun because I didn't feel I knew where I was to go next half the time, or why I even care.
I started this game because it was a highly rated story driven game (knowing it would be punishing) but I found the lack of story didn't give me purpose enough to keep playing.  My son felt the same and actually quit it before me (after going through the capital as well).
There are SOOOoooo many other games that are more ejoyable with better storytelling.

I've played and finished many hard games (Cuphead, Celeste, getting over it) and a hard game is like riding a bike. Some are harder than others, like having to learn how to ride while on a steep hill, or having to learn while riding on rough terrain. None the less, any time you fall while trying to ride can be linked back to you're inability to do so. Aka, "skill issue." Elden Ring on the other hand is like trying to ride a bike, on a hill, with rough terrain, while your drunk father throws rocks at you and pushes you off the bike. This is why I particularly didn't enjoy Elden Ring, because while the games stated previously are hard, they make it to where you're in control on whether you win or lose (the rough terrain/hill). Elden Ring is unfair due to conditions outside of your control (the drunk father hurling rocks).

Firstly, while this game "encourages" exploration, they make sure its no better than fighting bosses with an inconsistent spread of difficult areas, traps that'll teleport you to over leveled areas that you can't escape from, and having sights of grace respawn ALL enemies you've defeated. This makes exploring very slow, with it only becoming easier with finding better gear. Except the really good gear is by defeating bosses, and the ones that aren't are hidden behind invisible walls or cliffs. There are ones you can obtain through quests, except there's no quest log so keeping track of quests is only fun if you have a guide. Unless you already have experience playing souls games, guides are almost required to play Elden Ring if you want to play with an actual good build and weapons.

The biggest example I know with this game being over the top with unfairness is the area with invisible black knife assassins. There is no way you can see them coming unless you have the sentry torch, which can only be bought at the hermit merchant shack. This is the only item in the game that allows you to see invisible enemy's and is the only place you can get it. Not only that, but the game never directly/indirectly tells you how to get this item. This is what I mean by Elden Ring being over the top unfair, it consciously makes it impossible to do parts of the game unless you have previous knowledge on how to do it because it won't tell you. It's why so many people play this game with a guide, because if they didn't, they would spend hours running around like a headless chicken trying to figure out things like this and quests until they stumble upon the answer. This isn't just making it hard, it's making it confusing, which is far worse.

The story (while good) is anything but linear, in order to understand what's happening in the game, you have to watch 10 hour youtube videos on the game's lore. Don't even bother trying to play with friends in this game too as they can only join during boss fights. Also god forbid if you're friend joins one time to do a boss for shits and giggles, you're world will be forever open to be invaded by people with over powered gear and levels that can't be stopped from killing you unless you kill them or rage quit.

Any criticism thrown towards this game has been deflected by hardcore fans with the notion that those who don't enjoy the game are simply "bad" at the game. They refuse however to acknowledge that gamer's who are displeased with this game, and how it intentionally causes problems outside of the players control, would in turn cause them little pleasure in trying to finish the game. The main pleasure you get from beating Elden Ring is the testament that you beat something built to be intentionally unfair, however do the ends really justify the means?

I acknowledge how many awards, and how many people applaud the game, and I get why. The game is beautiful, the combat is terrific, and the different builds make customization in this game wonderful. I don't wish for people to read this review to persuade them that his game is bad. I want instead for those reading that are obsessed with the game, to try and understand those who try Elden Ring and decide its not for them. Not everyone is willing to spend countless hours on a game that will cause them so much negativity, and that criticism about the game is just as valid as its praise. For anyone reading this deciding now whether they should try the souls genre, please consider what I've written. With the thought on whether you're ready to commit tens to hundreds of hours for a game that will do everything in its power to bring you pain. There's much joy and awesomeness to be found here, but only if you're willing to deal with the game hurl rocks at you. Players too if you summon someone.

The only way the Souls formula could have been developed further was by taking it open world, and for me that ruined what made the Souls games appealing in the first place. I hoped some things would have been improved but alas it was more of a miss than a hit for me.


- STILL cannot freely experiment with weapons as you are limited in how many you can upgrade per run.
- STILL frame-locked at 60fps, no ultrawide support, you can mod these in but it requires disabling online play which severely impacts your game experience.
- Copy-pasted dungeons and bosses. 
- Bloated game systems, way too many items. 
- Pretty much every major boss is designed against solo play as you are constantly spammed with adds so you have to rely on spirit summons/co-op, lest you "git gud".
- Most of the NPCs have names beginning with G, R and M - gee, I wonder why. I don't remember who any of them were.
- Way too big. I tried to do everything in one playthrough and now I can't bring myself to begin a second one. Not to mention I don't think I can tolerate more of this game in its DLC.
- Obscure quest objectives with very specific triggers. You can easily get certain NPCs killed without even realising.
- And many other little things that really detract from what the game could have been.

Did it deserve GOTY? Maybe, for its setting, visuals, music/audio etc. It also opened up an entire franchise to new players, who can now go and experience the other Souls games and understand what made them compelling. Personally, the only times I really enjoyed it was in the "legacy dungeons", which were basically small, self-contained Souls levels - as it should have been in the first place. I would have much preferred a linear sequence of dungeons compared to the overwhelming number of areas you have to go out and explore, where the difficulty is not carefully crafted so you can really roadblock yourself. This guarantees that some players will have a terrible experience and will put the game down, instead of focusing on defeating the same boss as everyone else.

As a fan of Soulslikes and Fromsoft games in general, I wanted so hard to like this game. Everyone and their mother is praising it. It's over 90% positive. I don't get it. I tried three times to get into it and jus can't. I even got through most of the game once, before I just gave up at the frost dragon.

I played every Soulslike under the sun : DS, DS2, DS3, Bloodborne, Remnant 1 and 2, Nioh, Code Vein. Even Soulsvania like Grime and Hollow Knight. I beat each of those game several times, including optional challenges. Had fun dying and coming right back. Fighting the same bosses over and over until I mastered them and was able to beat them.

Elden Ring is the logical progression of the obsession for difficulty for difficulty's sake. How do you make sure veteran players still struggle on every boss? Just make sure said bosses chain attacks hyper-fast, give them hyper-agression to make healing difficult and make them two-shot the player. Enter a new boss fight? Here's thirty attacks you have to dodge-roll. Good luck.

I just don't get why Fromsoft games have evolved into roll-fests and everyone seems to find that engaging. Souls games used to be about positioning and careful engagement. Bosses would actually telegraph their attacks. Now, you just bash your head against the moveset hoping to get lucky enough to dodge all of the attacks.

Unfortunately, Elden Ring's bosses do not give you a feeling of pride when you beat them. Just relief. And that is its greatest sin.

The open world is also its greatest weakness. Once again, I do not understand the praise it's getting. Vast areas of emptiness dotted with reused assets. Have fun doing the exact same cave/mine/tomb with literally some layouts repeating. Then at the end a reused boss you'ce fought several times already. Or two at a time.

Speaking of bosses, I hope you like doing them several times. Because you're going to fight boss A, then B, then A and B sequentially, then A and B at the same time, then those bosses as regular enemies for some reason. The amount of filler boss battles to artificially fill the gigantic empty world is staggering.

And finally, the lack of polish is astounding. The upgrade materials are literally all named the same, but with a different number. The camera betrays you all the time. Hitboxes are funky. Enemies' AI is not made for an open world. Fromsoft get away with so much because of their name, it's crazy.

So in the end, I suggest playing better games like Remnant or Grime. These games are more polished, better designed and still remember what fun difficulty looks like.

A few pros for me: [olist]
[*]Game is pretty damn well optimized for what it is, something that's a rarity nowadays and can be beautified at your own risk using third party software.

[*]Combat is relatively pretty fun, but this is also going to be a con later in regards to Balancing, the overall scope of combat however is impressively flexible and offers more than what other games had before.

[*]The locations are varied and for the most part visually stunning, there is no denying that the art design team is the lead carry for what this series is and this has been proven time and time again in Fromsoft's history.

[*]It was functional on launch. Again. Huge for the year it released. Not just on optimizing but there's very few things that will break, crash, or outright cause anything negative to your PC like overheating or using more resources than it should to render things from halfway across the game world.
[/olist]

And now the part that'll lead to the searing backlash, the Cons, because yes this game has flaws and some are Glaring:[olist]
[*]The OST is probably the most disappointing in this game compared to any other modern release made by fromsoft. Where there's a good boss track, there's usually 3 filler tracks for other bosses and then an unnerving amount of silence while exploring that immediately follows. An Unforgiving Game, and So Shall My Review Be.

As a seasoned Souls veteran who has seen the rise and fall of countless Chosen Undead, Ashen Ones, and Hunters, I came into Elden Ring with a healthy mix of excitement and caution. I finished the game, dedicated time to exploring its vast world, and now feel ready to offer my perspective. Brace yourselves: Elden Ring is an unforgiving experience—and my review will reflect that.

Let’s start with the obvious. Elden Ring is ambitious, breathtakingly beautiful, and undeniably vast. But, as the saying goes, “vast like an ocean, yet shallow as a puddle.” It’s a game that prides itself on being difficult—brutally so—but unlike other Souls games, the challenge here often feels like an artificial mechanism designed to trap players in a replayability loop. Rather than tuning the beloved Souls formula for this open-world format, Elden Ring leans heavily on unbalanced difficulty to obscure its more glaring flaws in both gameplay and world design.

The scaling and balancing? Blatantly unfair at times, as if the developers chose frustration over finesse. Some bosses are colossal damage sponges with unpredictable move sets, while others feel overtuned to punish players for the sake of punishment, not for growth or mastery. This is a sharp contrast to previous Souls games, where difficulty felt purposeful—tough but always with a sense of progression and fairness. Here, the formula cracks under the pressure of its ambition.

Then there’s the persistent problem that haunts every Souls game: the clunky camera and input lag. Even with all the polish Elden Ring received, the hardest boss remains the camera and control responsiveness. Nothing in The Lands Between is as fearsome as the moment the camera spins wildly in a tight space, causing your death through no fault of your own. These legacy issues drag down what could have been a more fluid experience.

In the end, I would recommend Elden Ring, but only at face value—if you’re a Souls veteran willing to accept its flaws and revel in its punishing world, you’ll find enjoyment here. For others, especially newcomers, it’s important to understand that Elden Ring isn’t for everyone. It demands patience, tolerance for frustration, and a willingness to forgive its design missteps. If that sounds like your kind of adventure, then welcome to The Lands Between—but don’t say I didn’t warn you.

It just feels like open world dark souls if the souls games had a bright atmosphere. This is probably just nitpicking but I wish we could get something that isn't just a medieval fantasy souls like. Now for the biggest problem. The difficulty scaling is absolutely ass. Beyond ass even. In all of the other games you feel the progression. The bosses typically get harder enough to pose a challenge that feels like it should. Naturally progressive. There are spikes here and there but it always feels perfectly paced.
