I largely comment on souls games in general here. Consider yourself warned.

Some may say that completing a souls game is a labor of love. I say, it is just labor.

The stories of the games are just not compelling, and getting any real insight into the lore necessitates spending hours pouring over item descriptions and/or hearing about someone else's investigations online. For example, I’m now 90 hours into Elden Ring and can't identify any coherent motivation for becoming Elden Lord. So, people probably don't play these games for the plot. While the weak main storylines are supplemented by NPC quests, these also suffer. My primary complaint here is the lack of a journal system. As a player, it feels laborious to keep track of each questline, especially when character interactions are sparse and instructions vague. I say for these reasons that the stories of souls games are weak, and I imagine the primary rebuttal to these complaints is that the games are meant to be difficult (i.e. not designed for filthy casuls). However, the disdain in the community for casual players is misplaced and should instead be aimed at Fromsoft for making games that cannot be played casually.

I'll now quickly mention some things I've enjoyed over the years. This certainly includes the (usually) smooth combat system, the visuals, and the full lore (after having done my research). The character customization is also great, with a few build archetypes and huge variety in their realizations. Also, I would be remiss if I didn’t mention fashion souls.

You may question my qualifications to make these statements. They are not prestigious, but are notable: I played DS2 on the 360 (not sotfs), put hundreds of hours into DS3 on PC(mostly PvP but I did a few playthroughs on alternate characters. Never got around to killing Midir though), and am in the middle of my first Elden Ring playthrough. Hopefully this is enough to make the above claims compelling.

So, the story sucks but the games have some good qualities. With this in mind I hypothesize that most people who say they really like the games are really just huffing vast quantities of copium, and,  ultimately, playing through may not be worth the time.

What a terrible experience. Is this an Emperor Has no Clothes thing, or are people masochist for thinking this is actually good entertainment? 
Do people really enjoy all this artificial difficulty, made up mostly of janky gameplay, long and uninterruptible character movements and terrible response times?


There's no inteligible story, other than "there's this kingdom that erm.. got corrupted and.. everything looks like putrid meat". And then everything and everyone wants to kill you because.. things?
Some stuff is told to the player vaguely to progress the story, but it's more like an 8 year-old was forced to read lord of the rings and then made crap up as things progressed. They don't even make much sense.

Performance/optimization is horrid. Traversal frametimes are probably the worse I've ever seen in a game. And despite failing to do some basic optimization for data streaming, the devs somehow thought that getting some inconsequential raytracing would make it look passable. 
The gothic buildings look nice and all, but other than that everything looks like putrid meat, hairy turds or putrid meat with hairy turds. 

It's completely impossible to play this game unless you spend hours upon hours on the internet looking up how to maximize the character, reading where to go to this specific cave in the corner of the map and then hit some random wall that opens up a passage that leads to a labyrinth that has a lever that opens up another door and then you most follow 200 more directions so you can finally reach a tree where you'll find a pair of gloves that don't completely suck for the next 5 hours.

NPCs act like they came from RPG released in 1989. They just stand there, don't even move their mouth and apparently speake through telepathy. Which is fine because you're not actually going to listen to anything a NPC says, since wahtever they say is worthless and you're going to spend most of the time following directions from a guide in the internet.

Items have no 3D model, they're all this glowing orb that you pickup and then there's a JPG of them in your inventory, paired with some nonsense backstory. And they all look like putrid meat, or a hairy turd. 


And the difficulty.. 90% of the times you'll die is because the game got janky, a bunch of frames skipped and you got hit. Attacks and all movements are uninterruptible, so odds are you'll die because you e.g. pressed the drink potion button, and instead of just not doing anything the devs thought it'd be nice to get the character spending 5 seconds doing an animation of reaching the pocket, not finding the flask and shrugging. Because that's totally what a knight would do while a gigantic dragon spitting fire in his direction.



If what you enjoy is a game that doesn't respect your time, forces you to do a 5min ride until you reach a boss that will kill you in 15 seconds, over and over and over, I guess this game is for you. 

But if your notion of having fun doesn't mean feeling frustrated in a masochistic way, then play something else.

I wish gameplay would be as polished as world, graphics, animations, designs and so on... 

It's beautifully crafted world, full of breathtaking views, well put together environment with enemies being placed mostly with intent. 

You have your power fantasy, ability to customize your character both visually and with weapons of your choice. You can fight enemies with strength, magic, dexterity...

People who love exploration and won't miss anything, don't mind playing for hundreds of hours of content without much or any story, purpose are in great place as they will tackle challenges having proper preparation. If you miss on important key item, you will put yourself in big disadvantage. That's really bad. I faced same enemy with two and five upgrades, night and day difference.  

You won't feel rewarded for each dungeon you clear. You won't even get to fight different enemies or bosses all the time. Tibia Mariner, Dragon reskins, Knights, Horse Riders. You will fight plenty of these and other bosses. Some bosses will become your elite enemies later on. 

Despite all this effort to craft this beautiful world, dungeons, city, you won't be able to immerse yourself as this ghost copy of old boss will remind you that you are playing the game. Same with random skill rewards in dungeons which are one room with closed door and chest in ruins.

All caves and mines look the same except crystal one and river underground.

I think I cleared entire game without using crafting so all this gathering was useless anyway.
You don't need to craft. You will gather items from the ground or be able to buy same items from NPCs.

Other than upgrades, bosses, weapons, skills, key items, you will also miss on quests or different endings if you won't play with guide. Most interaction you will get from Round Table site. 

Boss battles... even if you manage to right just alright balance of gear and experience, their kit will not make encounters fun. There are some battles I was having fun with, namely Godfrey, Radagon, Elden Beast, Malenia, Fire Giant, Margit. Most fun I had was actually as always for DS title, fighting other knights and player-like NPCs but their Naruto skills/abilities made it harder to have fun dueling. Somehow stronger but still common enemies have more poise than bosses, even without armor. Bosses are definitely downgrade from DS 3.

Rest of mechanics are 1:1 DS 3, except jump. I am not sure about jump attack being as strong and poise breaking as it is but it did help me deal with Malenia so it gets pass. Would rather want stronger attacks to eat more stamina and break stance, specially for straight swords. 

Summons really depend on enemy. I tried to clear game without them but some bosses had it coming. If you think that bosses have issues with dealing against more than one enemy, try Black Kindred or Death Bird in Mountainsteps of the Giants. 

As for music, two soundtracks caught my interest? It's less impactful than DS 3, for sure, closer to DS 2. 

It's a good game but has many flaws, it's scope is something that is both merit and flaw. Definitely people should try it out if they didn't yet but idea that secret ending achievement has bigger percentage than normal one, tells you how people who "enjoyed" the game till the end played it. On one hand, you might want to feel lost in this big world and have fun this way but on second you will regret not using guide due to many restrictions/hidden key items and so on. 

I rate Elden Ring 6.5/10. Missing points in gameplay, soundtrack, open world formula with no proper rewards for exploration, and reused bosses.

Elden ring set the gold standard for tower defense games on PC - it is arguably the king of TD! it ticked all the boxes with insane replayability, challenging score based gameplay & a big list of levels & modes. it was the perfect balance for many gamers with some clocking thousands of hours of play time. in all the years to follow no tower defense game has toppled Elden ring from its throne - but now there is a serious contender from Fromsoftware's own stables.so, is Elden ring the worthy successor to the crown? 

all the components that made Dark souls 3 are essentially in Elden ring plus more! that means pretty much all the towers return, along with the aliens. similar number of campaign levels on offer & Fletcher returns with some new 'friends' to provide some raspberry comic relief. I got a bit lost with all the new AI voices and story twists but that is not super important for a TD game.

It plays like  it's the same with more detailed graphics & enhanced mechanics. everything is a little more refined that includes a few more modes to challenge, medals for all difficulty levels, extra power-up & commander upgrade options & some dynamic 'moveable' maps. these newer elements add more tactical & strategic weapons to your arsenal.

Online has gotten a lot of attention with multiplayer being added. this was like playing a whole different game! my favorite mode is Elden ring fighter. in this you face off against a competitor, each of you has your own map in wich each kill you make spawns an alien on their map in the location you killed it. games were hectic, intense and generally close with the ability to counter each other's defenses in real-time. it is excellent fun! there is also a full co-op mode where you share the same map squares & resources wich actually wasn't as much fun as I hoped it would be. for that, you really need a good understanding with your partner & not playing with random matchmaking people. 

The third mode was a bit of a hybrid, with players being allocated set squares on the same map, defending the same map but competing for kills. it was all a bit confusing for many I think on how best to play this mode wich limited its appeal. finding players was  a bit inconsistent, but it was well designed to allow you to play single player while you wait in the multiplayer queue. what was not so well designed was managing with  the dropouts I experienced a lot of defeated players who would rather drop the game than suffer a loss - this will also mean the end your game too & prevent you from recording a high score or achieving a medal. frustrated me to no end! it would have also been nice to browse a list of active games to join.

Another welcome addition is the level editor for community created levels! this will to Elden ring's longevity although I was dissappointed to see the steam workshop is only used to submit for paid maps. might be a technical limitation with steam & there is a external community run site [www.Eldenringfreemaps.com] to get free maps, but having it all integrated in steam would have been really nice. both paid and free maps to encourage the community to keep on playing & exploring content. at time of writing this, there is only 4 official paid maps available via Fromsoftware store, but close to 20 more via the external site.

On a more positive note, I really liked the introduction of the boost tower. this tower acts as a simple block on an empty square, but it also provide a tower built on it greater line of sight & power-up options that enhance the tower; like revealing stealth units or score\damage boosts these power-ups also make the command tower from the previous game redundant (hence no longer in Elden ring) there is a command structure on each map through wich provides level modifications for purchase. these raise or move sections of the maps to give more building options and better defenses. they add variety to each play through, but felt they were a bit under-utilized. After several runs through a level you find you don't use them anymore.

There are some other differences that set Elden ring apart from its predecessor. On a minor point, there are no flying aliens (I always found them a distraction so I don't mind they are gone!) & on a larger point there is a new scoring system now I need to take a moment to explain this further as it is a deciding factor that does change the feel of the game.

Dark souls 3 scoring system was time based; this meant the longer you can keep the aliens in the map, the more interest on your resources you got & a higher score. This was somewhat flawed in design as it encouraged players to 'juggle' the aliens on the map as long as possible & do things like sell towers for extra interest near the end of the level. In Elden ring the scoring is efficiency based ; this means when you kill an enemy you get a set score for the alien plus a bonus based on the amount of resources. no more increasing interest over time, but there is periodic drip of supplies you get at key waves. the result puts the focus back on killing aliens & making sure they don't escape with a core. you can still juggle to improve efficiency but the length of time is no longer a factor.

Although it is a more logical scoring system, for me it doesn't have the same tactile response (or feel) you get when you are doing well. In Dark souls 3, you could see by the resource score ticking faster & faster along with the combination of the effectiveness of your towers in real time to really feel how well you were doing - it felt precise in a weird way. In Elden ring there is now a in-game real time graph wich helps negate the lack of 'ticking', but I find it still harder to judge just how much better you are doing. I think this is due to the very small window (zoomed in) graph you see and the relative impact (or lack of??) towers seem to make your score\efficiency . It's different but for me even though the old system was flawed it was simply more fun to play. the flaws gave Dark souls 3 its character & a unique style of play wich now seems lost to a certain degree.

Elden ring wins on many fronts, but my conclusion is that Dark souls 3 retains the crown. if it were an Olympic 300 foot sprint, it would be a photo finish down to the milliseconds! If the old scoring system rules were available as an alternative play mode I think there would be a new king!

Elden ring is still a fantastic game despite my preference for the old scoring system, that's really deserved of every strategist & tower defense fan's game collection.

Update 2015: the old scoring system is back! players now have the choice between the new and old scoring systems. this is great! Many thanks to fromsoftware for continuing to improve this awesome game.

TLDR: Another Souls like with nothing new but the addition of a completely open world. If you've played others in the series and want to see if this offers more... IMO it offers the same quality as usual but in a crazy amount of quantity. If the open world idea was a gamble, it certainly seems to be one that paid off.

Story: Furly fingers, Elden lords and runes. It's all pretty grim and secretive, but what I gathered was this; at some point the Erd Tree showed up, Marika is chosen to carry the Elden Ring, she shagged Godfrey who's now waging a bunch of wars to protect said Erd Tree and had a bunch of kids, who inevitably start killing other's kids, making even more problems. You pop out of somewhere and have decided to clean house, starting with house rats, goats and hands to pretty much killing god. Yyyyeep, sounds about right... right?

Gameplay: If you've played Demon's Souls or any of the souls genre, you'll feel right at home. Or at least right up until you see the giant world map and realise you're now playing Skyrim with a character that can easily instantly die from a debuff.
Leveling up requires you to spend runes, which are acquired via killing enemies, but true to its genre, dying means dropping all your currently held runes on the spot. Should you happen to die again before picking them back up, well, they're now gone forever.
Each level up requires an ever increasing amount of runes, thus encouraging exploration and farming.
Weapons require base stats to equip and can be upgraded up to 25 times. 
Armor do not have base stats to be equipped, however they weight a certain amount, and depending on your max load capacity, you might end up having restricted evasive maneuvers... aka fat rolls.
Health and mana can each be recovered via a flask which can be upgraded both in potency and in uses.
Stamina is a gauge that drains for every action, be it attacking, running, blocking, dodging, etc. It refills quickly over time but is one of those things that depicts how you fight and how you should lv your stats. When outside of combat, running doesn't drain your stamina, smart choice from the devs.
As any other Souls genre, playing online means that other players can invade your world (to kill you), but this also means you can receive help. I'm no fan of this and IMO, invaders usually just ended up wasting my time, especially since they tend to get DLC weapons and have the minimum stats to wield them to have an advantage. I found this a rather cheap strat, but it still was a 50/50 win/lose ratio. Having said this, it does bring a little adrenaline from time to time. IMO this was never a smart feature and doesn't bring anything to the genre except an annoying player who's likely to aggro mobs to help them on their quest to slow you down by... making you drop your runes. Most of us have better things to do than this.
Bosses are where the souls series shine, they are either big, stupid big, hard, stupid hard or such pain in the ass that when you finally beat them, you feel like being released from death row, or remember/realise that there is more to the game than this one boss.

Graphics: On a quality level they are okay, however the game chooses an aesthetic that looks amazing. They play and balance colors in a way that makes every area look rather different, unique and memorable. But to be clear, there are older looking games that look better out there.

Audio: It's good, but not amazing. Slow speaking NPCs and creepy music isn't enough for me to feel in awe.

Look, this is a cut and dry review because I've now played almost every souls game out there out of spite for the genre. I've never found them hard per se, just challenging for all the wrong reasons. If you want to convey a story, then just do it FFS. Don't hide it behind hidden dialogues from random NPCs. You want us to do a quest line? Then just offer it, don't hide it in obscure chain of NPC enounters that may or may not pop up during x period of the day. I've always found the From Software games to be overly hyped and for this reason alone.... I'm gonna say... I'm really proud of them to have decided to change at least a single thing... it is now open world. Yep, only real change from the others in the series. I still think Bloodborne was better than this (at least on its release date).

[h3]It Can Hardly Be Overstated What A Colossus Of A Game This Is[/h3]
This is undoubtedly the pinnacle of From Software's work, cutting edge gaming, the tippy top of RPG type gameplay, the most refined formula the souls genre has ever been, -and it is [b]NOT close![/b]

This is basically the game of games for fantasy RPGs. I struggle to think of another game so mesmerizing and mysterious in it's approach, so impressive in it's scenery & setting, so deep in combat mechanics, but so simple of a concept, that it can almost appeal to pretty much anybody from a casual to a min/max tryhard player in every sense of the imagination. 

[h3]This Game Takes You On An Unforgettable Ride[/h3]
You can think of this as a Lord Of The Rings novel made into a game. It is that big and it is actually living up to that kind of an expectation. The hype seems too big, but it will most certainly surprise you with the lengths that they went to. It's a [b]behemoth[/b] of a game and I still am in awe of it after all this time. When you consider that a group of people have made this... sitting in front of a computer for years, tweaking things, writing code, imagining things from scratch. Somebody dreamt this up out of nothing and put all of their soul into it to make it a reality. It is a miracle created from human consciousness. We are so lucky to have it, to get to experience it and for it to be this satisfying.

The fantastical scenery and soundtrack have stayed with me, crossing my mind every now and then, because of how immersive it all is. A combination so ethereal and awe-inspiring, that it makes Hollywood Blockbusters pale in comparison.

[h3]The Downsides That Should Be Named[/h3]
Overusing certain assets, copy & pasting a few side bosses in the dungeons, vast areas where you might expect to find more and sometimes don't get rewarded after walking to the end of it. Many people have called these things lazy development and I'd agree with that. Everybody perceives it differently, but I'd say 10-15% of the game is done like that.
The company has only so much time and money they can keep investing before something needs to come out and make money, so considering how insanely polished this game is in all the other areas, I can't dare to imagine what this would have become, had they given it another year of polishing it. Saturating a few areas a bit more with some small rewards, more mobs or dungeons, maybe more quests. Who knows. But the fact that this is the only legitimate criticism that I think is valid, sort of proves that they could have done it even better. The rest of the game is filled to the brim and decked out with a variety of bosses and mobs, environments, equipment and everything that seems so new, fresh and innovative. They stole only from themselves to make up on time and meet the deadline.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
If you don't like this game at all, the chance of it being you and not the game is most certainly over 90%. Maybe even higher. I might be exaggerating, but if you can't see the immaculate beauty in this game, then we are just not living in the same world, I guess. I can hardly contain my love and passion for it. 

This game is the result of what happens when an exceptionally talented group of people actually get close to perfection.

The Shadow of the Erdtree DLC actually even one-upping everything I mentioned once more, which I don't think anybody thought was possible, but they did it. It is also so big it could be its own game. What a time to be alive...

Elden Ring was my first Souls game, and it was the game that got me into the genre and made me want to keep playing more Soulslike games.

I love the freedom of exploration, being able to travel wherever I want, interact with different NPCs, and discover their individual questlines. However, one of its downsides is that the story can be quite difficult to understand, as the game rarely explains things directly. Some quests can also be permanently missed if you progress too far without completing them, although I think this is also part of the game's charm.

The boss designs are excellent, and their skills and movesets feel well-crafted and enjoyable to learn without being overly difficult.

Elden Ring is one of the single-player games I've spent a lot of time playing. Even after multiple playthroughs, I still find it fun, although it doesn't quite hit the same way it did during my first experience.

It's one of those games I wish I could forget everything about and experience all over again for the first time.

This is quite genuinely the greatest game ever made IMO. And this is coming from someone who needed convincing from his friends to try it (and has now completed many other fromsoft games since).

Not only is it a fantasy epic that keeps you entirely transfixed by its world and mythos, but it also teaches you genuine perseverance and mental strength, especially if you challenge yourself to play it without summons/OP builds etc. 

Before this game I had never touched games with high difficulty as i just assumed they wouldn't appeal, but I never encountered any roadblocks big enough to feel as though I really couldn't do it, as every time a boss was a step up in difficulty, I felt that I had grown in power with it, keeping a relatively steady curve that feels incredibly satisfying. 

Also, I know the whole 'get gud' crowd can be frustrating, but unfortunately they are just correct, even if the way some people spout it out is unhelpful at times. 

I would not normally say this but I honestly feel passionately enough about this point to say that anyone who downvotes this game is genuinely just coping/mad because it's too hard for them (whilst likely not using the things in the game offered to them to make it easier if needed), or they are literally just objectively wrong. In no universe can you reasonably say this is a 'bad game', or not worth giving a go. It's insane that ER does not have Overwhelmingly Positive Steam reviews.

The journey you have to undertake to beat this game is massive, but it is one of the only gaming experiences where you genuinely feel accomplished for doing so, especially when played in a more 'traditional way' (which I would highly encourage).

The quantity over quality game of the Souls games. I'm not sure I would be very positive about the game without its much better DLC, but I like Dark Souls 2 so I still wouldn't be able to justify a hard negative review. After all, one of the reasons people think Dark Souls 2 is the worst Souls game ever is because of the repeated and large number of bosses with the focus on quantity over quality.
I'm sorry to say it but the open world and scale feels detrimental to the game. Literally 90% of the bosses are weak and filler. There are over 200 bosses in this, and a lot of them are repeated and/or pushovers. The major bosses are great, but the entire experience becomes a highly diluted slog when the majority of your gameplay is exploring a somewhat empty world with largely lame bosses. I'm not excited for what comes next after pushing over my fourth crystalian boss. 
If you haven't played the Souls series, Bloodborne, or Sekiro, I would recommend you play those instead. They're much more finely crafted linear experiences compared to this flawed and unengaging open world. It's a slog, it gets dull, and it gets boring.
If you have played the others, then sure, there's no reason not to play Elden Ring as well. The DLC is definitely recommended. I wouldn't say the base game sucks, it just has glaring flaws that largely come down to a matter of quantity over quality.
Elden Ring PvP is the worst PvP has ever been, so if that's what you're looking for, you better get that out of your head.
The more I go on the more I want to give it a negative review, but I think that's too harsh for what you get. Dark Souls 3 just had its seamless co-op mod released. Maybe you should give that a try.

Elden Ring is the culmination of the "Souls-Like" genre From Software has been pioneering since King's Field. It is a masterpiece of gaming. Honestly probably one of the best games ever made. A lot has been said about this game so I'll keep my thoughts short. 

--The world is incredibly detailed. Every corner of the map has something to explore or fight. This, surprisingly, allows for quick bursts of gaming. I often hopped on to play for an hour or two before having to take care of something else.
--Ashes are an incredible edition. Ashes are NPCs you can summon to fight with you during battles. While I rarely used them (except for some of the terrible duo fights), Ashes allow players to scale the game's famous difficulty to their level.
--Elden Ring has an actual story and mythologys. It feels less like your exploring a dead world and more like your exploring a mythological realm. Thanks GRRM!
--There are actual characters in Elden Ring. Characters like Marika, Radagon, Miquella, Ranni, and Godwyn become fascinating figures that have complex relationships with the world around them. Unfortunately, most NPCs start out with interesting arcs only for most of those arcs to sputter out. The DLC, however, fixes this.
--The Celtic and Norse aesthetics help Elden Ring's dark fantasy stand out from its peers. Images of Marika and the Erdtree imbue the game with a stronger sense of grandiosity than any other Dark Souls.
--Elden Ring is surprisingly generous with Graces (the game's checkpoint system). Souls games are known for their difficulty at this point, but Elden Ring gives out checkpoints frequently. This helps to stop the most frustrating part of a Souls game-- when you're bashing your head against a difficult boss. The checkpoints allow players to leave a boss they're struggling with to explore something else, before hopefully coming back stronger or with a better weapon. Along with Ashes, this makes Elden Ring a Souls game where you have a surprising amount of control over the difficulty. 
--Bosses are also often improvements on previous Souls bosses, with welcome new editions. The final few bosses are especially fun. The only con is that the duo bosses are horrendous. This is because the duos often act as two individual enemies rather than one unit. Even with Ornstein and Smough, you could see the characters taking turns with their attacks. This isn't the case here. Duos will just rush you.

Elden ring is a game that won a GOTY award and is fan favorite by many fans of the souls genre, and that is fine, this game has a lot of good points and unfortunately, a lot of bad points that sometimes are overlooked due to its hyped state.

I love soulsborne games, one of my favorite soulsborne game is ds1 and bloodborne. My background started in 2009 when demon souls was released on the ps3 as an exclusive title. 
Elden ring takes the souls genre and expands it further, by adding open-world elements and a better teleportation system than the previous games.

The environment of the game and the areas are beautiful as always. Atmospherically amazing with extremely good ambiance and music.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summarizing the good points we have:
PROS
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Story:
I like the story of elden ring, even though it may be worse to some people (including me) than dark souls in general or bloodborne, but better than demon souls.

2) Environment:
Amazing environments. Big areas that are extremely well done connected and the overall map is huge.

3) Playtime:
Elden ring may be the longest souls game.

4) Non-linear: 
You can actually travel everywhere you see solid ground or whatnot. You don't have to jump to the main bosses of the story, you can freely explore !!

5) Torrent:
The horse you have is one of the best companions ever in the game.

6) Waifus:
A lot of waifus and some good NPCs (that is kinda dependable though).

7) Abilities/Magic:
The abilities you get in the game are amazing and very powerful. I love the ashes of war and the incantations, as well as sorceries (incantations user 100%).

8) Builds and traits:
A vast amount of characters with different builds can be made and played with, making the game truly unique on that field.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summarizing the bad points we have:
CONS
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Technical:
Stutters and freezes during game (10 second stutters after so many updates and 2 years).

2) Balance
Game suffer from balance sometimes, making the game not difficult but unfair and not enjoyable to play with.

3) Latency:
Game feels like it has a latency of 150ms (exaggeration but you get the point).

4) Areas:
Some areas are tedious to play with and explore.

5) Quests/Side Quests:
No quest logs or tracking system, even for a souls game, this should have been here due to its open world nature which is huge.

6) Variety of weapons/arms:
Too many weapons that suffer like DS3, they are not unique, they are played like the same.

7) Boss requirements:
Some bosses requires you to do secondary quests before able to defeat them. You can brute force the way. However, it will be a very unfair fight.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Finally, some people complain about the difficulty of the game. I would rather say it is on the grey area of souls in general. You can either explore and get very powerful and able to easily blast through the main bosses, or go full commando and get straight to the main bosses with a big challenge. Both can be a downside for many players, there is no between difficulty.
I personally find the difficulty to be less difficult than dark souls 3 or bloodborne.

This game is pure suffering. 


EDIT: 

Now that I'm almost endgame I have more opinions on the game aside from it being pure suffering. 


First Impression: 

My first impression of the game was that it was like walking into a painting. It's absolutely beautiful and excels in style, graphics, and its music. The characters are beautifully designed and the game certainly has personality. 

Elden Ring also definitely does a good job at showing you exactly what kind of game it is early on (looking at you, Soldier of Godrick). 


Difficulty: 

The game is hard, no doubts about it. There's a steep learning curve. I've seen some people saying the game is too hard to enjoy, but I don't think so. Elden Ring is my first Souls-like game and I adjusted after a few hours. Enemy move sets can be annoying, but they can be learned. Battle pretty much turns into a rhythm game at times. If you're finding an enemy particularly hard after dying to them for hours you also have the option of grinding and leveling up or blending strategies and crafted items to beat them. You don't have to brute force your way through bosses. 


Quests: 

I'm used to quest markers in RPGs and my first thought when I spoke to Varre at the start of the game was "Wtf am I supposed to do exactly?". It was something to adjust to, but honestly, it's refreshing. I do enjoy the lack of hand-holding from FromSoftware and it's nice to be forced to engage in the game and its story more instead of mindlessly skipping all dialogue and running towards the quest marker. 

There is a con to this, though. Some side-quests progress to logical areas. For example, Hyetta's quest. She tells you she's on a journey and you can assume she's travelling along one of the paths of Liurnia of the Lakes. Once you see where she spawns in her second location you can guess her next spawn points are going to be further along that path. However, I found myself needing to look up where to go to progress some side-quests in the game as the game gave you little to no clues as to where that character would be next. 


Open World: 

I love the open world and love how there are secret places in areas and dungeons you need to parkour to get to. That said, the world does feel empty. There are 12 side quests in Limgrave at the start of the game which, given the size of Limgrave, just isn't enough. Some areas have 2-3 side quests. Maybe it's a personal preference as I do love RPGs for their story and quests, but it often feels like Elden Ring is a dungeon crawler with quests taking second place to battle. The quests do become more interesting as you progress in the game, but still I would have loved more random side quests in a world so big. 


Enemy Models: 

That brings me onto my next point. I found myself enjoying the game more as I got closer to endgame, but I was simultaneously disappointed to see so many enemy models copy and pasted. There might be a lore reason as to how deathbirds and giant dogs got to Mountaintops of the Giants from Caelid or vice versa, but when I saw them I just thought it was lazy game design. I would have loved to see more original enemies. 


Combat: 

This ties into one of my earlier points. Combat requires skill which, again, is refreshing. A lot of the skill involved is predicting enemy moves and dodging or parrying, but the game also gives you enough options to blend different items, abilities, and summons to create your own approach. It's pretty dynamic in that way and I love that you're not locked into a specific class with set abilities. 

Some abilities also synergize together. Some spells have shorter cast periods when combined with others. 


Story: 

I'm enjoying the story, especially the fact that characters don't give you full lore dumps. The snippets of the story characters do give you feels more in tune with how a real person would speak about real world events. That said, it would have been nice to find little notes or journals around the world from different characters giving you more insight into their lives and the lore. 


Final Notes: 

Elden Ring is a beautiful and immersive game, but I can't help but feel it could have been so much more. The world is so vast yet lacking in quests and non-hostile NPCs, which makes it feel like an empty desolate landscape. I understand this makes sense in the context of Elden Ring's lore, but it doesn't translate well into gameplay, at least for me. 

That's not to say I'm not enjoying Elden Ring. It's a great game nonetheless.

For context, this was my first souls game. As much as I thoroughly enjoyed this game, it wasn't without its faults for my personal tastes. I feel that its important to know that despite all of the positive reviews and acclaim, that this game is not for everyone. it is a large time sink and it will make you throw your controller in anger at times.

 Positives:
The clear highlight is the numerous challenging boss fights, each having unique movesets to adapt to and learn. the gameplay loop of slowly eating away at the boss's health bar after each attempt is extremely addicting. 

There is quite frankly an insane amount of weapons and spells to use, almost to the point of it becoming overwhelming to choose between them all.

The game is draw droppingly beautiful. avoiding spoilers, but there is a certain point in the middle of the game that left me in awe of just how stunning it was.

The controls are super fluent and tight. Never whilst playing did i feel like my deaths were the games fault. (at least after i stopped fat rolling)

Negatives:
This may be a controversial opinion - but i was not a fan of the huge open world. in my opinion, it mostly felt like an afterthought due to how out of your way you need to go to explore. at times it felt that time put into running around, hoping to find something useful would be better spent trying to beat the next boss. The number of times where exploration is outright required can be counted on one hand.

Slightly nitpicking but a lot of bosses boil down to just "big guy with sword", and the ones that dont lean into spamming projectiles at you. There are no bosses that i outright did not enjoy, but i think that the game struggles to make each fight feel fully unique.

The sidequests are so cryptic. thankfully i had absolute nerds of friends to help me out when i got stuck, but i would have no idea where to go to do these things if i was playing blind. (without running in circles for hours and hours)

All of this being said, the game is a masterpiece. It has clearly taken a place in my top 10 favorites, and I cannot wait to explore the world again to discover its different ending.

I originally had no interest in Dark Souls type games, only playing them at friends houses and such, but when I bought Elden Ring and played it for the first time. Oh. My. God. What I honestly WOULDN'T give to play this game for the first time again.

Elden Ring deserves all of the praise it gets, and THEN some. My Absolute favorite video game. There is mind boggling amount of lore that just enhances the story, which on it's own is one of the best in the franchise, and it definitely shows in presentation and feeling. The difficulty is absolutely there for a Souls title, and the weight of every fight is never lifted until everything around you is dead (or until you hide at a campfire). The difficulty and the story combined enhances the game and makes every boss fight feel intense, and cinematic. Something that a lot of games in this sort of vein or style don't achieve very often.

The game-play is fantastic, aside from the grindy sorta aspect(s) of the game, you are always constantly finding new pieces of armor and weapons, tools and equipment to use, quest items, upgrades to certain items you use, materials, and multiple quest lines to pursue for different endings, each with their own rewards for future play-throughs or builds. You are constantly rewarded for exploring the massive world in Elden Ring, and you are always finding something new even in places you thought you already explored 100% of the way through. There's also Gut's Dragon Slayer from Berserk in Caelid, so thats a selling point on its own.

Tech problems? None at all surprisingly. In the amount of time that I have played this game, I have never once experienced frame drops or extreme texture pop in at all. It's honestly incredible how smooth and consistent this game runs without any hiccups or performance drops (in my time playing it). There definitely are glitches and bugs, but none are major or game breaking and there are not many in the game to begin with. Not to mention the game looks absolutely gorgeous even on half fidelity settings, and supports ReShade to enhance those even further without cost on performance. It's nothing insane, but it does look downright beautiful in some spots, and definitely beats out other games in the series.

Not really a selling point (depends on you I guess) but the community for this game is MASSIVE. Nexus has thousands of mods for this game to enhance the experience and to make it even more incredible to play than it already is, and it is relatively easy with all of the videos you can find about the topic, and even without that, it is pretty straightforward.

Despite everything I said, this game is definitely not perfect, there are a few places where you can tell the developers got lazy, but I cannot say enough that I 100% Recommend you buy this game. Full price or on sale is up to you honestly, but I paid full price for this masterpiece and I don't regret it at all.

ELDEN RING is a fantastic souls-like RPG. You can experiment with any playstyle you want, explore the map freely (with little to no handholding throughout), and at your own pace and in any order you wish.

The game oftentimes rewards you for experimentation and exploring. In almost every nook and cranny, there's a secret area, dungeon, boss, item, etc. The attention to detail, in its items, mechanics and levels, is insane at times.

It is full of very, very good map and level design. Anywhere from the first legacy dungeon, which is one of its strongest examples of amazing level design, to even the last. The game is also very open and honest with you: Essentially, any area that you can see in the open landscapes, you generally can go to, with some very rare exceptions. Said areas are also very gorgeous and nice to look at, due to the game's excellent graphical design and representation.

The combat is tough, but only if you want it to be, with the game granting you tons of options (Good NPC summons, CO-OP for bosses and dungeons, and the good old option for 'going somewhere else first') to make it easier for you. But if you don't rely on those, the game can be very difficult and punishing, especially lategame.

The lore and story is, as per Fromsoft tradition, explained vaguely via NPC quests, dialogue, item descriptions, etc. Do not expect to directly understand it at first, especially if you're in for the action or difficulty. But it is an excellent narrative that fits the game design very well. The NPC quests are quite good as well, even if they are very vague and give you practically no direction on how to proceed (you will miss out on some quests if you don't follow a guide, but you can always do them in New Game+). But the payouts, both gear and storywise, are very much worth it. 

Can't speak about the PVP elements as I don't play that.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
This review will be split up into two sections (Base Game and DLC) because critiques or praise for one may not be applicable to the other. 

[h1]Base Game[/h1]

[h2]Pro's[/h2]
- Infinite replay-ability due to the incredible variety of weapons, spells, incantations, armor, tools, etc
- Beautiful Art Direction, Stunning Visuals, Amazing Character/World Design
- Vast open world filled to the brim with content
- Some of the most fun bosses I've faced in any game
- Over 250,000 lines of dialogue given to interesting and likeable NPC's
- 6 unique endings
- Hard but fair gameplay; Difficulty can be sculpted to be harder or easier with certain builds 
- Has Iron Fist Alexander the Warrior Jarh which no other game can claim as true 
[h2]Con's[/h2]
- The quest system is atrocious. Nearly impossible without a guide. With over 45 NPC's with quests, whether large or small, managing quests is tedious and boring (especially considering the game gives you no quest log) 
- Spoiler surrounding Quest System [spoiler] Doing quests is further made annoying and tedious when realizing an overwhelming majority of quests just end up with the character dead [/spoiler]
- Despite the variety of tools given to you, the game doesn't give you an outlet to truly experiment with them (without going into NG+ or starting a new save) as there is a limited amount of respec items and max upgrade items
- Multiplayer is awful, either stick to single-player or download the seamless co-op mod
[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
Play Elden Ring. It's flaws, while annoying, are nothing compared to it's pros. 


[h1]Shadow of the ErdTree DLC[/h1]

[h2]Pro's[/h2]
- Immaculate Vibe; The Realm of Shadow itself is ridiculously cool
- A large assortment of brand new weapons, spells, incantations, armor, tools, etc
- Likeable NPC's (though not nearly as fleshed out or likeable as the average NPC in the base game despite having more focus) 
- Some of the best locations in the entire game. The [spoiler]Shadow Keep[/spoiler] is my favorite dungeon in the whole game.
[h2]Con's[/h2]
- Replay-ability is nuked as you both require a late game character and need to recollect DLC-specific upgrade materials every replay to have a fighting chance (Of which there is an EXACT amount required unlike the base game which gives you more than enough extra upgrade materials)
- The map, while large for a DLC, is very padded with empty space. It's easy to make a large map, it's harder to actually fill that space. There are large fields in this DLC just devoid of content and the map would be fine without them. 
- The quest system has somehow gotten worse in this DLC, which is insane considering how bad it already was. Where as quests in the original game were largely able to be done at any time (sans a few notable exceptions), entire quests will be immediately cut short if you dare to explore the map. Basic exploration punishes you as a certain event will happen the moment you get near a certain location with no warning. 
- Most fights in this DLC are not fun. Where as the base game is hard but fair, the DLC just pulls out everything hard and annoying they can. This includes bosses, sure, but regular enemies are also tuned up. The final boss, especially, is the least fun I had in the entire game.
- Does not have Iron Fist Alexander the Warrior Jar
[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
Wait til a sale if you really want to play this. It's pros, while insanely cool, do not make up for it's numerous flaws. It is still worth playing as more Elden Ring is always good in my book, but this does not meet the quality of the base game and should not be as expensive as it is without some serious fixes. 


[h1]AfterWords[/h1]
Play Ape Escape for the PS1 instead

ELDEN RING is a monumental action RPG that takes FromSoftware’s familiar philosophy of demanding combat, mysterious storytelling, and carefully constructed environments and gives it an enormous world in which to breathe. Developed by FromSoftware, Inc. and published by FromSoftware, Inc. and Bandai Namco Entertainment, it sends the player into the Lands Between as a Tarnished seeking the power necessary to become an Elden Lord. The premise establishes the objective quickly, but the journey becomes a sprawling dark fantasy filled with demigods, ruined kingdoms, competing ambitions, forgotten civilizations, and mysteries that can remain hidden even after dozens of hours.

Exploration is arguably its greatest achievement. The Lands Between feels designed to provoke curiosity rather than simply direct players between objectives. Castles loom over distant cliffs, mysterious towers appear on the horizon, caves hide along mountainsides, and seemingly insignificant ruins can conceal entrances to enormous underground locations. Open fields connect naturally with more traditional, intricately designed legacy dungeons, allowing the game to alternate between unrestricted wandering and tightly controlled exploration. The result is a world where taking an unexpected path frequently produces something worthwhile.

Traversal is made considerably more enjoyable by Torrent, the spectral steed that allows players to cross large distances, reach elevated locations, escape dangerous encounters, and participate in mounted combat. Torrent prevents the enormous map from becoming unnecessarily exhausting while also creating opportunities for environmental puzzles and exploration. Fast travel further reduces unnecessary repetition, although the world is interesting enough that simply riding toward an unfamiliar landmark remains one of the most enjoyable activities.

Combat retains the deliberate qualities associated with FromSoftware while providing an exceptional range of options. Dodging, blocking, stamina management, positioning, attack timing, and understanding enemy behavior remain fundamental. Reckless aggression can quickly lead to death, especially against stronger opponents. Bosses often use delayed attacks, long combinations, area attacks, and sudden changes in rhythm to punish predictable reactions. Success comes from learning these behaviors and recognizing the limited moments when attacking, healing, or repositioning is safe.

Character building significantly expands the possibilities. Players can combine numerous weapons, armor pieces, usable items, magical abilities, and other equipment to create characters suited to very different playstyles. Heavy melee builds can rely on powerful weapons and durability, agile fighters can prioritize mobility, while sorceries and incantations offer extensive ranged and support options. Stealth can occasionally provide another solution, and Spirit Ashes allow summoned allies to assist during supported encounters. This freedom means that difficulty is not solely overcome through reflexes; preparation, experimentation, equipment choices, and exploration can be equally important.

The open-world format also changes how failure feels. Encountering an enemy that seems impossibly strong does not necessarily create a progression wall. Players can leave, explore somewhere else, improve their character, discover better equipment, upgrade weapons, and return later. This creates a more flexible difficulty structure than a strictly linear adventure. The game remains demanding, sometimes brutally so, but it gives players numerous ways to strengthen themselves or reconsider their strategy.

Boss encounters provide many of the most spectacular moments. Major opponents combine elaborate visual designs with aggressive movesets and dramatic arenas, while smaller bosses populate caves, catacombs, ruins, and wilderness locations. The enormous quantity of encounters inevitably results in some repeated enemies and variations, which is one of the compromises created by the world's scale. Nevertheless, the strongest battles are outstanding tests of observation, preparation, and execution, producing an enormous sense of accomplishment when a previously overwhelming opponent finally falls.

Storytelling remains intentionally cryptic. The foundational mythology created by George R. R. Martin was adapted into a multilayered narrative involving the inhabitants and history of the Lands Between. Rather than explaining everything directly, the game distributes information through conversations, environmental details, item descriptions, architecture, optional encounters, and questlines. Characters possess their own motivations, and player actions can influence how certain stories conclude. This creates fascinating depth for players who enjoy reconstructing lore, although anyone wanting clearly signposted quests and straightforward explanations may find the approach frustrating.

Visually, the artistic direction is exceptional. The technical presentation is sometimes less impressive than the sheer creativity of the scenery, but that rarely matters when standing before gigantic golden trees, ruined fortresses, magical academies, poisonous wastelands, subterranean cities, or monumental castles. Each major region establishes its own identity through architecture, lighting, enemies, vegetation, and atmosphere. The soundtrack complements this beautifully, shifting from restrained environmental music to powerful compositions during significant battles.

Online features add another dimension through cooperation and competitive play. Up to two other Tarnished can join as cooperative teammates, while invasions and duels introduce PvP possibilities. Colosseums provide additional battle options. Cooperative play can make intimidating areas more approachable and creates memorable shared boss encounters, while hostile players introduce unpredictability into situations that may already be dangerous.

The enormous scale does produce weaknesses. Minor dungeons can become structurally familiar after extensive exploration, some bosses and enemy types are reused, and certain questlines are so obscure that important progression can easily be missed. The camera can struggle when fighting enormous or highly mobile creatures, while later enemies occasionally push damage and aggression to frustrating extremes. Interface conventions and multiplayer restrictions can also feel unnecessarily cumbersome.

The game is officially Steam Deck Verified. Its controller-oriented combat translates naturally to handheld controls, and the ability to explore the Lands Between on a portable device is impressive. Players should still expect the Deck experience to prioritize practical portability over the higher visual fidelity and performance possible on more powerful hardware, but it remains a highly appealing handheld option.

Replay value is enormous. Alternative builds, hidden locations, optional bosses, different quest outcomes, multiplayer, numerous weapons and spells, multiple endings, and New Game Plus provide strong reasons to return. A second journey can feel surprisingly fresh when approached with a completely different character build, particularly because accumulated knowledge changes how intimidating previously difficult regions feel.

Ultimately, this is an extraordinary fusion of open-world exploration and challenging action RPG design. Its greatest accomplishment is not simply its size, but how consistently that size encourages curiosity. Discovering a hidden elevator, strange NPC, underground civilization, powerful weapon, optional boss, or entirely unexpected region creates a sense of adventure that few open worlds sustain so effectively. Repetition, cryptic quests, occasional camera problems, and uneven difficulty prevent perfection, but they are outweighed by tremendous combat depth, freedom, atmosphere, exploration, and replayability.

If you’re reading this wondering whether it’s worth it: just do it. Buy it. Play it. Lose sleep over it. Question your life choices later.

"Ash and Grace: A Tarnished’s Lament"


Borne from the Lands Between in shrouded fate,
A Tarnished rose, defiled, yet not too late.
With ghostly grace and Maiden's waning call,
He tread where proudest warriors dared to fall.

The Erdtree loomed, resplendent, cold, and high—
A silent god etched in the ashen sky.
Yet splendor rots where golden boughs once grew,
And thrones lie cracked, where Elden Lords once slew.

Through Limgrave's fields where spectral wolves do howl,
Past Stormveil’s gates, ‘neath Godrick’s stitched-on cowl,
He bled and battled, blade on tarnished blade,
In hopes the world could still, somehow, be made.

Liurnia wept in mist and broken lore,
A lake of lies, of glintstone, loss, and war.
With moonlight eyes, a Queen who lost her trust—
Yet from her ruin rose magic from the dust.

Caelid's red and festering decay,
Where stars fell silent, time had lost its way.
A cursed knight danced amid the crimson rain,
And met the Tarnished, not in hate, but pain.

Each Shardbearer, a soul in shattered pride,
The madness, rot, or hunger none could hide.
He felled them not for glory or for praise,
But for the promise of the Golden Blaze.

Yet trials cut much deeper than the sword,
And who dares seek to rule without discord?
The path to grace is soaked in blood and sin,
Each rune amassed a burden held within.

In Farum Azula, where the winds deny
The breath of gods, and dragons scorch the sky,
He faced Maliketh, the Beast of Death's own core,
And learned what law was buried in war.

With ash upon his cloak and soul grown old,

[h1]Elden Ring – 100% Completion Review[/h1]
[i]All achievements earned, every ending unlocked, every boss defeated, every dungeon cleared[/i]

[b]Elden Ring is not just the best open-world game FromSoftware has made. It is one of the most rewarding games to complete in its entirety.[/b]

You are the Tarnished, cast into the Lands Between to carve your fate through ash, rot, and ruin. The narrative is fragmented and obscure, but it invites obsession. Piecing together its world means reading item descriptions, following cryptic questlines, and dying in a hundred different meaningful ways.

[b]Combat is phenomenal.[/b]
Every weapon class feels handcrafted. Build diversity is staggering. Enemy design is grotesque and varied. Boss fights range from majestic to soul-crushing, and even the reused ones demand new strategies depending on context and terrain. A 100 percent run forces you into every corner of the map and reveals just how much care was put into the game’s non-linear structure.

[b]The open world is unmatched.[/b]
There are no map markers, no checklist fatigue. Discovery feels earned. Entire zones can be missed. Optional bosses are some of the best in the game. Questlines branch and collapse based on tiny decisions. Finishing it all means navigating a web of hidden consequences and irreversible choices.

There are flaws. Input buffering, late-game scaling, and a few too many Evergaols stand out, but none of them diminish the experience.

[hr]

[b]Elden Ring is a towering achievement in world design, combat, and player-driven storytelling.[/b]
Completion does not dull it. It sharpens it. This is a world that does not care if you miss something, which makes finding everything all the more powerful.

Depending on your build, you can curbstomp basically anything in the game, and I found it fun to try stuff out till I got the right build combo for the challenge and got through it. I appreciate the exploration aspect and the world looks cool, etc, but what made the whole thing click was when I realized I didn't have to stick a single build at all. The game even actually provides the respec items as well, so this is intended to some degree, but I just rather do what from's other game series does (AC) and rapid-prototype builds until I find something that makes the fights actually fun to fight. Granted, in AC you build your AC and loadout on a per-mission basis, which isn't how ER is meant to work.

It's a bit cumbersome, but I'll take that if it means I'm actually having fun with the game, which is all that matters at the end of the day.

finished base game, SotE and played a bit with Ng+, time for a review...
Not a big souls game expert, I'm trying to remediate that now by playing most of the classics, ER + dlc just happened to be my 1st title (at least full 3d one, I've already did Mandragora and No Rest for the wicked which kind of sparked my interest in the genre)
Let me start with the bad, and as You will quickly notice, it's mostly nitpicking:
- no item filter - for a game that kind of expects You to hoard items (especially weapons and talismans) an item filter would go a loooong way, of course after tens/hundreds of hours you kind of know the icons by heart..but still
- another QoL I would like to see and connected to the previous point is the lack of item sets - I wish I could bind a full set with a hotkey (it was so painful for me to juggle between talismans for different encounters, or quick slot items like pots etc - again no filter which meant every time I needed to scroll tens of icons to reequip something I was looking for) 
- tooltips/item descriptions - it actually took me a good amount of hours into the game to notice that some items do actually have bonuses (like stat helms and such) and the only way to find it is to read the descriptions (which again are kind of hidden...), I mean You already have the status effect for weapons mentioned separately so why not mention everything else also?
- talking with NPCs / quests - I understand that part of the appeal of Dark Souls and ER is the obscurity (previous point regarding the item description kind of proves it also) but it seems to be a bit much sometimes...exploring a grace locking You out of a quest or expecting to click the same npc couple of times to finish the dialog proper is a strange design choice, again not a big deal, but I quickly noticed that if I actually want to see everything I probably have to follow a guide so that I don't screw up my playthrough.

And that is about it, now the good...well I'm not sure what to write other than the game is a modern MASTERPIECE.
All the important bits (music, ambiance, game-play, world-building, dialogue, enemy design, versatility of builds, combat mechanics) it's all TOP TIER. 
The game holds You by the throat and doesn't let go until You commit and finish the next encounter and then the next and the next, until the end of the game.
I really found myself caring for the NPCs around me (and for obvious reasons..spoilers I guess...I was damn sad so many times).

It's worth every dollar, it's worth Your time, You have to try it even if You think You are a filthy casual and are scared of the difficulty (in my opinion heavily exaggerated, yes it has it's challenges but also multiple ways to approach a problem with the multiple tools You are given).

Overall:
Elden Ring is a triumph of the action RPG genre, delivering a challenging and rewarding experience that will stay with players long after they've put down the controller. I never expected a video game to fundamentally shift the way I see art, storytelling, or even myself. But Elden Ring did exactly that. It isn’t just a game. It’s an experience — one that challenged me, humbled me, and ultimately transformed me.

From the moment I first set foot in the Lands Between, I was completely immersed. The world is vast, hauntingly beautiful, and filled with secrets that beg to be discovered. Every crumbling ruin, every eerie dungeon, every horizon painted in gold — it all feels alive, almost sacred. Elden Ring doesn't hold your hand, and that’s exactly why it’s so powerful. It trusts the player. It dares you to explore, to fail, to learn, and to grow.

The combat is tight and deliberate, yet incredibly varied. I could approach situations however I wanted — with brute strength, precise spells, stealth, or even just running away and coming back stronger later. Every death felt fair, and every victory felt earned. There’s something deeply satisfying about conquering a seemingly impossible boss after hours of trial and error. It teaches perseverance. It teaches patience. And most of all, it teaches you to believe in yourself.

But what truly sets Elden Ring apart is its storytelling — subtle, fragmented, and profound. The lore, much of it hidden in item descriptions and environmental clues, weaves a dark, beautiful mythos that I still think about daily. George R.R. Martin's influence is unmistakable, but it’s FromSoftware’s enigmatic style that gives the story its soul. It’s not spoon-fed to you. You uncover it, piece by piece, and you become the author of your journey.

I’ve laughed, cursed, cried, and sat in stunned silence because of this game. It rekindled a sense of wonder I hadn’t felt since I was a kid — that feeling of true adventure, of stepping into the unknown and becoming something more than you were. It taught me that beauty often lies in struggle, and that the hardest paths often lead to the most rewarding destinations.

Elden Ring changed how I see games, but also how I approach challenges in life. It made me more resilient, more curious, and more grateful for art that dares to challenge the player instead of just entertaining them. It is, without a doubt, the greatest game ever made.

I’ve always been a completionist, and before even buying Elden Ring back in 2023, I had already looked up a 100% guide, even though it turned out to be a YouTube playlist. After a while, I realized I was just copying what the person in the video was doing, without really understanding what I was doing or why. It didn’t even cover everything properly, so I eventually dropped the game.

Almost a year later, I decided to give Elden Ring another chance, this time using a really well-made spreadsheet that organized everything in a way that made sense. Once I got the hang of the guide, I stopped feeling overwhelmed and finally started to fall in love with the world and the characters.

This time, I truly did 100% of everything + DLC: every boss, questline, and hidden area, and honestly there wasn’t a single part that I found boring or poorly designed. It was a completely enjoyable experience from start to finish, one of those games that once you finish it, you immediately wish you could feel that sense of discovery and accomplishment all over again. It was also my first real Souls-like, and thanks to the insane variety of possible builds, I was able to find a playstyle that really suited me. Something I noticed though, was that Elden Ring gave me a kind of anxiety while playing. Not in a bad way, but in that tense, heart-pounding way that keeps you fully immersed. I even avoided playing it late at night because it made it harder to relax afterwards. Strangely enough, that tension became part of what made the experience so memorable.

In the end, Elden Ring became one of my favorite games ever, and that’s coming from someone who never really cared about Souls-likes before. It’s nice to find a game that feels this complete, alive, and rewarding to explore, and give you the feeling to replay it again and again.

I'm not sure how I feel about the open world in this game. On the one hand, it is incredible how much there is to find, and how good it feels to explore. There are ruins and NPCs and little bits of lore and items to find everywhere, and it definitely feels like you're being rewarded for exploring. The visuals -- the vistas! -- were incredible. The view from the Lakeview grace looking into Liurnia, the first entry into Caelid, seeing the Erdtree for the first time; there's just so many awe-inspiring views in this game. Everything looks incredible, and each biome is beautifully crafted, with believable transitions. 

However, all that freedom comes at the price of purpose -- I had a lot of trouble understanding where I was supposed to go. Usually when this happens in a game, the difficulty of a given area will tell me, but this isn't just any game. It's a FromSoft game. Which means that a spike in difficulty can be because I've gone the wrong way, or simply because I need to get good. There's that guidance from the grace, but sometimes there's two that point in different directions, and even if there's only one, it might just lead you into a brick wall like [spoiler]Margit[/spoiler], when you're actually supposed to explore more. So I did explore more. And probably too much, because I overshot the average playtime quite a bit, and I was massively overleveled. Luckily I suck at the game, so it didn't trivialise the game for me, but I did do some areas way out of order, which led to some parts being incredibly hard and others pretty easy.

Also, the mini dungeons were cool initially, but they started to repeat a bit too much, and the lack of narrative cohesion and flow made them more administrative than exciting. It was nice to be able to find them, but all of them being so similar kind of sucked the joy out of it; I eventually stopped exploring them much, and just went for the main dungeons, which feel handcrafted (sometimes by a sadistic madman, but handcrafted nonetheless) and has that narrative cohesion and flow that makes it feel real and alive.

As for the combat and bosses, I really enjoyed it. The combat feels smooth and responsive, and I like the pace. My biggest complaint is the arbitrary waiting in the middle of attacks the bosses and enemies do to catch you out. I suppose it just takes some getting used to, but it was annoying. I much prefer the enemies that just attacks you straight with natural feeling movements, so I can intuitively dodge, rather than just rote learning the pattern and wait times. (However, I should say that learning to look for the actual attack definitely improved my ability to sightread the micro movements that gave away the incoming attack, which felt pretty cool.)

I beat most of the main bosses, and some of the major optional ones, and though beating [spoiler]Malenia[/spoiler] was certainly my highest achievement, my favourite encounter was [spoiler]Elemer of the Briar[/spoiler], whose armour I eventually donned. When I finally beat him, I got a Sekiro-esque feeling, where it felt like I actually understood his moveset and could sightread his attacks. Dodging and blocking and attacking at the right moments, like a dance. The feeling after beating him was maybe the best moment I had in this game.

So, while I think the open world loses a bit of the magic of the linear dungeons I've come to love, this is still an excellent game, and an excellent open world. It has all the combat and bosses I love from previous Soulsborne games, with an absolutely massive open world that is a delight to explore (for the most part).

I’ve been playing the soulsborne series for a long time and Elden Ring has satisfied most of my expectations.

What I’ve always loved about the soulsborne series is its ability to make me fear the unknown in all of my first playthroughs. By that I mean every area/place we explore we’re bound to see something scary, challenging, interesting or outright strange. Elden Ring takes that element up a notch by throwing us into a giant open world to explore with little direction. Everytime I explored the world I was constantly on high alert and forced to choose my fights carefully. On the topic of exploration, it’s very easy to miss certain areas, dungeons, bosses, NPC and weapons due to how vast the world of Elden Ring can be. I ended up missing a lot of NPC sidequests and a few optional bosses. 

The gameplay mechanics are mostly taken from Dark Souls 3, aside from the jumping mechanic which came from Sekiro. There’s a lot of new weapons, magic to choose from and many weapons from previous titles have also carried over too. The armour design in Elden Ring is probably my least favorite in the series. Some armour are too bulky, too slim or too specific to the point that mix matching aka fashion souls is kind of hard to pull off, so I just ended up wearing the same sets throughout the whole game. The soundtrack is alright. Some of the boss themes were good, most of them were kind of generic sounding epic boss music. For the most part it didn’t wow me as much, but the background music in certain parts of the game does a good job in setting the mood and making exploration or farming not as monotonous. 

Now, onto the biggest problem and probably the most controversial topic on Elden Ring, the difficulty. Elden Ring is definitely a punishingly tough game. This is most likely due to how overly aggressive and deceptive the enemies and bosses have become. Attack animations have unnatural delays or vague movements that make it difficult to determine an opening. Chain attacks are abundant and extremely long to the point where our stamina is drained and we are forced in a 50/50 situation at all times. AOE magic is spread wider than ever to the point where we just have to take the damage. And everyone is either as fast or faster than us. Combined, these elements create a punishing combat system to overcome with little room for error or forgiveness. At times, it made me wonder whether learning some of these fights was even worth the effort.

Overall, I would recommend any long time soulsborne fan to try Elden Ring. Just keep in mind that the combat is not the same as the previous title. For newcomers curious about the series, I suggest starting with Dark Souls III first. Jumping straight into the Elden Ring without prior experience could be a frustrating introduction.

Elden Ring is overall a good game, unfortunately it has both really good high-points with really bad low-points. The first half of the game is really well executed in my opinion, bosses are unique, difficult but fair and the overall game has a reasonable difficulty curve. The game gives you decent access to a variety of different ways of doing damage, whether you want fast and weak, slow and strong, range or melee, magic of different kinds etc. so there's something for everyone.

Unfortunately the latter half of the game can be quite the chore. Areas feel significantly more empty, both in terms of bosses, mini-dungeons and larger dungeons, as well as in random discoveries. The first half of the game is littered with these things so you can always find something interesting to explore, interact with or engage in combat. After a certain point however these things are mostly missing and areas become large mostly empty zones you run through simply to reach the next required boss-fight.

Quality of bosses also takes a nosedive in the second half of the game. For one particular boss (but there are multiple) this largely comes down fighting the camera. Bosses that are very large are not enjoyable to fight in this game, as you won't be able to see any/most of the enemies "tells" for what they are about to do (because you are so close when you attack that the enemy can't fit on the screen). This means you are left with a couple options, either become psychic to see the future, repeat the fight until you happen to get lucky or play very safe: run in after an attack get a single small hit in, then run super far away just in case they attack. The first option is rather impractical, the second is arguably not that fun and the third is tedious, leaving you with no fun way to finish the fight. I have yet to fight a rather large boss in this game were I'm not spending just as much time fighting the camera as I'm spending fighting the boss.

Another issue with boss quality later in the game is that their core moveset is just less fun in my opinion. More bosses move quickly whilst still hitting really hard, near all of them have WAY too many faints and have a ton of large AOE attacks where it isn't always obvious where you get hit. AOE attacks in particular make a lot of bosses irritating for me, as they serve as a way for the boss to force you to flee far away, which is fine, except they do this really often. In addition a lot of AOE damage is just unintuitive to dodge. Whilst hitboxes for most physical attacks in this game are done extremely well, some hitboxes like fire don't make it obvious where you'd get hurt.

Overall this leads to the latter half of the game feeling like quite the chore as I'm playing through, that was true in my first, and every subsequent playthrough.

One pet peeve I also would like to add: Please FromSoftware, just please stop trying to make this a platformer, you're very bad at making platformers. The movement in this game doesn't work well for platforming at all and the sections you put together are very poorly done, stick to what you're good at.

So why am I still recommending the game? Because the game looks great, runs fine even on older systems (I did most of my first ~70 hours playing on a mid-range PC from 2015), has beautiful environments and an amazing soundtrack. The combat is addicting, the freedom in playstyle and builds provide excellent replay value and there are a lot of really well designed boss-fights. The second half of the game can drag on and the quality is noticeably lower, but my overall experience of the whole game was without a doubt great.
