As my first game of the genre, it is memorable and I took my time, mostly exploring the gorgeous world.  I am glad to have used a guide for some parts and I did save scum endings (I'm a working adult ain't nobody got time for that) they were nice, albeit mostly short. 

I would recommend anyone who has the time to delve into the game and enjoy its mechanics play, regardless of the "git gud" sentiment. How one spends their free time is up to them because we all have free agency :) 

Despite how big the game is though, certain mechanics like madness spells are lore relevant and important, but fizzle out too quickly. The entire plotline and mechanics surrounding it are cool, and supposed to be powerful, but at the end of the day are not.  It's also frustrating to say that my favorite boss (Radahn) lore wise is INCREDIBLY powerful, but his boss fight is so weak. There is a disconnect because mechanics that are hyped up to be strong, yet fall short by miles. When you engage with the world and create expectations based on what characters are saying, only for them to be dashed it does take away from the game.

I will say the second half of the game is primarily a boss rush and that took away from the hundred+ hours of exploration, as I was just fighting the same boss on repeat. For the genre of the game, it makes sense, but I think it takes away from the overall experience. 

I spent many hours dying and running around looking at how in-depth the world and its zone were. From the empty fields of Limgrave, toxic pools of Caelid, ruined lakes of Liurnia, desolate volcano of Altus, shining brillance turned ashen capital Leyndell, supernatural underground zones, freezing storms of Snowfield, and crumbling ancient architecture of Farum Azula, there is character. So much character it feels awful getting into the second half of the game that has much smaller zones that feel like just large dungeons. 

In a world of happy endings, Elden Ring rarely has a quest end positively. It does help build the world as a dark and depressive environment, where people are forced to make the best with what little they have. My first quest ever involved a blind girl at a cart asking me to find her father in a castle and the result made me sad. The writing is there, but you can tell what George influenced. He has the capacity for a great fantasy setting, but likes to write some morally messed up story lines, especially with Marika/Radagon. 

The DLC will be played another day, but as someone who tried to do everything, it is a lot and was a great journey. My attacks had "oomph" and the possibilities to spec your build into something unholy is always an attractive option. Enjoy the freedom of the system and what the game has to offer yourself.

So I want to preface this by saying that the game is good. Though there are many flaws with it, it’s a good game. And to bring up something now, the build variety is definitely 100% the best part about the game in my opinion. You are somewhat limited, but you can stretch anything to fit the theme you want to go with for your build. The open world is pretty neat too. I personally don’t think it was fully flushed out, there’s still a lot of wasting your time to go off on a 3 hour errand for a better talisman, or armor set that fits your build. There’s also this point a little over halfway through the game where you just walk for 30 minutes with nothing to do. It’s very annoying because for the rest of the game, there was usually optional content once every 2 minutes or so, but here its so barren with nothing to do.

I think the main reason why people will dislike the game is because of the bosses, and that’s what I believe as well. If you want top-notch boss quality, play Dark Souls 3, Sekiro, or Lies of P. I personally think that those games absolutely sweep Elden Ring in terms of bosses. Elden Ring bosses usually fall into one of two categories. The first one is where bosses delay 80% of their attacks long enough for the sun to devour earth before they end up swinging, or you have the boss that snorted too much cocaine 5 minutes ago, and will not stop attacking for the life of them, and there’s very little in-between. If you do want to make this easier, then by all means use an overpowered build, or use spirit ashes. They both make the game a bit easier. Alternatively, if you don’t really care about how fun a boss is to fight, and really only care about whether or not the fight looks cool, then this game and Nightreign are right up your alley. Most of the major bosses in these 2 games focus on that aspect, and you’ll have a lot of fights with cool attacks and cinematic arenas. Overall, I genuinely believe the game is in a state of limbo, that will tip a certain way depending on what you would rather fight. honestly in my opinion, the biggest reason to get this game is to download the convergence mod (no i'm not kidding). it's just a better elden ring in almost every way possible, and is definitely worth trying out.

TLDR: ask yourself if you would have a ton of fun exploring the world and preparing your build. If you really don’t like bad bosses, then I would say skipping it wouldn’t be the worst idea. Alternatively if you like the cinematic bosses, then definitely pick the game up.

After 184 hours, I can confidently say Elden Ring is one of the best games I’ve ever played.

The world is absolutely massive and beautifully designed, and it constantly rewards curiosity. Every direction you go leads to something interesting — a hidden dungeon, a terrifying boss, a strange NPC quest, or a breathtaking view. Exploration actually feels meaningful, not just like empty space between objectives.

Combat is challenging but extremely satisfying. It pushes you to learn enemy patterns, experiment with builds, and improve as a player instead of just relying on better gear. There are so many playstyles (strength, dexterity, magic, faith, hybrids, etc.) that the game stays fresh even after dozens or hundreds of hours.

The atmosphere, music, enemy design, and lore are all top-tier. Even when the game is brutal, it never feels unfair — when you fail, you usually know why, and when you finally succeed, it feels incredible.

You should buy this game if you want:
• A huge open world that respects your freedom
• Deep, rewarding combat
• Tons of content and replay value
• A game that actually trusts the player and doesn’t hold your hand

If you enjoy exploration, challenge, and immersive worlds, Elden Ring is absolutely worth your time and money. Highly recommended.

My first soulslike. It was miserable for the first 5 hours, but became completely enthralling and addictive after I learned how the game works. How important vigor and upgrading weapons is, how I-frames work, what the game is trying to teach you with certain situations. After that, it became one of the most refreshing and engaging gaming experiences I've had in years. It's genuinely incomparable to anything else I've tried.

The euphoria that comes with besting a difficult foe is very, very visceral. There is also a great sense of terror & self-preservation with actual stakes on the line. It also feels like a breath of fresh air for a game to treat you like an adult.

Most people don't care about lore, neither did I for the most part, but after getting immersed and binging a few videos while farming, I have come to appreciate the game's themes alot more. As for the story you experience directly, the game does a great job putting you in the driver's seat of anything interesting. If something cool happens, you get to be there for it and see it. The characters are also quite well written and very well voice acted. It is very easy to get attached to the characters. I love Hewg & Roderika and I make an effort to kill Seluvis with my own hands whenever possible.

As for the price, if we go by the classic "1 euro = 1 hour of fun" metric, this game could easily cost 614 euros and be worth it to alot of people. However, in the real human world, the absolute maximum I would ever pay for any game of any kind would be 40 to 60 euros. And for that price, the game better be... Well, this. It's extremely replayable, I'm on my second campaign now trying one different playstyle with one different weapon out of dozens and hundreds, and I'm still discovering new things in the world I hadn't seen before.

Is this game and this style of game for everyone? No, definetly not. But you absolutely must try. And you must be willing to engage with it on it's terms. Because if it IS for you, it is fucking fantastic.

So I would start off this by saying I'm not a 'souls' player. I've never followed FromSoftware from the beginning and never played Bloodborne or Dark Souls and don't know if I intend to, so I'm one of the unlikely people to recommend this game for several reasons.


[h2] Graphics and Visual Design [/h2]

In similar vein to previous FromSoftware games, the world of Elden Ring has this really unique what I would describe as 'Super gothic' look. Grandiose cathedrals, castles, massive temples, all with this overt medieval and Christian/religious theme. It is really unique and absolutely beautifully done. What I was really surprised by was how successfully the world was designed so you can enjoy some truly incredible vistas and viewpoints from specific angles based on how you would arrive at a particular area. To control that movement flow in an open world game is not easy and I had some truly 'oh wow that is beautiful' moments in this game. The Lands Between is a unique and diverse place with danger lurking at every corner, but also the lands themselves tell a really vivid story. Initially I thought the tombstones everywhere were a bit morbid but I then realised it is all very deliberate to tell a story. The world of the Lands Between is a broken one, hence why it all feels quiet and dead, but also beautiful in a way one might experience walking through ancient ruins of a once great empire.

[h2] Gameplay and difficulty [/h2]

Ok this is probably where I will get some flack for my opinion. I think the combat 'can' get a little bit ridiculous, especially as a melee combatant. I think my main gripe that I have with the game is not that mobs and bosses hit hard and are very punishing - I've played games like that before and had fun. I don't think it's just about 'getting gud', but rather that there 2 totally different speeds and standards for bosses vs players. Bosses will be moving and hitting at warp speed while players will be limited by very visually cumbersome manoeuvres with animations that won't be able to be interrupted once started. This can make the gameplay quite frustrating at times as it forces a very careful and telegraphed gameplay to ensure you only attack during small windows of opportunity. There were times where I killed bosses during 40+ min fights where I had to dodge perfectly for 8-10 boss hits in a row just to get in maybe 1 quick attack before having to start the cycle again. That to me is not really fun and doesn't allow for a full use of mechanics and it encourages use of cheesy tactics. That being said, the game does give you a variety of ways to approach each boss through thousands of combinations of skills, speels, specs, weapons, builds, talismans, etc. I'm sure with enough research and patience, anyone can end up trivialising a boss by tailoring their approach to that particular boss fight. I would say that on the overall, once I hit a certain level, boss fights became more fun as I felt I had more tools at my disposal to balance out fights, rather than getting annihilated in 2 hits.

I think the combat is not really where the difficulty lies, but in honesty (and again maybe I'm just a filthy casual) but at times I found it frustrating just how little the game tells you about how to achieve things and the ridiculous expectation on players to just 'know' things. The amount of guides and googling I had to do to figure stuff out in this game - it made me wonder how long it would have taken me to figure out on my own. For instance,  (Light Spoilers) - There's 2 medallion halfs you must find before you are able to use a lift to access a certain area. Now I will acknowledge you can bypass the lift through a different path, but when I got to this point there was no indication where those two halfs would be. I happened to stumble upon one because it was in a fairly easy to access Fort but the other half I wouldn't have had a clue were it not for online guides. And that is the case for a lot of stuff in this game. There are truly important and indispensable objects in this game that are hidden somewhere that would be really tricky to find out as a new player on your own. So therefore, unless you enjoy extensive exploration over tens if not hundreds of hours, guides are probably your friend here.

[h2] Exploration and Story [/h2]

These two aspects were my favourite and what made Elden Ring a great game. I mean, when you get George RR Martin to help do the worldbuilding, chances are you will get a truly interesting story. Elden RIng has probably the most extensive, intricate, at times contradicting and yet fascinating stories and lore I have ever seen. Truly unique and complex, if not a bit confusing at times. There are very few cutscenes in this game, with most of the story told through item descriptions, small pieces of dialogues with a handful of NPCs, and through the visual design of the world. You are left to sort of piece together the story through reading items and exploration, which is done really well and gives a real sense of achievement when you get to the bottom of a story. Also, might seem contradictory with what I said earlier in terms of exploration being sometimes needed for really important items, but when it comes to the overall ability to stumble upon amazing places by accident, this game is no joke. I was able to just follow my curiosity and find amazing and incredibly detailed places that were always meant to be discovered in less than obvious ways, and I will always appreciate a game that has the courage to truly reward a sense of curiosity and attention to detail. It is not profitable or easy to justify to create game levels and entire areas that maybe 5% of players will experience, yet Elden Ring achieves that again and again and it truly makes you wonder what other secrets lie around the corner.

[h2] Final Thoughts [/h2]

With all that being said, I can totally see the hype, and it is justified. Elden Ring is a truly unique and beautiful game, crafted with love and attention to detail. It is probably one of the few games that really respects the player as an intelligent individual with agency and the game expects a lot from its players. but it also rewards them with a great experience in return. For those who are more casual I would say don't worry too much about boss difficulties. Yes, there were some that made me nearly smash my keyboard, but overall it was a net positive experience. My only wish is that they would just make it easier to find important items and locations in this game and that combat was a bit snappier and faster-paced, but otherwise a really solid game with some of the best world building and visual design out there.

MY SCORE: 9/10

An open world Dark Souls 3 with an insane amount of content. DS3 and Elden Ring go toe to toe, however the latter ups the level. The high production value is clearly visible. A masterpiece in its genre and an overall great game. 


+ Just like with the DS series, you're given plenty of tools and ways on how to get the job done
+ Amazing level design in terms of environment and exploration
+ Some locations like the castle area or the underground world feels like a DLC
+ Insane amount of weapons, gadgets and spells 
+ The game's content is vast. It packs so much content. It feels like Elden Ring is a combination of Dark Souls 1 to 3
+ A overall more "consumer friendly" storytelling where you can at least gripe some bits on what is going on and why you do what you do
+ The save points are better placed compared to DS3. A feedback FromSoftware took to heart. For instance, the so called grace, aka bonfires are placed in a fair and reasonable manner. Sometimes you are able to respawn close to a boss fight or event
+ Some great boss designs like "Godrick the Grafted" 
+ Plenty of challenging side and main bosses across the map. However there is a huge BUT as you'll see more below
+ The DLC is phenomenal and it almost feels like a game on its own
+ There are plenty of mods that elevates the game even more
+ It is challenging and it forces you to adapt and make you a better player
+ The world is insanely huge and you get more than what you pay for

Side note: Overall Boss designs and boss fights are generally better in DS3



The reason why I cannot give it a 10/10:

	- The UX/UI hasn't fundamentally changed. There is no significant improvement. There is always room for tweaks. I would've wished for a more "modern" UX/UI which involves better and faster handling of items and weapons. 

	- The same, if not minor degrading quality of available outfits similar to DS3. I did not see any improvements. There are just 2-3 knight outfits that I really like or find usable. I mean the game is built on the fact that you should CUSTOMIZE your character at the start of the game. But when it comes to dressing up your character, the choices are really bad. I don't see any improvements in that department either! 

	- Weird, grotesque helmets and the proportions are still bad. For instance if you use certain helmets, you end up with a deformed head. Usually long, thin and not in proportion to your body size/build. It looks stupid!!!! I just don't understand FromSoftware why they neglect this department?? I'm a designer myself and this really, really bugs me to the core. 

	- Many huge boss creatures perform the same obnoxious, circus-like jumps and acrobatics. Let's take a tiger or lion boss: 10x the size, massive, weighs maybe 3t but jumps like a circus master. Another massive creature and boss, has a ball like shape. Does a 90 degree angle jump, goes straight up and falls down. The same pattern to many other similar massive bosses. This 90 degree high jump with that weight, ok…. Annoying AF! 

	- Things are still a little bit obscure but less all over the place like in Dark Souls. While there is an incredible amount of content, the problem is that you can also get easily LOST. The game of course won't tell you much and obviously won't hold your hands. You're pretty much on your own. 

Having said that there's no overview of current and past objectives like for example in Assassins Creed and other games. It will not specify the current "mission"  or journey in the menu or map. 

	- The map and navigation system feel outdated. I especially mean the UX/UI on how to handle and place marks and waypoints on the maps . The navigation and map system is simply BAD. For example you can only set 5 waypoints. Exchanging and managing waypoints and markers is plainly horrendous. I want waypoint 2 to become no 4 instead etc. You got to delete all waypoints and create a new one.


Everything is said about the game already. It is a game that is fundamentally like an art of piece from its time, crafted with passion, Japanese creativity and precision.

For all souls like gamers - this game is a must!

Elden Ring is special. I feel like FromSoft has been building up to this game since the first release of Dark Souls, possibly longer. This game is extremely well made and stunning in every sense of the word. I can talk about how beautiful the world is, how amazing the story is, how fine tuned and gratifying the combat is, how much fun it is to explore but I know you have heard that all before.

As someone who has played DS1, DS3 and Bloodborne I am used to some of the basic knowledge of how these games work. It is tricky though, because this game falls victim to one of the sharpest learning curves out there. It is difficult to call this a negative because I feel that this is part of what makes this game so special. I am a firm believer that this game would not work in a world without the internet. I feel like the meta of searching how to do some niche thing and finding an entire community of passionate people enjoying the game is part of the experience itself. Talking with your friends who have played it and explaining different tactics, gear, secrets and more is part of the fun. This game is not friendly, and I am not referring to the fact that it is "hard", but that it intentionally does not guide the player in any way. Yes there is a tutorial but most of the games mechanics are not explained in any way and just left for the players to experiment and find themselves. I spent my first 30 hours in the game when it first came out not understanding how Ashes of War worked. Not until I picked the game up again and started over recently did I start to understand how the combat worked fully.

I think the best example of this is the story of Elden Ring itself. A player can play hundreds of hours of the game and not understand a single thing of what's going on. Not understanding what NPCs are talking about, not understanding the overarching plot, maybe they dont even understand who Michela is (the key character in the story). Not until I started watching lore videos did I start piecing everything together and start to appreciate the impact someone like George RR Martin had on the creation of this game. Everything is not there to serve you, it just is. I think this is kind of magical in a way, breathing a sense of life into the world, as if it has always been there and you are just a passerby of this breathing beautiful world.
This is how all of the mechanics in the game feel, from the exploration to the combat to the obtuse side quests. Its tricky because if it was executed in any other way I would say this is just bad design but I believe it is the intentional fun of it. They want you to research, they want you to learn. By the time you finish Elden Ring for the first time, if you start all over from a new save you will undoubtedly be a better player because you have taken the time to learn and understand how the game works, not just because your end game character is level 150+.

This game is not for the causal player, and I am not saying that to gatekeep, I am saying that because I don't think you will be able to enjoy Elden Ring in any casual way, you absolutely have to “lock in”. It's funny to see when people are in the middle of their first playthrough because I have seen it basically take over their consciousness, once it starts, it works its way into your brain and it's hard to not stop thinking about it. I know that happened to me.

If you are willing to give Elden Ring your time and energy, you will not regret it. It is absolutely fantastic.

This game was my first souls-like ever. It introduce a genre of games that I never would've thought to pick up. Now, over 300 hours later (and somehow convincing my wife to play it with me via Seamless Co-Op), it's safe to say that this was the best investment in a game I could've ever made.

If this is your first "Souls" game, Elden Ring is hard. But you know, so is life. It teaches you a valuable lesson without you ever having to get off your chair: it's not a matter of IF your reach your goals, it's WHEN and HOW. My first attempt at this game, it took me ~70 hours, and that's relying HEAVILY on the wiki for anything quest or location related. My second playthrough? 30 flat, and that still with exploration and taking things at my pace. My point is: it's a learning curve, and it's worth the struggle.

I then took it upon myself to beat every Dark Souls game to see the progression of how Elden Ring came to be, and dare I say after beating all of them, Elden Ring is truly FromSoft's greatest work. FromSoft took everything lacking in the DS franchise and completely put it on its head.

DO NOT SAY THIS GAME ISN'T FOR YOU. It is. It is for anyone who has any semblance of interest in fantasy/action/RPG. Just because you died 30 times and are bashing your head against the wall (I've been there a lot), it doesn't mean you're bad. It just means it wasn't time for you yet.

Не буду уподобляться игрожурам диванным, которые бы вычленили каждый аспект и оценили их отдельно по мнимой 10-балльной шкале или шаблону. Искусство судят в целости. Обзор представляет из себя хаотичный поток мыслей, посетивших автора на всех этапах игры. Это взгляд с перспективы человека, в чьей жизни Elden Ring не является первенцом из серии Souls. 
Игра удивительно хороша подкована технически. За всё время в ней я ни разу не сталкивался с вылетами или грубыми падениями кадров. Подловил себя на мысли, что ПК релиз, функционирующий настолько же безукоризненно как на эталонных консолях, сейчас уже как что-то из ряда вон выходящее. 
Японцам удалось нащупать баланс между плавной игрой и безумно красивой, местами гиперреалистичной картиной. Учитесь, янки!
При исследовании очередного сегмента карты, приходящейся лишь крупицей исполинских габаритов открытого мира, я думал: "А насколько большой и величественной архитектура тут ещё может быть?", наравне с мыслью "Насколько долго я могу просто бездействовать и созерцать?". Множество сюрреалистичных замков, крепостей, священных башен с величавыми мостами. Обожаю! Эта игра - как кладезь архитектурных изысканий, которые бы никогда не увидели жизни в нашем мире. В купе со своей дальностью прорисовки внушает тебе свой подлинный масштаб, свободный от игровых условностей. Столица Междуземья, Лейнделл - Город, обрамлённый золотом. Город Богов. Одним своим видом он заставляет тебя, сновидца, поверить в события, предшествовшие твоему появлению, как и в те, приведшие к его падению. Нарратив через левел-дизайн работает здесь на полную катушку. Elden Ring не ставит себе целью объяснить игроку все происходящее. Игра не использует кат-сцен, диалогов(за исключением немногих, которые ничего не объясняют), или рассеянных записей с информацией. Вместо этого она подогревает и дает пространство для воображения игрока, как сновидца. Все, что он видит, это последствия давно минувших событий, приведшие сказочное, некогда цветущее королевство в упадок. Big FAN. 
По боевой системе ничего не скажу. По степени интересности и разнообразия даже на пол пяди не Sekiro. Уникальность каждого из 10 предлагаемых классов - ложь. Как и раньше, ты или маг или воин. Какой в них смысл, если даже при своевременной прокачке я могу использовать любое оружие и в любой комбинации без ограничении? В этом плане игру очень легко сломать, я считаю. За счёт открытого мира и в теории безграничного потенциала для прокачки любой босс может превратиться в шутку(впопич привет). Как решение этому я не вижу и искусственное усложнение (игра без прокачки, игра со стартовым оружием, игра с одним заклинанием и т.д). Если игра сама по себе не может предложить достаточно испытании, а игроку приходится придумывать себе условия самостоятельно, то игра крайне безграмотно сбалансирована на фундаментальном уровне. В Dark souls у тебя было меньше шансов перекачаться и соответственно выпутываться приходилось на относительно равных условиях. Кривая сложности была круче. В Sekiro прокачка не давала тебе почти ничего. У тебя был меч, протез и набор инструментов на него. Вывозить оставалось лишь на мастерстве боя и комбинации подручных средств, и это было здорово. 
Пришло время для главных претензии: Чем этот мир начинен и как игра перерабатывает врагов, выставляя их за новых. 
За пределами ключевых областей, которые я возвеличивал ранее, совершенно нечего делать. Львиная доля карты - это пустышка, утыканная низкоуровневыми мобами и под копирку сделанными руинами с данжами. К середине игры всё исследование сводится к рутинному посещению 2-3 точек интереса области на коне и без намёка на энтузиазм. Изнутри все подземелья ничем не отличаются, для всего один алгоритм: найди рычаг, открой дверь, срази мини-босса. В конце получишь сундук-ловушку или предмет для крафта. ЗАЕБИСЬ.
Крафт - это новая фича-рудимент. Не знаю, зачем она в такой игре. Вспомнил однако фар край и 10-летнего себя на архипелаге. Очень сомнительное решение в итоге.
Переработка врагов. Нейроболван утверждает, что в базовой версии игры насчитывается суммарно [u]165–238[/u] основных и несюжетных боссов. Цифры впечатляют, но если вычесть рескины уже ранее побежденных, упомянутую сумму можно делить на 10. Получаем 20-30 совершенно не похожих друг на боссов. Все остальное - [u]раскраски[/u] для них. Вот и вся философия игры с её иллюзорной громадностью. Долго не мог смириться этим. Думаю, эта истина стала решающей в моей неприязни к ней. 
Отрицать колоссальность и влияние на индустрию Elden Ring однако нельзя. В тот год жанр обозначил свое место под солнцем и стал определяющим на поприще. Рекомендую ли я её? Скорее да, чем нет. Полюбить не смогу и фиолетово всем.

I have never properly played a Soulsborne game before and this is my entry into the series. I however do have some familiarity with other Soulslike games (Black Myth: Wukong, Silksong?) and have a FCG (fighting game) background. Please understand that my opinion comes from [b]my perspective as a hardcore gamer who has never played a FromSoft game.[/b]

First off, the negative: This game... is frustrating. Really frustrating. I understand to that players of the game love to make the argument that you can just make an OP build and explore and level up so that bosses get easier. While this works decently well in the early game, even without knowledge of how to make a build, in the later game, it is very difficult. Especially if you don't know what sort of armaments or talismans exist, didn't learn important mechanics in the early game when you were a bit information overloaded (as a new player to the series), or simply missed important things during exploration, with it so easy to forget or not know where there still is to explore. Nearing the end game, I found myself so frustrated with the final boss that I ended up searching up online on how to beat it [spoiler]-- getting in-game practice was tough since I had to beat Radagon every time beforehand to even get an attempt at Elden Beast with my melee only build. I eventually I searched up where to find Holy defense, good holy armor, etc., [/spoiler] As a gamer who likes to not rely on external learning outside of the game for singleplayer experiences, this felt like a huge defeat for me. The same happened with me missing the summoning bell. Since the final boss was the last part of my Elden Ring experience before writing this review, it did leave a bit of a bittersweet taste in my mouth. I did not feel a great sense of satisfaction for beating that final bit in the way that I did. 

With that out of the way, the good: Due to the fact that the bosses and enemies are so hard and how FromSoft designed the world, the world does feel more full and rich. You are just a tiny feeble speck in this massive world where castles and bridges and foes are consistently 5 to 10 times the size of the player. You often don't feel like an overpowered god and it brings a sense of overcoming hardship that ties in really well to a lot of the reasons we as players play games at all: A sense of achievement. Making your unique build (even if you don't really know what you are doing) is still fun as a new FromSoft player, and most bosses do make you feel amazing after you try again and again to eventually overcome, (whether through how you speced your build in its RPG mechanics, or just through learning boss patterns and punishes.) Seeing familiar concepts from fighting games (iframes, recovery, startup, active frames, hitbox analysis) is nice and some new ideas to me like stance and stance damage make for a really clean combat system.

Aside from praise, some small nitpicks:
[list]
	[*] A lot of the mine areas felt very same-y and didn't feel as fresh and give that amazing feel of exploration that the bigger castles/areas do. Going from mine to mine feels very bland and formulaic. Same with some of the minor bosses, which feel a bit cut and paste.
	[*]Due to how FromSoft tackled open-world level scaling, some areas you come across late in your playthrough sometimes are way too easy and lose that sense of wonder that you get when discovering an area roughly when you are supposed to for the first time.
[/list]
But with all my frustrations and nitpicks aside, my overall experience of playing the game was very good and I still think the feelings I had overcoming bosses and exploring the grand world more than makes up for it and this is definitely one of the better games of this gaming generation. Is it a masterpiece like they say? Idk, but it sure is a fun game to play.

If you are a new player to FromSoft games like I was and considering buying this game, I do NOT recommend it if:
[list]
	[*]You dislike games with very precise combat systems.
	[*]You aren't OK with some repetitive grinding of tech skill AND you aren't willing to seek help outside of the game.
[/list]
[b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
	[*]Beautiful art design, sound design, open-world level design, and overall well executed on most fronts
	[*]Rewarding RPG mechanics as well as rewarding Boss/ combat encounters
	[*]Quite content-rich
	[*]Unique and rewarding experience of overcoming hardship that is very hard to get from any other AAA developer.
[/list]
[b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
	[*]A lot of important systems are easy to miss or hard to learn without external help (wiki, youtube, a friend watching you play, etc.)
	[*]Chance of repetitive or poorly balanced "side" content
[/list]

First of all, the first gameplay experience is unmatched.
The world is insanely beautiful, the characters are memorable, and the voice acting is perfect. Every line feels heavy and meaningful. The dialogues hit hard...you can feel the weight behind them.

About the Difficulty :

The game’s difficulty depends entirely on how you choose to play.
Yes, skill matters...but even a noob like me can finish this game.

If you decide to fight bosses without summons or without some broken one-shot build, the game becomes hard as hell. You’re forced to rely purely on skill.
Summons, on the other hand, make the game much easier.

For me, Mimic Tear carried my entire playthrough, even against Malenia, and I was using a pretty random build to be honest.
For some reason, Mimic Tear didn’t help much in the Radagon fight...but Tiche absolutely did.

I personally don’t want to spend hours fighting a single boss. My first playthrough took 94 hours, and even with Mimic Tear helping me, it already took a long time. Without Mimic Tear, it would’ve taken me way more than that...there’s honestly no way I could’ve completed the game.
That said, there is one thing that genuinely made the game harder for me...and I’ll explain that in the “What I Hate” section.

What I Loved About the Game :

The beautiful environment goes without saying, but exploration is the real star of Elden Ring.

This is the only game where I explored this much. I’ve never explored any other game the way I explored this one...not even Red Dead Redemption 2 or The Witcher 3, where exploration is also a huge focus. Everywhere you go, something is waiting for you...a boss, a weapon, a Somber Smithing Stone, or even something you didn’t know you needed.

Even when I found items I wasn’t interested in, it still felt satisfying. Exploration never felt wasted.
Even after exploring for hours, I still feel like there are so many things left to discover.

Honestly, 60–70% of my playtime was just exploration, not boss fights ...and I loved every second of it.

One more thing I absolutely loved was weapons, especially my favorite one.. the Uchigatana with the Unsheathe skill.
I honestly can’t explain how satisfying that weapon feels. I used the Uchigatana for almost every boss in the game, right up until I found Rivers of Blood. The Unsheathe skill just hits different.

I know the Uchigatana isn’t really a late-game weapon...at least not with the skillset I have...but it’s still my favorite weapon in the game, no lie.

As for the story… I’ll be honest I barely understood anything except “Put these foolish ambitions to rest.”
I’ll definitely watch lore videos later. I’m just bad at grasping stories when the narration isn’t direct. But I’m sure it won’t disappoint.

Boss designs and movesets are also fantastic.

What I Hated About the Game :

This is purely my opinion nd you don’t have to agree.

The combat.
I don’t enjoy dodging 3–4 attacks just to land one hit or only to get interrupted or staggered while using a skill attack. Many weapons have amazing movesets, but the real question is ...can we actually use them effectively? I’m not so sure. Maybe skill issue from my side ..but srsly.

Another thing I hated was how the dodge  works.

Dodging doesn’t always respond instantly if you’re already attacking or stuck at the end of an animation and that often gets you hit.
My first Soulslike game was Black Myth Wukong, where dodging is instant. No matter what you’re doing...if you press dodge, you dodge.

That’s why combat in BMW feels so much better and more satisfying to me than in Elden Ring.

That’s exactly how I wanted Elden Ring’s dodge to feel.
If dodging worked like that, half the game would instantly feel easier. And that’s why BMW felt much easier to me compared to Elden Ring. If instant dodge were removed from BMW, it wouldn’t be any easier than Elden Ring at all.

This is honestly the only major thing I hated about the game.

Final Verdict :

Despite my complaints, I absolutely loved exploring this world, and overall, I enjoyed the game a lot.

I’ll still say it straight: Elden Ring is a 10/10.
You won’t regret buying this game and giving it a shot.

This was my first Souls experience, and interestingly, I held onto this game for almost a year after purchasing it before finally committing to the journey. Looking back, I’m glad I never gave up.

Elden Ring taught me more than just how to play a difficult game — it taught me to keep trying, learn from failure, and never give up.

[b]Pretty much every dragon boss is a copy and paste of the last with a different status effect.[/b] It really makes dragons feel like more of an inconvenience because you'll get good at fighting them by your second or third dragon boss. They should be way more threatening and keep you on your toes with mixed up movesets. Instead, they become old very quick. (this doesn't only apply to dragons, however they make for a great example)

[b]Elden Ring also has some of the worst implementations of duo bosses I've seen in the series.[/b] Duo bosses' attacks don't compliment eachother whatsoever, they're too independent to the point where it's like you're fighting two boss battles at the same time instead of a single 2v1 battle. The constant rushing of some bosses in this game really doesn't help either.

I'll use Valiant Gargoyles as an example:
One of their attacks is an AoE that does both instant damage and poison build up, which is fine. We've seen attacks like that hundreds of time before. Where the issue lies though is that you're sometimes put in a situation where this AoE attack is near unavoidable because the second Gargoyle wants to get up your backside CONSTANTLY, which leads you to being stuck in a poison AoE whilst also try dodge wild swings from another enemy. You're pretty much guranteed to take damage and you just have to take it. That's not a "git gud" moment, that's just poor boss design.

[b]Some boss strings are so quick they're almost impossible to dodge completely.[/b] This wouldn't be an issue if dodging the first attack of a string would give you an improved opportunity to evade the rest of said string, but with some bosses that isn't the case. The player's movement doesn't match the speed of some of the flurries thrown at you.

Luckily, this is a pretty uncommon occurrence and so it doesn't affect the majority of bosses, but it is still a very clear issue with balancing in this game...

[b]With all that being said, Elden Ring is still a very fun experience.[/b] Moving to an open world map offers for a lot more exploration and secrets that previous souls games. There's a whole bunch of NPCs to interact with and side quests to complete, which will keep you occupied for hours. There's a huge range of weapons and spells to find throughout your playthrough which really adds to the freedom of stylising your builds.

I do have other critiques and complaints about this game but it'll turn this into a much longer review than I'd like to make it.

And if you're someone who has already played Elden Ring and hasn't given the Dark Souls series a try yet, I highly recommend you give it a shot. It's a much more linear and more hardcore experience than Elden Ring but it makes beating it all the more satisfying.

[h2]Elden Ring is a great game, yet with glaring issues when you scratch the surface! Oh thee, lowly Tarnished...[/h2]

Elden Ring was my first Souls game, yet I've seen playthroughs of the Dark Souls games, so I was pretty aware of what to expect when I started playing. Struggle... struggle... and yet more struggle. My aim was to do a blind playthrough, but I quickly decided to check out some "non-spoiler" guides to actually enjoy the game. Overall I did have a great time, yet at times the game was insanely frustrating and unfair, which was to be expected. The game is wellmade, yet has some glaring issues...

[h3]Positives:[/h3]
1. The combat: Overall a great feeling when you manage to progress through parts of the game or killing a hard boss that you've been struggling on. There's a lot to learn and master, which improves your performance over time. Just get to grinding!
2. Builds: Anything and everything can work on any build, some things are obviously better (even broken) than others. You can choose yourself if you want to play with them and cheese bosses.
3. Difficulty "settings": Being able to play with OP builds/weapons, summons (spirit ashes) increased my enjoyment by a lot! I would've needed probably around 200-300 hrs to finish the game without them. Wiping on bosses for 100+ wipes is simply not enjoyable for me, but hey if you like that, go for it! "Unless you kill the boss on first try without summons and being full-naked with no weapons, then it's not a legit kill!", just touch grass lol!
4. Exploration & The Aesthetics: The Open World is simply amazing. I spent the first ten hours just exploring Limgrave (1st zone) and bonking around. It was great and I kept finding new secrets all the time. 

[h3]The negatives:[/h3]
1. Reused assets: There's simply *too much* in the game. Side content such as catacombs, mines, mobs etc are just copy+pasted in several locations. The first few "secrets" are hype to discover, but finding the roughly same layout of catacombs with the same boss after 50+ hrs is simply not fun. I think the game would've been better with a smaller and more compacted design (fewer unique bosses/zones), with a smaller map. 
2. Controls: The mount (Torrent) is amazing, but the [b]mount controls on PC are HORRIBLE![/b] I can't count the amount of times I've died due to the goat simply jumping off the map, even if my input was the opposite way... Not to mention the JP-path to the [b]Frenzied Flame in the severs... I spent like 30 mins and 20+ deaths trying to get down there, because my character randomly kept overshooting/moving on landing etc[/b]
3. "Punishing gameplay": The difficulty of the game is FINE and Souls games are supposed to be challenging and punishing. To a degree I would even say that they are supposed to "waste your time", until you "git gud". However... there are a lot of elements that are simply unfair. Many aspects (maps, bosses, mobs) are deliberatly designed to make you ragequit. I don't mind the challenge, but it should at least be a "even playing field", where you can learn.
4. The tryhard community: Holy... reading the input of parts of the Souls community makes me question my life choices. Can you just let people play the game THE WAY THEY WANT. If you want to play it as a "no-hit, naked, no ashes"-playthrough, then do so. Stop bothering people who use spirit ashes, summons etc. You can enjoy the game the way you want, and others are entitled to the same...

[h3]Overall a very solid game. Punishing & challenging, yet very enjoyable. Would strongly recommend, even though its apparant flaws![/h3]

I love it when multiple aspects of a game combine together to form a cohesive whole that exceeds the sum of its parts. Elden Ring, unfortunately, failed do that for me. And while I don't want to not recommend a game I had a lot of fun playing, there are just too many seemingly small irksome factors here that compound to produce a somewhat tedious experience for me where every time I'm about to enter a boss arena, I shudder at the thought of having to spend the next hour or two (or four) grinding that boss. Keep in mind that I'm no expert at this game, obviously; I've yet to beat R+EB & M (I'm sure everyone understands who I'm referring to). I simply did not have the heart to continue playing Elden Ring and this review serves as my closure so that I don't keep ruminating over it afterwards.

As I stated before, I have many "minor" gripes with this game.
[spoiler]
[h2]1. The Gear Upgrade System[/h2]
Let's start with an easy one. Elden Ring, is significantly more open than previous games. It has a bunch of cool weapons, spells, incantations and items to enable further exploration and every time I see a new exciting looking item, I want to try it out immediately and to this end, ER does have a re-spec system. But in classic FromSoft fashion, it is quite limited.

I can only re-spec my character if I have a larval tear in my inventory. So, every time I want to change my build after finding a new item or in response to a boss, I need to go take a massive detour and try to find larval tears on my own, or look up the wiki and go on a much smaller detour. You can guess my preference. Not only that, after the re-spec, I also need to upgrade my new shiny weapon/staff/seal so that it does not do terrible damage, which means, you guessed it, more massive detours (or wiki-powered smaller detours).

I just wish that ER had the following two QoL upgrades in order to incentivize exploration, if at least for the first playthrough (I know that during subsequent playthroughs, players either look up or cook up a build and beeline towards the items they want while ignoring everything else).
[list]
[*][b]Free re-specs[/b], similar to games like Divinity Original Sin 2.
[*][b]Smithing stone transfer[/b]: If I am to re-spec my character, chances are my previous fully upgraded weapon is now completely unusable anyway. So why not just let me transfer the +X upgrade to my new weapon. Of course, if I have two +25 (or +10) weapons and I want a +25 seal on top of that, I [i]have[/i] to farm, but exchanging one +25 weapon for another +25 weapon does not feel "unfair" to me at all. If I lose the ability/desire to use a certain weapon, having it rot in my inventory while I have to either find more stones or farm more runes to buy stones feels tedious.
[/list]
[h2]2. Enemies[/h2]
[h3]2.1. Design[/h3]
To me souls games live or die by their enemies. These games are not the most flashy/combo-driven and have relatively simple weapon movesets so most of the fun comes from fighting interesting enemies. But enemies in ER just have ridiculous physical form and movesets. Some of the most annoying enemies are either massive and have hitboxes that greatly exceed the dodge window or are so ridiculously fast that they attack non-stop and constantly hitstun. Allow me to list out some [b]large[/b] enemies that have what feels like a million health and also do a million damage.

And then some ridiculously fast/multi hit enemies like rats, the blob with a million arms that has a wild combo, Grafted Scions, black-knife assassins and the insect guys that shoot the 100 needles also fit this mold. And then, in classic Souls fashion, there are enemies that cast insta-kill clouds.
[h3]Placement and Scaling[/h3]
Outside of some enemies being inherently annoying, their placement and scaling, especially in late game areas, feels to me as if I'm supposed to avoid them altogether. In the mountaintops, the only enemies I found were giant crows, giant t-rex dogs, giant hands, rune bears and so forth. Catacombs now have the giant stone dogs as normal enemies. The Zamur heros are also just normal enemies now. The haligtree branches also has those massive trumpet bubble guys. Not to mention the giant ants in Ainsel that do a ton of damage.

On top of this ridiculous placement, the damage they deal is also outrageous. One strike from any of these enemies does like 50-75% of my health bar at 50 vigor. Some kill in one hit or one hitstun combo. Fighting one such enemy takes like 2-3 charges of my flask on a good day which quickly gets tedious.
[h2]3. Bosses and Rhythm[/h2]
ER has good bosses, outside of the obviously annoying ones. But I can't help but notice that every boss has an unstoppable flurry of 5-7 piece combos paired with a highly off putting rhythm. ER almost feels like a turn based game to me where the boss does a 7 hit combo while I dodge, then I get like two seconds to counter-attack wherein if I am not in the exact place to strike back, I lose that opportunity. Even staggered bosses require stamina to reposte, so while I stand around recharging my stamina for one second, the boss has already recovered.

The rhythm of the fight also just seems to demand rote memorization. I can't seem to extrapolate the rhythm or tempo of the whole fight by sampling a handful of random moves in my first few attempts. I just feel like every move is uniquely timed to catch rolls and dish out maximum punishment. Unless I can just out damage the boss, and there are builds capable of doing that, I just feel like I have to experience every single move first hand over the course of 2-3 hours before I can finally make any progress. This has been a real bummer for me, especially in the case of Rhadann (Starscourge), Maliketh, Godfrey, Malenia and Mogh (sewer and palace). The attacks these bosses do seems almost randomized where sometimes the exact same combo ends after 3 hits and other times is immediately followed up by another combo basically obliterating my punish window, punishing me instead for daring to attack after what felt like (and was in 60% of the cases) the final hit of the combo. After this happens a couple times, I am just afraid to go in again, what if there are more follow up hits? After like 20 attempts of failing to make heads or tails of the fight and making zero, I am forced watch a YouTube guide breaking down every single move and possible follow up which I then internalize and beat the boss in the next 5 attempts. This does not feel fun to me, it feels like I'm learning an instrument that I can't even play a song in.

Just for illustration, the rhythm of these fights feels something like this:

one . . . two . . . . . . . . three FOUR . . five

orr, maybe like this:

. . . . one TWO THREE . . four . . . . . . five

or perhaps:

. . one TWO . . . . three FOUR

or most likely, all of the above in a single fight, where every single move has a distinct rhythm and the rhythm of one chain of combos simply does not apply to another. I could go on but I am literally hitting the character limit.
[/spoiler]
[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
I really want to like ER. Heck, if I persisted, I could probably beat both M and R+EB in due time but I just couldn't bring myself plough on; it does not feel rewarding for me to do so. This is also, in part, because the DLC seems to exaggerate the exact same things that I've disliked about the base game. Maybe I can come back to it in 6 months and enjoy it again in the way I have enjoyed the earlier parts of ER but for the time being I feel like I'm done.

My journey with soulslikes started right here with Elden Ring. The world is masterfully crafted brutal, harsh, mysterious, and filled with stunning locations. Unlike many other titles, this game doesnt treat the player like an idiot. The obscure side quests add a lot of flavor, theres zero chance you wont miss something during your first playthrough. The combat system is excellent, with beautiful animations and spectacular effects for spells and incantations. While the difficulty especially the overused delayed attacks can be off putting at first, the game becomes even more enjoyable once you master the mechanics. As an RPG fan, the open world really spoke to me, though I understand its not for everyone. Personally I think it gives the game much higher replayability than the linear Dark Souls titles, as every new run can feel completely different.

Now, what you really need to look out for is the lack of a save anywhere feature... just kidding! Honestly, one of the main issues is those previously mentioned delayed attacks practically every single enemy has them! Another downside is the heavy boss recycling. I would also point out that the rewards for clearing catacombs are often unsatisfying, usually just being spirit summons. And finally, optimization issues? Im not sure what to call it exactly, but there are micro stutters that can ruin a fight. I dont think its a hardware issue, even after upgrading from an RTX 2060 to a 5060 Ti 16GB and from an i5-10400F to an i7-11700K, absolutely nothing changed in that regard. Interestingly, these stutters dont occur at all on a handheld like the Lenovo Legion Go.

Overall, I highly recommend it, a game easily worth hundreds of hours. Definitely in my top 10.

When I first played Elden Ring, I thought it was great, but not necessarily one of my favorite games. A big part of that is that I have a ton of respect for the world design of the original Dark Souls, and I feel like Elden Ring's Open World can lose a lot of the marvelously layered world design that makes Dark Souls legendarily fun to explore. The fact of the matter is that this is partially the case, but it is part of what makes Elden Ring legendary. 

Elden Ring is one of the greatest Dungeon Crawlers of all time. Most people do not think of it as one, but it is. Sure, the open world is gorgeous and well-designed, but I actually find its endless vaults and tombs to be marvelously compelling. The better designed "Legacy Dungeons" are obviously great, but this game is a fantastically fun one to play through when you delve below the earth to see what's hidden in the old and forgotten places. I imagine that it's only better with some sort of randomizer and I cannot wait for the days when I've forgotten enough about Elden Ring to by surprised by it once again.

From the creators of Bloodyborne and Dark Souls, you essentially get a glorified dating sim that is confusedly also an open world RPG. The areas are vast and beautiful yet the main attractions remain the women in this game. You have Ranni the Witch. I don't need to tell you how popular she is. Let's just say 4373 is a large number for people dedicating "art posts" to her. Then you have Melina, your first maiden. That childhood friend/neighbor girl character who has been helping you along the way throughout out your quests and just waiting for you to notice her. Soft spoken yet meaningful in her words and easy on the eyes. Just don't show her the three fingers, she's not into that...Then you have Fia. The deathbed companion. The character you go to after dying to the boss over and over again. Why? Because if you can't feel the warmth of a woman's body in real life, might as well pretend to feel it in a triple AAA game from Miyazaki. And to maintain realism, whenever you hug her you get debuffed, just like how it feels to hug women in real life; it doesn't last long, its lackluster, and you keep coming back for more while losing your grip on reality. Then you have Hyetta. She's the gal with an appetite. Feed her some grapes and she'll be over the moon. Feed her enough, and she will show you her three fingers (pun intended). You also have the amazon goddess of snoo snoo herself, Nepheli...the one with daddy issues. I know Gideon said he "adopted her" but...cmon. The guy who is all knowing wouldn't know how to court a barbarian women? Really?. That aside, the cutest one...the tsundere that sets your heart on fire...Dung Eater-chan. I swear...his eyes are as brown as the left over basketball sized chocolate mud babies I leave in my toilet after a hearty Taco Bell breakfast. A character of rigour and personality. 

The characters are as diverse as the regions you play in. The weapons are unique and all usable up to end game. The only regret I have with this game is not being able to continually fight bosses like you could in Sekiro for example. That was a huge missed opportunity. 

TLDR: You either get frame Moghed or you mew hard enough to be Elden Lord. In essence, a game I will never put down and the true successor to Dark Souls.

Definitely my favorite game of all time. First I'm going to talk a little about the lore because it's probably my favorite part of the game. The lore is extremely deep and well-hidden, but not so well-hidden that it's almost impossible to make reasonable guesses on past events (looking at you, Dark Souls II). The lore community is still very active and come up with new hypothesis all the time.

      The combat is very good, and spells can often mesh well with your regular weapons. The main bosses are all really great, and PvP is fun (especially at lower levels). There are lots of unique consumable & throwable weapons and buffs, lots and lots of decently unique spells (although there is one particular group of spells that are just slight variations of the same thing). There are a huge number of weapons, and special "ashes of war" you can attach to them which give an extra special attack on top of their existing moveset (even bows and magic staves can have them).

      The exploration is also pretty good. The game does tell you where to go to an extent, but there are no minimaps, or giant markers on your screen, or even on-screen instructions, only what NPCs tell you in the game, so you get to make all of the decisions on where to go instead of the game directing you around. Exploration is driven by "I wonder what that thing over there is". 
      It is a large game, but the game does a decent job at hiding exactly how big it is on your first playthrough, so it shouldn't feel too terribly daunting at first. There are also lots of little minor locations, caves, and dungeons for you to do. They can be a repetitive, but they contain lots of useful loot, and the puzzles tend to get harder & dungeons get longer as you get further into the game. The game is also absolutely beautiful; everything looks like a painting. In my opinion, even better than Dark Souls III environments, which are also incredibly beautiful.

      The DLC is very very excellent, even better than the base-game in my opinion. It feels completely packed compared to the base game, and the bosses are generally very good, challenging, and rewarding. The dungeons are much more unique, even with unique bosses you can't fight anywhere else, unlike the base game dungeons. Also the weapons and spells are all really cool and fascinating, and every single location is just so beautiful and unique. It's crazy!!!

      At full price, this game is worth it.

[h3]A generational game, but not without flaws[/h3]

To preface this review: my only experience with any souls-like was 'The First Berserker: Khazan', and I never finished it.
Actually, I almost never finished Elden Ring either. A few hours in, and I was ready to quit, but the sheer number of players glazing this game was bugging me. "What do they see, that i dont?''
I couldn't tell you exactly when I found my answer; it was more of a gradual experience. But I do now understand, even if I don't fully agree.

The [b][i]world[/i][/b] that's built here is amazing. The ambience and overall vibes made me feel like this was a living, breathing realm full of despair and danger. Even without many cut scenes, I could still grasp the severity and gravity of the events that had taken place. (even if most of the time i had no idea what was happening in the story)

The [b][i]combat[/i][/b], while at times was a little frustrating, is still one of its best features. The build diversity and scope are something special that I can't really find a comparison to in anything else I've played before it. 
The bosses, too, were imaginative and challenging, and more than a few times I found myself jumping out of my seat and slamming my desk in excitement after I defeated them.

There's more I could praise, but I won't, because so many reviews have already done that. So instead ill bring up a few of the [b][i]negatives[/i][/b] that i dont see mentioned very often.
The target locking in this game is dreadful. I swear I died more times to this than actual bosses. It's mostly fine when you have a single enemy to deal with, but as soon as there are multiple targets, it fails miserably.
The other massive flaw I feel this game has is with its in-game systems/mechanics. I can't think of a single game I've ever played that required me to tab out and Google as many times as this. It really was ridiculous. There is just so much that isn't explained or explained well, and most players will miss out on a lot of content or waste a lot of time without Alt-tabbing and turning to guides. 

Overall though, I'm happy I put the time in and finished it. It was a great adventure.

The world is massive, beautiful, and full of secrets that make exploration genuinely rewarding. Every time I thought I had seen everything, I found another hidden cave, underground city, or boss waiting to humble me in ways I didn't think were possible.

Despite its difficulty, the game never feels unfair. It challenges you to adapt, improve, and occasionally question your sanity. And when you finally defeat that boss you've been stuck on for hours, the feeling is unmatched.

This game has replaced OOT and DAO as my all time favorite RPG. What an epic game, no price scumming, brilliant level design, intelligently designed puzzles, and insanely awesome bosses. The combat has a steep learning curve, it took me hours to kill the first proper boss and I nearly uninstalled. After 84 hours I ran Miyazaki's gauntlet and became Lord of the Frenzied Flame. (no summons or magic for people who care)

Audio, and world building are the best I've ever seen in a game.

There are some downsides though: no real MKB support, roll on button release none negotiable is insane, lock on for as necessary as it is can be awful, shockwaves linger really long and have strange hitboxes, and some of the bosses scope is too ambitious and the fights are just weird. Verticality with the enemies move sets is generally a problem with them missing when they really shouldn't and there's a fair amount of flying enemies and uneven boss arenas. Also some of the quests are legit impossible to figure out without a wiki which is a shame because many are cryptic but you can figure them out on your own and it's really rewarding when you do.

Overall though this game is a masterpiece, I can't imagine the herculean effort it took to make this game. Watching the credits roll seeing all the people who worked on this, the coordination it must've taken to get this all to come together is awe inspiring. Truly the best modern game, I wouldn't be surprised if this is the best game to come out in my lifetime.

One of the best games I've ever played.

Elden Ring gave me a sense of exploration and adventure that very few games have managed to achieve. The world is massive, beautiful, and full of secrets. Almost every time I thought I had seen everything, I discovered another hidden area, boss, or questline. The freedom to build your character however you want is fantastic, and the boss fights are some of the most memorable I've experienced in gaming.

The amount of content is incredible. Even after finishing the game and earning all achievements, I was still finding new locations and optional bosses. The atmosphere, music, art direction, and lore are outstanding.

That said, I do have a few criticisms. One issue I really disliked was how certain interactions temporarily lock the player's actions. For example, when picking up an item or interacting with doors, the game can prevent you from attacking or reacting, which can feel unfair in dangerous situations.

Another problem is the repeated use of bosses. While the game has many amazing encounters, seeing the same bosses reused multiple times becomes noticeable and somewhat disappointing, especially in the late game.

Some questlines are also extremely obscure and can be very difficult to complete without using external guides.

Despite these issues, Elden Ring is still an exceptional experience and easily one of the greatest games ever made. It's a game that I will remember for a very long time.

What can I say about Elden Ring?! It is perfect in every single aspect, from the vastness and beauty of the open world down to the smallest detail hidden in a minor dungeon.
Even Vincent Van Gogh would have been amazed by the starry sky of the Siofra River, the Eternal City of Nokron, and Nokstella. The art direction is majestic; Leonardo da Vinci himself would be intimidated by the architecture, from the most basic houses to Stormveil Castle, Raya Lucaria Academy, all the way to Maliketh’s arena.
​It’s a game that will leave you breathless instantly and every single time; it will be one of the best memories you’ll ever have. It is a title that teaches PATIENCE, DISCIPLINE, PERSEVERANCE , and ADAPTABILITY.
​The lore is beautiful, incredibly vast, unlike any other game known to date. There are, however, some minor issues: the game demands a very high level of attention, and you will often need internet guides. It’s an experience packed with content, but the direct storytelling is weak and unclear; a lot of times you don’t immediately understand what is happening, and you will definitely need to watch an explainer video about the story. Once you do understand it, though, you’ll realize the game feels like it was created by aliens.
​It would have been great if there were more cutscenes, more NPC encounters, and much more explicit storytelling, maybe even with a voiced protagonist. On the other hand, Elden Ring is also praised for its silence and that calm that makes you feel completely alone in this gigantic world. The lore has very few plot holes, which doesn’t hurt the experience simply because the narrative is so multi-layered.
​You will definitely need video guides during your days in The Lands Between. Many things are hidden from a casual player, and progressing through certain quests is complicated, something that unfortunately broke my immersion a bit, since I had absolutely no idea what to do.
​To make up for it, though, the enemies designs are truly unique and fantastic  down to the most useless enemy in a dungeon.
Every boss is special, with different patterns and attacks, and the variety of builds is insane. You can go from a build with a sword and knight armor to being a naked man with a jar on his head for a helmet and a medieval cannon as a weapon. The item variety is incredible, and I don't know if another game will ever reach these levels.
​What else is there to say? The game is immense, the music is majestic, and it would be impossible to write a review that does it complete justice. It’s not for everyone due to its difficulty, but it’s completely worth it... even if by the end you probably won't have a desk anymore (luckily, mine is still intact). Getting the Platinum trophy for Elden Ring and achieving the goal of becoming Elden Lord is worth every single ounce of effort, and it's something you will never forget. An absolute, insane satisfaction.
​This game is, and always will be, SOLEMN!.

Mine dignity? Forfeit.
Mine productivity? Cast into the abyss.

"WHERE THE F*** DOTH I GO NEXT?"

I began this game as a warrior seeking glory, and ended as some deranged medieval accountant calculating how many times a spherical rock must commit suicide before I can afford a slightly better sword, whilst consulting YouTube sages to determine whether I have accidentally doomed an NPC's entire bloodline by opening the wrong door.

I've been deciding whether or not I should even write a review for this game. I am going to note that this is my absolute favorite game of all time. It's beautifully handcrafted to perfection. This review includes both the DLC and the base game.

As I said, Elden Ring is my favorite video game of all time. I love the contrast between the base game and the DLC, you have this luscious, full of life and spark walking through what feels to be a fairytale, yes at times it's really bleak, yes the lore of the characters are depressing as hell once you research and really take your time to get into it (which I highly recommend, George R.R Martin did the best job with storytelling I have ever seen). Miyazaki had put his all into this one game from everything that he had learned making soulsborne for the previous ten or so years. The story is top notch, the graphics are wonderful, walking into Limgrave for the first time and seeing the Erdtree glowing on top of you with the wildlife around you. Ugh it's just so beautiful but morbid at the same time, I wish I could see that for the first time again. I could just get lost in all of the side content because the characters that you meet as you explore and connect with really makes you feel a connection to them that you can't help but want to complete their questline. I have never played a game that I have ever felt that it wasn't made by humans except this one, that might seem weird first glance but everything in this game feels really cathartic once you get the hang of it. Figuring out your build, figuring out what your favorite affinities are, you have such a wide variety of options. Bleed and holy are my favorites. 

The DLC on the other hand.. It's bleak, it's really dark. It feels like you're just a wanderer in the middle of nowhere roaming around in a world that wants nothing else for you to be dead. The scadutree fragments are really cool but I felt a bit more connected to the base game personally. I'm not saying the DLC is bad whatsoever, it absolutely feels much more rewarding once you beat literally any boss in it. The difficulty ramped up 10x which I don't mind at all, I found myself out of my house thinking about the different builds I could use for a certain boss, the weapons, and the ashes of war that would help me all the way through it. It's awesome. Elden Ring is a masterpiece. Please play it

This game is MASSIVE! Every time I thought there couldn't possibly be more, the game showed me how horribly wrong I really was. It's also very difficult. Fortunately, there's so much to do, that you can easily get lost, increase your level, and come back and find the fights to be much easier. There are tons of well hidden secrets to discover. The massive amount of weapons and armor allow for a ridiculous number of playstyles. If you don't like hand-holding in video games, you won't find it here.

Cooincidentally, as this is my first experience with a FromSoft game, my biggest gripe about the game is that they REALLY leaned into the no hand holding. There is no quest log, you lose your runes (currency/experience points) when you die, which I'm really not a fan of. There are secrets hidden in places I imagine most people never found or if they did, found by complete accident as the hints they do give are vague at best. The DLC, if you bought it, can be missed. If you don't find the skippable boss you have to beat in order to access the DLC, you just can't play it. 

All of the irritable stuff aside, the sheer scale of the game allows for a playtime that makes it well worth the money spent if you enjoy overcoming the challenges. The community has made plenty of guides as well, so if you want the full experience but don't want to spend a year figuring it all out, they've got you covered. A lot of the quality of life issues can be overcome with mods as well if you're comfortable with that. As as someone who was intimidated by these games since they first became popular, I'm happy to have given it a try, as it's now one of my favorite games of all time.

Pros: Great combat, great exploration, awesome side quests, great music, great characters

Cons: Multiple enemy bosses, immunity bosses, and rough endgame moments

Overall: I never really liked Souls games because they seemed way too hard and confusing. As it turns out, they are only confusing if you are new to the franchise. I tried this game on and off for years, quitting each time because I just didn't get it. I finally took the time to research how all of the game's systems worked. Once I did that and picked a build that sounded fun, it was smooth sailing. To be fair, I did use a guide for the whole playthrough. I have a job, and FromSoft doesn't like to explain anything, so a guide just made my experience much better. While playing this, I had so much fun that I revisited all of the other FromSoft games, and Elden Ring is for sure their best game. The exploration is fun and rewarding, the combat is unforgiving but fair (sometimes), and the satisfaction from beating a difficult boss or area is unmatched. I wouldn't recommend this as your first FromSoft game, but if you have some experience, there is no better title. However, I did find myself hating a couple of things, which soured my time a little. Multiple-enemy bosses such as the Valiant Gargoyles pissed me off to no end. It feels like the developers couldn't come up with a new, interesting boss, so they just copied and pasted an existing one. The difficulty of these fights felt more unfair than anything else in the game. Bosses having total immunities to certain status effects also felt very bad. I used a bleed build, so several bosses (including the final one) were completely immune to the setup I had been using for 60 hours. It feels stupid for a build to be horribly crippled; a status reduction is fine, but total immunity is bullshit. Lastly, the exploration basically dies at the Mountaintops of the Giants. That area is so miserable to "explore" that the discovery aspect of the game essentially ends there—the exception being the Consecrated Snowfield, which mostly just acted as a way to finish upgrading my weapon and get to Malenia. Even with those flaws, I really enjoyed my time and see why many people call this game a masterpiece.

Grade: S
