 Kinda hard to really properly judge a game like Elden Ring. Not only was it continuation of a somewhat niche genre created by FromSoftware but it's evolution from the Dark Souls series to this game was so spectacular that said fact alone is probably enough to give it a positive review.

 But that would not suffice so let's continue.

 For anybody that has played any of the Dark Souls games this game will feel quite familiar and yet it's scale makes any of the previous games feel almost tiny.
 The open world is huge and for anybody planning on exploring all of it best to say goodbye to at least 50 hours purely on that alone.
 And for fans of the previous games the legacy dungeons will be the much needed breath of familiarity. Almost maze like level layout for many of them, often equipped with dangerous traps or falls and even more dangerous bosses in their final rooms.

 The combat feels very similar to Dark Souls 3, almost to the point that anybody who has played and liked that game has a duty to play this one.
 There have been some important changes to said combat though. For one we now have a dedicated jump button and the ability to use said at will jump to chain into a jump attack.
 That jump attack is how one now deals with enemies hiding behind shields, among many other methods. And it is also now heavily used for level traversals.

 Equipment deterioration has been eliminated from the game. So no more durability stat on weapons and the like.

 The open world features a mount for you to use for rapid movement and said mount also allows attacks while mounted. For some enemies or bosses in the open world this new combat method makes the encounter a joke BUT be warned that taking enough damage to your mount will despawn it and kick you to the ground at which point you will be extremely vulnerable. Taking damage then is probably at the same level as getting a backstab or maybe even worse, don't know exactly since it only happened to me maybe once.

 With such a huge game comes also a huge variety of weapons, spells and armours. Might actually be a bit too much now that I'm trying to remember most of them. But aside from the annoyance of getting loot that is not well suited to your build I do not see much of an issue with the sheer numbers of tools you have at your disposals for combat.

 And speaking about tools for combat this is probably a good spot to mention one of the other additions to the game that did not exist in any of the souls games, spirit ashes.
 Very early one you can get a item that lets you summon the spirit of fallen soldiers or heroes. This is a separate mechanic to the normal summon mechanic from the Souls series.
 Summoning in the old games was used primarily for coop and sometimes summoning NPCs for certain bosses and with certain conditions met. Said summoning feature always had the drawback of increasing the health bar of the boss for which you summoned help.
 Spirit ashes do NOT have that penalty, which means that for all intents and purpose using it is almost as pressing a button to lower the difficulty.
 Now I am not saying that people should not use it or that those who do are somehow lesser at the game, especially since I like to use them a lot as well, but I cannot deny that for some bosses using spirit ashes basically trivialises the fight.
 If you are a experienced souls player then using them in very early fights is probably the best example of how jarring the difference of difficulty exists in the usage or not of just 1 item in the entire game.
 And saying that I will also mention that some of the boss fights in the middle of the game and later seem rather purposely designed for you using the spirit ashes. 
Or in other words: They usually feature a very tough duo of bosses that leave you so little room for mistakes that you will almost certainly use the spirit ashes or even just summon other players.
 Oh and on a final note regarding these spirit ashes.
 One of them is a mimic of the player and is in 99% of cases the best one to summon. Especially if you are using a melee tanky build.


 Anyways the only other major change related to the combat is probably how PVP is handled in ER compared to the previous games.
 In the older games using semi-rare consumables that allow you to summon other players, and also usually increase you maximum health, would also flag you for possible invasions from other players.
 In ER this has changed so much so that "non-consensual" PVP is not really a thing anymore, or well at least not as much as previously.
 Now you can only be invaded if you:
 1. Summon other players for COOP or
 2. Equip a very specific item

 So if you are playing solo you will NEVER be invaded by other players. Any invasions while playing solo are scripted NPC invasions.

 To be honest I am not quite sure how to feel about this change, on the one hand being invaded in the previous games could get annoying but it also help make the games feel alive and could break any monotony setting in.
 And for people looking forward to PVP this change also made the experience of invading somebody a very different experience than before.
 
 Previously chances were good that you would invade a solo player just going through the game. NOW you know that when you will finally hit a host for invading your are either outnumbered from the start or facing a player that is intentionally allowing PVP so is most likely experienced and ready for the fight.

 
 Moving on from combat, the world is just a work of art and a joy to experience for the first time. Jumping freely at will and the new mount also make the exploration more enjoyable then before.
 What might not be as enjoyable for some is the new crafting system.
 
 If you ever got tired of going back to NPCs for arrows or other consumables then you might actually like this system that allows you to craft almost any kind of consumable outside of combat.
 Personally I kind of like it since going to merchants for arrows was always a hassle to me but this new change did mean that I now had to pay attention to weeds, flowers and the like to be sure have a sizable supply of materials.
 The crafting system also meant that a lot of drops and loot found through out the world is just crafting materials. And let me tell you there are few moments more disappointing than fighting a bunch of hard enemies to get to a chest only to find a damned flower inside it.

 Regarding the story and everything associated with it. It's the same FromSoftware formula:
 You are more or less a nobody that fate is not allowing death to take until you "fixed" the world in one way or another.
 Very few NPCs that you can actually talk to and even fewer quests from them that are understandable or easy to follow to completion.
 Again sounds very much like the previous games.


 The bosses have probably never been quite so impressive or larger than life, and I don't just mean their size.

 The amount of characterization and flavour that these new bosses hold is a whole different level than the majority of bosses from the Souls series.
 Hell the IP holders certainly agree with that statement if they are willing to make a movie featuring said characters.

 Oh and speaking of bosses:
 Even for a Souls veteran some of the bosses in this game are bordering on plain old unfair territory and I think in the future FromSoftware will probably have to innovate boss fights in other ways than just pure mechanical difficulty.
 Still each boss does have at least 1 weakness so the game is not unwinnable, especially when using spirit ashes.


In conclusion:
 For anybody that has played and liked any of FromSoftware's games there is very little here that could turn you away in my opinion.
 Maybe there has been some lowering of difficulty in some areas but I would say that the harder bosses do make up for that. Whether that is to your liking is a different matter.

 And for anybody new there is probably no better entry point

Probably the best game I have played in over a decade or more.

The story and lore is top-notch. Every experience of the story makes you feel like you are investigating the lore and finding it out as you go. There is no hand-holding and you need to figure everything out on your own.

The amount of weapons and armour in this game, puts essentially every other game to shame.

The amount of spells you can unlock, whether through doing missions, finding secrets or completing stories is amazing.

You can attach "Ashes of War" to most weapons and entirely customize their effects and abilities, while the weapons that cannot be customized, are highly unique with wicked cool effects and spells of their own.

Even the "Spirit Ashes" that you use to summon and assist you in hard areas have entire storylines and secrets to them... one of them in the DLC has such a great story to it, that it is worth it to mention - Jolana and Anna. (Starts off as only Jolana, but if you find her sister, you can combine them together and have 2 very strong allies for essentially any boss fight... that is, if you didn't find the Silver Tear Ash and make a copy of yourself.)

Now - the DLC...

The DLC of this game is bar-none, the best DLC I have ever purchased (Shadow of Erdtree), it adds easily 2/3rds of an entire game, some of the best weapons and equipment in the game, some of the best spells in the game, some of the best bosses in the game and some of the most cinematic experiences for the bosses.

The newest DLC that was released - Tarnished Pack, is also great! It is inexpensive and opens up what is normally end-game gear, for starting classes. (Milady, Leda's Sword, Rellana's Twin Swords = DLC, Idus Sword = Tarnished. Light Greatsword is my favourite, so I am biased...)

The PvP in Elden Ring is also much better than most other Souls Games, where most Souls Games didn't seem to level limit invaders, so you would get wiped by high-level players. The worst thing of Elden Ring PvP are "Twinks", players who have 1k+ hours in the game, but start new characters and invade at low levels, to kill "noobs". However, there is a mechanic to help that as well, where you can choose to be a "Hunter" and get summoned into other peoples worlds to defend them from invaders. (About 70% of me entering someone's world to defend them, turned into me just duelling the invader. The emotes/gestures are great and you can communicate really well with just gestures and how you move your character, so, like in For Honour, most people who are about to start a 1v1, do an emote/gesture to show they want a clean duel and to show respect. So, even the Elden Ring "culture" and player-base, is largely Honourable and most of everyone is here to have fun and be challenged. Few players cheap it out just to win and the only players that "cheap it out" do it via Roleplaying, so they might be roleplaying an Assassin and they might backstab you while they are invisible!)

Even if you beat the game in NG+7, the game can still be played and have fun in the Colosseum, where you can play PvP all-day if you want. (The game just turns into For Honour Duels at that point, which is half the fun of that game as well.)

If you like hard, fun, rewarding combat - buy the game.

if you want hilarious situations - buy the game.

If you want one of the most beautiful environments in the industry - buy the game.

If you like spells, magic, and customization - buy the game.

If you want to get lost, just exploring a giant world, adventuring without the game holding your hand at every step, turn and mission of the game - buy the game.

Very cool game with a lot of really beautiful locations, fun exploration, and challenging combat (this is my first Dark Souls game but I'm told this is to be expected). There are lots of truly-interesting lore concepts that are tied together with a hair-thin thread; I think it's best absorbed as abstract fragments of story rather than trying to piece together a cohesive larger narrative.

I recommend playing with some kind of walkthrough/guide if you care about any particular questlines, items, or endings. The *fun* difficulty comes from the fights. The *less fun* difficulty comes from obscure and hard-to-follow questlines--NPCs will disappear to locations you have no way of knowing and expect you to stumble into them three times in the correct order or whoopsie, you've locked yourself out of a quest you didn't know existed. Sometimes you're expected to rest and come back and talk to the same NPC multiple times to get new dialogue, but nothing indicates that you're supposed to do this. Several times I returned to a location to find that someone I'd completely forgotten about had died offscreen in a way that was theoretically supposed to mean something to me. Overall I really enjoy playing and the questlines are fun to complete, it can just get frustrating trying to follow a particular story and not having any way of knowing what to do next.

With any other FromSoftware game I wouldn't have even cared to leave a review. insanely hard fights just for the purpose of being hard and making the player suffer, impossible to comprehend lore, and toxic wannabe philosopher fan bases; but the titular game, ELDEN RING, is really quite different, and quite good.

Though the formatting of incredibly punishing combat has remained the same, the formula of which it is presented is wildly fun and unique compared to other games by the same dev team. Stuck on a boss? You have a massive and deep world to explore and level up in to strengthen yourself before returning. Like character customization? ELDEN RING has one of the best character creators I've ever had the pleasure of playing with possibly hundreds of builds to play around with in the Lands Between.

Graphically the game is beautiful as well, even if turned to potato settings.

Where this game still fails a bit: In terms of actual roleplay there isn't much, most dialogues consist of you just pressing "Accept" or "Decline" with often times the Decline option lacking consequences; There are a few endings to play towards, but a good number of them are extremely similar.
Then onto lore; from what I know the lore and background lore of the game is it written with a lot of passion, with even a helping hand from Game of Thrones writer George R.R. Martin being lent. However like most FromSoftware games, it feels very much as if it doesn't actually want you to learn it. The general information about the world and its characters is all extreme conjecture and bias, which can be good for a complex world; but having no (at least to my knowledge) concrete way to learn the definitive lore is a bit wacky to me.


All in All; a very good game, and for hardcore fans of the medieval video game genre, it is a must buy.

Elden Ring is definitely one of the most immersive and best gaming experiences I’ve ever had. Literally a massive achievement in every part of game design. Even despite having so much difficulty and frustration through the bosses, dungeons, etc., I still don’t think I can ever get an experience like this from any other developer. It’s packed from start to finish with content in a world that’s so dense and rich.

There’s just something special about simply existing in this world and then slowly understanding the history, conflicts and circumstances that brought everything to where it is in The Lands Between. After finishing the game, I decided to watch a bunch of lore videos. It really hit harder thinking about the grand moments when I understood the actual weight behind them, realizing that the journey through this broken world has ultimately meant. 

Elden Ring’s story is completely outstanding in its own regard. In the fantasy open world, it depicted the cycles in terms of generational and familial tragedy, the cycle of violence and the hope of a brighter future. It's clear that the vision of the story is so well directed, well driven and how almost every mechanic ties into this game. I really love that the game never tells you that there’s not a single correct way to fix everything because either; you’re given this world that’s already been shaped by countless of failures, ideals and conflicts, and then you’re left to decide what kind of future should come from it, even if it means embracing something completely unknown. 

Overall, this game has been frustrating to the max lmao. But it’s overwhelmingly beautiful, mysterious and genuinely breathtaking. An insanely, well crafted game that’s impressive in its technicalities and somehow just those things make Elden Ring truly the experience instead of it just being a game.

After Dark Souls III introduced me to the Souls formula, Elden Ring felt like the natural next step and apparently all those hours spent learning to "git gud" actually paid off.

I had very similar feelings about Elden Ring to the ones I had about DS3, although this time around I found the experience somewhat easier. Not because the game doesn't have its fair share of difficult bosses and encounters, but because I already knew what these games expected from me. DS3 had taught me to be patient, learn attack patterns, adapt and try again rather than immediately panic when something wanted to murder me.

And yes, I'm still a magic user. Some things never change. 😅

The move to an open world worked beautifully for me. There's an enormous amount to explore, and discovering completely new areas while simply wandering around the Lands Between was one of my favourite parts of the experience.

The Eternal Cities were easily my favourite locations. Nokron and Nokstella have such a beautiful, otherworldly atmosphere that discovering them for the first time really stuck with me.

My favourite boss, though, has to be Rennala, Queen of the Full Moon. Maybe there's a slight magical bias there... 🌙

I enjoyed the story and lore as well. Like Dark Souls, Elden Ring gives you a world where there's always more beneath the surface if you're willing to look for it, and piecing everything together is part of the experience.

The soundtrack is fantastic too, especially some of the boss themes and, as seems to be becoming a tradition with games I love, several tracks inevitably ended up on my Spotify playlists.

Shadow of the Erdtree was also a great addition and gave me another reason to return to a world I'd already spent so much time exploring.

Dark Souls III taught me how to "git gud". Elden Ring gave me an enormous world in which to put that lesson to use.

And, naturally, I did most of it by throwing magic at things from a safe distance. 🧙‍♂️✨

Elden Ring – A Masterpiece with Some Flaws

I first bought Elden Ring in 2022, but despite spending over 200 hours on Steam, I never managed to finish it. Part of the problem was my approach: I relied on walkthroughs that explained almost everything, which made the experience unnecessarily slow and, eventually, boring.

Later, I decided to give the game another chance on PlayStation, this time with a different goal: completing it and collecting all the trophies. That approach worked much better for me. After spending another 100 hours on PlayStation, I finally achieved the Platinum trophy.

Now that I've completed the game, I can confidently say that Elden Ring is a masterpiece. It's beautiful, ambitious, and filled with incredible details. However, even a masterpiece isn't without flaws.

1. An Excessively Large World

Elden Ring's world is enormous, and while exploration is one of its main attractions, its sheer size can become exhausting. Some players may enjoy getting lost and discovering things along the way, but for others, constantly wandering around without a clear sense of direction can become frustrating. I have nothing against open-world Souls games, but I think Elden Ring sometimes takes this concept too far.

2. Overcomplicated Level and Path Design**

In traditional, linear Souls games, finding hidden paths, discovering shortcuts, and struggling to reach a particular item or boss can be a rewarding part of the experience. However, in a massive open world like Elden Ring, this design philosophy can sometimes become more frustrating than enjoyable. The combination of an enormous map and complicated paths doesn't always work in the game's favor.

3. Unbalanced Boss Difficulty

I feel that FromSoftware struggled to find the right balance between freedom, accessibility, and genuine difficulty, particularly when it comes to boss fights.

The difficulty curve can feel inconsistent. You might spend hours struggling against one boss, only to defeat the next one surprisingly easily. It's almost as if the game can't decide whether it wants to be extremely challenging or relatively accessible.

Of course, difficulty is subjective, and different players will have different experiences. But for me, the inconsistency between boss encounters was noticeable.

Final Thoughts

Sometimes, it's simply impossible to satisfy everyone with a single experience, and Elden Ring is a good example of that.

Despite my criticisms, I believe the game deserves every bit of praise it receives. FromSoftware did an excellent job with its storytelling. The cutscenes are captivating, the major bosses have their own identities, and I would even argue that Elden Ring represents a significant evolution in storytelling compared to Miyazaki's previous works.

Its art direction is simply outstanding. It's the kind of artistic vision that makes a game memorable for years, something that graphical fidelity alone cannot necessarily achieve.

Interestingly, as I'm writing this review, I'm completely exhausted by Elden Ring. Its enormous world, constant exploration, and lack of straightforward progression sometimes made the experience frustrating. Its open-world design was both one of its greatest strengths and, at times, one of its most exhausting weaknesses.

Nevertheless, Elden Ring is worth your time. It's more than just a video game; it's an artistic achievement that offers an experience you simply cannot get from watching a movie or reading a book. Interactive worlds have their own unique way of telling stories and creating memories.

Give it a try. It's an experience worth having.

Wow, what a game. Probably the best open world game I’ve experienced. My first playthrough was well over 100 hours and I still missed some of the content. This world is absolutely full of things to see and explore, and it is absolutely beautiful. The world and aesthetic are peak fantasy and is what makes this game a masterpiece in my opinion. There’s so many options for weapons and builds, it's insane. Incredible boss fights and soundtrack as well. The storytelling is vague but I think that’s what the Souls-like games do best, you feel like you are experiencing this story as a real and insignificant part of this larger world, the story doesn’t revolve around you as the protagonist. 

The biggest thing that bothered me was the quests. You genuinely could not complete most of these quests playing the game blind, characters would disappear, die or lock you out of parts of a quest because you took one step in the wrong direction, or didn’t do some hyper specific action related to that quest. This game does not hold your hand at all but I feel it goes a bit too far in that aspect, a lot of important details will be missed. There’s also the difficulty at times, and things will feel unfair but persevering is worth it. 

The DLC had more of what I enjoyed, but also the things I didn’t. Trying to navigate the DLC map was an absolute headache, and different regions would have wildly different difficulty that didn’t seem to follow a coherent pattern like the base game does. 

Despite that I consider this game a master piece and easily sits within my top 3 favourites, and I pray for more Elden Ring content some day.
